title: The Traitors: Bombshell confession as faithfuls finally turn the screw
text:
Bombshell confession in The Traitors as faithfuls finally turn the screw
- Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
With the traitors still riding high following last Friday's episode, could they really just walk it to the final? It was time to find out.
Having been bestowed with the almighty power of the double dagger - well, metaphorically speaking, at least - King Kenny held all the cards, choosing to use his special power of a double vote to send another faithful packing.
As cliffhangers go, it wasn't hugely thrilling for viewers at home, given that the pair up for banishment - Sharon Rooney and Joanne McNally - were both faithfuls.
Nevertheless, it left a big impact on the faithful crew as they realised they had let the traitors land yet another blow ahead of Friday's final.
"We've got to pull something out of the bag," said frustrated faithful Michael Sheen later. He wasn't wrong.
Joanne got teary as she departed and joked "she was premenstrual," before revealing she was "a hardcore faithful".
Maya described her as a "ball of fun", while Kenny put on his best acting skills in the aftermath by pretending to be struggling with having the deciding vote, even comforting poor Sharon. Give that man an Oscar.
Meanwhile, James Blunt was on the hunt for whiskey like a teenager at the end of a house party: "Where do they keep the stiff stuff?" he asked himself, finding only a tray of empty glasses.
Murder was soon on the minds of the traitors again as the dastardly trio of Kenny, Maya and James A trudged up to the turret.
"The life of a traitor... it's not for everyone," said Maya. And that probably includes James A, although to be fair, he has shown a bit more enthusiasm for some pantomime villainy in the last couple of episodes. More on him later.
"Let's have faith," said King Kenny without a hint of irony.
As ever, James B was as far off the pace as me in the year 11 cross-country race.
When Leigh-Anne Pinnock, probably the most astute faithful of the series, brought up James A being a potential traitor over breakfast, James B sarcastically replied: "I think that's a good theory to start banishing the most innocent."
Sharon - aka Poundland Poirot - failed to appear in the dining room, having been chosen for the chopping block so soon after escaping banishment, throwing all the faithfuls into more confusion. She was getting a bit stressed, so it was probably for the best.
Michael had a warning for the traitors though, giving his most rousing oratory since his motivational speech for the Welsh football team ahead of the 2022 World Cup.
"Traitors... today is going to be a living hell for you, I am going to push and push and push and you are going to suffer today. This is the apocalypse.
"Vengeful daddy is in the house today."
Theories were soon flying left right and centre, with Bash throwing the spotlight on "the head of the round table" Michael, Kenny putting suspicion on James B, while Romesh pointed the finger at actual traitor Maya, shock, horror.
And the obsession with the peacock perfume wasn't going anywhere.
Finally Michael 'Vengeful Daddy' Sheen seemed to be on to something, telling a shell-shocked Maya in the kitchen: "I think you could be a brilliant traitor, and if you and Kenny paired up, amazing."
She was probably relieved when the jeeps turned up for another day trip, and Romesh was all of us with his hilarious reaction to news of yet another insane mission.
On being told by host Claudia Winkleman that they had to find the severed heads of some of the murdered celebrities and reunite them with the head of the buried body, he got the giggles: "It's just so ridiculous. I love it though!"
James B tried to get one group in the Frankenstein-style lab to sing his hit Beautiful - which had Leigh-Ann and Michael bopping along but by the puzzled look on Kenny's face, he had clearly never heard it. Awks.
This mission was a bit of a rehash of the wailing in the well challenge from the first Celebrity Traitors series, with Claudia going full headteacher and cheering - or should we say, shouting - the teams on.
Digital versions of the dead celebs in bell jars had to be matched to the correct gravestone in the castle gardens.
"Seeing Ross's face when he was alive was enough to give a man pause, let alone when his dismembered head is looking out at you from a pickle jar," quipped Michael.
Back at the castle, it seemed that Michael wasn't the only one starting to turn up the heat on Maya.
Romesh and Bash decided she had gone under the radar long enough: "One of the greatest gliders in the game. Maybe Olympic level gliding," mused Bash. And King Kenny was also in their sights.
And so to the penultimate round table. (A shout out to Claudia's sequin-tastic midnight blue trouser suit).
Michael was under the spotlight first due to his presence, intelligence and status as "the father of the table."
In turn, he first went back to his previous suspicion of Leigh-Anne on the night of the murder in plain sight, accusing her again of using her Big Mix dance with Miranda as a distraction.
Romesh put heat on James B due to his vocal accusations, which were often wrong.
The quiet ones - traitors James A and Maya - were then questioned by Michael and James B, who soon honed in on the murder in plain sight, working out that Maya, Kenny and James A were in the library at the end of the night when Ross was killed.
Vengeful Daddy was indeed in the house, and James B was on the money for once. Credit where it's due.
Then the bombshell of the series - something that has never happened before in the history of the show.
James A, who failed dismally to defend himself against Michael's accusations, clearly couldn't take any more and confessed he was a traitor at the table.
"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.
"I've had a unique experience on this that no-one has had before, I wanted to be a faithful and that's all I wanted to be. But I couldn't just say 'guys, vote for me.'"
At least no-one had to explain their decision when they all wrote his name down on the boards.
And as Michael and Maya stood round the firepit before heading to bed - or the turret in Maya's case - she looked like a dead woman walking. And DI Sheen is on her case.
The Celebrity Traitors final will be shown on BBC One and iPlayer from 20:00 GMT on Friday. You can also follow along on our live page from 18:00 GMT on Friday.
description: Could the faithfuls finally come good in Thursday's penultimate episode?

title: Sir Patrick Stewart: A life in pictures
text:
Sir Patrick Stewart: A life in pictures
Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart rose from humble beginnings in his native Yorkshire to become a global superstar whose work became immortalised portraying characters on some of the most popular sci-fi franchises in history.
The star, who won acclaim on both stages and screens, died at his home in Los Angeles on Thursday after a career that spanned more than seven decades. He was 86.
Born in 1940, his mother was a textile worker and his father was a former military officer whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had a profound impact on his mental health.
He grew up poor, and later spoke to journalists about witnessing his mother being abused by his father.
Young Patrick's love of drama came at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
He went on to star in countless Shakespeare plays. One of his earliest breakout roles was in 1970's Two Gentlemen of Verona, which also featured his rescue dog, Blackie, playing the role of the dog Crab.
His expertise in Shakespeare led to play a major role in the 1976 BBC television series I, Claudius.
In 1981, he was featured in 1981 fantasy film Excalibur, bringing him one step closer to his future sci-fi career.
Sir Patrick has won numerous awards, including a Grammy and two Laurence Olivier Awards. He was also nominated for a Tony, along with multiple Golden Globes and Emmys over the years.
His iconic voice and facial expressions saw him star in both the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, helping to spawn a generation of global sci-fi fans.
In 1987, he took on the role of Jean-Luc Picard on popular TV series Star Trek: The Next Generation. Tapping into Star Trek fandom earned him millions of adoring fans around the world.
His scores of sci-fi fans reached new heights with his starring role as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, which began in 2000.
He reprised the role multiple times over decades through the Marvel Cinematic Universe, including in 2026 in Avengers: Doomsday.
description: His career on stages and screens spanned seven decades but came to be defined by his roles on some of the most popular sci-fi franchises in history.

title: Joanna Wietrzyk: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race says she made wrong decision
text:
'I made the wrong decision,' Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race tells BBC
An Australian athlete has admitted making the wrong decision and putting others at risk by continuing to race after soiling herself during an endurance sports event.
Speaking exclusively to the BBC ahead of her return to the sport, Joanna Wietrzyk suggested her determination to win the Hyrox race in Beijing in September had clouded her judgement: "It was my decision to continue racing so I take full responsibility for that."
Challenged over why she carried on, she said: "I didn't really think about those around me… the decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect."
The 24-year-old said that the experience and subsequent backlash was "traumatic". She also said she had considered walking away from the sport, in which she holds a world record.
Hyrox sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, in northern Germany, and is now held across the world.
Roughly halfway through her event last month, Wietrzyk suffered a bout of diarrhoea. Images of faecal matter on parts of her body were then shared widely online.
Asked whether officials should have stopped her, she said no-one encouraged her to do so at the time.
Hyrox's co-founder, Moritz Fürste, has issued an apology saying it had been a mistake not to react immediately during the race.
New rules have now been introduced giving race directors the power to remove athletes if their vomit, urine or faeces pose a risk of contamination or threaten the welfare of themselves or others in a race that is primarily held indoors using shared equipment.
Although initially defiant in a now-deleted Instagram post, Wietrzyk apologised in the week after the Beijing event and said she would forfeit the win and retroactively withdraw from the race.
Due to compete in Hamburg on Friday, she said she was "nervous" about her return and hoped that the high-profile incident would not define her.
"I don't want it to become my identity," she said.
In her first interview since Beijing, Wietrzyk said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning but had gone into the race "feeling fresh, feeling really, really good".
"It was a very sudden experience," she told the BBC.
"It wasn't until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive person… and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing.
"Obviously I did put other people at risk," she admitted.
Hyrox China has since reportedly refunded some competitors their entry fees.
Wietrzyk also said she regretted an initial social media post published after the race which included the words "Go hard or go home" and "a win is a win". She said she had been in "flight or fight mode" as she sought hospital treatment.
"I didn't really account for what the public would have seen that situation as."
Challenged over whether her apology could be seen as an effort at damage limitation, or too late, she said that she hadn't expected so much exposure from the incident.
"I needed those days to reflect on it and process it."
Speaking about the mentality of elite athletes, she said: "They're so hyper-vigilant on winning and doing the best that they can, putting their training to good use and showcasing their fitness to the world."
After reflecting over the past weeks, she said: "There is more to life… than just racing and just winning."
After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from future events.
Speaking about the comments and photo shares online Joanna Wietrzyk said there had both been support, to make sure she was OK, but that it had also shown social media can be a very "toxic place".
Wietrzyk told the BBC that it had been a "mentally and emotionally taxing period" and she had not expected the global scrutiny, saying her family had also received threats.
"[It] was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays, especially from someone who's 24, just out there racing.
"Yes, I did make the wrong decision but I don't believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online… At the end of the day I'm only human."
Wietrzyk said had been trying to stay offline and had sought to "isolate herself from the world" for a time: "I can't do that forever."
"I still have so much more I can achieve in this sport so I think, for me, my mental resilience is the key here where I can inspire others through what I've been through."

title: China made Real Madrid's Mbappé apologise over Mao remark - but many people don't know exactly what he said
text:
China made Mbappé apologise - but many don't know exactly what he said
On Monday night, as Kylian Mbappé was attending the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, he was also becoming the centre of a huge controversy on Chinese social media.
Football fans had stumbled upon a clip of him joking about the meme that makes him "laugh the most" - where his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao Zedong, who oversaw one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
The controversy spread like wildfire as Chinese brands cut him off one by one and China Media Group, the parent group of state broadcaster CCTV, suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches. A foreign ministry spokesperson said: "Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
But on the Chinese internet, few were explicitly spelling out those words and actions, or even using the name of Mao - who remains a near-sacred figure in the country.
China's sophisticated censorship system, which cuts 1.4 billion people off from the global internet, meant many didn't know exactly what had happened.
The accusation of "hurting the feelings of the Chinese people" alone seemed enough to trigger a tsunami of anger, amplified by social media algorithms and a heavily controlled internet, where people are wary of disagreeing with the majority view.
It wasn't long before Mbappé, one of the biggest football stars in the world, said he was "sincerely sorry" for his "ill-judged" comment. His club, Real Madrid, and the Spanish league La Liga, also issued apologies. China is a huge market for the world's most popular sport.
Beijing later confirmed it was taking the footballer's apology "seriously". China Media Group has yet to say whether broadcasts will resume.
But the anger online lingered.
"An apology is the least he should do, but I don't forgive him. I support a ban on him," read a top comment on Weibo.
Mbappé did not mention Mao by name in the interview, but many felt any joke that involved the founder of Communist China crossed a line.
"Do you know who you hurt? He is the spiritual pillar of the Chinese people," read one Weibo comment liked by more than 700 users.
"He's the most important figure in our history. Do you think a simple apology can make everything okay?" another wrote.
Ironically, despite the heavy backlash, many on Chinese social media are still asking what exactly the French forward said. They tried AI chatbots, which are just as censored as the Chinese internet and couldn't provide any answers. Others attempted to explain, but skirted around any mention of Mao.
References were made to "the person on the 100 yuan note" and "the teacher", a title Mao once used for himself. Screenshots of the meme and interview were shared, with both the word "dictator" and Mbappé's face blurred out.
Neither the Chinese foreign ministry statement nor the apologies issued by Mbappé, Real Madrid and La Liga mentioned Mao directly.
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976.
Despite the turmoil of his rule, including the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society, he remains a revered figure in China.
A portrait of Mao overlooks Beijing's Tiananmen Square, a symbol of how central he is in the modern Chinese imagination. Unlike other former Chinese leaders, his embalmed body is placed on public display there, drawing tens of thousands of visitors every day. In recent years, there has been a revival of interest in him among young people, who read his works and watch clips of him on social media.
Chinese history books downplay the devastation during Mao's rule. The Chinese Communist Party's verdict on Mao is that his achievements outweigh his mistakes. In their eyes, he is "a great revolutionary and a great Marxist".
But outside China, history sees Mao as both a revolutionary and a dictator. And so reactions among the diaspora - dissidents as well as people whose families fled China decades ago, in the wake of Mao's rule - was very different.
"You don't need to apologise, you are not wrong," a highly liked comment written in Chinese under the football star's X statement read.
"The ones who should apologise are the CCP; they kidnapped the Chinese people and brainwashed them," another Chinese user wrote.
On X and Threads, neither of which are accessible in China, the controversy spawned even more memes. Some feature Mbappé's face on other images of Mao, while others go further, placing him on the body of current Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
And then there was the rest of the internet which was simply puzzled.
"It's honestly hard to understand... It seems like people aren't allowed to speak out against their leaders. And they expect the whole world to think the same way they do? That's ridiculous," read a top comment under Real Madrid's apology on Instagram.
"How dare you call a dictator a dictator? Terrible," another user on X wrote.
description: His comment about Chinese leader Mao sparked anger but censorship left many wondering what exactly happened.

title: 'My six-year-old cries herself to sleep': How fireworks affect people with autism
text:
'My six-year-old cries herself to sleep': How fireworks affect people with autism
Although she is only six, Grace Miller already knows what to do when fireworks season arrives every year.
She will head to her bedroom, pull the door closed and the blinds down, and try to hide from the barrage of noise happening outside.
However no matter how much effort Grace puts in, she is often left crying and deeply distressed by the constant explosions during October and November.
Grace, of Kirkintilloch, has autism and is among those - adults and children - whose sensory issues are affected during the period around Bonfire Night.
Grace's mum Laura has set up a petition on Change.org calling on East Dunbartonshire Council to introduce firework control zones in the area, similar to the approach already taken in some parts of Glasgow and Edinburgh.
She feels while it is known that animals can be easily distressed by the amount of noise created by fireworks, the effect it can have on people with conditions like autism are less publicised.
For Grace, diagnosed with autism two years ago, the impact every autumn is considerable.
"She's funny, outgoing, just a beautiful wee girl – but when something like this happens she goes in on herself and hunkers down," Laura told BBC Scotland News.
"You feel absolutely powerless when it all kicks off every night. Your children look to you for protection and for you to come up with a solution, but in this case you can't.
"She has so much distress when it starts and is often crying herself to sleep.
"The narrative is usually about animals, but vulnerable people in the community are mentioned far less. I'm not asking for fireworks to be banned, far from it – but do they need to be so loud and so constant?"
People with autism can be more or less sensitive to sensory experiences, with the impact varying from person to person.
In Grace's case, loud noises can upset her heavily, effectively triggering what is often called a sensory overload - where a person becomes overwhelmed as a result.
Grace now uses ear defenders every night, but they only muffle the sound rather than blocking it out entirely.
In recent years the National Autistic Society have issued guidance aimed at helping people with the condition cope with fireworks season, with suggestions for easing stress and anxiety.
Laura would like to see more local authorities use the powers granted to them via the Fireworks and Pyrotechnic Articles (Scotland) Bill in 2022.
Since then, both Edinburgh and Glasgow City Councils have brought in firework control zones for parts of each city, after constant problems with anti-social behaviour around Bonfire Night.
They stop people from setting them off on private property, but organised displays are allowed.
East Dunbartonshire has not had problems to that degree, but it is the sheer number of fireworks, being set off day in and day out, that Laura struggles with the most.
"I don't want to ruin anyone's fun but this is a real struggle," argues Laura, who is also mum to 10-year-old Aidan and is married to husband Scott.
"It is not just 5 November and at the new year, it is here, there and everywhere from October onwards. If it was a couple of days and that was it, it would be a lot easier to cope with."
'There is a real impact fireworks have'
It is not just children who can be affected badly by fireworks.
Jonathan Blythe, 41, has Asperger's Syndrome and dreads the autumn arriving, as he know it will bring a nightly din with it.
"We've been hearing fireworks almost every night, sometimes even during the day," he said.
"My partner and I can't even relax and watch television together in the evenings without me becoming distressed by the fireworks."
Jonathan lives in the Barmulloch area of Glasgow, which is not covered by a fireworks control zone.
He says one recent experience saw him become so panicked that he left his house, got in his car and drove around for hours to find somewhere that was quiet.
"This really is affecting me and my day-to-day life, there is a real impact fireworks have on people like me."
East Dunbartonshire Council told BBC Scotland News it would be happy to speak to Laura about fireworks in the area.
However it has also stated in documents that misuse of fireworks is "relatively limited in number across the East Dunbartonshire area" and that it does not receive many complaints.
In correspondence with local politicians the council said control zones are intended to respond to significant disorder, and not be a "catch-all solution" if people have trouble with fireworks.
Laura feels that is not an acceptable answer, and intends to keep pushing for change, including with her petition.
"It's hard for someone to understand unless you have someone that is neuro-divergent in your family.
"Since Grace was born, there have been challenges but we have rode through them together, and we will keep doing that with this as well."
description: Grace has autism, and is among those - adults and children - who find the period around Bonfire Night to be highly distressing.

title: I gave birth in ambulance amid staff shortages at local hospital
text:
I gave birth in ambulance on A96 amid staff shortages at local hospital
A woman gave birth in the back of a moving ambulance after being told the specialist care she might need was unavailable at her local hospital.
Hannah Smith, 39, lives less than 20 miles from Dr Gray's Hospital in Elgin but it has only accepted low risk pregnancies since services were downgraded in 2018.
Instead she was sent to Aberdeen Maternity Hospital - 60 miles away from her Moray home - but her labour progressed so quickly her baby boy Braeson arrived before she could get there.
"I don't think anyone should be put into that position," she said. NHS Grampian said it was sorry about the "poor experience".
It is at least the third time a woman has had to give birth at the side of the A96 since 2018, with two other cases reported by the Press and Journal in 2021 and 2022.
Hannah had wanted to give birth at Dr Gray's, which is about half an hour from her home near Buckie, rather than travel about an hour and 40 minutes to Aberdeen.
However, because of her age, her IVF pregnancy, and the possibility she might require an emergency Caesarean section, she had been advised to have the delivery at a hospital with full consultant-led maternity services.
A Caesarean section, or C-section, is a surgical operation to deliver a baby through a cut made in the mother's abdomen and womb.
She had previously undergone an emergency Caesarean with her first child two years ago.
Hannah woke at about 03:30 on 11 October believing her waters might have broken.
Initially her contractions were mild, but by around 06:00 they had intensified dramatically.
Her parents began driving her towards Aberdeen, but after contacting maternity triage they were advised to meet an ambulance in Keith for the remainder of the journey.
By coincidence, one of the paramedics who arrived to help was Hannah's second cousin.
"It was just nice to see a familiar face," Hannah said.
But shortly after leaving Keith, with her mother also in the ambulance, Hannah realised her baby was about to arrive.
"I could feel it and I said 'no, he's coming'," she recalled. "And from there it was literally seconds and that next contraction he was out."
Her son was born as the ambulance crew searched for somewhere safe to stop near a farm track, just off the main A96 road.
They were about 50 miles (80km) from Aberdeen and 19 miles (30km) from Elgin.
Hannah said she felt immediate relief when she heard him cry, having feared something might go wrong so far from hospital.
Despite having given birth, Hannah still had to complete the journey to Aberdeen Maternity Hospital. She said she asked to be taken to Elgin instead, but was told she had to continue to Aberdeen because that was where she had been booked in.
She said the journey was particularly uncomfortable due to bumps and roundabouts.
"I was terrified that I might drop him," she said.
Hannah said she understood why doctors wanted her to give birth somewhere with specialist support available, but questioned why that care was still unavailable closer to home.
She believes she would have reached Dr Gray's before her baby was born had she been able to go there.
"We would have made it if we'd gone to Elgin," she said.
Instead, the specialist hospital birth she had been advised to have became an ambulance delivery.
"Instead of consultants I ended up with a paramedic and my mum as the midwife," she said.
"It was nice in the end but it could have gone very differently.
"If anything had gone wrong with me or with a baby it wouldn't have been such a pleasant experience.
"I feel like Moray mums have been put on the back burner, that their maternity care isn't as important because they live in a rural situation."
She praised the ambulance crew and staff at Aberdeen Maternity Hospital for the care they provided.
For now, Hannah is recovering at home and enjoying life with her newborn son and his two-year-old brother Alvah.
But while her story had a happy ending, she fears further delays could put other mothers at risk.
"I'm not the first mum to give birth on the A96 and I probably won't be the last," she said.
"I think just delaying it is going to put more women at risk."
It was announced earlier this month that the restoration of full maternity services at Dr Gray's Hospital had been delayed until next year.
Maternity services were downgraded in 2018 due to staff shortages, meaning most expectant mothers in the area had to travel to Aberdeen or Inverness for births.
Currently low-risk pregnancies are being accepted at Dr Gray's.
The aim had been to have a full consultant-led maternity service by the end of this year. NHS Grampian said it would now instead be done "as soon as is safely possible" next year.
Katie Colville, director of midwifery for NHS Grampian, said: "While we are pleased mum and baby are doing well, we are sorry Hannah and her family had a poor experience.
"We want as many women in Moray as possible to have the choice of giving birth at Dr Gray's, closer to home and with the people who matter to them, and this type of experience only reaffirms our determination to deliver that as soon as safely possible.
"That said, for some women and babies, the specialist care available in Aberdeen means that planning to give birth there will always be the safest option."
She said extensive arrangements were in place to support women who need to travel and to minimise the need for journeys during labour.
"Sometimes, though, labour is unpredictable and circumstances can change quickly," Colville added.
"We know how long Moray families have waited for the return of full consultant-led maternity services at Dr Gray's, and this is why we're so determined to finish what we've started."
It comes as a nationwide review of Scotland's maternity services is ongoing.
Chaired by maternal and child health expert Prof Christine McCourt, it will pay particular attention to how care is provided in rural and island communities - with specific focus on services in Elgin, as well as Caithness and Wigtownshire.
Prof McCourt is due to submit her findings and recommendations in July next year.
description: Hannah Smith was travelling to Aberdeen Maternity Hospital as she could not go to Dr Gray's in Elgin.

title: Scottish police to target online gangs forcing children to self-harm
text:
Scottish police to target sadistic online gangs forcing children to self-harm
Detectives in Scotland have joined international law enforcement in targeting online gangs which groom and coerce children into acts of self-harm.
Officers are hunting members of loose online networks of sadists known as "The Com", which mainly targets girls on gaming platforms and social media.
The groups, mostly comprised of teenage and young adult males, have risen in prominence in recent years after cases involving sextortion and hacking, as well as self-harm encouragement.
So far, there has been one arrest in Scotland, while there have been a handful of convictions in England.
The Molly Rose Foundation - a suicide prevention charity helping young people and families victimised by the network - said the groups "represent the gravest risk to children online".
Warning: This article contains distressing content
Paul, not his real name, is a detective constable working in Police Scotland's internet investigations unit.
In a locked room at the force's Scottish Crime Campus, he is showing the BBC images on a computer sent to the team by the National Crime Agency (NCA).
Flagged by National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in the United States, the material was eventually passed to Police Scotland and on to Paul's desk.
He now has the job of sifting through horrific images of abuse and injury in order to identify the victim, as well as the Scottish perpetrator.
"Unfortunately, we are getting a lot of self-harm imagery," he tells BBC News.
"There's nearly a thousand images in this particular case, and we need to go through every single one of those."
Abuse for 'kudos'
This case is linked to a Com group - a violent collective that uses mainstream social media platforms to manipulate and blackmail girls into harming and abusing themselves.
Often, the police say, this is done by the group for "kudos", or clout, from their peers.
On the screen, one image show a young girl's arm covered in blood. Another shows blood used to daub a symbol on to a bathroom wall.
Paul alleges the girl in the case was directed to harm herself by someone she met online - understood to be a young male in Scotland.
"Usually, it's a young girl in these particular cases," he said. "We're finding a lot of vulnerable young girls that are between 11 and 17.
"Unfortunately, we discover down the line that there are other vulnerabilities that [perpetrators] are exploiting."
Among the pictures are occult or Satanic sigils, a way for the abusers to appear "as extreme as possible", says Paul.
He continues: "It's very common, but I don't think they believe these Satanic things.
"With these particular groups anyway, it's about how extreme, how much exploitation can you inflict on an individual.
"It's about how much control you can get, up to the point that they're getting them to self-harm."
The Com - short for "the community" - are loosely-affiliated online groups involved in acts of abuse, financial crimes and extremism.
Groups involved in recent court cases include "The 764" and "CVLT". However, membership and group dynamics shift over time.
In May, the NCA said it was investigating around 200 cases involving these networks, while there have been a number of convictions.
In August, 20-year-old Justin Swaddle was jailed for two years for blackmailing and coercing more than 100 victims into acts of self-harm, including carving his online username on their bodies.
Det Ch Insp Craig Faulds - who leads efforts targeting groups' links to Scotland - described the crimes as "an evolution of online child abuse and sexual exploitation".
He told the BBC that often abusers will target their victims on "innocuous gaming platforms".
He continued: "It can move to social media platforms, messaging services and online forums.
"We are seeing cases where perpetrators online are targeting young vulnerable people, usually girls, and they are manipulating them, they are coercing them into sharing indecent images of themselves.
"Some of the more serious cases are seen by coercing individuals to cause acts of serious self-harm.
"We have identified victims and perpetrators in Scotland. And we are at the stage of mapping this threat to understand significance and the prevalence of it."
Who are the abusers?
Hazel Stewart, who works for the NCA's Threat Leadership team, described the prevalence of Com groups are "low-volume, high-harm", adding: "The scale doesn't matter, it is the harm that is being caused."
She told the BBC that the abusers themselves are often young males who have been socially isolated or bullied.
"They find their own identity online, they can be whoever they want to be," she said.
"And therefore they are encouraging those that are vulnerable, usually young females... seeking them out, say, on suicidal ideation sites or eating disorder sites, and encourage them into more private spaces."
Stewart explained that abusers form relationships with victims and "be very supportive at first" before encouraging them to carry out harmful acts.
"It might be a small cut at first. Or it might be harm to a pet, or a sibling," she said.
"That harm will escalate and the grooming and manipulation continues, and the victim is in a situation where they can't escape."
Stewart described the threat as a "global problem" and said the UK was working with law enforcement in the USA, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, as well as Interpol and Europol.
The Molly Rose Foundation has recently warned about Com networks. Its chief executive Andy Burrows said it was "becoming the frontline of child protection online".
He said that online safety regulator Ofcom had been warned about the threat of online gangs and had been slow to respond - a "failure" that he said highlighted weaknesses in the Online Safety Act.
He continued: "These networks represent the gravest risk to children online, with every UK police force investigating Com cases, the threat is real and widespread.
"It's also clear that these risks exist beyond just social media, on gaming platforms and encrypted messaging apps, which is why Andy Burnham must move beyond a blanket social media ban and incentivise all online platforms to become safe for young people as a price of doing business in the UK."
An Ofcom spokesperson said: "The threats posed by Com groups are a particular concern for Ofcom, and we're working closely with law enforcement and child protection agencies to tackle them.
"Where services fail to comply with their duties, we've shown that we won't hesitate to act."

title: What makes a golden eagle chick called Beaky Junior so important?
text:
What makes this golden eagle chick so important?
A golden eagle chick has become the first to fledge from a nest on a managed grouse moor in the south of Scotland.
The bird - Beaky Junior - hatched in a nest in a secret location in the Moffat Hills, at a site used for recreational gamebird shooting.
It comes after a Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) report revealed that two-thirds of UK persecution incidents involving birds of prey had occurred at similar sites.
And it is being considered a "hugely significant milestone" by those running a project to boost golden eagle numbers in the region.
Dr Cat Barlow, chief executive of Restoring Upland Nature (Run) which is behind the scheme, said they had received "incredible support" from landowners and gamekeepers.
The project to relocate birds from the Highlands to a secret location in the Moffat Hills started in the summer of 2018.
Numbers in the south of Scotland had fallen to a handful of breeding pairs but they are now at a record level of more than 50 - despite some setbacks.
Birds have been shot at or killed and that is why the birth of Beaky Junior - one of five golden eagle chicks successfully fledged in the area this year - is being seen as so significant, since it happened on a managed grouse moor.
Earlier this year, the RSPB report highlighted 182 confirmed persecution incidents involving birds of prey in Scotland over a 10-year period.
It said they were widely scattered across the country but the majority - 64.3% - had occurred on land managed for gamebird shooting.
Against that backdrop, the efforts in southern Scotland to encourage estates and conservationists to work together are seen as particularly important.
Beaky Junior was even named by local gamekeepers in recognition of the "key role" they have played in helping golden eagles thrive.
Barlow explained: "It is wonderful to see a golden eagle hatch, fledge and fly freely from the newly-established nest of a translocated golden eagle that has made its home on a managed grouse moor in the Southern Uplands.
"This reflects the incredible support we have had from landowners and gamekeepers – from translocations in the Highlands, to continued monitoring and protection of birds and eyries on their lands and estates.
"Indeed their support has been absolutely vital to our success in restoring the population of golden eagles to record numbers."
She said the fledging of five chicks from the nests of birds they had translocated to southern Scotland was a "hugely significant milestone".
Barlow added that it gave "genuine hope" in the battle to reverse biodiversity decline and ensure future generations across Scotland, England and Wales could experience the "incredible sense of awe" when seeing a golden eagle.
Michael Clarke, who chairs Run, said individuals from "all walks of life" had helped the birds to thrive.
He added that they would continue to monitor the impact of the golden eagles on the area "with support of land managers, gamekeepers, farmers and the wider community".
The chief executive of landowner body Scottish Land and Estates, Sarah-Jane Laing, said it was thrilled to hear gamekeepers had named the chick.
"Beaky Junior's arrival serves as a powerful example of what can be achieved when land managers and conservationists unite behind a shared vision, grounded in trust and genuine partnership," she said.
"Seeing this magnificent species return to and flourish in these landscapes is something we can all take pride in."
The gamekeepers involved asked to remain anonymous in order to protect the location of the bird.
Speaking on their behalf, Mark Ewart, regional co-ordinator at the Southern Uplands Moorlands Group, added: "It is incredibly rewarding to see gamekeepers celebrated for the important role they have played in the success of Run's South of Scotland Golden Eagle Project.
"Monitoring and providing the right habitats for golden eagles and other species to flourish is an important part of what gamekeepers do on a day-to-day basis.
"To encounter golden eagles daily is the ultimate indicator of the success of the project-gamekeeper partnership."
description: The bird's arrival on a managed grouse moor in southern Scotland is seen as a key moment for the species.

title: Gareth Ward defends Michelin-star Ynyshir after food hygeine debacle
text:
'I run a spotless kitchen', says Michelin-star restaurant chef in wake of food hygiene debacle
The chef at Wales' only two-Michelin-star restaurant has defended the way he operates his kitchen after the venue came under scrutiny over food hygiene standards.
While chasing a third Michelin star, Ynyshir was handed a one-star hygiene rating in February and told to improve due to concerns about raw and undercooked foods.
The news made global headlines and was a blow to Ward and his team, but in Apple TV's documentary series Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars, Ward said Ynyshir was "an incredible place".
"There's nothing in there that's amateurish," he told the programme. "I run a spotless kitchen."
Ward, who co-owns the restaurant near Machynlleth in mid Wales, added the hygiene rating had hurt, "because we are only trying to be the best".
"Whether you're a cafe, or a pub, or a two-Michelin-star restaurant. We've all got the same rules," he told the eight-part second series of the show, which follows elite chefs and their teams.
"But we go above and beyond everything to make what we do safe."
Ynyshir was previously ordered to stop serving raw lobster after Ceredigion council found "significant hazards" were not properly identified.
The restaurant received its first Michelin star in 2014 and its second in 2022, becoming the first and only restaurant in Wales to hold two.
It missed out on a third star at the ceremony this year.
The 16-seat restaurant serves Japanese-inspired raw dishes as part of its nearly £500 a head 30-course tasting menu, and accused inspectors of not understanding its specialised procedures.
By August, the council had reinstated its five-star hygiene rating after it found the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".
But, for Ynyshir, the scrutiny was a major setback, and Ward shared his frustration in the documentary.
"I'm very proud of my whole team and my business, and what we've achieved," he said.
"It's obviously massive in the media, which anyone instantly jumps on and thinks it's about cleanliness," he said. "I run a spotless kitchen.
"When something like this happens you're a bit blown away."
Ward said the restaurant served a lot of raw food and did a lot of things "that aren't normal".
"We have done some things wrong, but we don't deserve everything [we were accused of]," he said.
"It's just, we dare to be different."
He said the inspection left him feeling the weight of responsibility, with more than 30 members of staff and the business potentially at risk.
Management of food safety at Ynyshir was categorised by inspectors as needing major improvement, as was cleanliness and condition of facilities, while "hygienic food handling" was rated "generally satisfactory".
A dirty floor, inadequate hand-washing facilities in some areas and broken equipment posing a potential contamination risk were also identified in the inspectors' report.
Ynyshir responded at the time, saying the inspection "identified a small number of minor issues typical of a busy professional kitchen situated in the countryside of rural Wales" which had been "rectified immediately and in full".
It said biological testing, at "significant cost" to the restaurant, had "conclusively confirmed that our techniques are safe, compliant and appropriate".
It said at the time it was prepared to work constructively with the council but expected "an informed, consistent and fair assessment process that recognises the realities of modern, non-conventional restaurants".
When Ynyshir was reinspected, Ceredigion council said the "business had addressed all matters identified during the original inspection".
description: Chef Gareth Ward defends how he operates in documentary after Ynyshir got a one-star hygiene rating.

title: Ceredigion heart attack patient had 140-mile round hospital trip
text:
Heart attack patient, 83, had to drive four hours for hospital appointment
An 83-year-old recovering cancer patient who has suffered two heart attacks was forced to drive himself on a four-hour round trip for medical tests.
Charles Swift was referred to Withybush Hospital in Haverfordwest, Pembrokeshire, for tests on his heart in August - he lives in Borth, Ceredigion - which is 70 miles away.
He made inquiries about getting non-emergency transport but was refused by a call handler from the Welsh Ambulance Services Trust (WAST) when he told them he owned a car.
"I can't understand why pensioners have to run about in their own car," he said.
WAST said it was not always able to meet the increasing demand for transport, and changes were underway to improve the service.
Swift, who has been treated for three types of cancer and has had two heart attacks, said when he rang hospital taxis, he was asked if he could walk, climb stairs and owned a car.
When he replied yes to all three, he said he was told: "You'll have to use that then.
"I don't understand. What's the difference if you've got a car or not? I'm 83. It's not a good journey to do. It was tiring."
On another occasion, Swift was told on a Friday afternoon that his hospital transport for an appointment in Haverfordwest on the Monday had been cancelled, leading him to cancel the appointment.
When he got hospital transport for a subsequent appointment, he said it was "very pleasant, no problem at all".
Hywel Dda University Health Board's website says patients travelling to and from hospital are normally expected to organise their own transport.
When that is not possible, some patients could be eligible for non-emergency patient transport provided by the Welsh Ambulance Service, but must meet eligibility criteria.
This includes receiving regular dialysis or cancer treatment, needing a stretcher or oxygen or needing to travel in their own wheelchair.
Public transport is not a realistic option as trains from Borth to Haverfordwest take a minimum of three-and-a-half hours in each direction.
Councillors in Ceredigion have made calls for better hospital transport systems in rural areas.
One of them, Hugh Hughes, met Swift shortly after his first appointment when the health board wanted him to go back for a second one.
He said: "He was distraught. He didn't know how he was going to manage it. He was absolutely exhausted after the first experience."
After Swift's initial request for transport, the ambulance service reviewed his phone call.
According to Mark Harris, WAST's assistant director of operations, the transport would not have been refused if the service had more information.
"We've changed our processes now, and we've put some training out to our call taking team, so when Mr Swift rings again, he'll get a different answer," he said.
Harris said the demand for transport and the distances travelled to appointments were increasing, placing a strain on resources, which could lead to the cancellation of transport.
"We are seeing an increase in the volume of journeys we have to cancel where the demand exceeds our available resource," he said. "So we will get occasions where we have more work than we can fit on our vehicles within a day [and] we're in the middle of a significant improvement programme now to address that."
The councillors and voluntary organisations involved in patient transport have said that, even when a patient gets transport, bookings are frequently cancelled the day before the appointment.
Hughes said: "We've got a very good hospital in Bronglais just on our doorstep yet many of the services seem to be migrating further south.
"We've got to accept there will be occasions where you have to travel. But this seems to be becoming far more prevalent."
Dolen Teifi - a community transport service based in Llandysul - has 42 vehicles and 160 volunteer drivers covering Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire.
The charity's manager Rod Bowen said drivers make about 50 journeys to hospital appointments each week and had noticed that the ambulance service's capacity "has been stretched".
While the non-emergency ambulance service is free, Dolen Teifi charges an average of 57p a mile to partly cover its costs.
"The demand for hospital appointments has gone up," added Bowen.
Bowen said the charity had taken 145 calls in the past two months when hospital transport had been cancelled the day before an appointment, and it was able to help in about a third of cases.
"We've been able to fill that gap, and it's quite an important gap to fill because basically that means the person can actually get to the hospital for their appointment," he added.
"We've seen a huge increase of people having to travel past their main hospital door to a hospital that could be anything up to 40 to 50 miles away."
Bowen also said longer journeys for appointments were more common and older patients were "not really comfortable" driving to hospitals in unfamiliar areas.
Hughes said the health board and the ambulance service needed to work together as people were "falling through the net and are not getting the transport they need".
Andrew Carruthers, chief operating officer at Hywel Dda health board, said the board covered a large rural area and it was "aware of the challenges that some of our patients face especially when they have to travel longer distances to access specialist treatment."
He added it worked closely with WAST, and it would raise concerns to see how "transport options available for our patients" could be improved.
description: Charles Swift faced a 140-mile round trip to get to a hospital, but had to drive himself.

title: Spain train crash: Young athlete and former minister among victims
text:
Young athlete and former minister among victims of Spain train crash
A 24-year-old athlete and a former government minister are among the victims of a deadly train crash that killed 69 people near Urda in central Spain on Wednesday morning.
The crash, between a high-speed Renfe train and a stationary Iryo train on the same track, also injured more than 100 people, many seriously.
The impact caused carriages to derail, and there are fears the death toll could still rise, with reports of family members searching for missing relatives in hospitals across the region.
The bodies of those killed have been taken to the main forensics institute in Toledo, where families have been giving DNA samples to help identify them.
The crash is the second rail disaster in Spain this year, and the worst in the country's history since 2013.
Who are the victims?
Julieta Gallego
Julieta Gallego, 24, was a Spanish long jumper who competed for Madrid athletics club, AD Sprint.
"The entire club is heartbroken," it wrote on Instagram.
The Royal Spanish Athletics Federation (RFEF) announced her death, expressing its condolences to her family, friends and teammates.
Gallego regularly competed in Spanish club championships, local media outlet ABC reported, and had a best jump of 5.9m (19ft 3in).
Raúl Chapado, president of RFEF, told the outlet that her death is a "blow that strikes at the very heart of the athletics family."
"Today, the sport mourns the passing of Julieta, a life ahead of her that has been unjustly extinguished".
Fátima Báñez
The death of former employment minister Fátima Báñez, 59, was confirmed by the Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE), which she chaired.
"Her warmth, generosity, and commitment leave an indelible mark on businesses and the entire CEOE team," it said in a statement.
Báñez served in the government under former Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy from 2011 until 2018, and was the first woman to hold the role. In 2012, she introduced controversial labour reforms that made it easier for companies to fire people, sparking mass protests across the country.
Following news of her death, Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso paid tribute to her, saying she would be "deeply missed".
"Spain loses a great political figure," she said.
José Manuel Chacón
The Civil Guard confirmed the death of its officer José Manuel Chacón, 31, in a statement expressing its "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.
Antonio Montero Domínguez
Finance and tax lawyer, Antonio Montero Domínguez, was remembered as a "meticulous professional" and "tireless worker" by legal news website, El Derecho.
His death was confirmed by Spain's tax authority, where he had been an inspector between 2012-2016.
Additional reporting by Sarah Rainsford, Madeleine Lake and Tom McArthur

title: Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
text:
Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.
Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.
Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.
Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.
Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.
She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term.
"I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.
In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.
However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.
Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.
By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Amazon shares hit
Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Microsoft cuts AI spend
Wall Street's reaction to Microsoft's update was more muted, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.
description: Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its AI own search summaries were affecting ad revenue.

title: Murder charge dropped after non-suspicious death
text:
Murder charge dropped after non-suspicious death
A man who was arrested on suspicion of murder will face no further police action in relation to the death of a woman, which is no longer being treated as suspicious.
Devon and Cornwall Police officers were called after a woman's body was found at an address on Teignmouth Road, Torquay, just before 21:00 GMT on Tuesday.
A forensic post-mortem was carried out on Thursday which the police said found no evidence to suggest the involvement of a third party, and that the most likely cause of death was believed to have been from natural causes.
A man in his 50s from Torquay who was arrested on suspicion of murder will face no further police action in relation to the woman's death.
Det Insp Jason Kelly said: "We would like to thank members of the public for their support and patience during this investigation.
"Our thoughts remain with the family of the deceased."

title: Youths caught trespassing at Leweston School grounds in Dorset
text:
Youths caught trespassing on closed school grounds
Youths wearing balaclavas were caught trespassing on the grounds of a closed private school, police have said.
The six people were attempting to gain entry through a window at Leweston School, near Sherborne, on Thursday afternoon, Dorset Police said.
Officers attended and located the youths before contacting their parents or guardians, who then came to collect them. One was taken home by police.
The century-old private school posted a shock announcement on its website this week that it would not reopen after half term.
The Catholic boarding and day school wrote: "We are very sorry for what this means for our pupils, their families and our staff, and for how little notice we have been able to give."
The school's alumni include actress Kristin Scott Thomas and Baroness Dido Harding, who ran the government's Covid-19 Test and Trace programme in England.

title: Venezuela opposition leader María Machado calls for elections upon return
text:
Venezuela opposition leader María Machado calls for elections upon return
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado is calling for elections to be held next year.
During a news conference in Caracas on Thursday, the Nobel Peace Prize winner said the country's move toward democracy was "irreversible".
She also thanked the Trump administration for opening the "floodgate to freedom" by capturing her opponent, former President Nicolás Maduro.
The same day, Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, said elections would be held and that her government should oversee a "transition of this magnitude" - which Machado dismissed as illogical. Rodríguez, who was Maduro's vice-president, did not set a date for voting.
Machado said there would be elections in 2027, but also did not offer an exact timeline.
The transition in Venezuela would be "irreversible, organised, pacific", Machado said standing before a slogan which read "Let Us Be Free".
Her return to the country comes after she repeatedly made earlier efforts to re-enter Venezuela, and failed.
Last year Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat and in darkness to travel to Norway and accept the Nobel Peace Prize. Soon after, in January, the US seized Maduro.
The Trump administration then backed Rodríguez as leader. She was sworn in as interim president and later signed an oil deal that granted favourable terms to the US.
Although it remains unclear what Machado plans to do next, she has previously said she would run for president again if an election were held. Her ability to return to her country was contingent on approval from the Trump administration.
Speaking about her return, Machado said she had heard one word repeated by the thousands of supporters who thronged her route into the capital - freedom.
"I come to carry out a task and complete a mandate," she said.
The opposition leader said she had not received a message or invitation to meet from Rodríguez, and would not personally participate in election negotiations between opposition representatives and the government.
But she wished them well in their work, she said, in order to see the electoral body reformed so that every Venezuelan, inside the country and abroad, could vote.
Shortly before Machado's news conference, Rodríguez delivered a speech in a conciliatory tone, saying she had "instructed the security agencies that no one be detained without judicial order, except in cases of flagrant commission of crimes".
Rodríguez also spoke of "the doors being open" in Venezuela to returning exiles and talked of dialogue and building consensus.
description: Machado, who was in exile for nearly a year, said the transition in Venezuela's government would be "irreversible, organised, pacific".

title: King Charles in Guyana as Bahamas visit declared 'diplomatic success'
text:
King Charles arrives in Guyana as Bahamas visit declared 'diplomatic success'
King Charles III has arrived in Guyana for the second leg of his Caribbean tour, following a visit to the Bahamas that Buckingham Palace described as a "sensitive balancing act" and a "diplomatic success".
The main themes of the two-day state visit to Guyana will be the environment and sustainability - alongside the growing commercial ties between the UK and Guyana.
The King is due to have an audience with President Irfaan Ali and will attend a state reception celebrating the 60 years of bilateral relations betweeen the two nations.
After visiting Guyana, the King will travel to Antigua and Barbuda, where he will open a major Commonwealth leaders summit in his role as the head of the "family of nations".
Guyana - formerly British Guiana - is the world's fastest growing economy due to the discovery of oil reserves there in 2015.
More than four fifths of Guyana is covered by rainforest and it has one of the lowest rates of deforestation in the world.
Cultural exchanges will also feature with a group of bagpipers from the National Piping Centre in Scotland joining the royal tour.
As the King left the Bahamas on Thursday to fly to Guyana, his spokesman said the islands he was departing had "a special place in the King's heart".
"The great wall of cheers he received when greeting crowds will echo long in his memory - and be a source of tremendous pride and encouragement as the tour continues to Guyana, and Antigua and Barbuda."
The two-day trip to the Bahamas saw the King meet young boxers, environmentalists and politicians.
He also joined the dancing in a Junkanoo parade to celebrate island life.
In his only public speech of the tour so far, delivered during his first engagement in the Bahamas, the King referenced the UK's involvement in the slave trade acknowledging the "suffering of the past."
His spokesman said: "The King had hoped the visit proved an opportunity to celebrate and reaffirm the modern partnership between the Bahamas and the UK - and to address the shared challenges of the future and also to acknowledge the great injustices of the past in a respectful way."
The tour comes amidst renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in the slave trade and to offer reparations - compensation from those countries that profited from the trade in enslaved men and women.
A small number of protesters were at some of the King's engagements in the Bahamas, with campaigners holding signs saying "pay us what you owe us" but their presence did not disrupt events.
The Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting (CHOGM) being held in Antigua and Barbuda from 1 November will discuss the legacy of slavery. The King will deliver a speech as Head of the Commonwealth.

title: Sir Patrick Stewart: Actor who moved effortlessly between Star Trek and Shakespeare
text:
Sir Patrick Stewart: Actor who moved effortlessly between Star Trek and Shakespeare
Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, was a stage and screen great who balanced Hollywood stardom with an equally stellar career in classical theatre.
While many actors are typecast, he moved effortlessly from Shakespeare and Dickens to the command of the USS Enterprise and his famous wheelchair in X-Men.
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.
One of the world's most versatile actors, he mastered both comedy and tragedy, science-fiction and historical drama - despite the entertainment industry's traditional dislike of bald heads.
Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire on 13 July 1940.
His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.
His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had shredded his mental health.
"My father was a very potent individual," Stewart later recalled. "It was said that when he strode on to the parade ground, birds stopped singing."
But Alfred Stewart had become a quick-tempered man, suffering from what would now be called post traumatic stress.
He was prone to drink and often took out his frustrations on his family - although Patrick himself was never the target of his fists.
Young Patrick's love of drama developed at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He found the predictability of dramatic performances a welcome change from the turmoil of his home life.
He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a journalist and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.
He also threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
But he found it impossible to concentrate on both his job and his acting. Eventually his editor told him to choose between journalism and the "foolhardy" acting.
Stewart picked up his typewriter and walked out.
At the age of 18, he had the traumatic experience of losing all his hair, a huge blow to an aspiring actor and self-conscious teenager - who worried that girls would no longer find him attractive.
He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company - playing a variety of roles across the company's repertoire.
And when not appearing as Oberon or Enobarbus, he made his TV debut as a fireman in a 1967 episode of soap opera Coronation Street.
His Broadway debut came in 1970 as Snout in Peter Brook's critically acclaimed production of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Over the next two decades, Stewart appeared in a variety of television roles without threatening to become a major star.
In 1974, he played Lenin in the BBC's 13-part drama series The Fall of Eagles.
He was a conspiratorial Roman soldier in the hugely popular I, Claudius and a Soviet spy in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy and Smiley's People.
In 1984, Stewart left the RSC and moved to the National Theatre. By then in his mid-40s, he had only ever been unemployed for three weeks, but was rarely cast as a main character.
He had landed a number of supporting film roles: including playing Guinevere's father in Excalibur, a warrior-minstrel in Dune, and a riding instructor in Little Lord Fauntleroy.
And he was the voice of a small character in the animated film of Richard Adams' novel The Plague Dogs.
But even he described the first half of his career as "sound but never spectacular".
Then came the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
A producer named Robert L Justman was intent on reviving the Star Trek franchise, and was looking for a successor to William Shatner's legendary James T Kirk.
He had hoped to find a sexy, hirsute Frenchman to play the role - but chanced upon Stewart giving a lecture to his wife's Shakespeare class in Los Angeles.
Justman turned to his wife. "I said I think I've found our new captain," he said.
Stewart was intrigued but sceptical.
He knew nothing about the original Star Trek and his great friend, Sir Ian McKellen, told him not to throw his stage career away on a wild goose chase into space.
But in need of a boost to his finances, Stewart signed a six-year contract, firmly believing the show wouldn't last and he'd be back on the boards before long.
"Everybody told me it would be a flop," he recalled. "A friend of mine said, 'Get a suntan, make some money, go home.'"
He was, however, pleased that the producers didn't mind his baldness.
He'd tried wearing a wig in early screen tests, but it looked ratty and - in the end - Star Trek's founder Gene Roddenberry told him to ditch it.
"In the 24th Century, they wouldn't care if Picard was bald," he said.
Stewart, who was billed by the New York Times as "an unknown British Shakespearean actor", found it hard adapting to his new job.
After his stage experiences, he found the 20 hours a day on set tiring, and he also struggled to work with a fairly laid-back and fun-loving US cast.
His decision to call his fellow actors together and give them a lecture about behaving more seriously failed to gain him popularity.
"It was really awful, being dressed down by the captain," said Brent Spiner, who played Data, the android. "We really thought, 'Well, please, get over it'."
Eventually Stewart softened, insisting that every member of the cast told at least one joke a day.
Despite his initial reservations, Star Trek: The Next Generation both survived and prospered - making its star a very wealthy man.
Captain Picard was supposed to be French, but displayed a surprisingly English regard for both Shakespeare and Earl Grey tea.
And, after playing all those Shakespearean princes and dukes on the London stage, Stewart became fiercely proud of him, and of the show's ability to connect with younger audiences.
In addition to the television series, Stewart played Picard in four Star Trek films. But while commanding the Enterprise, he managed to not neglect the theatre.
With his new-found celebrity, the parts he was offered improved greatly.
For years, he performed a one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol on Broadway - playing all 40 characters.
In 1995, he appeared as Prospero in a memorable performance of The Tempest and, two years later, he starred as Othello - who he presented as a white mercenary in a black African nation.
But his Star Trek success limited the roles that Hollywood was prepared to offer him.
"No director wanted to cast this grand, deep-voiced, bald English guy," he told the Times. "Because everybody knew he was Picard and couldn't possibly be anybody else."
Eventually, he took the role of Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise, essentially playing a telepathic Picard in a wheelchair.
His co-star was Sir Ian McKellen - the friend who'd warned him to avoid Hollywood - in the metal-bending role of Magneto.
Alongside his work in America, he won critical acclaim opposite Harriet Walter in Antony and Cleopatra in 2007.
And, in the same year, he played Macbeth for the first time - despite a 30-year age gap between him and Kate Fleetwood, playing Lady Macbeth.
But the critics refused to complain.
Critic Nicholas de Jongh decided it was "the best Macbeth I have ever seen", and hailed him as "one of our finest Shakespearean actors".
In 2010, Stewart was awarded a knighthood for his services to drama.
In 2009, he again teamed up with Sir Ian in Waiting For Godot.
It was a moment of personal fulfilment for Sir Patrick who, as an awed teenager, remembered watching Peter O'Toole in the play at the Bristol Old Vic.
His deep and authoritative voice made him much in demand for voice-over roles - including a reprise of his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek video games.
One female interviewer once gushed that "just hearing him order breakfast is rather thrilling".
He also voiced a host of TV commercials both in Britain and the US.
Away from acting, he was a passionate political activist and a long-time supporter of the Labour Party, as well as a campaigner for victims of domestic abuse.
In 2013, he married his third wife - singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell - in Nevada.
Sir Ian McKellen officiated at the ceremony, which had to be restaged at a Los Angeles restaurant when someone discovered that his legal power to do so did not extend to the Silver State.
A year later, the two knights took their talents to Broadway, alternating performances of Waiting for Godot with Harold Pinter's No Man's Land.
Sir Patrick made a video for Amnesty International on the subject of domestic violence, referencing his father's brutality towards his mother.
Once named the third greatest Yorkshireman after Michael Palin and Sean Bean, he never lost touch with his roots - keeping a house in God's Own Country, and remaining a lifelong supporter of Huddersfield Town football club.
Forthcoming projects had included a final performance as Professor Charles Xavier in Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday, which will be released this Christmas.
And, if millions remember him only as the somewhat taciturn commander of the USS Enterprise, that prospect was not something that worried him.
"For huge numbers of people I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that's fine," he said. "I really believe we created an admirable individual."
description: The English actor began his career on stage before finding fame as the captain of the USS Enterprise.
