title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
text:
Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
According to protocol, the president will appoint a party leader whom he believes has the best chance to form a majority government. That leader has up to 42 days to achieve this, before the task passes to a second nominee who is given 28 days. If that nominee is unsuccessful, a period of 14 days is granted to a third candidate, after which, if no government has been formed, new elections will be called.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.
description: The PM's Likud party has alleged foreign interference and said Arab-led parties "stole" the election after his coalition lost its majority.

title: 'Respected and beloved': Tributes pour in for Sir Patrick Stewart
text:
Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86
Sir Ian McKellen has led tributes to Sir Patrick Stewart following his death at the age of 86, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation".
Tributes to the renowned British actor have poured in since his death at his Los Angeles home after "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia was announced on Thursday.
"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," Sir Ian, Sir Patrick's X-Men co-star, said.
Famous for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek, Sir Patrick was a versatile actor who won multiple awards, balancing Hollywood roles and a career in classical theatre.
William Shatner, who also helmed the USS Enterprise in Star Trek, said Sir Patrick brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did".
"Captain Picard stood for the best of us and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work," Shatner added.
Stewart depicted Picard in more than 170 episodes of the hit sci-fi TV series between 1987 and 1994, as well as in four feature films. He returned to the role for Star Trek: Picard in 2020.
Dame Judi Dench said she was "shocked" and "very sad" to hear of Sir Patrick's death, adding: "He's never been one of those actors who never felt like it that night, he was always very, very committed... He'll be much missed and he was much admired."
George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in Star Trek, said the actor "inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity".
Sir Patrick would later be celebrated for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier - most commonly known as Professor X - in the X-Men film franchise.
Hugh Jackman, who starred alongside him in the franchise, called him a "tremendous friend and man", saying: "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today."
Sir Ian, a longtime friend of his X-Men co-star, who officiated his wedding in 2013, said Sir Patrick was "defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire".
"You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues."
Sir Ian recalled first meeting Sir Patrick as young actors in the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and how he had expressed caution over him taking on the Star Trek role.
"He took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did," said Sir Ian, who appeared with Sir Patrick in a 2009 theatre production of Waiting for Godot.
He added that while the US had become Sir Patrick's "adopted home", he "never forsook his origins" growing up in Yorkshire, and said "the proudest achievement of the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic, was his appointment as chancellor of Huddersfield University".
Sir Ian noted that Sir Patrick's final film appearance will be as Professor X in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday film. Marvel Studios described him as "a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman".
The Academy dubbed his voice "unmistakable", adding: "Whether commanding the bridge of the Enterprise or guiding a generation of young mutants, Sir Patrick Stewart brought a tenderness to his characters that made us feel we knew them."
Sir Patrick died on Wednesday "in the loving care of his wife", a statement from his family said. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," it added.
The veteran actor is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, as well as by his two adult children from his first marriage, Daniel and Sophie Stewart.
'One of greatest stage actors ever seen'
Born in the town of Mirfield in 1940, Sir Patrick's love of drama began at school where he was introduced to Shakespeare and his first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
When Sir Patrick was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010, he said he owed "literally everything" to his former English teacher who first encouraged him to perform.
His first foray into professional acting was when he joined the RSC in 1966, going on to play King John, Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream and Henry IV.
The RSC described him as a "colossus of both stage and screen", remembering him as "one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation" whose contribution to the company was "beyond measure".
Dame Harriet Walter, who first met Sir Patrick in his theatre days more than 40 years ago, said his passing was like a "huge giant tree has fallen in the forest".
"He had fire in his eyes and you were absolutely in the room with him," the Succession actress told BBC Newsnight. "I've never heard a bad word against him. And I think the world's going to be very poor without him."
Theatres in London's West End will dim their lights for two minutes on 3 November in his honour.
Hannah Essex, co-chief of the Society of London Theatre and UK Theatre, called him "one of the greatest stage actors this country has ever seen".
As well as having roles in films such as Safe House, Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the original Dune, Sir Patrick continued to appear on TV throughout his career, making guest appearances on Frasier, Futurama and the Simpsons.
US actor and animator Seth MacFarlane, who grew up as a fan of Sir Patrick, said he was "gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend" as they worked together on Family Guy, American Dad! and Ted.
MacFarlane described him as a "rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great and a great writer sound masterful".
Comedian Ricky Gervais, whose BBC programme Extras Sir Patrick guest starred in, described him as a "legend".
Sharing a video of the pair giggling in a set of bloopers for the series, Gervais said: "I still can't believe he agreed to do this scene. And he didn't even mind when I ruined every take."
Sir Patrick was a lifelong supporter of English Football League club Huddersfield Town, which called him a "titan of his craft".
"Fiercely proud of his Yorkshire roots, Sir Patrick was a Terrier in every sense, and we're proud to have counted him as one of our own," the club added.
Alzheimer's is the most common type of dementia, while Lewy Body Dementia is another common form caused by abnormal protein deposits, which cause a loss of cognitive function.
The Alzheimer's Society CEO Michelle Dyson said Sir Patrick was an "extraordinarily talented and much-loved actor, admired by millions around the world", adding: "His death is a heartbreaking reminder of the devastating impact dementia has on people and families across the globe."
The actor became a campaigner on domestic violence in later life, including becoming an ambassador for domestic abuse charity Refuge in 2007, after witnessing his mother suffer violence at the hands of his father.
Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, Refuge's board chair, said it had been a privilege to "watch his endless devotion" to the cause, adding that he "broke down barriers and taboos on the subject".
Andy Burnham considered Sir Patrick to be "one of the very best" who "never forgot his working-class Yorkshire roots".
"He brought joy to millions," the prime minister's spokesman said on his behalf. "He always stood up for what he believed in, including through his campaigning to help those affected by domestic violence.
description: The actor died in Los Angeles following a "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

title: GCHQ intern who took data home loses bid to cut sentence
text:
GCHQ intern who took data home loses sentence appeal
A GCHQ intern who was jailed for endangering national security by taking top secret data home has lost a bid to reduce his jail term.
Manchester University computer science student Hasaan Arshad breached tight security rules when he used his mobile phone to remove material from a computer system at GCHQ and transfer it to his private computer on 24 August 2022.
The 26-year-old was jailed for seven-and-a-half years after he admitted an offence under the Computer Misuse Act and two charges of making an indecent photograph of a child.
On Thursday Lady Justice Cockerill refused Arshad permission to challenge his sentence, saying there were no arguable grounds that the sentencing judge was wrong.
GCHQ is the UK's intelligence, security and cyber agency and plays an important role in keeping the country safe, in conjunction with MI5 and the Secret Intelligence Service (MI6).
The court heard how Arshad, from Rochdale, Manchester, was coming to the end of an industry year placement with a technical development team at the site in Cheltenham, Gloucestershire.
Arshad had undergone GCHQ induction and was required to sign the Official Secrets Act.
He was motivated by a desire to complete the project he had been tasked with as his placement was coming to an end.
Prosecutor Duncan Atkinson KC told the Old Bailey last year that Arshad's actions "lost a tool" being developed at GCHQ, risked exposing the identities of 17 GCHQ colleagues, and undermined the trust of partners, which "created a significant risk of damage to national security".
Rupert Bowers KC, representing Arshad, argued the sentencing judge had made the sentence too high for a first-time offender.
He said Arshad had "noble if misguided" intentions and no "corrupt motive".
Bowers said: "This is an exceptional case because of the motivations and the intentions.
"Yes, a serious offence has been committed by someone who was reckless, but he has not committed it intentionally to harm national security."
At the Court of Appeal on Thursday, Lady Justice Cockerill said the judge had given "careful consideration" to Arshad's "age, immaturity and neurodivergence" and had rightly taken into account the serious harm to national security which could have been caused.

title: Littlewoods regeneration to go ahead without Twickenham Studios
text:
Littlewoods project backed despite studios pull-out
The company behind plans to regenerate Liverpool's landmark Littlewoods building said the project was still on track despite proposals to bring a film studio to the site falling through.
Capital & Centric - which has been involved with the Edge Lane site for more than a decade - confirmed that Twickenham Studios was no longer going to be involved.
There had been plans to turn the famous Art Deco building into a "Hollywood of the North" film production and post-production complex.
Speaking after Chancellor John Healey announced a £20m funding package for the scheme in Wednesday's Budget, Capital & Centric's John Moffat tried to allay concerns of "another false dawn" for the site.
Twickenham Studios - involved in making high-profile films such as War Horse and The Iron Lady - was announced as an "anchor tenant" in 2018, planning to take up to 85,000 sq ft (nearly two acres / 0.8 hectares) of the complex.
Even after a major fire in the buildings that year, Twickenham Studios said it was still committed to the project and said the same in 2024, despite having dissolved a company it had set up called Twickenham Studios Liverpool Ltd the year before.
Moffat confirmed to BBC North West Tonight that the film studio had pulled out of the project.
Twickenham Studios have been contacted for comment by the BBC.
'False Dawns'
Liberal Democrat councillor for Gateacre in Liverpool, Kris Brown, told the BBC the Littlewoods project simply could not afford "another false dawn".
"I think the sheer scale of the project meant this was never viable without the government stepping in," he said.
"But if we can get it under way it would be a great thing for Liverpool, the North West, and the UK.
"We cannot afford any more false dawns though.
"Developers must get a contractor in place and we need full transparency on this and a plan - should this not work out in the future."
Moffat said he was confident the project would be completed and ultimately generate jobs and money.
"It does need more than £20m but this unlocks further funding," he said of the chancellor's investment announcement on Wednesday.
"The site's made a huge amount of progress.
"Obviously we had some grant funding.
"We've spent that remediating the site, getting it structurally stable.
"This now is the next step moving us from ambition into action and actually delivering the scheme.
"I understand people's scepticism but, as a business, this is what we do up and down the country.
"We take sites that people think are beyond regeneration and we bring them back and we turn them into really exciting places and thriving economic generators - which is exactly what this site is going to be.
"It's going to generate thousands of new jobs and hundreds of millions per annum for the local economy."
Lynn Saunders, head of the Liverpool Film Office, said the site was needed to support the demand for creative spaces in the city region.
"I've been providing evidence for the past 15 years why we need to build infrastructure in, for example, film and TV," she said.
"Productions are flocking here but there isn't ancillary space, workshops or innovation space."
"This isn't a film and TV dedicated site, it's creative industries.
"It's about providing a focal point to develop skills for creative industries.
"I think the announcement by the chancellor gives this scheme a massive boost.
"It will allow all the various different public agencies and the private sector to look at the city's potential.
"Why not Liverpool?"
Jimmy Mulville, managing director of Hattrick TV productions, shared a similar view to Saunders.
"I think Liverpool is the most 'film city' outside of London," Mulville said.
"It kind of makes sense that you have a state-of-the-art studio here.
"It's about time I think.
"It's such a fabulous city to shoot in - the locations are brilliant.
"I've spoken to many producers who shoot locations here but then are forced to go down south to Pinewood and Shepperton to complete their production."
He added: "If this building was in London, it would have been redeveloped many, many years ago."

title: Leicester woman jailed for role in prostitution ring
text:
Woman jailed for role in prostitution ring
A woman who was part of an organised crime group that trafficked women into the country for prostitution has been jailed.
Leicestershire Police said Wai Sin was part of a group that moved victims from brothel to brothel - with a premises in Leicester "one hub on the carousel".
The force said the "operation was like a conveyor belt, delivering a steady stream of women to Leicester to have sex with men for money".
The 63-year-old, from Leicester, was sentenced to five years and four months in prison at Leicester Crown Court on Thursday.
She was also handed a slavery and trafficking prevention order for seven years, having pleaded guilty in July to conspiracy to arrange or facilitate the travel of another person with a view to exploitation, control prostitution for gain and transferring criminal property.
A police operation took place at an address in south Leicester in January, the force said, where Sin was arrested and several mobile phones recovered.
Following an examination of the devices, officers said they found evidence of the phones being used to advertise women for sexual services on two websites.
'Deliberate and exploitative'
The adverts contained details of services provided at the premises and when officers attended, they found large amounts of sexual paraphernalia.
Between May 2025 and January, 27 women were trafficked through the business, the force said.
Once Sin had the money in her account, a "significant amount" was transferred to accounts in China.
The defendant operated several bank accounts, police said, with more than £135,000 banked between May 2025 and January.
Det Con Natasha Panchal said: "This was a deliberate and exploitative operation run for profit, in which women were treated as commodities.
"It was clear during the investigation that Sin was part of a network of people who exploited women for their own financial gain.
"Up to 11 men would visit the premises throughout the day and the victims were made to work long days.
"Prior to the arrival of each victim, the defendant would advertise them for sexual services on two websites. More than 24 adverts were identified and all were taken out with one of Sin's two telephone numbers as the point of contact.
"The women they exploited were vulnerable and they took advantage of that for their own gain."

title: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
text:
'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."
description: A temporary ceasefire has brought rare quiet to Kherson, offering its residents a glimpse of normal life before fighting resumes.

title: More than 43 million ballots cast so far in midterms early voting surge
text:
More than 43 million ballots cast so far in midterms early voting surge
With less than a week to go until the US midterm elections - which will determine which party controls Congress for the next two years - more than 43 million Americans have already voted.
Data from the University of Florida Election Lab indicates that four to five million early votes have been cast each day, a much higher rate than in most previous elections.
Texas has seen the highest above-average turnout rate so far, says Professor Mike McDonald, who runs the database. Hispanic communities are also seeing a much higher turnout than usual.
Overall turnout appears on track to outpace 2020, and even possibly 2018, which beat the 1914 record for overall turnout in a midterm election.
Texas has already surpassed its 2022 numbers by around 1.75 million voters, says McDonald. More than 5.8 million ballots have been cast in the Lone Star state, which has emerged as a key battleground that could decide which party controls the Senate for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Data from states where voters are required to register a political affiliation during the primary elections, when voters choose their party nominees ahead of the general election, indicates an increase in votes cast by Democrats.
The number of early ballots cast by Republican-affiliated voters remain generally similar to 2022.
Early voting is also up among voters who chose to not register with a specific party, McDonald says, however the data does not show which candidates they chose.
Figures on Thursday show that 44% of early ballots have been cast by Democrats, and 31.2% by Republicans. A further 24.7% were attributed to voters who had no party affiliation. However, that's just for the roughly half of states that require voter affiliation.
Three states require voters to submit their race when they register - North Carolina, Georgia and Florida. Data from these states shows an increase in votes cast by Hispanic and black communities, while voting among white people is on par with 2022 early voting figures.
"That makes sense because communities of colour are more frequently part of the Democratic coalition, and whites are more frequently part of the Republican coalition," McDonald says.
Texas does not require voters to provide party affiliation or race. But the data still shows a surge in voting by some counties on the border with Mexico, which are comprised of more than 90% Hispanic people.
"When I look at those counties, what I see is some of them are going to beat their 2022 turnout in just the early vote alone," says McDonald.
Early voting has boomed in recent years, driven by the Covid pandemic when more states began offering early voting options, including both in-person and by mail.
In the 2020 election, when voters were picking both the next president as well as their lawmakers, more than two-thirds of all ballots were cast early. Half of those early votes were also cast by mail.
Voters increasingly prefer to vote in-person, even when voting early, says McDonald. They are also returning their ballots earlier than in previous elections.
He adds that he believes this could be due to concerns about postal voting, but says there is not data to indicate what could be causing this. Postal votes are more likely to be disqualified due to errors, he notes, and says some voters could be concerned about meddling in the US Postal Service.
Some officials have already confirmed records being broken. On Thursday, the city of Minneapolis said that it has set an early voting record for a non-presidential election.
Early voting will soon taper off, as states start cutting off early voting as an option in the days before the election on Tuesday, 3 November.
Correction 30 October: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that some states require voters to register a political affiliation, however that refers to the primary elections and not the general elections taking place on 3 November.
description: Hispanic voters have helped drive the early voting numbers, which appear to outpace overall turnout for previous elections in some battleground counties.

title: Broken hospital tap wastes a million litres of water
text:
Broken hospital tap wastes a million litres of water
More than a million litres of water may have been lost by a broken tap left running at a hospital for almost three months.
Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board said the tap, in Ysbyty Glan Clwyd's emergency department, was fixed on October 26 - but a sticker by it shows the matter was reported on 7 August.
According to the Let's Save Water campaign, funded by water companies, a running tap wastes 10 litres a minute, which is 600 litres an hour or 14,400 litres a day.
The health board said any decision to remove the facility from use had to be balanced against potential impact on patient care.
From 7 August to October 26 is 81 days, including start and end days.
That means as much as 1,166,400 litres of water may have gone down the drain at the hospital in Bodelwyddan, Denbighshire.
According to Welsh Water it charges £1.5889 per 1,000 litres for non-households, which comes to £1,853.29 for 1,166,400 litres.
Not-for-profit Waterwise, which dubs itself the UK's leading independent voice on water efficiency, was appalled.
Chief executive Nicci Russell said: "This is an absolutely horrific waste of water when we can scarcely afford to be wasting water.
"The climate change committee is telling us drought is one of our top three climate risks.
"Our current water systems are not even fit for the current climate let alone what is coming - parts of Wales are still in drought."
Russell said water scarcity was a national emergency.
She said: "Identifying leaks of this kind is one part of the problem. This hospital clearly did identify it - it would be interesting to know how long it was before it was reported."
According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, Denbighshire County Council member Chris Evans was sent a video of the tap, shot on 11 October, by a constituent.
He said: "It sums up what is wrong with Betsi, that they can't even sort a running tap that's been running since August."
Ysbyty Glan Clwyd is managed by Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, which has been in special measures for much of the last decade.
Evans said: "Things are not getting any better with the health board, are they? If we can't sort the basics out, how are we going to sort these things out for the patients?
"It's not good for the environment. It's a waste of water. Why can't we just replace the tap? It shows how bad Betsi is."
Water watchdog Ofwat said: "Finding and fixing customer-side leaks is essential to achieving better water resilience, securing water supplies for everyone.
"By proactively identifying and fixing leaks, customers can reduce their water bills and minimise the risk of costly property damage and unexpected repair bills."
Betsi's operational estates chief, Arwel Hughes, said: "The fault reported to our estates team was identified as a minor drip from a specialist clinical tap, which subsequently deteriorated to a more substantial flow.
"Although a replacement part was ordered from the manufacturer promptly, repair was delayed until Monday 26 October due to supplier lead times."
Consideration, Hughes said, was given to emergency department's requirements.
"Any decision to isolate or remove the facility from use had to be carefully balanced against the potential impact on patient care, including the availability of essential handwashing facilities within a busy clinical environment," he said.
"We are currently working with our suppliers to review and improve the availability and lead times of specialist replacement parts, in order to reduce future repair times."
description: The matter was reported on 7 August but not fixed until 26 October.

title: Delivery of new CalMac ferry MV Glen Rosa put back to February
text:
Delivery of new CalMac ferry MV Glen Rosa put back to February
The expected handover date of the long-delayed CalMac ferry MV Glen Rosa has been put back by another two months until next February.
The dual-fuel ship being built by the state-owned Ferguson shipyard was expected to be ready by the end of the year, and had originally been due for delivery in 2018.
Transport Secretary Stephen Flynn said he had been told by the firm's boss that the yard could deliver the ship by the end of the year but officials had recommended a short delay to allow for the fitting of redesigned propellers.
Ferguson Marine is still assessing the impact on overall cost for the ship, already well over £200m which is more than four times the original contract price.
In a letter to Holyrood's transport committee, Flynn said: "Ferguson Marine has assured me that Glen Rosa can be delivered this year, however the handover will now be scheduled to take place in February 2027.
"This enables new propellers to be fitted and the ship's liquefied natural gas (LNG) fuel systems to be filled and commissioned only once.
"Doing this work now avoids the need to recall the vessel later."
Why does the ship need new propellers?
MV Glen Rosa and its identical sister vessel MV Glen Sannox are the first LNG-powered ships of their kind ever built in the UK, but construction has been blighted by design challenges and disputes over who is blame for the problems.
When Glen Sannox entered service on CalMac's Arran route in January 2025, nearly seven years later than expected, it quickly won praise from ferry users.
Two months later, however, a weld opened up near the stern of the ship, causing a small leak.
It was quickly fixed, but subsequent investigation concluded the underlying problem was excessive vibration when the ship was moving astern in harbour - which was itself linked to the design of the propellers.
These propellers, along with the ship's rudder, gearboxes and dual-fuel propulsion system, were all designed and supplied by the Finnish firm Wartsila.
Wartsila has spent months redesigning them, and new ones are expected to be fitted to Glen Sannox when it goes for its annual maintenance in December.
Glen Rosa is currently moored on the Clyde at Inchgreen for the final phase of construction but will have to enter dry dock before similar work can be carried out.
Multi-agency decision
Flynn said the decision to put back the delivery date yet again was recommended to him by a multi-agency group comprising ferries procurement agency CMAL, ferries operator CalMac, Ferguson Marine and Transport Scotland.
He said there was an opportunity to fit the new propellers to MV Glen Rosa in January, by which time it would become clearer how the redesigned propeller blades were performing on Glen Sannox.
He said it had been agreed this made more sense than handing the ship over with the older propellers, then withdrawing it again in order to have new ones fitted at a later date.
Transport committee convener Willie Rennie, however, said new delays were "completely unacceptable".
He said: "When the Cabinet Secretary next appears before the committee on November 18, he will need to be fleet of foot in providing concrete answers as to why, under his tutelage, islanders must suffer the consequences of yet further delays and over the winter period too."
Sea trials scheduled for November
In a separate letter to the transport committee, Ferguson Marine confirmed it had yet to carry out builder's sea trials of MV Glen Rosa, which were expected to take place in October, but these were now scheduled for November.
Chief executive Graeme Thomson said this delay was due to a number of system issues that had been identified, which was a "normal part of commissioning a vessel of this complexity".
Thomson said the decision to fit the new propellers to the ship prior to handover amounted to "extra scope" and would take place in dry dock in late January.
He said that for safety reasons it was not possible for the ship to enter dry dock with LNG on board, so the commissioning of the LNG systems had also been put back until the work was complete.
Thomson said that once builder's sea trials were complete he would give the MSPs a "substantive update" on the outcome, the revised handover schedule and the "cost impact of the change".
Builder' sea trials are the first in a series of at-sea testing voyages of a ship, which are followed by owner's acceptance trials and a final regulator approval process.
Once delivered, CalMac will also want to conduct its own crew familiarisation and berthing trials before the ship begins carrying passengers.
The two ships were initially expected to cost £97m when they were ordered from the Port Glasgow firm in 2015 but the repeated delays and technical problems have resulted in a succession of large cost increases.
An extra £150m has been required to finish Glen Sannox, and the latest estimate for completion of Glen Rosa is £197.5m.
These figures are over and above the £83m paid out prior to nationalisation, and do not include £45m of written-down government loans to the shipyard.
Ministers have said the loans were were not directly related to the troubled ferries but that is disputed by the yard's former owner.
Last month, BBC Scotland News revealed that Glen Sannox had experienced a large and uncontrolled venting of flammable methane gas during its first year of operation, due to the failure of a valve which was part of Wartsila's engine system.
The ship has not operated on LNG since the incident, although CalMac says it is safe to do so following the fitting of an upgraded valve and monitoring equipment.
description: The state-owned Ferguson shipyard has now been asked to fit redesigned propellers to the ship prior to handover.

title: Big Ben restorers to fix Cricklade's toppled Jubilee clock
text:
Big Ben restorers to fix toppled Jubilee clock
A 125-year-old Grade-II listed clock which was toppled by lorry is to be fixed by restorers who previously worked on Big Ben.
Erected in 1898 to mark Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, the clock outside the Vale Hotel in Cricklade, Wiltshire, was damaged after being hit on Tuesday evening.
It is now scheduled to be fixed by the Cumbria Clock Company, which helped restore Big Ben during the £80m renovation of the Elizabeth Tower in Westminster.
On assessing the damage to the landmark, Cumbria Clock Company owner Keith Scobie-Youngs, who grew up in the area, said he had never seen anything quite like it.
According to Cricklade Town Council, the clock had been fixed before after it was hit by a military vehicle in 1945.
Scobie-Youngs, whose company has been maintaining the clock since 1989, said the internal mechanisms of the structure and the electrics had been removed, but a larger vehicle was needed to move it from the ground.
He said recovering the smaller pieces of the clock already had stopped people from taking away "trophies".
He said the process of restoration would take at least 12 weeks and they hoped to keep as much of the original clock as possible.
Scobie-Youngs said he had a "full workshop" of people "capable of repairing cast iron" and "fabricating other structures to fit inside".
"When it does come back it will look exactly as it does now but perhaps a little bit stronger," he added.
A lamppost was also damaged in the incident, entering a window of a guest room at the Vale Hotel.
The hotel said it was planning to get a structural engineer to assess whether there was other damage.
Local residents have expressed their shock at the damage and at seeing the landmark on the floor, with the local rugby club describing it as being "tackled" to the ground.
Pauline McManus, who lives locally, said the clock was "part of this town" and that she had confidence it would be put back together.
Meanwhile, resident Ceri Whitehead, who has lived in the town for 12 years, previously said: "It has always been there, it's like part of the furniture and it's definitely a focal point especially with Christmas coming up - they decorate it."
Describing clocks as "important milestones", Scobie-Youngs said they were "important touchstones for local communities".
"Every community will have stories about those clocks," he said.

title: Paris suburb shooting suspect targeted people of Muslim or African appearance, prosecutor says
text:
Paris suburb shooting suspect targeted people of Muslim or African appearance, prosecutor says
A man suspected of a deadly shooting near Paris last week has admitted targeting people of "Muslim, African or North African" appearance, prosecutors say.
A man was killed and seven people including a child were injured last Friday when an attacker opened fire as he drove through two western suburbs.
On Thursday the suspect was charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office (PNAT) said.
President Emmanuel Macron called it a "racist terrorist attack" and anti-racism demonstrations have been held around France.
Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was killed in the shooting.
Three of those wounded were still in hospital with one in critical condition, terrorism prosecutor Olivier Christen told reporters.
The suspect, named in French media as 39-year-old Kevin T, chose Trappes and nearby La Verrière because he saw them as a "hotbed for Islamists", he said.
Kevin T had denied any "terrorist intent", insisted his actions were "legitimate" and said he "feels no regret", Christen said.
Police found "weapons or weapon components" in the suspect's home as well as books including a Quran, a Bible and Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf and stickers celebrating the hard-right National Rally (RN) party, Christen said.
Kevin T told investigators that he had designed the stickers with slogans such as "long live France, RN, proud to be French" himself and had them printed more than a year ago, Christen said.
But the suspect also told investigators he was not a member or supporter of any political party.
On Wednesday Macron said that "certain political movements on the far right" including the RN and "those close to them" had allowed a climate of racism "to take root".
Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a prominent RN lawmaker, retorted that it was the president himself who had allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish.
France's presidential elections is six months away and RN leader Marine Le Pen is currently leading opinion polls.
description: Kevin T has been charged with murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise.

title: Botox providers may be regulated in Guernsey
text:
Health mulls regulation of cosmetic industry
Providers of botox and fillers in Guernsey could be regulated under new plans from the Committee for Health and Social Care (HSC).
The suggestion was included in the committee's workplan for this political term, alongside plans to regulate medicinal cannabis clinics and give people who aren't doctors powers to prescribe medicines.
HSC's top priority remains plans to develop a new model for care in Guernsey, which could see patients paying more for healthcare in the future.
As part of its workplan for the term, HSC has highlighted there was no regulatory framework for private or voluntary sector homecare providers, which presented a "critical risk" according to HSC.
HSC stressed there was a particular concern about the risks posed by the unregistered workforce when it came to home carers.
Alongside aesthetic treatment providers HSC is also looking at regulating psychotherapists, counsellors and alternative therapists.
As part of developing a new model for healthcare in Guernsey HSC has committed to reviewing its contract with the Medical Specialist Group which provides secondary healthcare locally.
Deputy George Oswald who leads HSC said: "This work plan sets out an ambitious programme for the political term, centred on creating a more sustainable health and care system, without compromising health outcomes.
"Delivering it will require difficult choices, as well as close partnership working across government and with healthcare providers, charities, staff and the wider community.
"By investing in prevention, supporting people to live independently and modernising our services, infrastructure and technology, we can build a system that is better equipped to meet the changing needs of our islands."
Subject to the availability of resources HSC may look at proposals for the introduction of allergen regulation.
The committee also said it was keen to explore allowing the long-term care insurance fund to pay for care delivered in people's own homes, not just residential or nursing homes.
HSC is the sixth committee to publish its workplan for the rest of this political term, after the committees for the Environment and Infrastructure, Economic Development, Education, Sport and Culture, Housing and Employment and Social Security.
The Committee for Home Affairs hasn't published its workplan for this political term, and it remains unclear when it will do so.

title: Swindon teacher who drove to pupil's house in night banned
text:
Teacher who drove to pupil's house in night banned
A teacher who told a pupil she had "a real effect" on him before later entering into a sexual relationship with her has been struck off.
Mark Fletcher, 45, behaved "inappropriately" towards a pupil at Ridgeway School and Sixth Form College in Swindon, Wiltshire, in 2019, including driving to her home in the night and emailing her outside school hours, a Teaching Regulation Agency (TRA) panel found.
The relationship became sexual after the pupil left the school. Fletcher was suspended in July 2023 after she disclosed the relationship. He disputed all allegations.
A TRA professional conduct panel found his actions amounted to misconduct of a serious nature and ruled he should be banned.
Fletcher, who joined the school in September 2009, sent the pupil numerous emails from his personal account, many during the night or in the early hours of the morning, the panel found.
The pupil said Fletcher drove to her house at about 01:00 BST on 30 August 2019 and she "snuck out" to meet him. They talked until about 06:00 BST.
The panel heard that the pupil said Fletcher had told her: "You're not gonna tell anyone are you?" When she replied "no", he responded: "Good, I trust you," or words to that effect.
Emails sent in July and August 2019 included Fletcher telling the pupil: "It is rare to meet someone who changes who you are", and "Do you actually want to meet up and talk... Free most days from midnight... I can do tomorrow/the early hours of Saturday".
No police action
The pupil said that until December 2019, their relationship involved nothing physical beyond hugs, but included regular emotional conversations about how they felt about each other.
She said they began engaging in sexual activity that month, meeting late at night in Fletcher's car.
Police investigated allegations against Fletcher but took no further action. The case was referred to the TRA on 22 November 2023.
The panel report said Fletcher made no admissions and the case had proceeded on the basis that he disputed all allegations.
"The panel was satisfied that the conduct of Mr Fletcher amounted to misconduct of a serious nature which fell significantly short of the standards expected of the profession," it concluded.
"Accordingly, the panel was satisfied that Mr Fletcher was guilty of unacceptable professional conduct."

title: Samaritans closing and merging branches in north of Scotland
text:
Samaritans confirms closure of branches in north of Scotland
Samaritans has confirmed the closure of four of its branches in Scotland.
The sites in Stornoway, Thurso, Orkney and Shetland are to shut as part of wider changes to the suicide prevention charity's UK operations.
Its branch in Elgin is to be merged with Inverness.
Neil Mathers, executive director for Scotland, said the charity was moving to fewer, larger branches to "strengthen volunteer capacity and provide more reliable support".
Mathers said callers would be able to reach a volunteer more quickly, particularly during times when callers wait too long for an answer.
He said: "Volunteers are at the heart of everything we do, and we are hugely grateful for the dedication and compassion shown by volunteers all over Scotland.
"We recognise that it is difficult for volunteers to hear their branch will close or change."
Mathers added: "Although the way we organise our listening service is changing, our commitment to communities remains the same.
"We will continue to be visible and active across Scotland, working with volunteers and partners to maintain local presence, outreach, and representation."
description: The charity says it is moving to fewer, larger branches to help it provide a more reliable support.

title: MI5 false evidence in neo-Nazi spy case a serious failure, says intelligence watchdog
text:
MI5 false evidence in neo-Nazi spy case a serious failing, says intelligence watchdog
The man responsible for overseeing the conduct of the UK's intelligence services has said that MI5 lying to multiple courts while defending a violent neo-Nazi spy is as "serious as anything" he has ever dealt with.
"Oversight depends on candour," said investigatory powers commissioner Lord Leveson. "Failings of candour undermine the entire basis of oversight and accountability."
His office, the Investigatory Powers Commissioner's Office (IPCO), investigated how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts concerning the abusive informant known as agent X, as first exposed by the BBC.
IPCO's report, released earlier this year, found one senior officer lied repeatedly while another misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.
It also criticised other senior spies and found "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.
MI5 said it accepted the report's findings "without reservation" last month. The High Court is due to decide soon on what action, if any, to take against the agency or its staff.
In comments to mark the publication of his annual report on Thursday, Lord Leveson said the "case of agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as commissioner".
"False evidence was given to the High Court and the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and the prime minister directed me to find out how that happened.
"My investigation has now concluded and found that both IPCO and the courts were misled."
The IPCO investigation examined how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the violent neo-Nazi informant.
He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while he was under police investigation.
The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block our investigation into X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.
MI5 claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from Beth and everyone else, leaving her at a serious disadvantage.
But what MI5 said was untrue. It had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.
A senior MI5 officer had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist. He even wanted me to meet the agent. In doing so, he repeatedly departed from the NCND policy.
That officer was found to have repeatedly lied by the IPCO investigation. He has resigned from MI5 since the BBC exposed what happened.
The IPCO also oversees and regulates MI6 and GCHQ, as well covert powers and agent-running by police forces and other agencies.
Its annual report revealed that errors by MI5 involving agents increased from four in 2017 to 21 in 2025. In the same period, errors by MI6 decreased from 10 to three.
It also criticised the National Crime Agency (NCA) for failings in how it managed a juvenile criminal informant, meaning a child under 18 who was being used by the agency.
It found that the NCA did not inform Lord Leveson of the fact it was running a child informant within the required time period, and a senior NCA officer wrongly extended the authorisation well beyond what is legal.
It also found a failure to record the circumstances which would justify the absence of an "appropriate adult", and that the child was "tasked to engage in criminal conduct" without the protection of a valid legal authorisation.
Lord Leveson said the agency's conduct fell "well short of what the law requires" and said he had written to its director general.
He also expressed concern with GCHQ, saying it "still cannot tell me what has happened to removable media that may hold sensitive data, years after I first raised it with them".
The report revealed the spy agency now estimates there are "thousands" of memory cards, hard drives and other portable media items it can neither find nor account for. The report stated that "these items are utilised extensively and are an essential component of some of GCHQ's operating processes".
"We remain very concerned about this issue and are disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate", said Lord Leveson.
description: Lord Leveson says MI5 lying to multiple courts was as "serious as anything" he has dealt with.

title: Canada 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski found guilty of fraud
text:
Canadian 'Crypto King' found guilty of fraud
A Toronto jury has found self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski guilty of fraud, after hearing evidence he stole millions of dollars of investor money and spent it on private jets and other luxuries.
The jury quickly reached its verdict on Thursday, convicting the 27-year-old with one count of fraud over C$5,000 ($3,600; £2,900), after just hours of deliberation.
Throughout trial, Crown prosecutors called over a dozen witnesses, including investors whom Pleterski had cheated, and accountants and financial experts who testified on his scheme.
Pleterski pleaded not guilty and represented himself at his trial, cross-examining only one witness. He presented no evidence and did not testify.
The Canadian man was charged in May 2024 with one count each of fraud and money laundering following a 16-month joint investigation between Durham Regional Police and the Ontario Securities Commission.
The laundering charge was later dropped.
At the time, Durham Regional Police Chief Peter Moreira said it was potentially the biggest-ever fraud case in the region.
During Pleterski's trial in Ontario's Superior Court, Crown prosecutors presented ample evidence of his lavish spending using investor funds, according to local media.
He is believed to have taken more than C$36m from investors, and spent about half.
They said he used the money sent to his company AP Private Equity Limited to buy multiple trips on private jets and spend about C$5.6m on luxury vehicles.
Prosecutors also said he used the money to spend C$45,000 a month on a lakefront mansion in Burlington, Ontario, while racking up C$4.9m in credit card bills.
Bankruptcy proceedings had shown Pleterski also bought a McLaren and BMW for his parents - who had given him C$50,000 as a crypto investment - along with a Louis Vuitton bag, Burberry coat and a 2017 Bentley Bentayga.
Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora said during closing arguments on Wednesday that "Pleterski was no 'Crypto King'".
"He was a thief. A thief who stole investor money and used it as he pleased," Aurora told the jury, according to CBC News.
Things came crashing down for Pleterski ahead of his May 2024 arrest.
In December 2022, he was kidnapped in the middle of the night in downtown Toronto, with his captors demanding a large sum for his release.
"I'm sorry, I really am, I didn't want to or mean to ruin anyone's life," a bruised and bloodied Pleterski said in a video obtained by CBC News.
He was released three days later, after being tortured, including with waterboarding, cigarette burns and beatings with golf clubs.
He returns to court on 13 November for a sentencing hearing.
description: Prosecutors had accused Pleterski of stealing tens of millions of dollars of investor funds to buy himself a range of luxuries.

title: Scam sees 'bogus' callers pose as Suffolk Police officers
text:
Scam sees 'bogus' callers pose as police officers
Residents are being urged to be vigilant for scammers after a police force received reports of "bogus" callers pretending to be its officers.
Suffolk Police said there had been "multiple reports" on Wednesday and Thursday of scammers calling members of the public and falsely claiming to be police officers.
According to the force, the fraudsters appeared to have phoned from a cloned number, meaning calls made back to it would be routed to the Suffolk Police switchboard.
Suffolk Police and Suffolk Trading Standards said anyone who receives a call from someone claiming to be an officer should call 101 to check their identity.
"If you wish to check their identity and a crime number you have been given, we advise you hang up and call 101, ideally from a different phone," the force said.
"An officer will never mind waiting for you to check their identity via the control room. Please share this message with anyone who you think may be vulnerable.
"We are aware of other forces reporting similar incidents in recent days."
How can I spot a scam call?
According to Suffolk Police, police officers will never:
• Ask for bank details or PINs
• Request cash or bank card handovers to couriers
• Demand money transfers to other accounts
• Ask for payment of fines or fees over the phone
• Request access to your computer or passwords
• Ask you to "assist" in an investigation by doing any of the above activites

title: Sex offender jailed after meeting up with police in Reading
text:
Sex offender jailed after meeting up with police
A registered sex offender who thought he was meeting a 13-year-old following sexual communications online was arrested after instead being met by police.
Thomas Reeds, 25, from Ashton-under-Lyne, Greater Manchester, was arrested after travelling down to Reading to meet the child in April.
He was jailed for seven-and-a-half years after admitting 18 offences, including engaging in sexual communication with a child.
Reeds was already banned from having unsupervised contact with children under 16 following another court appearance at Manchester Crown Court in April 2024.
After officers arrested him, they found Reeds was in contact with other children and that he was in possession of 15 indecent images of children.
At Reading Crown Court on Friday, he pleaded guilty to the offences.
They included three breaches of a sexual harm prevention order (SHPO), eight attempted breaches of a SHPO and making indecent images of a child.
Det Con Stuart Robertson, from SEROCU, said: "Thomas Reeds posed a significant threat to children and took active steps to pursue and facilitate sexual offending.
"We welcome this sentence which reflects the seriousness of these offences and demonstrates our commitment to identifying offenders, safeguarding children, and bringing those responsible before the courts.
"Anyone who has experienced sexual abuse, or who has concerns about a child, should report it to police.
"Information provided by the public plays a vital role in protecting vulnerable people and preventing harm."

title: Ex-Top Gear host Richard Hammond's new Abergavenny life wild swimming and food festivals
text:
Ex-Top Gear host Richard Hammond's 'brave' new Welsh life wild swimming and running
Former Top Gear star Richard Hammond says he has swapped vintage cars for food festivals and running as he settles into life in a Welsh market town.
The 56-year-old bought a £2m Georgian mansion in Llanwenarth, near Abergavenny in Monmouthshire, in November 2025 following his divorce from wife Mindy after 23 years.
The presenter previously told BBC Wales he had "never been happier" since moving into the 19th Century home, and each week he has discovered a new reason to be "delighted that I live there".
With Bannau Brycheiniog - Brecon Beacons - in his back garden, Hammond told the High Performance Podcast he had taken up open water swimming as he becomes "braver" than he has ever been.
Hammond said it only took him a couple of visits to the property for him to realise that he "loved it".
"The Brecon Beacons National Park is the other side of my right-hand fence," he told the Telegraph.
"I can walk up the Sugar Loaf Mountain in an hour and 20 minutes or I could be getting measured for a new suit or buying a coffee in 20 minutes."
His home is currently being renovated to include car garages, a padel court and guest accommodation.
He recently made headlines for saying he would "find a way" to share his space with rare bats that have paused his renovation plans.
He said: "I just have to work with the bats. I like bats. You don't move to where I've moved and try to stamp all the nature out."
At the beginning of 2025, Hammond announced that he and his wife Mindy, who share two children, were separating, just three months after his father died of cancer.
It also came around the time of the final Grand Tour episode which brought his 22-year broadcasting career with Jeremy Clarkson and James May to an end.
Since then, he has been rebuilding his life in Wales, and said his energy levels had "been replenished".
"I'm now far braver and do things I would never have done," he said.
He has even joined an Abergavenny running club, bringing his 5k time down to under 25 minutes, and taken up open water swimming in the Lake District as he keeps pace with new girlfriend Keira "Kiki" Glen.
"Basically, she did a triathlon and I went to support her," he told the Telegraph.
"They were all having such a great time and buzzing afterwards, so I signed up for next year and got swept along."
While you would expect that classic cars and motor racing still feature heavily in his life, Hammond is aware that his priorities have shifted.
Rather than attending the Goodwood Revival festival this year, he was sampling cheeses and whiskies at the Abergavenny Food Festival.
Hammond is probably best-known for his time on Top Gear, which was revived in 2002, and went on to become one of the BBC's flagship shows at the time.
But he was unsure whether the formula would work today because it was a "completely different time".
In August, it was announced the show, which has been off air since Andrew "Freddie" Flintoff was seriously injured in a crash while filming four years ago, is coming back.
"The BBC will bring it back because it's an old brand, it predates us by decades," Hammond said.
"The car is the second biggest outlay people have."
Hammond's daughter Izzy has inherited her father's love of cars and the pair now co-present on the social media channel DriveTribe.
Hammond said he was "sure" she would be interested in a role on Top Gear some day.
"It'd be good to see some females on those shows," he said.
"Half the drivers are. TV has a role to play in representation. It's important, nobody's going to step into an arena unless they see somebody that represents them."

title: Chef jailed after filming 'shocking' attack on ex-partner
text:
Chef jailed after filming attack on ex-partner
A chef who threatened to decapitate his ex-partner in a "prolonged and vicious" attack, which he filmed on his mobile phone, has been jailed.
David Thompson, 49, burst into the victim's flat in Harrogate while she was watching television, before stamping on her, hitting her with a stereo unit and smashing a glass vase over her head.
York Crown Court was told the woman, who said she had feared she was going to die, suffered extensive bruising and cuts to her hand and knee, caused by shards from the glass.
Thompson, of The Square, Hillam, was jailed for three years and eight months after admitting attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm.
The court heard how, when Thompson got into the flat, he shouted: "It's a good job I didn't bring my cleaver around or I'd chop your head off right now."
Prosecutor Oliver Norman said he then kicked the woman in the head "with full force" before stamping on her.
The barrister said Thompson then dragged her to the floor and, while she was curled up in a ball, smashed the vase over her head.
Police were called by the woman's neighbours who had heard her screams and "loud crashing sounds".
During the hearing, the court was played footage from his mobile phone in which she was seen pleading with Thompson to leave.
In it, she screamed: "Help me, help me. Stop it please. Please help me somebody."
When officers arrested Thompson, it was evident he had been drinking and had blood on his shorts and trainers.
He initially claimed he had acted in self-defence and said he "should have killed her", the court heard.
'Shocking attack'
The attack happened in June 2024, a year after the pair had split up.
The court was told they were initially on good terms, but when Thompson found a new partner the relationship with his ex had soured.
In a statement read out in court, the victim said during the attack she "closed her eyes believing she was about to die".
She said she had since suffered from severe anxiety and depression and was unable to work.
Defence barrister Oliver Connor said Thompson had mental-health problems and had lived a "law-abiding life" since the attack, continuing to work as a head chef.
Passing sentence, judge Sean Morris described the attack as "shocking".
"What you did was go round to her flat where she was on the bed and you subjected her to a prolonged and vicious attack," he said.
"You threatened to kill her, you kicked and stamped on her head, leaving your own footprint in her flesh."
Thompson, who has a previous conviction from 2016 for battering another former partner, was also given a 10-year restraining order banning him from contacting his victim.
Det Con Rebecca Foster from North Yorkshire Police said: "Domestic abuse can have a devastating and lasting impact on victims. We would like to commend the bravery of the victim in this case, as well as the members of the public who intervened and contacted police when they realised something was wrong.
"We welcome the sentence handed to Thompson and hope it provides the victim with some reassurance as she continues to recover from her ordeal."

title: Married man jailed for grooming 'vulnerable' teenage girl
text:
Man jailed for grooming 'vulnerable' teenage girl
A married man who groomed a "vulnerable" teenage girl for months before booking her into hotels for sex has been jailed for 11 years.
Shoaib Mohammed made contact with the girl on Snapchat when he knew she was 14, then after encouraging her to send sexualised images, arranged for her to leave home in Leicester and meet him in Sheffield, where he took her to hotels for sex.
The 34-year-old, from Sheffield, had pleaded guilty to five counts of sexual activity with a child, one count of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, and three counts of possessing indecent images of a child.
He was sentenced at Leicester Crown Court on Thursday.
The court heard Mohammed knew the victim's age when he began grooming her through electronic communication in 2021, and that he was significantly older than her at the time.
Judge Keith Raynor, sentencing, said the defendant "groomed her and manipulated her" over a period of months.
"The contact was to such a degree that the victim thought that [the defendant] and her were boyfriend and girlfriend," he said.
"You acted as her mentor and confidant, but you also wanted to drive a wedge between her and her friends."
The judge said the victim was "struggling emotionally" at the time and worried about impending GCSE mock exams, which Mohammed was "fully aware of" and exploited.
"At this stage you had one thing on your mind, and it was to abuse her sexually," he said.
Mohammed arranged for the girl to travel from her home in Leicester by train and meet him at Sheffield, after which he drove her to a quiet street in the Manchester area and had sex with her in a car.
They then went to a series of hotels in Sheffield over a number of days, where he repeatedly left her alone for hours while he carried on with his normal life.
In one case a receptionist challenged Mohammed as he tried to book into a room with the victim, which the judge said showed "a great professionalism and absolute sense of duty".
The victim's family reported the girl as missing, which the judge said "must have been one of the most terrible things for a parent to have to do".
Mohammed went into "a panic" when he learned police were searching for the girl, the court heard, and he drove her back to Sheffield railway station, after which she returned to Leicester and her family.
Mohammed was arrested by police soon afterwards, but the court heard he only pleaded guilty to the offences as a trial was set to begin earlier this year, with the case having been listed and relisted numerous times.
As well as a custodial sentence - of which he must serve at least two thirds - he will be on extended licence for three years, and will be subject to a sexual harm prevention order for 15 years.
In a victim impact statement she read out herself in court, the victim said she had been left fearing she was pregnant after the incidents, and now had problems trusting people and making new relationships.
She also said the long delay between the abuse taking place and the sentencing had had a significant impact, but added she was determined to speak out.
"It has been another period of my life spent carrying what happened to me while waiting for justice," she said.
"I'm here for the girls who are too afraid to speak. I'm here for the women who were never believed.
"I'm here for the children who were never given the chance to tell their story."
Her mother also addressed the court, saying hearing about the pain her daughter had suffered was "incredibly difficult" and adding the delayed proceedings have had "a massive impact" on everyone involved.
Judge Raynor said the victim's account was "one of the most impactful statements that I have ever heard in my judicial career", and praised her for speaking "eloquently about the fear she experienced as a 15-year-old".
After telling the court the backlog of cases in England and Wales was between 82,000 and 100,000 cases, he said the delays in this case reflected the "unfortunate state of the criminal justice system".
He also offered commendations to the Leicestershire Police officers leading the investigation for their work over the past five years.
'Years of work'
Following sentencing, Nicola Potts, from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Mohammed "preyed on a young victim while posing as a caring friend and romantic partner", with the defendant's actions delaying the arrival of justice for his victim.
"The evidence that this man groomed and abused the victim in this case was conclusive," she said.
"However, his continued denials have taken years of work to bring him to justice as we built a case that stopped his lies in their tracks."
Det Con Daljinder Gill issued an appeal for "anyone else who may have experienced similar behaviour from Mohammed or who has concerns about contact they have had with him" to get in touch with officers.
"If anything about this case feels familiar to you, please come and speak to us," he said.
"You will be listened to, taken seriously and supported."

title: Poundland staff stage Walsall HQ protest after jobs potentially at risk
text:
Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators
Chants of "save our jobs" filled the air outside the Poundland headquarters as workers protested while the chain edged towards collapse.
The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which will give the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.
On Thursday afternoon, dozens of staff members gathered in Walsall armed with placards bearing a range of messages, including "people before profit" and "Gordon Brothers, 12,000 jobs are not a write off!".
The board of Poundland Limited said it "recognises any sale process creates uncertainty" and thanked staff for their support.
The decision to appoint administrators comes after managing director Barry Williams told the company's 12,000 staff the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.
It is understood the firm's owner, Gordon Brothers, wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.
Kelvin Blake, who attended the demonstration, has worked for Poundland for 25 years and said the announcement had seen morale among the team plummet.
He told the BBC: "I feel like the Gordon brothers have treated us with contempt, as if we don't exist.
"We are the ones that make the money, but we feel like we've been used and abused."
A team leader, who did not want to be identified but has worked for the company for more than a decade, said staff were "really upset" and "saddened" at the announcement.
"We have all worked tremendously hard to save the company, and we've been successful," they said.
"We've turned it around and this is a profit-making business that is not suitable for administration.
"We've completed that turnaround as we set out to do. There are other options, we are successful and there is a way forward.
"We love this company."
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1.
A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.
Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer, leaving it on the brink of collapse.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.
Bally Auluk, national officer for the USDAW union, said: "The government needs to do more to step in, not only to help Poundland but retail going forward.
"How do you put a company that is going from strength to strength into insolvency, saying that it's not fit for purpose? It's one thing only and that's greed. It's totally unacceptable.
"Now you have the potential of these guys here along with thousands of colleagues around the country being out of a job despite their best endeavours to help make this company a success. It's a national scandal."
The company's founder, Steve Smith, started with a market stall in Bilston selling items for £1, with the first Poundland store opening in Burton-upon-Trent in 1990.
Smith sold his shares in the firm for £250m in 2006.
