title: Armed police train for an attack on nuclear shipment from Dounreay
text:
Armed police train for an attack on nuclear shipment from Dounreay
Armed police have for the first time tested a scenario where an attempt is made to attack and steal a shipment of radioactive material being transported from the Dounreay nuclear power plant.
The Civil Nuclear Constabulary exercise involved armed attackers deliberately crashing a car to stop a lorry reaching Georgemas Junction, a railway station about six miles from the plant on the north Caithness coast.
In real-life situations, the station has been used for transporting radioactive material from Dounreay to Sellafield in Cumbria for reprocessing or storage.
The training exercise included an employee at Dounreay, near Thurso, being "arrested" in connection with the attack.
The Civil Nuclear Constabulary (CNC) worked with Police Scotland and other emergency services during the exercise held late last month.
A workshop was also held involving police, Highland Council, Dounreay and the Vulcan Naval Reactor Test Establishment.
Vulcan, which sits next to Doureay, is a military facility used for testing prototype nuclear reactors for submarines.
'Really challenging'
CNC said months of planning went into preparing the exercise.
Exercise and resilience manager Steve Warren said: "This was a scenario that had not been exercised or tested before, meaning we were asking a lot of everyone involved."
Ch Insp Dave McIntosh, of Dounreay's operational policing unit, said the training had placed personnel in "really challenging circumstances".
He added: "I'm very proud of them, they did a really, really good job."
Dounreay was built as an experimental nuclear reactor site in the 1950s and is now in a years-long process of being decommissioned.
description: The Civil Nuclear Constabulary exercise involved a car deliberately crashing into a lorry containing a cargo containing fake radioactive material.

title: Lincolnshire council leaders react to delay in major shake-up
text:
Leaders react to delay in major council overhaul
Council leaders in Lincolnshire have given their reactions after plans to redraw the county's local authority map were put on hold.
An expanded City of Lincoln Council and a Lincolnshire unitary authority had been planned as replacements for the seven existing district councils and Lincolnshire County Council.
But Lincolnshire is among 14 areas where local government reorganisation (LGR) has been halted.
Some council leaders said the news was disappointing but others said it would allow more time for the proposals to be looked at.
The government said on Thursday that other major shake-ups in Derbyshire, Devon, Hertfordshire, Kent, Lancashire, Leicestershire, Nottinghamshire and Staffordshire had also been sent back for further review.
The plans had previously been paused in September after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.
In a Commons statement, Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said the government was "withdrawing the decisions announced in July" for the nine areas.
LGR was due to be the biggest change to the local political scene for a generation, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
Grantham Independent councillor Paul Stokes, deputy leader of South Kesteven District Council, said: "This latest announcement does, at least, allow more time to get LGR right for South Kesteven and Greater Lincolnshire, and will allow the original proposals and the evidence they contained to be looked at again."
But East Lindsey District Council leader Craig Leyland, a Conservative, said: "This unfortunately adds confusion from the disastrous way that LGR has been dealt with by this particular Labour government."
Reform UK's Lincolnshire County Council leader Sean Matthews added: "I'm not surprised if residents are confused about what is happening.
"But while the uncertainty continues in Whitehall, rest assured we're focused on getting on with the day job and delivering services that support our residents, our communities and our county."
Richard Wright, the Conservative leader of North Kesteven District Council, said the announcement was "disappointing".
However, City of Lincoln Council leader Naomi Tweddle, a Labour member, said: "It is encouraging that ministers now want to look again at housing growth, travel-to-work patterns, potential boundary changes and financial sustainability – all areas that our proposal was designed to address in detail."
North and North East Lincolnshire would not have been affected under the LGR shake-up.
Reconfirming local elections in May next year would go ahead based on existing council boundaries, McMahon said plans for elections to shadow councils – set to run for a year before taking over from the current authorities – would now be held in May 2028.

title: What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
text:
What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?
Chancellor John Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have both spoken of their desire for the benefits bill to come down, but the government has not yet laid out a timetable for any reductions.
Their political opponents have criticised them for a lack of detail on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, accusing the government of delaying difficult decisions over cuts.
Official forecasts released alongside the Budget indicate welfare spending is going to increase by £79bn in cash terms over the next few years.
BBC Verify has taken a look at the numbers behind this thorny political issue and some of the difficult options the government have to bring down welfare costs.
How much is being spent on welfare?
The official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates in its latest forecasts that the cost of the welfare system will rise from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2032.
The OBR's figures include spending on pensioners, which accounts for just under half of the total. The majority of this cost is on the state pension.
However, if we look at the size of welfare spending relative to the size of the overall economy the OBR's projections are less dramatic, increasing from 11.1% today to 11.3% of GDP in 2032.
Total welfare spending would also remain below the peak of around 12% of GDP in 2013 following the global financial crisis, leading some economists and researchers to question the idea that welfare spending is out of control.
But there are some welfare costs that are rising rapidly.
Spending on health and disability related benefits, in particular Personal Independence Payments (PIP), is up sharply since the Covid-19 pandemic.
Accounting for inflation, spending on working-age disability benefits increased from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026.
Inflation-adjusted welfare spending remains lower than 2013 because several other working-age benefits, such as Universal Credit and housing benefit, were cut by Conservative-led governments as part of their austerity programme from 2010 onwards.
So spending in some parts of the system has come down while it has risen in others - and there could be a connection.
Some researchers think the post-2010 welfare cuts to benefits might have created an incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead to protect their living standards, therefore shifting costs around the system rather than generating lasting savings.
The problem of Neets
Many also see a specific problem regarding the growing number of young people in the welfare system claiming benefits, including PIP.
Official figures show the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neets) has risen by around 230,000 since 2019 to just under one million.
Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many off benefits and into work.
His interim report in May estimated that annual PIP expenditure on 16 to 24-year-olds rose from £1.3bn in 2020 to around £3.2bn in 2025. It also projected this cost would reach £6.5bn and cover 700,000 young people in five years' time.
PIP claimants can be in work, but official statistics show that only around one in five are.
What could cutting the benefits bill mean?
Politicians are often unclear about what they mean by reducing spending on welfare.
In March 2025, former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer's government presented a plan which it said would save £5bn a year from health-related welfare spending by 2030 by tightening PIP access and reducing the value of health-related Universal Credit payments.
But official forecasts made it clear that annual spending on health-related welfare in cash terms was still set to rise after the reform, just not as rapidly as the path it had previously been on.
However, at the time the OBR did forecast the plans would help put overall UK welfare spending on a "slightly downward trajectory" as a share of the economy over the medium term, rather than remaining flat as had been previously projected.
So this type of relative reduction in anticipated welfare spending, rather than a cut in absolute cash terms, could be what the government seeks to deliver.
Looming reports may offer options
The final Milburn report is expected in the coming weeks, as well as a separate final report from disability minister Stephen Timms into the options for PIP reform.
There has been speculation that these could recommend creating a new welfare system for people under the age of 25, so they are not eligible for PIP and receive lower payments than older people.
There are also suggestions Timms could propose a new PIP eligibility test to reduce access, although he was not specifically instructed to find savings.
Reforms along these lines could potentially make some savings to the welfare bill relative to the existing trajectory of rising spending, as well as reducing forecast welfare spending as share of GDP.
But some analysts argue that to be effective in delivering sustainable savings, such reforms are likely also to require the government to spend a lot more to enable young people in particular to get into and remain in work.
This was signalled by the interim Milburn report which noted that for every £1 the government spends on employment support for young people around £25 is spent on benefits, suggesting he could propose a significant increase in government spending on welfare-to-work schemes.
This means that any welfare savings could, in the near term at least, be offset by additional spending in other departments.
However, in the long term this approach could still deliver welfare savings if the employment support was effective.

title: Man pleads guilty to federal hate crimes charges over fatal Colorado firebombing
text:
Man pleads guilty to federal hate crimes charges over fatal Colorado Molotov cocktail attack
A man who had already been found guilty of firebombing a group of protesters advocating for the release of Israeli hostages in the US state of Colorado has now plead guilty to federal hate crime charges.
Prosecutors said Mohamed Sabry Soliman threw Molotov cocktails at the group of demonstrators in June 2025 - injuring at least 12 people, one of whom died.
He plead guilty in May to 101 state charges, including first-degree murder - resulting in a sentence of life in prison - but initially pleaded not guilty in the federal case.
Prosecutors want Soliman to be sentenced to life in prison plus 50 years over the federal charges, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He is due to be sentenced in January.
United States Attorney Peter McNeilly said the sentencing recommendation was driven by what the victims wanted.
In light of the plea, McNeilly said Soliman had dropped motions seeking to keep his family from being deported from the US in case they needed to be witnesses in his case.
Authorities said Soliman planned the attack for a year, watching videos on explosives before driving from his home in Colorado Springs to the Boulder protest.
While he hurled the Molotov cocktails at the crowd on 1 June, 2025, he shouted "Free Palestine". The group were members of Run for Their Lives in Colorado, which met weekly to support the release of Israeli hostages taken by Hamas during the 7 October attacks.
Karen Diamond, 82, died from injuries caused by the attack three weeks later. Her family said her husband, Lou, was also severely burned and had to recover for a month in a hospital burn unit.
Soliman, an Egyptian national, told police after he was arrested that he wanted to "kill all Zionist people", according to court documents.
He came to California in 2022 on a non-immigrant visa that expired in February 2023, according to CBS.
The firebombing escalated concerns about antisemitic violence in the US, taking place shortly after a fatal shooting outside a Jewish centre in Washington DC.

title: Boy who lost four fingers in firework blast issues Bonfire Night warning
text:
Boy who lost four fingers in firework blast issues Bonfire Night warning
A schoolboy who lost four fingers after a firework went off in his hand has warned other youngsters not to mess about with pyrotechnics ahead of Bonfire Night.
Riley Luke was eight years old when he and a group of friends found the discarded firework near their homes in Paisley, Renfrewshire.
They were handing it around and trying to light it when it exploded in Riley's hand.
Riley, who is now 12, was left with devastating injuries that led to him spending two weeks in an induced coma in hospital.
In the run-up to this year's Bonfire Night, the youngster has urged others to be careful around fireworks.
"Just think before you do it," he said.
"Let your parents do it instead of you so you don't lose any of your fingers, hurt yourself, end up in hospital or lose an eye."
His father Scott told how the youngsters had been tossing the firework to each other on waste ground when the accident happened.
He said: "Eventually, Riley was holding it and when it lit, it stuck to his hand.
"He was trying to get it off his hand and then within seconds it exploded, which resulted in losing four of his fingers and a good part of his palm.
"His thumb was blasted back to his wrist, part of his hand wasn't there and he had fingers missing."
Riley was taken by ambulance to the Royal Hospital for Children in Glasgow where he was in surgery for 14 hours.
He then spent around two weeks in an induced coma in intensive care with his hand stitched to his groin to restore blood flow.
He was released from hospital just a few days before Christmas.
Learning to write again
After returning home, Riley had to learn to write with his left hand and needed help putting his clothes on and cutting his food.
He said: "I had to get my teacher to help me write. I thought about writing with my left hand one day and then I just got, like, better and better at it.
"I was colouring in with pencils in the hospital and that was building my hand strength up."
Four years on, he still finds tasks like tying shoelaces and fastening buttons difficult.
However, his father says he has not let it stop him from joining in on activities.
"He's head-strong, he doesn't hold back. He still goes and plays on the scooters, bikes, just anything that a wee boy does, he does too," Scott said.
"It's just a wee bit challenging."
'Consider the risks'
On Bonfire Night last year, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said it received a total of 751 calls between 15:30 and midnight, and fire crews attended more than 250 bonfires.
Deputy assistant chief officer Ian McMeekin, who is head of prevention at SFRS, said Riley's experience was "a stark reminder of the devastating injuries fireworks can cause".
He added: "Fireworks are explosives and are incredibly dangerous if they've not been handled safely by an adult.
"We want to prevent fires, accidents and injuries from occurring in the first place.
"If you're planning on hosting a private event involving fireworks, consider the risks and always follow the Firework Code to keep everyone safe.
"Our community action teams across Scotland have been engaging with local schools to ensure pupils are aware of the dangers that bonfires and fireworks pose, and they will continue working with our partners to promote safety messaging."

title: South East local government reorganisation clarified
text:
South East council reorganisation plans clarified
The south east of England has been given clarity over local government reorganisation (LGR) plans before final decisions are made.
A two unitary council proposal for East Sussex and Brighton, excluding Falmer, is being taken forward, while West Sussex remains awaiting a decision and plans in Surrey are unaffected.
A plan, which would have seen all 14 Kent councils replaced by four larger unitary authorities, has now been withdrawn, though the government has stressed LGR is not cancelled.
Local government minister Jim McMahon told the House of Commons on Thursday "every area will have an outcome by early next year".
The plans have been controversial in Sussex from the start, with East Sussex County Council launching a legal challenge in protest and other local authorities considering the same.
It has now been confirmed East Saltdean, Peacehaven and Telscombe will be absorbed into Brighton and Hove City Council (BHCC), with Falmer remaining under East Sussex County Council control.
BHCC leader Bella Sankey said: "Bringing our communities together reflects how people live and it will give residents living to the east of our current boundary greater say over the services they already use."
However, Lewes District Council leader Zoe Nicholson said: "We are shocked and deeply disappointed by the government's decision to press ahead with proposals that our residents have resoundingly rejected."
Elections for the new-look councils will take place in May 2028.
The lack of decision in West Sussex has been described as "frustrating" by Chichester District Council leader Adrian Moss, who welcomes the proposed launch date being pushed back until 2029.
He says councils across West Sussex "have worked closely together to explore the opportunities and challenges presented by local government reorganisation" for more than a year and will be ready when a decision is made.
Worthing Borough Council leader Caroline Baxter says the ongoing review will "ensure that any decision in our area is given the time and consideration it deserves".
Separate from LGR, the first election for a mayor of Sussex and Brighton is still scheduled for May 2028.
Maidstone Borough Council leader Stuart Jeffery described the delay in Kent as "deeply frustrating", according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
The government also said it could not confirm yet if the county would be getting a mayor.
Both Medway Council leader Vince Maple and Kent County Council leader Linden Kemkaran welcomed the prospect, which remained at an embryonic stage.
While Surrey is unaffected by the latest LGR development, mayoral plans are not yet finalised.
A proposed agreement for Surrey to get an elected mayor was set out in the Budget, and Woking and Surrey Heath MPs, Will Forster and Al Pinkerton respectively, were pushing for consultation on Thursday.
McMahon said a consultation would take place "probably around December".

title: Gateshead dad who shook baby has jail term increased
text:
Dad who shook baby has jail term increased
A father who left his baby son permanently disabled after shaking him has had his jail term increased from four to six years.
Christopher Yates had consumed cocaine and 11 pints of lager before he shook his six-month-old son with the force of a "high velocity car accident," causing severe brain injury, blindness and a likely inability to learn to walk.
The 30-year-old from Gateshead admitted causing a child to suffer serious physical harm and was jailed for four years at Newcastle Crown Court in July, but the Solicitor General referred the sentence to the Court of Appeal.
Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr said: "The sentence imposed by the judge was not only lenient but unduly so."
Gemma White, for the Solicitor General, said Yates shook the baby five times, while yelling at him to shut up on 5 October 2025, but did not contact medics until six hours later when he claimed the child had fallen from a chair.
'Catastrophic injury'
The court heard Yates gained custody three weeks before the incident after the baby had been taken from his mother into foster care.
Family members were concerned Yates was not being supported by professionals and became easily frustrated with the child, the court heard.
Their concerns included him not clothing the child properly and his flat being a "mess" strewn with dirty nappies and empty alcohol cans.
White told the court the sentencing judge had not properly reflected the level of harm caused to the baby and had reduced the sentence too much to reflect Yates' ADHD, autism, depressive disorder and traumatic upbringing.
She said: "There was very significant use of force against a six-month-old baby which resulted in catastrophic injury."
'Red flags'
Rachel Hedworth, for Yates, said the sentencing judge had rightly reduced the sentence to reflect his mental disorder.
She said Yates had only discovered he was a father through a paternity test after the baby's birth, but had "put himself in the ring" to be the sole carer of the boy.
She said the baby was given to him despite authorities being aware he had been "self-medicating" with alcohol for "over half his life".
Hedworth said despite his family highlighting these "red flags", he received "very little" assistance from professionals.
She said: "Had his behaviour and his care of that child been monitored at a much earlier stage, then perhaps with some more advice and guidance he may have been helped."

title: Stockton Council to vote £13m Billingham town centre purchase
text:
Councillors to vote on purchase of town centre
A final decision on a proposed £13m purchase of a town centre will be put before councillors next week.
Members of Stockton's Labour-run cabinet will decide on 4 November whether or not to acquire the town centre from current owners Sheet Anchor Evolve.
The initial purchase and other works would be funded by a £20m grant which was approved by the previous Conservative government in 2023 and later confirmed by the current Labour administration.
Papers outline that, since 2008, the centre has had four private sector owners, "none of whom have invested in the asset", with the current owner indicating that it isn't planning "major repair and improvement works".
Speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, cabinet member for resources and regeneration Councillor Paul Rowling described the existing area as "quite run down".
Funding for the purchase needs to be spent by March 2028 and cabinet members will only be voting on phase one next week.
That would see the council take full control of the centre, carry out some repairs and demolish the vacant Queensway South building and the former library.
Rowling said the council's working valuation of the town centre is £10.75m and the cabinet will have to decide whether it can justify paying the higher asking price.
He said Billingham had been exposed to wider challenges facing high streets nationally, but previous owners "haven't helped much".

title: More than 100 jobs under threat at military safety gear factory
text:
More than 100 jobs under threat at military safety gear factory
More than 100 jobs are at risk at a Scottish factory which manufactures safety equipment for the military.
Gentex has announced proposals to close its plant at Stranraer where 111 people are employed and to make "changes" at its Letchworth site in Hertfordshire.
It said the move was part of plans to centralise its UK operations in a new facility in Haydock, Merseyside.
The firm said no final decision had been made but eligible employees would be paid until the end of next year - even if they are made redundant earlier.
Local MSP Finlay Carson said the loss of 111 highly-skilled jobs in the area was "hugely significant".
"This is not simply another company restructuring," he added. "It represents one of the largest private sector job losses our area has faced in recent years."
He called for an urgent, co-ordinated response from the Scottish government, Dumfries and Galloway Council and agencies including South of Scotland Enterprise.
He said: "We must use the time available to ensure affected workers are supported into new opportunities and that every effort is made to attract replacement investment to the area."
The Scottish government's Business and Fair Work Minister Tom Arthur, described the possible job losses as "deeply concerning" and said they would have a significant impact on the local community.
He said: "I spoke with Gentex this afternoon to better understand the reasons for this decision and to encourage the company to engage with South of Scotland Enterprise to explore any options to help the site remain open.
"The individuals affected by this announcement are our immediate priority. Should there be job losses, the Scottish government's PACE team stands ready to offer their full support to staff if any redundancies proceed."
Gentex produces safety equipment like helmets, headsets, visors and oxygen masks for the military, law enforcement and other industries.
The factory has a long history in the town, where it was previously owned by Top Tek, which manufactured helmets for Kangol.
From 1983, it was operated by Helmet Integrated Systems Ltd (HISL) before being acquired by Gentex in 2014.
The news was broken to staff at Stranraer and Letchworth earlier.
Andrew Wilde, senior director of operations at Gentex, said: "Our long-term European growth opportunities and customer needs are outpacing our current UK facilities, so we have conducted a detailed review into how we grow our operations."
He said they proposed consolidating their UK activities at Haydock, subject to a formal consultation process.
He added: "If the proposal proceeds, this would result in the closure of our Stranraer facility and changes at Letchworth, with a number of roles at risk of redundancy. The proposed transition would take place in phases over the next two years.
"We know how hard this news is for our colleagues in the UK and their families, and it's no reflection on them or their work. We're committed to protecting the pay of eligible affected employees through at least the end of 2027."
description: Gentex announces proposals to close its site in Stranraer, where 111 people are employed.

title: Wettest week for two years during named storms
text:
Wettest week for two years after named storms
England had its wettest week for two years, due to heavy rain from two named storms, Austen and Boelo.
The Environment Agency said the period between 20 to 27 October was the wettest week since October 2024.
A daily average of 55mm of rain fell across England in the seven days with as much as 87mm in the South West.
Much of the country remains officially in drought, with a severe drought in place across parts of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex.
The downpours meant England has now received 11% more rainfall than the long-term average for October, according to the Environment Agency.
River levels have increased at all but two of the sites the agency monitors.

title: Adur and Worthing Councils forecast £2.3m homelessness overspend
text:
Councils forecast £2.3m homelessness overspend
Homelessness and temporary accommodation is expected to cost two councils in West Sussex more than £2m over budget between them for 2026-27.
Budget monitoring figures projected overspends of £1.5m at Worthing Borough Council (WBC) and £760,000 at Adur District Council, with both identifying homelessness as a major pressure on their finances, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
The figures have been highlighted in a report which is set to be discussed by the councils' joint overview and scrutiny committee on 4 November.
Councillors have questioned when the overspending can be reduced and how, the report says.
Across all council services, the report showed WBC overspent by about £3.8m, while ADC spent £385,000 less than budgeted in 2025-26.
It said Adur benefited from tighter spending controls and Worthing was supported by an estimated £4.8m in exceptional funding from the government which, when added to the total budget, showed as an underspend.
Worthing is expected to use £3.7m of this support in 2026-27 and Adur is expected to have an overall underspend of £1.9m, according to its budget forecast.
Councillors also asked officers on the committee about the possible impact of changes to renters' rights legislation and additional government funding to help tackle rough sleeping, the report said.
It came after Chancellor John Healey announced a further £430m to help people sleeping rough in the 2026 Budget, saying it would help keep the government's offer of a route off the streets open for the rest of the current parliament.
A finance working group from the councils is continuing to look at their spending and plans for next year's budget, the report says.
It is due to report back to the joint committee in January 2027.
Both councils have been approached for comment.

title: Fish farm feed barge sinks in Loch Torridon following Storm Boelo
text:
Fish farm feed barge sinks in Loch Torridon following Storm Boelo
A feed barge sank at a fish farm in a Highland loch on Sunday following Storm Boelo.
Salmon firm Bakkafrost Scotland said no-one was hurt and all the fish pens at its Sgeir Dughall site in Loch Torridon remained intact.
The company said it was assessing the condition of the barge and its contents, and was considering the safest way to recover the boat, which was carrying food for farmed salmon.
A spokesperson said: "Protecting the surrounding marine environment is a priority, and we want to ensure that any recovery work is carried out safely and with minimal impact."
The spokesperson said the barge sank following a weekend of severe weather.
They added: "At this stage our focus is on completing the assessments and working with the relevant authorities and specialist contractors."
HM Coastguard said it was notified of the sinking on Tuesday morning.
A spokesperson said: "No-one was reported to be in distress and the Maritime and Coastguard Agency's counter pollution and salvage team was notified.
"The site is being monitored and no significant pollution has been reported."
Storm Boelo brought damaging high winds and rain and the Met Office issued an amber severe weather warning for most of Scotland from 21:00 on Saturday to 21:00 on Sunday.

title: Hundreds of GP surgeries lose online services after Silicon Practice collapse
text:
Hundreds of GP practices lose online services after collapse of tech firm
Patients in many parts of the country have been left unable to access their GP surgery online after a tech firm went into administration.
Silicon Practice ran digital services, including websites, online booking and consultations, for around 500 practices in England – just under 10% of the total.
Practices across the country, including in London, Gloucestershire and Norfolk, have reported problems. Services in Wales are also affected.
GP leaders said the problem would cause huge disruption, given the scale of online booking that now takes places.
Patients in areas that are affected are being advised they will have to make appointments via the phone. The NHS app is working.
Since last year, all practices in England have had to offer online appointment booking. Currently, more than 40% of appointments are made that way.
An NHS England spokesperson said while "the majority" of GP practice websites were running as normal, some using Silicon Practice will be affected.
"If your GP practice website is unavailable and you need help, you should contact your practice by phone or in person as usual."
'Hugely disruptive'
Affected practices have been contacted by NHS England with advice on how to maintain business continuity and minimise the impact on patient care.
Silicon Practice ran the digital tool FootFall, which it advertised as reducing patient phone calls to practices by 30%, by working to "free your reception team from routine admin and manage demand more efficiently. Proven in 1,000+ GP practices across the UK".
Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs, said: "GP practice websites are an increasingly important way for patients to access care, book appointments and find information about the services available to them.
"When websites are not working, it can be hugely disruptive for patients and place additional pressures on already stretched practice teams.
"It is vital that any disruption to practice websites is addressed promptly to ensure patients are able to access care."
She said affected practices must receive prompt, practical support from NHS England and local NHS organisations to restore their websites, minimise disruption and ensure patients know how to contact their practice and access the care they need in the meantime.

title: Ballots cast in Onchan House of Keys election to be recounted
text:
Ballots cast in election to be recounted
The high court in the Isle of Man is set to order a full recount of the ballots for one constituency in the recent House of Keys general election.
It follows a petition to the court by former Onchan MHK Julie Edge, who lost her seat in September's contest, after figures showed 79 ballots were unaccounted for.
The petition calls for the court to declare the election void, which would lead to a new election being held.
At a hearing at Douglas Courthouse, First Deemster Andrew Corlett called the situation "very unprecedented" pointing out the court had not dealt with an election petition before, and the recount would take place first with the rest of the petition dealt with afterwards.
In her petition, Edge said while it would not have changed the candidates elected, the "fact that ballot papers verified at the count are not accounted for calls the integrity of the count into question".
During the hearing, Attorney General Walter Wannenburgh stressed that it was an application "that does not rely on in any way a suggestion of corrupt or illegal practices".
Representing deputy returning officer for the count, advocate Jeremy Callin, Kathryn Clough said a recount would be a "sensible way" dealing with issues with some of the figures.
As well as the unaccounted ballot papers, the petition alleges the Notice of Result misstates the number of voters whose papers were not rejected.
In addition, reasons for the rejection of ballot papers do not match, a ballot count for a polling station was altered without date or recorded explanation, and candidates were not given reasonable opportunity to ask for a recount before the result was declared.
It also alleges postal ballots were opened without Edge or her agents present.
It argues that taken together "the election was not so conducted as to be substantially in accordance with the law".
The deemster said the recount would take place in a courtroom at the Isle of Man Courts of Justice in Douglas, but would most likely have to be done outside of normal working hours as the courts were "exceptionally busy" during the day.
The count will be carried out by Callin and his team and Edge and the other candidates who stood in the election will be allowed to observe along with members of the media, with the process overseen by chief registrar Stuart Clague.
A final order outlining the details governing the recount will now be agreed by both parties and the deemster before it takes place.

title: Bristol former boxing chief looks back on life as he turns 90
text:
Ex-boxing chief looks back on life at age of 90
"Being the son of a rag-and-bone man, I had to pinch myself being among all these superstars," says 90-year-old Fred Little, who enjoyed a remarkable career overseeing some of the biggest nights in professional boxing.
As well as being brought into contact with the likes of Tyson Fury, Frank Bruno and Ricky Hatton, Fred, originally from Barton Hill, Bristol, also worked in security for big stars such as Tom Jones.
As a boxing inspector, overseeing safety, regulations and medical standards, one of his standout memories came in Las Vegas, where he watched Roy Jones Jr take on Antonio Tarver in an atmosphere he described as "unbelievable".
Now, as he celebrates his 90th birthday, Fred is reflecting on a remarkable life that has taken him from wartime Bristol to top-flight boxing.
In his early life, Fred remembers his early childhood spent during the horror of World War Two. "We used to run down the street with airplanes on fire and bombs hitting houses," he said.
"We'd go to a communal air raid shelter and everyone's crying and screaming, it was terrible."
When Fred grew up, he became a welder, working on oil rigs around the world, including the Piper Alpha platform off Aberdeen shortly before the 1988 disaster in which 167 people died.
"I was inconsolable," he said of the loss of life. "I knew quite a lot of those blokes."
His career also took him across the United States, where he spent five years coaching football after leading a team from St Pauls in Bristol to victory in a soccer tournament.
'Most amazing life'
But it was boxing that brought him into contact with some of the sport's biggest names. Rising up to chief inspector for the British Boxing Board of Control, Fred oversaw everything from gloves and ring preparations to security, safety and ambulance provisions.
Fred also worked as security for entertainers including Shirley Bassey and UB40. He says one memorable encounter saw singer Elaine Paige dedicate a performance of the song Memories to him.
Looking back, he said: "I've had the most amazing life, I've done everything you can think of."
His daughter, Charlotte Maggs, said: "He is a very familiar face around Bristol and is hugely respected within the community and by the many people he has met throughout his life."
She added: "Over the years, he has battled numerous health problems, including suffering a cardiac arrest, which left our family fearing that we had nearly lost him."
And Fred's final wish is simple. He said: "When I'm gone, on my headstone just put: 'I have lived'."

title: Driver who killed man in Cudworth grass cutting row jailed
text:
Driver who killed man in grass cutting row jailed
A driver who ran down and killed a man during a grass cutting dispute has been jailed for nine years.
Mark Wigley, 60, hit 45-year-old Liam Green in a VW Touareg on Rose Tree Avenue in Cudworth, near Barnsley, at about 17:00 BST on 3 April.
Following a trial at Sheffield Crown Court, he was cleared of murder but convicted of manslaughter, while his daughter, Sarah Wigley, 39, and brother-in-law, Neil Shaw, 54, were cleared of all charges.
At a hearing earlier, Judge Graham Reeds KC told Wigley, of Royston Road, Cudworth: "It is a case where you used your car as a weapon and intended to hit him and cause some injury."
The dispute started after Green went knocking on doors offering to cut people's grass and came to the house of Mark Wigley's mother.
She became upset that Green had offered her the service for a £7.50 fee and sent images from her Ring doorbell camera to her family, who believed she was being harassed.
The court previously heard that Green had struggled with addiction.
The trio found Green after about 30 minutes, with Shaw driving a Ford Ranger to the scene, while Mark Wigley was driving the VW and Sarah was his passenger.
Judge Reeds said: "It is a mark of the breathtaking arrogance of you and your daughter, and the family members who referred to him in derogatory terms, that you collectively made no inquiry into why he was calling at pensioners' bungalows and just assumed that he was a drug user who was pestering older people for money.
"He was not, but that didn't stop you."
Joe Stone KC, for Wigley, said his client had asked his daughter Sarah to call 999 immediately after the incident, did not attempt to flee and did not drive over Green after the initial collision.
He said: "This is an accident that has happened almost spontaneously and has had devastating consequences for multiple parties."
Stone said there had been three witnesses who described Wigley's "shock and surprise".
"This is not a man who has just no previous convictions, he is someone with a whole raft of witnesses behind him that can testify to the type of man he is," he said.
"He has led an honest and industrious life to date."
In addition to his prison sentence, Wigley will be banned from driving for five years after his release.
'Good man'
The judge told him: "Liam Green's mother accepts that her son was no angel, but one thing the evidence in this case clearly demonstrated is that, regardless of what he might have done in his past, on this occasion he was doing nothing more than going to neighbours on the estate where his mum lived and trying to get work cutting the grass."
Laurie Hilton, Green's mother, spoke through tears about her son who "had only wanted to help neighbours with their garden".
She said that following his death, she struggled to go to the shops and could no longer eat chocolate or cheese, and onion on toast because it reminded her too much of him.
"I miss his phone calls of a night and I would say a big hug from mam and he would say a big hug from Liam," she said.
"He was a real mammy's boy."
Hilton added: "I will never see him again until I join him.
"Sometimes I pray for that day to come sooner. I am so miserable."
Shane Green, his brother, wrote in a statement that the impact on his family had been "unimaginable", while Green's ex-partner, Sally Wilkinson, with whom he had a son, described him as "a good man with a big heart and lots of love to give".

title: What the future holds for Oxfordshire and West Berkshire councils
text:
All change for Oxfordshire and West Berkshire councils
Hot on the heels of plans for a new Thames Valley mayor, the government has now approved proposals to scrap a number of Oxfordshire and Berkshire councils.
It means the authority you pay your council tax bill to and whose refuse collectors take your rubbish away may change from the one you are currently used to.
The government has said this will save money and improve services for residents.
Some council have also welcomed the proposed changes, which would see three new unitary authorities created, but others have called the decision "a disaster".
A unitary is a single tier of local government that handles all local public services, instead of splitting duties between two levels.
What will change?
Let's start with West Berkshire Council and two of its near neighbours.
The Berkshire council will cease to exist, as will the Vale of White Horse and South Oxfordshire councils, all three merging to create one new authority, Ridgeway Council.
Jeff Brooks is the leader of West Berkshire Council, and he believes having a bigger organisation will help everyone.
"We don't want to be a huge council but we're not the right size," he said.
"We'll now have bigger departments appropriately sized, and they'll have more capacity. That's a major step forward for our residents."
A new Greater Oxford
In Oxford the existing city council area will expand, both in terms of geography and power.
It will absorb areas like Kidlington, Wheatley and Berinsfield, bringing the population up to 240,000 people.
Susan Brown, who is the leader of the existing Oxford City Council, said the plan was about "building the homes we desperately need for residents".
"This is the best way of doing that, building them near the city, where people want to be, the homes are sustainable and the jobs are there to support people," she said.
A new Northern Oxfordshire Council
With 265,000 people, the Northern Oxfordshire Council will cover most of the old Cherwell and west Oxfordshire patch, excluding the villages now in the Greater Oxford area.
The government says the councils and their local MPs will now have approximately three weeks to digest the news and confirm they want to go ahead with the proposals.
Under the changes Oxfordshire County Council would be scrapped, and its leader Tim Bearder is critical of the plan.
"Services we currently provide across the whole county will now be split into three," he said.
"Anybody can see that increases costs and complexity which is the opposite aim to what local government reorganisation was meant to do."
He said he and his colleagues were considering their next move, which could involve legal action.
If the plans are agreed then elections for the new authorities would take place in 2028 with the new councils coming into being a year later.

title: Lib Dems and Reform in war of words over alleged shove
text:
Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.
The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.
Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.
The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".
The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."
Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.
However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph.
The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.
Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.
In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.
"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.
"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."
Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."
Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."
The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.
In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.
"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.
A spokesperson for the House of Commons said that a prayer card for Farage - the way in which MPs reserve seats in the Commons - did not "display a valid date stamp" and therefore "was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol".

title: Met refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan letter
text:
Met refers itself to police watchdog over letter about Meghan's father
The Metropolitan Police has referred itself to the police complaints watchdog over its handling of a letter with allegations against Thomas Markle, which was handed to his daughter, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019.
The letter, written by Markle's first wife Roslyn Loveless, is believed to have contained claims about Meghan's father.
Markle has strongly denied recent allegations that he had possessed images of child abuse, describing them as "sick lies".
The force said it had voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) "in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex".
The Met added that it intended to make further referrals to "relevant overseas law enforcement agencies", a process which it expected to be completed "in the coming days".
The letter that will be considered by the IOPC was sent to the Met's royal protection team by Roslyn Loveless, who divorced Thomas Markle in 1975 and died in 2024.
The handwritten letter was then passed to Meghan in January 2019, with the duchess saying last week that it had "made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father".
Meghan did not provide any details but said it had given her sufficient reason to not visit Thomas Markle and not allow him to meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lilibet.
Scotland Yard said the letter contained claims about offending outside the UK and that it had been forwarded to "the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness".
Confirming that it had referred itself to the IOPC, the Metropolitan Police said it was aware of media reports that it had try to obtain a copy of the letter.
"While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom," it said.
It added that the Met has carried out an initial review in recent days which has led to the voluntary referral to IOPC.
The watchdog will consider why the Met did not share the contents of the letter with other law enforcement agencies, in the UK or overseas, given that it contained claims of alleged offences.
There are also reports that the Met did not keep a copy of the letter and had to get one from the Sussexes.
Meghan said in a statement last week that she believed the allegations in the letter "were being investigated".
But the watchdog will have to consider what happened to the warnings.
There are also likely to be questions about what royal officials knew about the letter, which was sent when Meghan was still a working royal and which was forwarded to the Sussexes' office rather than to her personally.
Jim Gamble, former head of the Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre, previously told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he would have expected the police to have shared any warnings.
"If you get information that comes to you about someone from a foreign jurisdiction who represents a threat to children, there's a well-worn path and generally you'd expect a UK police force to share that information," said Gamble.
"I would have expected the Metropolitan Police to have gone to the FBI to say: 'Look, this isn't proven, it's an allegation, you might want to look at it'."
Noel Rasmussen, Thomas Markle's granddaughter and niece of the Duchess of Sussex, told the BBC that she was "deeply troubled by the questions surrounding the Metropolitan Police's handling of the information it received".
"If allegations of this seriousness were brought to the attention of authorities, it is reasonable to ask what steps were taken, why the information was not shared with other law enforcement agencies," she said.
"I believe those questions deserve clear, transparent answers."
Reports of the Met's handling of the letter emerged as Thomas Markle's son had told police in the Philippines about material that was alleged to contain sexual images of children he claimed to have found in possessions belonging to Meghan's father.
Thomas Markle had been in the Philippines in December 2025, undergoing hospital treatment, when Meghan wrote to him to end all contact.
Authorities in the Philippines have begun investigating the claims.
Philippine Police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from Markle's former home.
Four boxes of material - including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes - were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week.
However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr has strongly denied all the allegations against him. He has been backed by his daughter Samantha, who has dismissed the claims against her father as "fake".
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

title: Worcester content creator describes life-changing impact of stroke at 22
text:
'I had a stroke after a ride on a rollercoaster'
Up until spring 2025, the life of content creator and PR executive Saskia Bishop was a glamorous whirlwind.
When she was not unboxing beauty products on social media, she could be found enjoying herself at gigs or jetting off to Paris with her friends for the city's fashion week.
That all changed on 21 April last year, when the then-22-year-old fell ill with a terrible headache after getting off a rollercoaster at a theme park in Southend, Essex.
"I just got this massive sharp bang in my head. It was like a bomb had gone off," said Saskia, who lives between Worcester and Gloucester.
"I was in so much pain that I couldn't tell my parents what was going on with me."
Saskia was having a stroke - specifically, a brain bleed caused by a ruptured arteriovenous malformation, an abnormal cluster of blood vessels connecting arteries and veins.
She lost the ability to speak, began to vomit violently and became disoriented, as her dad Scott called for an ambulance to take her to hospital.
After time in intensive care and a 7.5-hour operation, she had to spend many months recovering.
It would be a month before she could speak at all and another three before she could hold a conversation, while she also had to learn to walk again.
About 18 months later, the 23-year-old said she remembered the whole experience from the second it started.
She recalled an "extreme amount of pain" and being very confused, adding: "I didn't know what was going on and I couldn't speak. I think I was most confused about that."
Scott said he was unsure Saskia would survive and described it as the "most haunting" experience of his life.
"Some of the emotions and feelings will stay with me forever," he added, though he said he now felt a deep sense of gratitude and relief for her recovery.
Saskia barely left the house for nine months and initially struggled to come to terms with how much her life had changed.
"I was very busy all the time, being your typical 22-year-old girl, and then within a second, I was immediately isolated from normal life," she said.
"That was really difficult, to be by myself all the time."
As well as suffering with neurological fatigue, Saskia said she developed a form of obsessive compulsive disorder and became sensitive to loud noises and bright lights.
"The smallest things will immediately zap your energy," she added. "Even having conversations were completely tiring me out.
"People just don't understand it and a lot of people who have spent a lot of time with me still don't understand it."
But along with support from friends and family, she said connecting with other people who had been through similar situations helped her to get through it.
"That really changed my recovery to make me realise I'm not alone," Saskia added.
Her story will be among those told on the Channel 4 documentary Trauma: My Broken Brain, due to air at 22:00 GMT on Monday.
She said doing the show was "very cathartic" and she wanted to help other young people with similar health problems.
"Everything I do will hopefully improve the world for young stroke survivors or people who have had a massive life shift in a split second," she said.
"It leaves you in a bit of an identity crisis, you're kind of lost."
Asked if she had any advice for those going through similar experiences, she urged them to stop comparing themselves to "who they were before".
"You'll see so much more progress because you're never going to be the person you were before and that's OK," Saskia added.
"You've had a massive life-changing event and that applies to anyone else who has had a serious life trauma that changes you over night."
Signs of a stroke
The NHS says the main symptoms of a stroke can happen suddenly and are remembered using the acronym FAST:
- Face: One side of the face may droop and it may be difficult to smile
- Arms: Weakness or numbness may make it hard to raise both arms and keep them there
- Speech: Speech may become slurred or confused
- Time: Call 999 immediately if you think someone is having a stroke

title: Men jailed for 'brutal' Fraserburgh street attack
text:
Men jailed for 'brutal' Aberdeenshire street attack
Three men have been jailed for what a judge described as a "brutal" street attack in an Aberdeenshire town.
Ewan McIntosh was beaten with a pole, kicked and punched during the assault in Fraserburgh in February 2023.
Connor Smith, 23, was convicted of attempted murder, while Bobby Hendry, 36, and Brandon Noble, 20, were convicted of assault to severe injury, permanent disfigurement and danger to life.
At the High Court in Edinburgh, Smith was jailed for five years, Hendry for five-and-a-half years and Noble for two years and eight months.
Lady Drummond told Hendry that he was significantly older than the other two accused and had a lengthy criminal record.
The younger pair of attackers were teenagers at the time.
The offence happened at Gallowhill Road, Viewfield Road, Queen Mary Street and Gray Street when the victim was pursued and attacked.
The judge said the victim suffered serious injuries as well as the attack having a psychological impact.
She said: "It was a sustained and brutal attack on the public streets of Fraserburgh."
She ordered that Hendry should be under supervision in the community for a further three years after his release.

title: Plans for north and south Derbyshire councils withdrawn
text:
North and south Derbyshire councils plan withdrawn
Plans for a major shake-up of local councils in Derbyshire have been withdrawn by the government.
On Thursday, ministers said plans to create a north and south council in Derbyshire - which they had previously given the green light - would now be reconsidered along with several other areas, including Nottinghamshire and Leicestershire.
Amber Valley leaders had recently started the process of a legal challenge against the plans, which would have controversially involved splitting the borough between the two new unitary authorities.
The government said every area would have an outcome by early next year and "all options remain under consideration".
Local elections will go ahead in May on existing council boundaries.
It is hoped the new councils will be established for 2029, with elections to shadow councils in May 2028.
Local government minister Jim McMahon told MPs the government was still committed to the process of local government reorganisation (LGR), but that it had listened to local political leaders.
The Reform UK leader of Derbyshire County Council, Alan Graves, said officials would be using the time to restart efforts to lobby the government for the county's preferred proposal.
"We welcome the additional time this provides to engage with government on our preferred option for uniting Derbyshire served by a single local authority," he said.
"This has consistently been the county council's preferred approach because it provides the strongest foundation for sustainable, high-quality services, delivers the greatest benefits from reorganisation, and avoids the disruption that would result from breaking up services that currently operate across the county.
"We will continue to work constructively with the government and our local authority partners as the new timescales are developed and the options are reappraised."
The leader of the Derby Conservatives, Steve Hassall, said the idea of local council reorganisation needed to be scrapped altogether, criticising the government's "indecision".
"It was never a good policy in the first place, and the fact that they cannot proceed with it as it was just demonstrates how poor it was," he said.
"What they do need to do is just resign this poor decision to the dustbin. Nobody wants it, it clearly can't work. The government just need to get a grip."
While Derby city and the majority of district and borough councils elsewhere in the county had been supportive of the north and south council plan, Amber Valley recently started the first formal step towards a potential legal challenge over the government's paused plans for LGR.
Under the plans, parts of Amber Valley in the northern council would include Aldercar and Langley Mill, Alderwasley, Alfreton, Dethick, Lea and Holloway, Hazelwood, Heanor and Loscoe, Ripley and South Wingfield.
Meanwhile, areas which would join the southern council include Belper, Denby, Duffield, Holbrook, Kilburn, Kirk Langley, Mackworth, Mapperley, Quarndon, Shipley and Smalley.
The Labour leader there, Chris Emmas-Williams, said he welcomed the government's withdrawal of its decision.
"Our position has consistently been that this was the wrong decision for our borough and its communities," he said.
"We look forward to further clarity from the government on the next steps and timetable for a new decision, to help our residents and employees understand what happens next.
"In the meantime, our focus remains on delivering the day-to-day services our residents rely on, which continue as normal."
Speaking to the BBC on a visit to Rolls-Royce in Derby on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he accepted the decision to withdraw the plans was "frustrating" for local leaders.
"There's definitely been a situation where people have put a lot of time into it and we haven't yet got the result that we need," he said.
"What I would say though is it's about better services in the long run.
"If you go through this process, in the end it gets you to a point where the councils will be set up better to support local people, so there is a prize at the end of the road."

title: Former Sheffield church leader and wife charged with rape
text:
Former church leader and wife charged with rape
A former church leader and his wife have been charged with several counts of rape dating back to 2008.
Police said Stephen and Janet Timmis, aged 68 and 61, of Psalter Lane, Sheffield, had each been charged with eight counts of rape against the same woman following a report of non-recent sexual abuse.
The charges relate to offences alleged to have taken place between May and September 2008 while Timmis was a leader at The Crowded House church in the city.
The pair have been released on bail to appear at Sheffield Magistrates' Court on 1 December, police said.
South Yorkshire Police said their inquiries suggested former church members may have information that could assist the investigation and urged them to come forward.
"Anyone with information will be offered appropriate support as required," they added.

title: Scottish prisons 'at the brink' after worst riot in a decade
text:
Scottish prisons 'at the brink' after worst riot in a decade
A riot at a young offenders institution last month was the worst disorder in one of Scotland's jails in a decade, the prison service has said.
Prison officers from four other jails were called in to restore control during the incident at HMP & YOI Polmont in September, which involved about 30 inmates.
Linda Pollock, chief executive of the Scottish Prison Service (SPS), said it was an example of "bubbling tension" caused by increasing overcrowding within the estate.
It comes after the Scottish government released projections estimating the prison population could rise to 9,450 next year – 1,650 over the current design capacity.
Justice Secretary Neil Gray said the government is considering reforms to "achieve a sustainable prison population".
Pollock said the predicted increase would make it impossible to safely accommodate prisoners and protect the welfare of staff.
Several prison officers suffered minor injuries in the riot at Polmont on 26 September.
Images released by the SPS to BBC Scotland News of the aftermath show panelling damaged and torn out, furniture broken and strewn across the hall and a glass window cracked and shattered.
Police Scotland is investigating the incident.
Pollock said the outbreak of disorder was "not unexpected" given the rising strain placed on prisons by the sharp increase of those held in custody.
"We did have disorder in Polmont, there was destruction there and we had to take control of the situation," she said.
"People in custody are becoming frustrated by the overcrowding conditions, the impact that has for them and restricting the opportunities they have for rehabilitation."
Pollock added: "We are seeing bubbling tension across the estate. We pushed our prisons to the brink and now we are at the brink and action needs to be taken."
Pollock highlighted the recent incident of interruption to the water supply at HMP Barlinnie as an example of the "fragility" of the Scottish prison estate.
She also warned that Scottish prisons were at serious risk of a return to levels of disorder "last seen in the 1980s" if conditions did not improve.
Two major riots, at HMP Barlinnie and HMP Peterhead, took place in 1987 as a result of poor conditions inside the jails - including 'slopping out', the practice of using buckets in cells as toilets.
On both occasions, prison officers were taken hostage.
Pollock said the current system was "close to breaking point" and that action was needed to ensure it "does not break".
Why are prisoner numbers so high?
About 8,500 inmates are currently held in Scotland's jails.
In May, a new record high for the prison population was set, with 8,603 inmates being held in a system designed to accommodate 7,805.
Since June 2024, about 1,600 prisoners have been freed early to ease pressure on the system, through waves of emergency releases and changes to the rules.
The automatic release point for some short-term prisoners was lowered last year from 50% to 40% and fell again in May to 30%.
The change did not apply to prisoners convicted of sex crimes or domestic abuse.
However, the number of inmates has remained well above the designed capacity, with about 700 more long-term prisoners in jail now than two years ago.
That has been partly driven by an increase in convictions over serious organised crime and historic sexual offences.
Pollock said special measures including two prisoners sharing cells intended for one had been introduced.
A new £209m jail, HMP Highland, is due for completion later this year to replace the 124-year-old HMP Inverness with capacity for 200 inmates.
Meanwhile, HMP Glasgow, a replacement for the 143-year-old Barlinnie, is expected to open in 2028 at a cost of almost £1bn.
The 1,344-capacity facility was originally scheduled to be ready in 2025 and cost estimates in 2022 put the final bill at £400m.
Phil Fairlie, assistant secretary of the Prison Officers' Association (POA), described the projected increase as "shocking and depressing".
He said the prison service would reach a point of "saying the doors are shut" to new inmates should the projections be accurate.
Fairlie said: "From the outset the POA said that the early release scheme would only provide temporary relief and that the spaces freed up would immediately be filled by newly convicted prisoners.
"We need urgent action to address the lack of prison accommodation and the understaffing of the prison estate, and vastly improved support for our members who are on the frontline of this crisis and working under intolerable pressure."
In June, the Scottish government launched a consultation on permanent new measures to address issues with overcrowding.
One proposal would change the definition of long-term prisoners from those serving four years or more, to those serving five years or more.
That would push some prisoners into the category where they would be freed automatically after serving less than a third of their sentence.
Another proposal would see the automatic release point for long-term prisoners - including killers, rapists and child abusers - changed to two-thirds of their jail term.
At present, if they're not granted parole, they are freed when they have six months left to serve.
Under another suggestion, judges would be encouraged to avoid issuing prison sentences of less than two years, up from the current presumption against sentences of 12 months or less.
The proposals followed a series of recommendations laid out in a report by the Scottish Sentencing and Penal Policy Commission and would require the backing of MSPs to come into force.
Gray said the Scottish government was increasing investment in community justice, but acknowledged further action was needed.
"To ease the pressure, we have maximised capacity across the prison estate by 640 over the past three years and we are building two new prisons," he said.
"Alongside expansion of the prison estate, the reforms will strike the right balance across custodial sentences, community sentencing and the need to robustly protect victims and the public."
Scottish Labour's justice spokesperson, Pauline McNeill, said the situation was "completely unsustainable".
She added: "The justice secretary must come forward with a comprehensive, long-term plan for tackling these issues, including evaluating proper alternatives to custody and supporting hardworking prison staff."
Scottish Conservative justice spokesman, Stephen Kerr, added: "The SNP's only answer is to water down the consequences for criminals after two decades of failing to build the prisons Scotland needs.
"Enough is enough. The SNP must stop putting the needs of offenders ahead of public safety."
description: The prison service said violence and destruction at Polmont last month was an example of "bubbling tension" caused by increasing overcrowding.

title: Oldham Coliseum's Macbeth cut short at Liquid and Envy nightclub
text:
Macbeth run cut short at Oldham nightclub
The curtain has come down early on a production in a town's last remaining nightclub of one of Shakespeare's most famous tragedies.
The Oldham Coliseum Theatre's version of Macbeth began previews at Liquid and Envy on 23 October and had been due to run until 7 November.
The theatre apologised and said all ticket holders would automatically receive full refunds. Cast and crew members will be paid in line with their contracts.
Oldham Council said it was disappointed and would work with the Coliseum's board to understand the "unforeseen circumstances" behind the decision.
A theatre spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to have cancelled Macbeth, and we recognise the disappointment this has caused audiences and the wider Oldham community."
They said cancelling a production was never easy, particularly after the considerable work involved, and that more information would be shared as soon as possible.
A council spokesperson said it wanted ticket holders to be reimbursed promptly and for cast and crew members to receive appropriate support.
"We will be working with the Coliseum Board to better understand the unforeseen circumstances that led to this decision," they said.
Former Coronation Street star Julie Hesmondhalgh, who recently starred in the BBC's Celebrity Traitors, is also offering refunds to people who donated to her fundraising appeal to help those who could not afford tickets.
Her GoFundMe campaign raised £1,855 from 53 donations, with an earlier update saying the money would allow more than 70 people to attend the show.
Hesmondhalgh apologised and asked donors to contact her directly to arrange a full refund.
The production, directed by Nick Bagnall, was set in the 1970s, with the nightclub transformed into a world of gangsters and casinos.
Speaking before the cancellation, Bagnall said: "I want to blow the dust off Shakespeare."
The theatre said the rest of its autumn and winter programme would go ahead as planned at venues across Oldham.
The Coliseum's permanent building on Fairbottom Street is undergoing refurbishment and is expected to reopen in 2027 after an additional £7m was agreed to fund essential work.

title: Hull exhibition charts Karl Bushby's 28-year global trek
text:
Exhibition charts Karl Bushby's 28-year trek home
Personal belongings and photographs from a man who spent 28 years walking from South America to Hull are to go on display.
Former paratrooper Karl Bushby set off on his journey from Chile aged 28 in 1998 and will return to his hometown city on Monday to a civic reception in Queen Victoria Square.
The now 57-year-old carried out his global trek with two self-imposed rules - not to use any form of transport to advance and not to return to the UK until his mission was complete.
The free exhibition at the Monocle building will feature photographs of his travels, diary excerpts alongside letters home to his parents and "The Beast" - a custom-built trolley that he used to transport his belongings.
The building's owner, Charlie Allenby, said Bushby's journey had "put Hull on the map alongside so many other great people from the city over the years".
"We're showcasing what he has achieved and it's important for people from far and wide to see and learn about what he has experienced, especially with his personal belongings being on display," Allenby said.
"If Karl's story can inspire one young person to take a chance and do something out of the box, it's absolutely worth it."
The exhibition will run from Tuesday 3 November until early 2027.
When Bushby returns on 2 November after his civic welcome, he will complete the last part of his journey by walking to his mother's home in east Hull.

title: Cryptocurrency fraudster stole £250,000 for spending spree
text:
Crypto fraudster stole £250,000 for spending spree
A woman conned victims out of thousands of pounds before spending almost £250,000 on jewellery, travel, home improvements, vehicles and takeaway food.
Nottinghamshire Police said Faisa Ali took money from a large number of investors for her cryptocurrency company, from 2021 to 2023, and made guarantees their cash could not be lost.
However, she sent a text message to the investor WhatsApp group in March 2023, which stated she had made poor decisions and lost all their money.
The 34-year-old, of Palin Street in Radford, Nottingham, was given a three-year prison sentence - suspended for three years - at Nottingham Crown Court on Monday and was ordered to carry out 300 hours of unpaid work.
The force said it opened an investigation after angry investors turned up at Ali's home and she called the police.
Officers said 23 victims, nearly all from Somali communities across the UK, including Nottingham, Sheffield, Birmingham and London, provided witness statements and one person had lost more than £40,000.
Detectives established Ali had been fully aware the value of almost all cryptocurrencies had fallen dramatically and consistently over the 18-month period she operated the scheme, but had continued to use money from new investors to fund a "luxury lifestyle".
'Calculating fraudster'
Bank statements from 18 October 2021 to 22 March 2023 showed she splashed out £76,140 on jewellery, £40,845 on travel, £65,183 on home furnishings and improvements, £41,625 on vehicle purchases and payments, and £24,030 on fast food.
The force said a proceeds of crime hearing, which is due to take place at a later date, could result in Ali being stripped of any cash and assets.
Det Con Simon Jones said: "This was a complex investigation into a calculating fraudster who systematically exploited the trust of numerous victims, stealing thousands of pounds in the process.
"Many of those targeted were not wealthy individuals. They had worked hard, saved carefully and, in some cases, borrowed money in the hope of securing a better future.
"For many of them, years and even decades of saving have been wiped out, leaving them with nothing."

title: Leeds student feared being 'killed' before rape - court
text:
Student feared being 'killed' before rape - court
A student feared she "would be killed" as she was led to the basement of a stranger's home before she was raped, a court has heard.
The woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was attacked at an address in the Hyde Park area of Leeds on 9 April this year, jurors at Leeds Crown Court were told.
Uvesh Vahora, 36, is standing trial for one charge of rape, which he denies.
Prosecutor Timothy Jacobs told the court the woman had earlier left her own house to buy food, but was approached by the defendant, who then took her to his own home and assaulted her.
In a police interview which took place the day after the alleged rape and which was played to the court, the woman said she had taken a dose of ketamine shortly before leaving the house.
She said that had resulted in her being "intoxicated" and "disorientated".
The woman said in her interview that she had no memory of how she had first encountered the man who attacked her.
However, she recalled being taken to a "messy" home, where she had her coat and phone taken from her.
She said she was then taken down to a basement room with a bed where she was raped.
She stated that the defendant then walked her back to her property where he promptly "disappeared", before she "broke down" and cried "hysterically".
'Vegetative state'
Describing the moment she entered the basement, she said: "I just remember I thought I'd be killed. I didn't know what was going on."
In the interview, the student recalled saying, "please don't hurt me" while she was attacked, as well as asking for her phone back.
Asked in her interview if she had consented "at any point to what was happening", the woman replied, "no, I wouldn't have done".
Jurors were told that in a police interview after his arrest, Vahora said he had found the woman struggling to unlock her door, before she told him she needed the toilet.
He said he had suggested she try her neighbours, but she did not want to because it was late.
Vahora said they then agreed she could use his toilet, and after going with him to the property, the woman had kissed him and initiated consensual sex.
The defendant told officers he then walked her home and they had exchanged phone numbers, jurors were told.
During a pre-recorded cross-examination of the woman, which was played in court, she was shown CCTV footage which the defence suggested showed her "voluntarily" going into the house of the accused.
The woman maintained she was in a "vegetative state" because of the ketamine she had taken and had no memory of meeting the man.
When it was put to her by Vahora's barrister, Richard Littlehales, that she had kissed the defendant, the woman replied, "I did not kiss the defendant, no".
The trial continues.
