title: Man found guilty of murdering 13-week-old baby in Kent
text:
Man found guilty of murdering 13-week-old baby
A man has been found guilty of murdering his girlfriend's 13-week-old baby in Kent.
Hunter Hodges suffered a "severe direct impact" to the head akin to that seen in "a high-speed motorcycle collision or a multi-level fall", Canterbury Crown Court heard.
Tyla Wharmby was caring for the baby overnight while his partner, Shannon Hodges, slept. He is not Hunter's biological father.
The 24-year-old man, of Prestedge Avenue in Ramsgate, had pleaded not guilty to murder and grievous bodily harm with intent, but was found guilty of both offences on Thursday.
The court heard Wharmby had visited a pornography website about 10 minutes before the child's mother called for an ambulance for the "lifeless" infant.
She told the 999 call handler: "My two-month-old son woke up this morning with a swollen head.
"It's really, really squishy.
"Every time I touch his head he screams."
'Everything was broken'
Hunter was rushed to Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother hospital in Margate on the morning of 15 July 2022.
The baby was airlifted to a London hospital where he died following a cardiac arrest that afternoon.
Forensic pathologist Dr Nathaniel Cary said Hunter's injuries were the result of severe trauma, such as being "thrown to floor or against a solid direct upright surface".
Consultant paediatric neurosurgeon Amedeo Calisto said: "Everything that could have been broken was broken here."
Wharmby's conversation with a police officer was recorded after staff at the Kent hospital alerted them to what happened.
He initially told police he had woken up at 04:00 to give Hunter some Calpol and give him his bottle.
Wharmby said he then woke up about half an hour later to the baby "screaming" with a swollen back of the head.
"I took him into his mum, we called an ambulance and now we are here," he added.
Wharmby was arrested later that same day.
"This was a deeply distressing case," said Det Insp Adam Marshall.
"Throughout this lengthy and incredibly difficult process, Hunter's loved ones have shown remarkable courage and strength.
"Despite their immense grief, they provided vital evidence and remained steadfast in their support of the investigation.
"Our thoughts remain with them as they continue to come to terms with their loss."
Hunter had been to the Margate hospital multiple times in the weeks before his death.
The baby had been repeatedly vomiting, had mottled skin and was crying more frequently, which the court heard are symptoms of Shaken Baby Syndrome.
His mother told hospital staff on one occasion: "Look he is really not OK. I'm not going to keep coming back up here to be rushed off with antibiotics."
Professor Safa Al-Sarraj, a consultant neuropathologist, said in court he had found signs the child had suffered a traumatic brain injury by "a similar shaking action", most likely inflicted within the month before he died.
Wharmby had denied shaking the baby during this time.
He is due to be sentenced at Canterbury Crown Court at a later date.

title: Southport attack victims' medical records 'accessed inappropriately'
text:
NHS staff may have inappropriately accessed Southport victims' records
Two more NHS staff are under investigation over allegations they inappropriately accessed Southport stabbing victims' medical records.
Liverpool Heart and Chest NHS Foundation Trust identified the cases while carrying out a "retrospective audit" of which staff had accessed information about the victims of the July 2024 attack on a children's dance class.
In May, the University Hospitals of Liverpool Group (UHLG) admitted that nearly 50 of its staff had wrongly looked at victims' medical files.
A separate investigation is also being held at North West Ambulance Service Trust in relation to staff looking up the victims of the attack without authorisation.
Youngsters had been taking part in a Taylor Swift-themed dance class at Hart Space in Southport when a knifeman fatally attacked Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and nine-year-old Alice Da Silva Aguiar.
Eight other children and two adults were injured, including Leanne Lucas, who was helping to run the class, and businessman John Haynes, who tried to stop Axel Rudakubana.
Liverpool Heart and Chest Hospital said it was "carrying out an investigation into two potential instances of inappropriate access connected to the Southport incident".
It added: "The cases were detected as part of retrospective audit and two members of staff have been placed on precautionary suspension whilst an investigation is concluded."
It said the case had been reported to the Information Commissioner's Office and the health regulator the Care Quality Commission.
The trust's medical director Manoj Kuduvalli said: "We are deeply sorry that this has happened.
"Our patients trust us with their most personal information at some of the most vulnerable moments in their lives, and any inappropriate access to those records is a serious violation of that trust.
"We have been clear with all colleagues that patient records must only ever be accessed for legitimate reasons connected to their role and the patient's care.
"We will not accept behaviour that compromises patient confidentiality or undermines the trust our patients place in us.
"We have spoken to those that are affected and will keep them informed as our investigation continues."
The data breach at UHLG happened at Aintree Hospital in Liverpool, where some of those injured were treated, in the days after the 29 July 2024 attack.
The BBC understands the three patients affected included Leanne Lucas and a 13-year-old girl who had been helping to supervise the dance class.
In May, UHLG described the breach as "inexcusable" and stressed that changes had been made, although no-one had been sacked.

title: Nottingham and Nottinghamshire boundary shake-up plans put on hold
text:
County and city boundary shake-up plans put on hold
Plans for a major shake-up of boundaries in Nottingham and Nottinghamshire are on hold.
Parts of the surrounding boroughs of Broxtowe, Gedling, and Rushcliffe were set to be merged with the city, with a new "Greater Nottingham Council" created to manage all the area's services.
A second unitary authority, called "Nottinghamshire Council", was also set to be established, comprising the districts of Ashfield, Mansfield, Bassetlaw, and Newark and Sherwood along with the remaining parts of the above three boroughs.
Plans were put on hold last month and on Thursday, the government confirmed Nottingham and Nottinghamshire were among nine areas where plans had been withdrawn and would be reconsidered.
The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) said: "Withdrawing these decisions does not mean reorganisation has been cancelled in these areas.
"All options and proposals remain under consideration in these areas and every area will have an outcome by early next year."
Some council leaders in Nottinghamshire had plotted to legally challenge the decision - including Reform-led Nottinghamshire County Council.
A spokesperson on behalf of the nine councils across Nottingham and Nottinghamshire said: "While it is disappointing that a final decision has been delayed, we welcome the further clarity provided by government on the next stage of the local government reorganisation process.
"The government has confirmed that the previous decision has been withdrawn and will now be reconsidered as part of a wider review. It has also made clear that Nottingham and Nottinghamshire remain part of the national LGR programme and that a new decision will be made based on the proposals already submitted."
Labour leader of Nottingham City Council, Neghat Khan, said she was "disappointed" by the decision but stood by the authority's proposals, saying she believed it was the "best route to stronger, more sustainable local government".
She added: "I know that further uncertainty is not good for our residents or our workforce.
"We will continue to engage positively with the process, and I will be writing to government at the earliest opportunity so that we understand what this means for Nottingham. For residents, there is no immediate change to local government or to the services we provide.
"Our focus remains on delivering for Nottingham people, ensuring that we are in the strongest possible position when the government reaches its final decision."
Councillor Mick Barton, county council leader, said the withdrawal of plans was the "right thing to do".
"I am really happy," he said. "There will be some unhappy people but they have made the right decision in my opinion.
"I'm really happy we stuck to our guns and put the judicial review in."
'Massive decision'
Councillor Sam Smith, Conservative leader of the county council's opposition, said the LGR process had been "a complete and utter mess from start to finish, and hundreds of thousands of taxpayers' pounds have been wasted on it".
Meanwhile, Labour East Midlands mayor Claire Ward said it was important for the government to get LGR "right".
"This is a massive decision," Ward said. "This is about making sure that those boundaries - those new authorities - are the right ones, and so they've taken the existing decision off the table, but they are looking at all of the same options again.
"And I hope that we will get a fairly early determination from the government, but I want them to get it right. And so, if that means they've got to take a little bit more time, so be it."
Soon after Andy Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, his government announced an abrupt "pause" on LGR in England in early September, while all options were put under further review.
And on Thursday it was confirmed only five of the original 14 regions - East Sussex, Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire and Worcestershire - will proceed.
Local government minister Jim McMahon told MPs the review had found the government's decision-making to be "robust".
"I want to be absolutely clear that this is not a reflection of the work underpinning those proposals," he added.
"I commit to coming back to the House with updates for another set of areas by Christmas, and every area will have an outcome by early next year."
Reconfirming local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries, he announced plans for elections to shadow councils, set to run for a year before taking over from old authorities, will now be held in May 2028.

title: Decision on 160,000-bird Sheriffhales chicken farm put on hold
text:
Decision on 160,000-bird chicken farm put on hold
A decision on plans for a chicken farm housing up to 160,000 birds has been put on hold after fresh concerns were raised about the scheme's environmental assessment.
The proposal for land south-west of Manor Farm in Sheriffhales, near Shifnal, Shropshire, would see four poultry houses built, each accommodating up to 40,000 birds.
Planning officers for Shropshire Council have recommended approval, saying environmental assessments found odour impacts would be minimal and operational noise levels low.
However, the application has attracted 1,494 objections, with concerns raised about issues including traffic, water quality and animal welfare.
Supporters of the scheme say it would boost domestic food production, support the agricultural economy and create jobs, while using modern systems designed to minimise odour.
The proposed development would also include feed bins, a feed-blending room, a dead bird store, underground dirty-water tanks, a biomass boiler house and a pond designed to temporarily store rainwater and reduce flood risk.
Sheriffhales Parish Council was among those to have raised concerns, citing previous issues linked to a former pig-rearing operation on the site.
Planning officers had recommended the application for approval, subject to conditions including the need for an environmental permit before the site could become operational.
But members of the council's southern planning committee were told on Tuesday that five extra detailed representations have been received since the publication of the committee report.
The submissions raised a number of technical matters relating to the environmental assessment accompanying the scheme.
Officers asked councillors to postpone consideration of the application so the new material could be fully reviewed and responded to.
The committee unanimously agreed.
If approved, the farm would employ two full-time staff. Birds would be reared for about 38 days before being removed, with around seven-and-a-half production cycles taking place each year.

title: Man sentenced for 'eye-wateringly violent' stabbing of dog
text:
Man sentenced for 'eye-wateringly violent' killing of dog
A man who hit his dog on the head with a hammer and stabbed her in the chest has been banned from owning or keeping animals for the rest of his life.
Glenn Tweedie pleaded guilty at Edinburgh Sheriff Court to causing unnecessary suffering to the black Labrador, named Caillie, who died of her injuries.
The Scottish SPCA were first alerted after their animal helpline received a concerned call about a dog 'screaming' at a property in Loanhead, Midlothian.
The inspector who attended said it was the "most eye-wateringly violent conduct" he had seen towards a completely innocent pet.
Tweedie initially told the inspector the dog had been euthanised at the vets but then confessed to killing her because he could not afford the vet bill.
He used a hammer to strike the dog twice, and then proceeded to stab her through the thorax, which killed her.
The inspector said Caillie was found at the bottom of a large ditch covered in branches.
A second black Labrador was also found at the property and has been taken into care by the Scottish SPCA.
The inspector said: "Tweedie wrongly claimed Caillie was in immense pain, but in fact it was he who caused his animal to suffer in the most unimaginable way – both physically and mentally.
"To then dump Caillie in a ditch shows Tweedie's complete lack of remorse and how little regard he has for animals."
Tweedie was sentenced to wear an ankle monitor for a year and given a community payback order.

title: A66 dualling scheme nearly doubles in length to nine years
text:
Road upgrade timeline almost doubled to nine years
A project to dual the A66 road, which runs across northern England linking Cumbria, County Durham and Yorkshire, has had its timeline almost doubled.
The Department for Transport (DfT) said work between Penrith in Cumbria, and Scotch Corner in North Yorkshire will now take nine years instead of the initial estimate of five.
The government said the move boosted affordability, but Westmorland and Lonsdale MP Tim Farron said: "Inflation in construction is ahead of regular inflation and so if you have nine years' worth of materials to purchase... that is certainly going to make it more expensive."
Previously the project was costed at £1.3bn, but reports suggest the bill has risen to £1.4bn.
The change to the timeline was announced as part of the Budget on Wednesday, after which a DfT spokesperson said it would be a "huge boost" for communities in the area.
"With the business case now approved, construction will start around Penrith, Cumbria, this winter, with at least 30% of jobs going to local people."
Delay 'leaked out'
The campaign to dual the A66 has been a long one. Plans were previously approved by the last Conservative government and then paused when Labour won the 2024 election.
The scheme was then re-confirmed in July 2025 and preparatory work has started on the route.
Farron, a former Liberal Democrat leader, said he was pleased the scheme was now progressing but angry the delay was "leaked out in the small print".
He said: "This is about saving lives, it's about protecting communities.
"It's also about making sure that we boost our economy and, given those are the really laudable motives for doing this, to make it take nearly a decade to deliver it is something that we are rightly angry about."
National Highways said the first section between Penrith and Temple Sowerby was expected to be completed by 2031.
A spokesperson claimed the project would "improve journeys, make the road safer and boost economic growth".
"We're building in stages, which keeps the project affordable while reducing disruption and minimising environmental impacts."

title: Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
text:
Burnham says he wants to cut welfare bill 'as soon as we possibly can'
Andy Burnham has said he wants to cut the welfare bill "as soon as we possibly can", but was unable to guarantee this would happen before the next general election.
Opponents raised concerns over the lack of details on welfare reform in Wednesday's Budget, after welfare spending was forecast to increase from £353bn this year to £431bn in 2031/32.
Asked whether he would seek to reduce the bill before the next election, Burnham told reporters: "We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we're working flat out to that end."
He warned against "crude cuts" and said he wants to get people into "sustainable employment". The Conservatives accused Labour of being "addicted to welfare".
The prime minister faced questions about his approach after the Treasury disputed that Chancellor John Healey had suggested to the BBC that the benefits bill will be cut before the next election, which must be held by August 2029.
When Healey was asked by the Today Programme on Radio 4 whether there would be a cut in the bill before polling day, he said: "There will be, there will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we'll do that in a Labour way."
But several Treasury sources took issue with this being interpreted as a promise to do so by the next election. Downing Street later said it was "not setting an arbitrary target or timetable".
The prime minister's official spokesman would not say whether the government's ambition to cut welfare spending meant reducing it below its current level, or ensuring that future spending rises at a slower rate than is currently projected.
Further details about the government's proposals are expected after two major reports are published in November.
These include a review of disability benefits co-chaired by Labour minister Sir Stephen Timms and one on young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) led by former minister Alan Milburn.
The two reviews were announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer after his attempt to make significant changes to the welfare system, including restricting eligibility for some health-related benefits, resulted in a mass revolt of Labour MPs and an embarrassing climbdown in June 2025.
Speaking during a visit to Derby, Burnham said the "big next priority in front of us" is the publication of the Milburn report.
He said: "We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There's no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible."
Pressed again for a timeline on his plans, the prime minister said: "We're working hard to cut the welfare bill as soon as we possibly can. But we're doing it in a way that supports people into work.
"If we just went and made crude cuts, in the end, that leaves people in crisis, and you spend more public money somewhere else, so it's about getting people into sustainable employment."
'Huge bonus'
Former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane said if the government could provide a plan to show "greater restraint" of the benefits bill, that would "play spectacularly well" with the financial markets.
Haldane, who has previously advised Burnham, told the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast: "If the government could get that through I think it would come with a huge bonus."
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch responded to the Budget by saying the country was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed, and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".
Reacting to government briefings and remarks on Thursday related to when a reduction in the benefits bill could take place, Badenoch said it "looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading".
She said: "Don't let anyone tell you this was a 'do no harm budget'. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they've harmed our national security."
Welfare spending is forecast to rise this year by £19bn to £353bn.
Watchdog and forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said this figure is expected to rise to £431bn in 2031/32, driven primarily by health-related and pensioner benefit spending.
Of the figure forecast for 2031/32, £209.8bn is on pensioners, including the state pension and winter fuel payments, while £110.7bn is on universal credit and legacy equivalents and £69.6bn is on disability benefits such as personal independence payments.
The government has already pledged to reform the existing state pension triple lock from 2030, and more proposals and changes to the welfare system are expected to emerge in the coming months.

title: Radical changes to make-up of Essex councils delayed
text:
Radical changes to Essex councils delayed
A decision on whether a radical reshape of councils in Essex will go ahead is now expected early next year, the government has said.
Plans to abolish Essex's fifteen councils and replace them with five super councils were withdrawn in September.
But on Thursday, the government said local government reorganisation (LGR) in the county was under review. Minister Jim McMahon told the Commons "all options and proposals will remain under consideration".
The Conservatives have described the government's handling of LGR as "a farce". Essex County Council leader Peter Harris, of Reform UK, said it needed to "get on with the serious business of running a council".
The government announced the five council model for Greater Essex would go ahead in March. It had received the most cross-party and council support at the time.
But Essex County Council sought a judicial review against the decision in the summer.
LGR plans for Essex, Norfolk and Hampshire were then withdrawn by the government in September, "in light of new legal advice".
The government said there would be "fresh ministerial decisions" going forward.
McMahon told the Commons "there is not a requirement for areas to develop new proposals" and they will "consider the proposals already submitted and the evidence".
There were four proposals for Essex originally put forward, including four and three council models.
Conservative MP John Whittingdale told the Commons that withdrawing Essex's plans six weeks ago had "paralysed decision-making".
The Reform UK leader of Thurrock Council, Richard Bingley, said there was "continued uncertainty" for authorities that made planning difficult.
"Thurrock and the wider Essex area are still waiting for clarity about our future," he said.
But the Labour leader of Southend City Council argued: "The government is progressing things at a greater pace than was anticipated."
Daniel Cowan said: "We will continue to robustly advocate that the five model is the best for Southend and Greater Essex."
Cowan argued there was clarity that the city council would continue to provide services until 2029, when new unitary councils would then take over.
Chelmsford City Council leader and county councillor Stephen Robinson, Liberal Democrat, said it was "vital" that all councils worked together "to protect public services, by making that [LGR] a smooth process".
"So I am disappointed that Reform-led Essex County Council still refuses to engage in that process," he said.
Harris said: "We need to get on with the serious business of running a council with a £3bn budget and ensuring that residents get the services they need and deserve."
BBC analysis of freedom of information requests and council documents showed that 11 of the 15 councils in Essex had spent a combined £5,497,711 on LGR so far.
The government announced on Thursday it was set to give Essex councils £2.25m to cover LGR costs.

title: Nine of 14 plans for council overhaul withdrawn following review
text:
Further delays for major council overhaul in nine of 14 proposed areas
The government has announced further delays to nine of 14 major council mergers, with only five now going ahead.
Proposals for 14 regions to undergo mergers of smaller councils to form larger unitary authorities was put on hold by Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner last month, following concerns around legal challenges.
Local Government Minister Jim McMahon has told MPs the review had found the government's decision-making to be "robust", but nine areas have now been withdrawn for further review.
Only five of the original 14 regions will be taken forward, after three more weeks of consultation. Shadow local government secretary Katie Lam condemned the latest news as "a farce".
Mergers will continue to progress in East Sussex, Gloucestershire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire and Worcestershire.
But the government is seeking "legal clarity" in the remaining nine areas, which are: Derbyshire, Devon, Hertfordshire, Kent, Lancashire, Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire, and Staffordshire.
In a Commons statement, McMahon said the government was "withdrawing the decisions announced in July" for those nine areas.
"I want to be absolutely clear that this is not a reflection of the work underpinning those proposals," he added.
The review will now focus on the nine areas where current plans have been withdrawn for further review, as well as four areas where plans were withdrawn in September, in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.
Two further areas, Cambridgeshire and West Sussex, are still waiting for merger plans to be agreed, totalling 15 regions where local government reorganisation plans remain undecided.
McMahon said: "We will move faster where we can, and some of the remaining areas may receive an outcome decision before others.
"I commit to coming back to the House with updates for another set of areas by Christmas, and every area will have an outcome by early next year."
Reconfirming local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries, he announced plans for elections to shadow councils, set to run for a year before taking over from old authorities, will now be held in May 2028.
Responding, Lam set out how the reorganisation had been beset by delays over the past two-and-a-half years.
"From start to finish this government's approach to local government reorganisation has been nothing short of a farce," she told MPs.
She added: "Naturally the taxpayer was left to pick up the tab for all of these delays - a bill which runs into the tens of millions of pounds."
Local Government Association chair Eamonn O'Brien called for a re-set of relations between the government and local councils across the country.
He said: "While today's announcement provides some certainty for some areas, many councils remain frustrated by the situation they have been placed in.
"All councils affected need urgent clarity on next steps and how costs already incurred will be met.
"There needs to be a reset in the relationship between government and councils on local government reorganisation, with local government fully engaged in shaping decisions from the outset."

title: Southampton drug dealer jailed for 3D-printed gun murder
text:
Drug dealer jailed for 3D-printed gun murder
A "weapons-obsessed" convicted killer who used a partly 3D-printed pistol to murder an intruder has been jailed for a minimum of 30 years.
Marcin Buryta, 32, found 45-year-old Piotr Pruszak at his home in Conifer Road, Southampton, in February and shot him four times, Hampshire Police said.
The defendant was a drug dealer who previously killed a man at a birthday party in his native Poland when he was a teenager, officers added.
He was jailed for life at Winchester Crown Court for murder, two counts of possessing a firearm and one count of possessing ammunition with intent.
Buryta phoned police shortly before 20:00 GMT on 11 February to say he had shot someone, the court heard.
He then continued to send and receive messages about the prices of cocaine and ketamine, police said.
At the address, officers found Pruszak with gunshot wounds from a Glock pistol, parts of which had been home-printed.
Police later found two more firearms, a loaded crossbow, a machete, a dagger, knives and knuckle dusters at the address.
During the trial, jurors were told Buryta was 19 when he fatally stabbed a man at a birthday party in Poland, police said.
Det Chief Insp Clair Trueman said: "Buryta is a man obsessed with weaponry, who didn't stop with the initial shots he fired that night, instead retrieving further ammunition and shooting again."
Previously, Pruszak's family, from Poland, paid tribute to their "beloved son and brother".

title: Harrogate law firm prepares to appoint administrator
text:
Law firm prepares to appoint administrator
A North Yorkshire law firm is preparing to call in administrators after four decades in business.
Berwins Solicitors, based in Harrogate, employs about 40 people and specialises in family, property, and wills and probate law.
The firm filed a notice of intention to appoint an administrator with the High Court on Monday.
It comes after Berwins celebrated its 40th anniversary at Cedar Court in Harrogate last month. The BBC has contacted the firm for comment.
A spokesperson from the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) said: "We are aware of the situation and are liaising with the firm as it effects an orderly closure.
"We continue to monitor the situation, and would only take action if the interests of clients were at risk."
According to the SRA, more than 200 law firms have closed in 2026 so far, including those which have ceased practising or merged with another company.
I added that, as it prepares to close, Berwins should be in touch with their clients throughout the process.
The Harrogate office was set up by Paul Berwin in 1986, which expanded to a Leeds office in 2013.
Berwin stepped down from the company earlier this year, with Danielle Day now listed as the managing director.

title: Bradford Council leader forced to backtrack on pool funding claim
text:
Council leader forced to U-turn on funding claim
A council leader has backtracked on claims £14.6m left over from a cancelled leisure centre project was not available to spend elsewhere in Bradford.
Reform UK councillor Stephen Place had accused Shipley's Labour MP Anna Dixon of making "false claims" after she said the money could be spent on other projects.
Dixon said she had forwarded a letter from government confirming the funding from the Local Regeneration Fund remained available to the council on 9 September, but Place said he had not received the letter until Wednesday.
He has now confirmed the £14.6m from the cancelled Squire Lane Leisure Centre will be retained by Bradford Council and can be spent on other projects.
Place said he had raised the matter with senior council officers in early September, but the executive had only received written confirmation from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) on Wednesday.
"We warmly welcome that these monies will not be clawed back by national Government and that they remain available as a capital grant," he said.
Dixon said Place had "wasted months, failing to make use of millions of secure government funding" and residents needed a "clear alternative plan for how this money will be spent".
"It should not have taken the Reform UK leader more than three months to publicly acknowledge this," she said.
"It is deeply concerning that the Reform leadership on the Council were willing to cancel a multimillion-pound project without a clear understanding of whether this funding could be retained for the benefit of Bradford."
The disagreement arose over claims that money given to Bradford Council by the government for a leisure centre at Squire Lane in Girlington, which was scrapped by Reform in July, could be spent to reopen Bingley Pool.
Dixon, campaigners and local councillors had called on the authority to spend the money on the pool, after Dixon said she had had it confirmed by Jim McMahon MP, minister for local government, devolution and regional growth, that the council could retain the funding.
Place, however, denied receiving the confirmation from MHCLG, saying: "Claims that Bradford Council has existing funding available to spend on Bingley Pool are categorically untrue."
Independent Bingley Councillor Joe Wheatley said he was "glad" Place had "woken up to the fact he has got a letter that we can spend that money on whatever we like".
Meanwhile, Jeremy Thackray, chair of the Friends of Bingley Pool, said Place had been invited to a meeting of the Friends of Bingley Pool on Wednesday evening, but did not attend.
"We know what our next step is but up until now we've been trying to work out what is the legal position of that money and it does seem like everything is coalescing around it's available, Bradford can spend it," he said.
"It seems everyone is coming to an agreement it is there and we can work out little administrative problems but in general Bingley Pool could be a place it could be spent."
Place said the council was not yet able to commit the money to a particular project but would "look to utilise them in future, to the benefit of Bradford residents".

title: Cows returned to field after moo-ving on to Leicestershire rail line
text:
Cows back in field after moo-ving on to rail line
Train services were temporarily held up after several cows broke through fencing and moo-ved on to a railway line in Leicestershire.
A spokesperson for Network Rail said it was reported at about 15:30 GMT on Monday that several cows were on the line at East Langton, in the Harborough district.
The cows were safely returned to their field just after 16:00, the spokesperson added.
On social media, officers from Leicestershire Police said fencing was repaired by Network Rail, before services were able to resume.
Network Rail apologised to any passengers whose journeys were affected.
The Leicestershire and Rutland rural policing team said the incident fell within its "rural policing stereotype".
"With obvious risks to passing trains, passengers and the livestock themselves, officers worked quickly to identify the farmer, locate the animals, safely remove the cattle from the tracks and secure the damaged fencing," it added.
"A great bit of teamwork from all involved, including the farmers' incredible team of dogs (nobody panic, they were never near the track).
"Please take this as a timely reminder to check your perimeters and ensure your livestock are secure."

title: Hedon man's epic South America MND challenge nearly completed
text:
Epic South America MND challenge nearly completed
A man attempting to run the length of South America to raise awareness of motor neurone disease (MND) is about a month away from completing his challenge.
Mike Humphreys, from Hedon, near Hull, set off from Argentina in March and is now about 40 days from reaching the northern tip of Colombia.
Despite recording a record-breaking 160 consecutive 50km runs, he said the challenge was "nothing compared with what people living with MND face every day".
Humphreys, who is no stranger to extreme challenges, said he would continue with them until a cure is found.
Having lost one friend to the condition in 2013, he is now supporting a second, Craig Eskrett, who was diagnosed in 2023.
He told BBC Radio Humberside: "Craig has inspired me every step of the way. The way he has adapted to everything MND has thrown at him is incredible, and honestly, if it wasn't for him, I would probably have given up by now.
"What I'm putting myself through is nothing compared with what people living with MND face every day. That's what keeps me going through the altitude sickness, the food poisoning and all the tough days on the road."
He added: "This isn't about me or about breaking world records. It's about doing everything I can for people affected by motor neurone disease, and raising awareness until we find a cure."
Humphreys, a personal trainer, was supposed to start the trip last year but was delayed when his van and running equipment were stolen.
After getting a new van, he started his challenge on 30 March in Ushuaia, near the southern tip of Argentina, and ran 50km (about 31 miles) on his first day.
He said he had since completed more than 200 consecutive days without a break, running at least the distance of a marathon each day.
He has previously ridden about 1,000 miles (about 1,600km) across Europe on a Chopper bike, ending at Val Thorens in the French Alps.
He has also run 30 marathons across Europe in 30 days.
Humphreys' other challenges, which his followers on Instagram help him to choose, have included running a marathon in ski boots and climbing a mountain wearing only flip-flops and swimming trunks.

title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
text:
Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.
Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.
Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.
The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.
The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.
Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.
Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.
Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.
According to the latest figures up to 30 September, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.
The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.
However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.
Rob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.
After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.
However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.
If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.
Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.
While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.
Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."
Pensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule change in a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.
Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".
He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."
Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.
However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.
The change applies to payments made from 28 October.
In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.
Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner".
Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".
She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system.
"Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."
Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.
The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.

title: Merthyr man saved by off-duty police sergeant after cardiac arrest
text:
'I died twice', says man saved by off-duty police sergeant
A dad who suffered a cardiac arrest and collapsed in a shop said his 12-year-old son could have lost his dad if a "hero" off-duty police officer had not saved him.
James Ashley, 52, from Merthyr Tydfil, had just finished parkrun and was shopping in Cwmbran when he was hit by a "wave of dizziness" and fell to the floor on 4 April.
Sgt Adam Hollings from Gwent Police was nearby and immediately started CPR.
"I clinically died twice but by the time the paramedics got there, I was sitting up talking... the difference with Adam knowing what he was doing is that my son didn't lose his dad as a 12-year-old," he said, and called him an "absolute hero".
Hollings, who has spent 21 years on the force, was awarded a Royal Humane Society Resuscitation Certificate for his role in saving Ashley's life.
"We're very lucky to have the first aid training that we do, and if we can occasionally be in the right place at the right time to help people out, then fantastic," he said.
The 40-year-old from Abergavenny told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast that even though he was off-duty his training and lifesaving skills kicked in and he acted on "autopilot".
He told someone in the shop to call an ambulance, and then used a defibrillator.
A defibrillator is a device that gives a jolt of energy to the heart. It helps get the heart beating again when someone is in cardiac arrest and their heart has stopped.
Ashley was taken to University Hospital Wales in Cardiff and has since made a full recovery.
"The difference with Adam knowing what he was doing is that my son didn't lose his dad as a 12-year-old," he said, calling his saviour an "absolute hero, a legend".
The pair were reunited a week later when Hollings visited in hospital.
"The nicest moment in all of it was meeting James and his family," Hollings said.
"Being able to see that me doing a little bit there got him to the hospital in time so he could have the lifesaving care that he needed, and know that he was there for his family, that's the real reward.
"But the award is lovely," he added.
Ashley said Hollings was a "lifesaver", but also "just a smashing bloke".
"We had a really good chat," he said.
Ashley had undergone first aid training himself from a previous job and said even though he was "rusty now", he encouraged others to use their skills if they have them or to get the training.
"If you think, 'Oh, you know, I'm sure there'll be someone there' and 'Oh, it's someone else's opportunity to do it' or 'I can't be bothered or whatever', you absolutely can make a difference to people's lives," he said.
"And it's not just maybe the person you save, it's the people around them who you're helping."
Sharon Owen, CEO of Calon Hearts, a Welsh charity that provides defibrillators and training, praised Hollings for his "quick thinking".
She said it showed "just how important it is to know CPR and have the confidence to act."
"When someone suffers a cardiac arrest, every second counts," Owen added.
"Don't be afraid of getting it wrong - call 999, start CPR and follow the call handler's instructions.
"Doing something is always better than doing nothing."
Owen said people needed to try to overcome any embarrassment they have about performing CPR on a stranger.
"Research shows that women are less likely than men to receive CPR, partly because people may feel uncomfortable touching a woman's chest.
"But when someone's life is at risk, embarrassment should not come into it. Everyone deserves the same chance of survival."
How do I perform CPR?
To perform CPR, follow these steps:
- If you find someone collapsed, make sure it's safe to approach
- Check if they respond by gently shaking their shoulders and asking them loudly "are you ok?"
- If they don't respond, shout for help and ask someone to call 999 or 112 for an ambulance, or put your phone on hands-free and call yourself
- Open their airway by gently tilting their head back and lifting their chin, and look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds for normal breathing
- Kneel by the casualty and put the heel of your hand on the middle of their chest. Correct hand placement for CPR on a person with breasts may mean that your hands may touch some of the breast. This is okay
- Put your other hand on top of your first hand and if you can, interlock your fingers
- Lean forwards so your shoulders are over your hands, keep your arms straight and press down hard to a depth of about 5-6cm before releasing the pressure, allowing the chest to come back up. Push at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute
- Listen to instructions from the 999 operator if you still have them on the phone. They will tell you what to do and help you to push at the right speed
- Continue chest compressions until emergency help arrives or the person starts showing signs of life and starts to breathe normally
Source: St John Ambulance
description: James Ashley from Merthyr Tydfil suffered a cardiac arrest in a shop in Cwmbran.

title: Wolves legends reunite for Black History Month film project
text:
'Racism can crush you, but I used it for motivation'
Three former Wolverhampton Wanderers footballers have reunited for a short film for You Tube paying tribute to the contributions of Black players over the past 150 years.
George Berry, Don Gardner and Bob Hazell met at The Junction pub in Wolverhampton as part of Black History Month to reflect on their experiences at Wolves, with each having played a significant role in the club's history.
Gardner was Wolves' first Black senior player, Hazell its first Black goalscorer, while Berry was the first Black player to lift a trophy for the club.
"If you're the only Black face on the pitch and thousands of people are shouting abuse, that's hard," recalled Berry.
Gardner said: "I never looked at it through the lens of colour. I didn't think of myself as a Black footballer, I thought of myself as a footballer who wanted to succeed."
The icon, who donned the famous gold and black shirt as a professional player in 1973, has been hailed by the club for "helping change Wolves forever for Black players".
Recalling the obstacles he faced in his career, the 71-year-old said racism was something he faced "all the time".
He said: "You'd be taking a throw-in and people would shout things at you from a few feet away.
"There were occasions when players, like Brendon Batson and others, had bananas thrown onto the pitch and there were monkey chants. That happened regularly in football during that era," he said.
"You'd also get abuse from opposition players. But often they were doing it because they wanted to get you off your game.
"Then after the match, those same players would come over and shake your hand and ask how you were.
"It doesn't excuse it but football was different then."
Gardner helped pave the way for fellow legends Hazell and Berry to join the squad.
For Berry, who joined the club in 1973 as an apprentice, there were many challenges to overcome, both on the pitch and in the dressing rooms.
"I remember when I first trained in the first-team environment that there were one or two things said. There was some 'banter' and some language that I didn't particularly like.
"But the worst stuff never came from your teammates, [it] was from the supporters or your opponents.
"But there are really only two choices you can make when you receive it – you either let it crush you or you use it as motivation.
"I chose to use it as motivation."
At Molineux, Berry reached the FA Youth Cup final, became a first-team regular and was voted Players' Player of the Year in 1979, before helping Wolves lift the League Cup the following season, their last major domestic title to date.
He added: "Not only the Black players, but all players who have had an influence on the club deserve recognition.
"As Black players, we played our part, and it's nice to see that being remembered."
Another player celebrated in the short film is Hazell, whose first goal against Manchester City in March 1978 made him the first Black player to score for the Old Gold.
Despite his triumphs on the pitch, there were barriers that almost took him away from the sport, he said.
"There were things that happened that I didn't even tell my family about. I knew if I told them everything, they'd have said, 'Forget football and come home'. But I needed football.
"Nothing was going to get in my way. I loved football too much, so I learned to deal with things and keep moving forward," he said, adding that a camaraderie among his fellow players helped him to push through.
"I remember things happening in matches where teammates would immediately step in and stand up for me.
"Years later, I'd mention those moments to them and they'd often have forgotten all about it.
"But for me, they meant a lot because they showed they had my back."

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand options for customers
text:
DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.
DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.
Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.
"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.
"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.
For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.
He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".
The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.
Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.
"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.
In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.
DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.
The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.
New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."
"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

title: Budget a 'mixed bag' for independent businesses, says restaurant owner
text:
Budget a 'mixed bag' for independent businesses
An independent restaurant owner has said the chancellor's Budget has not gone far enough for small businesses.
Kenny Mann, who runs Limas in Long Eaton, Derbyshire, said the raft of announcements on Wednesday was a "mixed bag" and felt more could have been done to help small firms.
He welcomed the relief on businesses rates, but added the increase of the minimum wage of 3.9% in April would effectively cancel it out.
Speaking to the BBC, Mann said: "Small businesses and independents are really going to struggle, I think, moving forward."
Limas opened in 2023, and Kenny said the first year was "incredibly tough" with inflation and the cost of energy hitting the hospitality sector hard.
He said the business was now ticking over nicely but that the measure of his success would be quite different to others.
"It's about keeping the door open, paying the bills, paying the VAT on time, making sure the staff are paid, rent paid, etc.
"So if you can count surviving and staying open as success, then at the moment we're successful. But to me, that's not success, and that's not sustainable for a long period of time."
Chancellor John Healy announced a raft of measures in the Budget more widely aimed at giving the country some "breathing space" from the cost of living.
The threshold at which High Street shops start paying business rates in England will be increased from £12,000 to £18,000, meaning businesses would pay no rates on properties with a rateable value below this level.
From 1 April 2027, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage will be paid £13.21p per hour, up 50p from the current £12.71 an hour.
The rate for 18 to 20-year-olds will rise to £11.27 an hour from 1 April, up from £10.85. For someone working full-time, that means an increase of £760 to their gross annual earnings.
The minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds is also rising by 3.9%, increasing from £8 an hour to £8.31.
Kenny, who watched the Budget in real time from his restaurant bar, said the chancellor was moving money around with no real benefit to him.
"There's obviously business rate reliefs, which will help in one hand, but the rise in national insurance minimum wage for those young people just means that you're taking from one and giving to the other.
"It's pretty much cost neutral, essentially, so it's not enough, it's not enough, and small businesses and independents are really going to struggle, I think, moving forward."
Max Andrew works part-time as one of Kenny's front-of-house staff.
He secured employment after a stint of work experience through school. He welcomed the rise in the minimum wage but he feels it could stop employers hiring more young people in future.
"It's good for people who are working, but if businesses are paying that bit extra, then they might not be able to afford more apprentices or younger people working.
"I do think it is good, but then at the same time, it might not help more young people getting more jobs."

title: Offshore workers turn to weight-loss jabs to meet new helicopter weight limits
text:
Offshore workers turn to weight-loss jabs to meet helicopter weight rules
Hundreds of offshore workers have been using weight-loss jabs to help meet maximum weight rules for helicopter flights due to come into force next week.
From Sunday, anyone weighing more than 19st 7Ib (124kg) in civilian clothing and footwear will be banned from taking a flight to an offshore platform covered by UK safety regulations.
When the new rules were announced last year, about 2,200 workers were over the limit but that figure has now fallen to fewer than 250, according to Offshore Energies UK (OEUK).
The industry body told BBC Scotland News that on one platform, 60% of staff had been taking weight-loss drugs and extra fridge space had been provided to keep the medications cool.
The average weight of offshore workers has risen over recent decades, and increased by almost 1st 7Ib (10kg) since 2008.
The new weight limit policy came after the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) warned that rescue winches - which are critical during offshore emergencies - cannot safely lift heavier people.
The figure was decided upon after factoring in the weight of the rescuer, stretcher and other kit that would add to the combined total.
OEUK health and safety manager Graham Skinner said a range of measures were being used to help offshore workers manage their weight, including gym equipment and healthier food options.
Alongside those, he said many had had chosen to make use of the latest medical advances in controlling appetite and digestion.
"What we know is that offshore workers are using weight-loss jabs regardless of the policies. Last year we saw in some cases 60% of workers turning up with weight-loss jabs," he told BBC Scotland News.
"That's brought our average weight down in a very short space of time. I think that's very common in society and it can potentially be a really useful tool if somebody's got a lot of weight to lose it can get them in a good place."
He said initially staff appeared to be funding the medication themselves, although he thought it possible that some firms were now supporting them with the costs.
Could some workers lose their jobs?
The weight-limit policy has been criticised by the RMT union which claimed there had been a lack of consultation, and that it could lead to experienced staff being excluded from offshore operations.
Earlier this year, BBC Scotland spoke to one occupational health expert in Aberdeen who said some clients were "really stressed" by the new rules while others had chosen to leave the industry.
Companies could offer staff alternative onshore roles but Skinner warned: "If somebody has chosen not to lose weight then there's a real possibility they could lose their job."
He said there were a number of safety reasons for having weight-limit controls such as working in confined spaces or ability to quickly exit a helicopter - but the actual numbers had been driven by the lifting capacity of the winches.
"It's the same winch on all search and rescue helicopters and if somebody needs to be rescued due to a health or safety incident the winch has limitations and we can't allow people to exceed those," he said.
Workers will be asked to declare if they are under the weight limit and this will be checked at the heliport.
He said employers in the industry had been working "really hard" to ensure as many staff as possible complied with the new rules and he hoped the number of staff over the weight limit could be reduced still further.
description: From Sunday anyone weighing more than 19st 7Ib (124kg) will be banned from flying to an offshore platform.

title: Jennifer Symonds drowning murder-accused pleads guilty
text:
Man pleads guilty to murder of woman found drowned
A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman who was found dead in the River Thames in Oxfordshire.
Nelio Gouveia, 45, of Phyllis Court Drive, Henley-on-Thames, required a Portuguese interpreter when he entered his plea at Oxford Crown Court.
The body of Jennifer Symonds, 44, was recovered from the river at Phyllis Court Club early on 6 March. A post-mortem examination showed she died from drowning.
Gouveia, who was known to Symonds, will be sentenced on 20 November.
When Gouveia pleaded guilty to killing Jennifer Symonds, three of her friends who were in court looked relieved and emotional.
In the dock, the defendant was dressed in grey with a pullover tracksuit top and looked down at the floor during most of the 10-minute hearing.
Det Insp Rob Underhill said: "My thoughts remain firmly with Jennifer's family, who have lost someone who was dear to them.
"Nelio's actions on 6 March were heinous, and I am pleased that he has pleaded guilty.
"This case demonstrates Thames Valley Police's commitment to investigating violence against women and girls."

title: Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself 'leader of Brazil' after election loss
text:
Flávio Bolsonaro calls himself 'leader of Brazil' after election loss
The defeated candidate in Brazil's presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro, has referred to himself as "leader of Brazil" in a letter he published on social media after leaving the country for the United States.
Bolsonaro lost to his left-wing rival, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the run-off on Sunday by a difference of 4.4 million votes, but has not conceded defeat.
In the letter, Bolsonaro alleges, without offering evidence, that he was the victim of "electoral fraud" and says that he will lead the opposition from the US.
He left Brazil on Tuesday after failing to comply with an order to surrender his passports, a decision which Lula described as "a shameful act".
Bolsonaro starts his letter, which he posted on his X account, saying "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the leader of Brazil".
However, he had posted a previous version, that was later deleted, in which he wrote: "I address the Brazilian people and the international community as the rightful president of Brazil."
Both versions repeat the allegation that Bolsonaro first made on election night, that an extension of polling hours on Sunday had benefited his rival.
In the letter, he says it was "an electoral fraud unfolding before my eyes".
The extension was requested by both Lula's and Bolsonaro's campaign teams, and the head of Brazil's electoral authority has said that the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the country's laws and constitution.
An analysis of election data conducted by BBC Brazil and BBC Verify has also found that only around 34,000 people voted during the extended hours - far lower than the 4.4 million votes that separated Lula from Bolsonaro.
In his letter, Bolsonaro also addresses his departure from Brazil - which caused confusion after he disappeared for more than 24 hours.
It later emerged that he had gone across the land border to Argentina, and from there flew on to Florida, following a brief refuelling stop in Ecuador.
Bolsonaro left after failing to hand in his passports to police - in defiance of a Supreme Court order, which had been issued as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering.
He has not been charged as part of the money laundering probe and denies any wrongdoing, calling the investigation a "politically-motivated witch hunt".
Bolsonaro added that he had never intended to leave Brazil, but argued that he was the victim of "political persecution".
He ended the letter by saying: "I left Brazil but I haven't abandoned Brazilians".
While Flávio Bolsonaro said that he planned to lead the opposition from the US, it was not clear how he planned to do that.
His party recognised the election result and while some of its politicians have described Bolsonaro as a "political exile", his campaign manager, Rogério Marinho, stated on Wednesday that "there is no evidence" of the electoral fraud that Bolsonaro alleges took place.
It is also not yet clear where Bolsonaro intends to stay or for how long.
His younger brother, Eduardo, has been in self-imposed exile in the US since March 2025, saying he was the victim of political persecution. The two siblings posted a photo of themselves holding a Brazilian flag on Wednesday.
The Trump administration has provided visas for Flávio Bolsonaro and his family but did not say what kind of visas they were.
The US president did not explicitly endorse Bolsonaro in the run-up to the election and told reporters he "won't get involved" when asked about Bolsonaro's allegations of election fraud.
Earlier in the week, he had said that "it looked like another rigged election," without providing any evidence.
And on Thursday, Trump told reporters that "the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil".
description: The defeated presidential candidate says he will lead the opposition from the US.

title: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
text:
Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".
Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.
A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.
It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.
It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".
This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.
The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of £65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.
The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.
If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.
It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.
The detail may come more quickly than feared. On welfare, the Milburn Review process is clearly heading for some sort of welfare-to-work scheme, even a separate system for younger workers.
It will cost money up front to subsidise work opportunities and hope to save more from welfare bills in the future. The chancellor saw at close quarters Gordon Brown do this twice two decades ago.
The Office for Budget Responsbility's (OBR) economic forecast showed the sheer rise in the welfare bill, which is set to jump to £431bn in 2031, if pensioner support is included.
There are two further areas where the chancellor laid down markers, with little fiscal cost, in terms of the long term plan.
On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power.
While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.
On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected.
There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.
How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge.
Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?
Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030.
The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.
A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.
But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.
description: Chancellor John Healey's plans fall short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.

title: Boys arrested in South Normanton after stolen bike report prompts police pursuit
text:
Boys held after stolen bike report prompts pursuit
Four boys have been arrested after a report of a stolen motorbike prompted a police pursuit.
Derbyshire Police said on Tuesday night, it was reported the bike had been seen driving dangerously in the Alfreton area.
Officers attended and saw a number of people on four motorbikes in Long Meadow Road, before they sped off. Two of the bikes were then seen again in Rodgers Lane and a pursuit followed.
With the help of a police helicopter, officers caught up with those two bikes in The Chine in South Normanton, and the four boys - 12, 15, 16 and 17 - were arrested.
A third bike was later found abandoned in Rodgers Lane.
Police said the 12-year-old was arrested on suspicion of dangerous driving, theft of a motor vehicle, possession of CS gas and failing to stop - while the 16-year-old was detained on suspicion of theft of a motor vehicle and possession of a bladed article.
The 15-year-old and 17-year-old were arrested on suspicion of dangerous driving, theft of a motor vehicle and failing to stop.

title: The South West reacts to Budget announcements
text:
The South West reacts to Budget announcements
Tourism and hospitality leaders have been reacting to this week's Budget.
Among the headlines in chancellor John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday were a £100 payment to help millions of households with energy bills, a VAT cut on electricity bills and a freeze on fuel duty, both extended to July.
It also announced Devon would get an elected mayor in 2028 white Cornwall was included as the only area on a pathway to become a Foundation Strategic Authority.
Sue Jewell, chair of South East Cornwall Tourism Association and a holiday accommodation provider, said the budget "gave with one hand and took with the other".
As part of the Budget legal minimum wage is to rise by 3.9% in April
Jewell said: "I think it's tricky because actually I would believe that quite a lot of people in our business anyway pay over the minimum wage just to retain staff.
"However because of the cost we've cut back on staff.
"Which is sad really because it's local people who could be having local jobs."
Dr Harry Pitts, senior lecturer in Politics at the University of Exeter's Cornwall Campus, said the £100 energy payment was one of the "small things to make life a little easier for some households in the immediate period".
Anyone living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment", funded by extra tax on banks.
The Budget announced the threshold at which high street shops start paying business rates in England was to be increased from £12,000 to £18,000, meaning businesses would pay no rates on properties with a rateable value below this level.
Toby Parkins, interim ceo at the Cornwall Chamber of Commerce, said he predicted this would benefit about 900 extra businesses in Cornwall.
"For the small business that is a big win," he said.
Helen Wylde-Archibald, from the Devon Chamber of Commerce, said she "welcomed some stability".
"The last two have been a bit scary for business," she said, referring to previous Budgets.
She added: "It doesn't necessarily give us all the conditions we want for full growth and strong growth, but the main thing was there was no broad base business tax rises and fuel duty remains frozen until July."
She said she didn't think there was enough in the way of announcements of more support for farming and food, and this had "an impact on the rural economy".
James Kittow, from Butcher & Grazier in Cornwall, said: "It just seems like we've been forgotten again.
"We're an industry that is ready, willing and able to help the country produce the food for the nation."
He added there was no change on inheritance tax for farmers. Since April, inherited farming assets worth more than £2.5m face 20% inheritance tax
"I'm looking to plan for a succession... we want to keep farming, we want to keep doing what we love doing but if we're going to get hit on the other end of it then it does make you think twice about what is all this for, and it's just so sad for the future farmers that want to come into the trade," he said.
'Existing property'
Andrea Drew, managing director at Lander Mortgage Services, said the key announcement relating to housing was a scheme for first time buyers, and a a "First Time Buyer Isa".
This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus.
"The only negative I would say... on new builds, the housing market isn't just all about new builds, it's about existing property... because not everybody wants to have a new build property," she said.
She added: "The other thing was about the increase in tax for landlords so, they're increasing the tax by 4%."
She said she'd seen landlords who decided to sell their property because of the amount of tax but tenants couldn't afford to buy the homes.
"What tenants need is more homes to choose from, not fewer, and they can't solve the housing shortage by destroying people who are providing the housing," she said.

title: Avon and Somerset Police chief calls for clearer e-scooter laws
text:
Police chief calls for clearer e-scooter laws
A police chief has said she would like the law clarified around the use of e-scooters, describing the current situation as "ambiguous" and "very difficult to enforce".
The chief constable of Avon and Somerset Police Sarah Crew has been on BBC Radio Bristol's hotseat with John Darvall, answering questions from listeners.
The conversation also covered officer numbers, the early release scheme, concerns around young people wearing balaclavas and the investigation into missing student Jack O'Sullivan.
Read our main takeaways from the show below.
Clear up law on e-scooters
E-scooter trials launched in Bristol and Bath in 2020, making it legal to ride a rental scooter within a designated area. But e-scooters that are not part of the trial cannot legally be ridden on public property.
That means a 15.5 mph rental scooter may be lawful in a trial area, while an almost identical privately-owned scooter is not.
The Chief Constable said the force has seized about 150 e-scooters this year, but would like the law to be clearer to help with enforcement.
She said there is a "lack of understanding" among the public about what is and isn't allowed.
"Every chief constable in the country would want this cleared up," she added.
More officers needed
Crew said she was "acutely aware" that the force is "under-resourced". A recent internal analysis suggested they need 100-200 additional officers to meet demand.
Across the country, the average number of officers is 236 per 100,000 people, and higher in areas with a major city. But in Avon and Somerset, there are 187 officers per 100,000.
"When there's an emergency, things that aren't an immediate or urgent threat to life at that moment back up and get into a queue", she explained, as she apologised to a stalking victim who waited 17 hours for a response.
The Chief Constable also said the early release of prisoners was also adding to pressures on the force, suggesting the cost to her force may be around £4 million per year.
"There is a system failure within our public services," she said.
Crew said police find themselves on the "front line" of dealing with a range of mental health and social care issues.
"If the root cause issues haven't been addressed in custody then they're in our communities," she added.
Concerns on balaclavas
Many callers wanted to ask what was being done about young people wearing balaclavas on bikes, which was described by one listener as "intimidating".
Police only have the power to ask them to take balaclavas off "in certain circumstances" such as protests where facial coverings have been prohibited and orders have been put in place, Crew explained.
In Nottingham, the city council introduced restrictions, giving officers the power to ask people to remove balaclavas if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or anti-social behaviour.
Crew said her force was committed to dealing with antisocial behaviour but declined to say whether balaclavas should be banned by local councils in the area.
"I didn't know quite the level of concern about balaclavas specifically," she said.
"If we [the police and council] are seeing a problem, we come together, we look to solve that," she added.
'No stone unturned'
The parents of missing student Jack O'Sullivan have said they want his case to be investigated by a different police force.
Crew said the force had already bought in expertise from elsewhere and was continuing to do so.
"We've brought in experts, specialists, we've had peer reviews, help from the National Crime Agency," she said. "Every line of inquiry has been followed."
"There is an investigator and a team at the College of Policing ready to come in and look at aspects of the force's investigation," Crew added.
Crew said: "Everyone has exactly the same aim, and that is to find Jack."
"I can't imagine how it feels to be Jack's parents. We will leave no stone unturned," she added.
