title: Young musician Daniel Towriss 'lives on' through new foundation
text:
Family set up charity in music-loving son's memory
A family has set up a charity to help aspiring musicians in memory of their music-loving son who died earlier this year.
Dan Towriss, 24, from Rotherham, was autistic and his sudden death in July "left the biggest hole in my heart", said his mother Jennifer.
His father, Nick, said the family had set up a charitable foundation in Dan's honour to help young people "learn music, experience music and find the joy in music".
The charity One More Song takes its name from something Dan used to do at the gigs he played, said Nick, who acted as his roadie.
Dan was found dead at his computer on 11 July by his mother and although he had been ill, the family said that was not related to his sudden passing. Tests are still being carried out to find out the cause of death.
Dan's funeral took place in August.
"Dan often struggled with his mental health, but music was his outlet," said Nick.
"A self-taught singer songwriter who just loved to play at any given opportunity, he gave so much of his time helping others, making people happy bringing them together."
Jennifer said the foundation would "mean other young people can also play and write music, sing, dance or perform and grow a talent and a confidence in music where they may have challenges they need a little help to overcome."
National music charity Young Sounds UK has underlined the importance of access to musical instruments and lessons for young people.
Its chief executive, Hester Cockcroft, said many of the talented people it supported had autism or were neurodivergent in some way.
"The benefits of confidence-building can be particularly noticeable where young people might struggle at school, maybe academically or because they've got additional needs," she said.
"To be able to express themselves creatively and emotionally is such a positive thing."
Nick said music acted as a social bridge that helped his son connect with other people.
"In his honour, we want to create a foundation where we can help young musicians between the age of 16 to 24 get into music, whether that's by donating musical instruments to them, or guiding them into pathways for singing lessons or performing," he said.
"The foundation is in its infancy but we want Dan's legacy to outlive us."

title: Stolen sousaphones and samba drums leaves music group 'absolutely gutted'
text:
Stolen sousaphones and samba drums leave music group 'absolutely devastated'
An Edinburgh-based community music group is appealing for help after a van carrying their musical equipment was stolen.
Oi Musica said the white Ford Transit van, nicknamed "Big J", was stolen between Sunday evening and Monday morning, along with nearly all their samba drums, two sousaphones, and much more of the group's equipment and personal belongings.
Speaking to BBC Radio Scotland, Oi Musica co-director Olivia Furness said: "I'm absolutely gutted, you know that sinking feeling that you get when you realise something like this has happened. I'm absolutely devastated."
She said the group, which specialises in large brass ensembles, street drumming and outdoor performance, was trying to keep going by using borrowed equipment.
Oi Musica was founded in 2011 and aims to use the music of street bands to bring people and communities together.
One of its main projects is Brass Blast, which is an award-winning project that offers accessible opportunities to learn an instrument and play in a band as part of an after-school programme.
Its aim is to increase the low number of disadvantaged young people taking up instruments in East Edinburgh.
The group had a range of events planned this week including the Brass Blast youth project and performances with primary school children in Greenock.
Furness said: " We are doing everything we can to keep our programme running, we didn't cancel Brass Blast on Tuesday.
"We managed to borrow drums from connections we have in the street band community.
"We're trying to keep our show on the road and keep our programme running despite this."
Furness said the response to the companies appeal for information on social media had been "incredible", with their Facebook post having almost 3,000 shares.
She called the support "really surprising and a little overwhelming".
The van was stolen from Westbank Street in the Portobello area of Edinburgh.
Furness said: "I don't think it was targeted for the contents, I think it's just quite a desirable van to steal."
"They're (the samba drums) not going to have a huge amount of value to a group of people that doesn't play those instruments, there is not a huge demand for them," she said.
Furness said the sousaphones, a large brass instrument like a tuba family which is designed to wrap around the player's body so it can be easily carried and played while marching, could have some value but they are really quite niche.
She hopes that the unique nature of the instruments will help them be spotted easier if they appear on musical instrument resale sites.

title: Plan to replace 11 Hertfordshire councils with four unitaries axed
text:
Hertfordshire councils' restructure plans dropped
Plans to abolish 11 councils in Hertfordshire and replace them with four unitary authorities have been dropped by the government.
It means elections for its existing councils will go ahead based on current county boundaries in May 2027, with shadow elections for any new authorities due to take place no earlier than May 2028.
Mayor of Watford, Liberal Democrat Peter Taylor, said: "This whole process has been a shambles. Today's announcement creates even more uncertainty for councils and local communities."
Local government minister, Jim McMahon, said "every area [in the country] will have an outcome by early next year", with plans for Hertfordshire's future remaining under consideration.
The proposals were unveiled in July, but only six of the existing 11 authorities in Hertfordshire supported the model of four unitary councils, with others preferring either two or three councils to serve a population of 1.2m.
However, local government secretary Angela Rayner announced a pause in the plans for the county in September along with 19 other areas, after receiving legal advice.
The government said it was now minded to go-ahead with reorganisation in five areas across the country, but will also consider the best way forward for all remaining areas, including Hertfordshire.
McMahon said: "All options and proposals in these areas will remain under consideration and I will approach all those with an open mind. As such, it should not be assumed that the same proposal will be automatically selected.
"We will move faster where we can, and some of the remaining areas may receive an outcome decision before others."
The changes are part of the government's plan for wider devolution of power away from Westminster, and ministers said the new all-purpose or "unitary" councils should have populations of 500,000 or more.
The government has also confirmed it will release half of the allocated transition funding, approximately £2m, to Hertfordshire in November, with the remaining funding provided once a final decision had been reached.
But Taylor said: "Proper assessments of the various reorganisation proposals should have been done before the government announced their decision in July.
"Hard-pressed councils have already spent a lot of time and money on this. Now we're left with even more uncertainty and rising costs.
"This is a terrible way to treat councils and communities."
However, in Wednesday's Budget, Chancellor John Healey said Hertfordshire could soon get an elected mayor, who would make key decisions about transport, housing and infrastructure.
The government said it expected elections for the role to be held on the same day as the shadow elections, in May 2028.
Angie Ridgwell, from the Hertfordshire Local Government Reorganisation programme, said: "While today's announcement means there is no confirmed reorganisation model for Hertfordshire, work across the county will continue.
"We will now carefully consider the implications of this announcement on Hertfordshire's LGR programme and the work to establish a Mayoral Strategic Authority for Hertfordshire."

title: Staffordshire ceramics firm takes 'giant leap' towards building on the Moon
text:
Ceramics firm takes 'giant leap' towards building on the Moon
A company says it has turned Moon dust into "solid pellets", which could pave the way to produce bricks on the Moon's surface.
Scientific consultancy firm Lucideon, based in Staffordshire, said the process involved firing electricity directly at the dust, which solidified it.
The innovation would help to "lay the foundations for humanity's next giant leap," said the company.
"It's not quite bricks yet, but it's on the way," said the company's chief executive, Tony Kinsella.
"If we are going to survive [on the Moon], the Moon still gets hit by objects from the rest of space. You need something that can be strong enough to withstand the odd pebble or rock missile coming in from outer space… so that's the 'why'."
The technology builds on decades of the region's expertise in ceramics to transform its traditional knowledge into advanced materials innovation, said the company.
The research was carried out as part of a programme funded by the European Space Agency.
The firm said sending materials to the Moon was too expensive because of weight and space constraints, meaning it would be better to use local resources to build extra-terrestrial habitats.
"Do we want to live on the Moon? Well, it's full of rich minerals," he said.
"It has been shown that gravity can help make some products that can't be made on Earth, and therefore it's a place we have to be, man has to be there," added Kinsella.
"I think we do need to go back to the Moon, not only because it's hard, but because it's valuable."
The firm said it was able to use its expertise in ceramic processing to turn the loose powdery material that blankets the lunar surface into a more solid material.
The process, known as sintering, is commonly used in the manufacture of bricks and many ceramic products.
"Our city is all about ceramics and its great history… but we also need to look at the future of ceramics," said Kinsella.
"All of this work is about ceramics and it's going to have such an impact on our living in every way – in energy, in how we live, in batteries, how we travel, and therefore, this is part of that new dynamic in the future of ceramics."
Kinsella said he believed there would be a "colony" on the Moon within his lifetime, even if it was just a few people.
"I think we will have a small colony of people who can reside on the Moon outside a spaceship for longer than a few weeks," he added.
"In an era defined by renewed momentum in space exploration, innovations like this will shape how, and where, humans live in the future," Richard Goodhead, from the firm, added.
"And in turning lunar dust into the building blocks of possibility, Lucideon is helping to lay the foundations for humanity's next giant leap."

title: Labour MP Tony Vaughan apologises over bullying and harassment
text:
MP apologises over bullying and harassment
A Labour MP has said sorry in the House of Commons following complaints over his behaviour towards a female member of staff.
It comes as the Independent Expert Panel published a report requiring Tony Vaughan to apologise for breaching Parliament's bullying and harassment policy.
The MP for Folkestone and Hythe was found by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards to have committed the breach after a constituency staff member complained he "behaved towards [her] in an overbearing and belittling manner".
Vaughan said on Thursday he accepted the findings in full.
"As a result of these behaviours, my former colleague was upset and humiliated," he said.
"My behaviour had a real and continuing impact on her and her family, and I am truly sorry for this."
The Labour Party said it "expects the highest standards of conduct from all our members and elected representatives.
"We have robust processes in place to ensure those high standards are upheld.
"It is right that Tony Vaughan has apologised following this independent process," a spokesperson added.
'Abuse of power'
Vaughan, who has represented his Kent constituency since 2024, was found to have hugged the complainant without consent at an office event.
He also took her personal mobile phone from her hand to join an online meeting without asking permission and failed to explain why phone calls between them had ended abruptly.
Vaughan appealed the Commissioner's findings, though the Independent Expert Panel confirmed the majority of them, according to Parliament.
The sub-panel stressed that "oppressive and bullying behaviour towards [MPs'] staff members is wholly unacceptable".
It added that Vaughan's actions were breaches of "basic boundaries and courtesy" - rather than failures in management - and an "abuse of his power".
The politician told MPs on Thursday that he was not "sufficiently alert" to the power imbalances between him and his employee.
He added he recognised his behaviour could well impact on "someone who is vulnerable whether or not that is known".
"I made mistakes," Vaughan continued.
The 36-page report said it took account of the impact of what happened on the complainant, who has a right to anonymity.
She said she was left feeling stressed, exhausted and offended, it adds.
The report also stated that Vaughan had "expressed genuine and thoughtful remorse".
He should be required to make an "unreserved apology" to the complainant and the House by way of a personal statement in the House of Commons Chamber, it continued.
"We consider that this achieves the appropriate balance and clear messaging required regarding the behaviour expected of MPs," the report said.
Vaughan added he had undertaken further training as a result of the incident.

title: Little Stonham crash victim was "special" teenager full of energy
text:
Tributes paid to 'special' teen who died in crash
A teenager who was one of two to die following a crash has been described as a "truly special person" who was "full of life and energy" by her family.
Amelia Miller, 19, of Stowmarket, was driving a red Peugeot 107 when it was involved in a crash with a silver Volkswagen Passat in Little Stonham on 18 October.
She was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge where she later died. Miller's male passenger died at the scene.
Her family members, Chris, Jo and Issac, have paid tribute to the "daughter, sister, aunty and cousin", who they said left school with "fantastic grades".
They added she had been a keen dancer before becoming a photographer, and loved heavy metal and rock music, as well as the "occasional farming song".
"She was only 19 and was so full of life and energy, a truly special person," they said.
"She loved the freedom of having a car, but her passion was motorcycles and she used to go for rides on her 125 looking for photo opportunities, which would normally include bikes or animals, often being goats.
"Amelia left an impression with everyone she met. She struggled with the school environment but left with fantastic grades.
"She really blossomed around adults in the workplace environment with her sharp mind and wit."
The crash happened in Debenham Road at about 10:15 BST. Police, paramedics, firefighters and an air ambulance were all called.
The occupants of the Volkswagen suffered minor injuries.
Police are continuing to appeal for witnesses to the collision.

title: Government withdraws contoversial plans for Leicester expansion
text:
Government withdraws plans for city expansion
The government has withdrawn a controversial plan to expand Leicester's political boundary.
On Thursday, ministers said previous proposals to create a greater Leicester council, absorbing towns and villages currently outside the city, would be reassessed.
The proposal to abolish the 10 existing councils in Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland and replace them with two larger unitary authorities has been taken off the table at this stage.
Local government minister Jim McMahon told MPs a new proposal for the political map of Leicestershire would be announced either before Christmas or early in 2027.
Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland are among nine areas, including Nottingham and Nottinghamshire, and Derby and Derbyshire, where decisions have now been withdrawn and will be reconsidered.
The government has revealed plans to go ahead in some areas, including East Sussex and Brighton, and Hove and Warwickshire.
McMahon said the government was still committed to the process of local government reorganisation (LGR) but that it had listened to local political leaders.
There have been numerous protests against the plan to expand Leicester by residents, who said they did not wish to be incorporated into an enlarged city.
Leicester city mayor Sir Peter Soulsby said: "I'm very disappointed the government is continuing to delay the decision on local government reorganisation for our area.
"This uncertainty will make it very difficult for us to proceed with the work needed to create a mayoral strategic authority."
The government had been accused of ignoring the result of its own consultation on the changes, which showed 87% of some 6,600 responses opposed city expansion.
Reform UK-led Leicestershire County Council has opposed the city expansion, threatening a legal challenge against it, and leader Dan Harrison said Thursday's announcement was "a victory for people power".
"Our legal challenge to a city expansion was already under way, and I'd like to praise our residents who have fought against this for a long time," he said.
"It's true that reshaping local councils can offer huge benefits. I remain convinced that the proposal we submitted to government, simplifying services, saving £40m a year and empowering communities, offers the best solution for the future.
"But national decision-making has been shambolic at best. The government asked councils to draw up proposals, agreed them, paused them, backtracked and now says there'll be updates later this year.
"You couldn't make it up."
Christine Wise, Liberal Democrat leader of Rutland County Council, said: "We've been waiting for the government to provide an update on LGR for almost two months.
"When the pause was first announced, we pushed ministers to use this time to reconsider their options and give us more evidence to support the decision they announced in July - placing Rutland into one of only two unitary authorities covering the whole of Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland (LLR).
"While it's encouraging that ministers are giving serious consideration to the concerns that have been raised, we will continue to push for the government to take an evidence-led approach to LGR. If LGR does go ahead, it must deliver financial sustainability, local accountability and better outcomes for communities."
Micheal Mullaney, leader of the Liberal Democrat group on the county council, said: "I hope the government will now scrap this unwanted change entirely or at least that any new decision would be better than the last one.
"It has been a waste of time and money."
Conservative leader of Harborough District Council Simon Whelband added: "The government's handling of this process has been deeply frustrating. Ministers have created enormous uncertainty, failed to properly address local concerns and left councils and their hardworking staff in limbo for even longer.
"We will continue to fight Leicester's proposed land grab and make the strongest possible representations to ministers.
"I will not accept any areas of Harborough District being included in any form of expanded city as part of a unitary council.
"This must be a genuine rethink, not another exercise in kicking the can down the road before imposing a decision from Whitehall."

title: Man sentenced after object from car smashed Essex Police vehicle
text:
Driver sentenced after object smashed police car
A man has been sentenced after failing to stop when an item flew from the roof of his car and smashed a police vehicle's windscreen.
Officers had been responding to an emergency on the westbound A120 in Essex at about 13:30 GMT on 19 December when the item hit their car.
Glenn Lillie was travelling on the opposite carriageway when a "large unknown item" came off the roof of his white Audi and flew over the central barrier at such a speed that it shattered the windscreen and covered officers in glass.
The section of the carriageway near Little Canfield was closed while both the police car and debris were cleared.
The 34-year-old, from Braintree, said he did not stop as he "considered it unsafe to do so".
He pleaded guilty at Colchester Magistrates' Court on 6 August to three counts related to danger of causing injury, as well as two counts of failing to stop or report the incident.
On 22 October, he was disqualified from driving for six months and given a 12-month community order including 140 hours of work.
He was ordered to pay £244 in costs and a surcharge.
PC Simon Bailey said the consequences could have been "devastating" if not for the "skill, professionalism and composure of the officer behind the wheel" to come to a controlled stop.
"Every driver has a responsibility to make sure anything they carry is properly secured before starting a journey," he said.
"This incident is a stark demonstration of how dangerous an insecure load can become."
Bailey added that their investigation involved "painstakingly" piecing together evidence, including the leftover debris and camera footage.
Caitlin Taylor, road safety manager at the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents, stressed that load security is a simple but vital part of road safety.
She said: "Unsecured loads can cause serious incidents, putting other road users at risk of injury or even death. To keep themselves and others safe, drivers should always ensure loads are properly secured before every journey and check them regularly during transit.
"Taking a few minutes to use suitable restraints such as straps, nets or covers can prevent debris from falling onto the road, and helps protect everyone using the road network."

title: Controversial plans for Devon councils withdrawn by government
text:
Controversial plans for Devon councils withdrawn
Controversial plans to replace Devon's local authorities with four new councils have been withdrawn by the government.
The plans announced in July proposed an enlarged Plymouth, Exeter and Torbay with a fourth council covering the rest of rural Devon.
Earlier this autumn ministers announced the plans had been "paused" pending a review.
Local Government Minister Jim McMahon promised Devon, along with all the other areas under review, would have a new set of proposals by early next year.
The changes are driven by the government's decision to replace the remaining county and district councils, like those in Devon, with unitarity authorities which deliver all council services under one roof.
Ministers also regard unitary authorities as the building blocks for devolution, although it was announced in the Budget that Devon could proceed with plans for a regional mayor ahead of the decision on council reorganisation.
The plans endorsed in July were those drawn up by the Labour-run city councils in Plymouth and Exeter.
They argued the large Devon Coast and Countryside Council covering most of the county was "specifically designed for rural and coastal communities, with services tailored to the challenges of dispersed, older, populations, market towns and isolated areas".
Critics dubbed it the "rural rump", an afterthought to the cities, and questioned its viability with almost all of Devon's major towns lying outside its borders.
Opposition politicians also said the proposals selected were electorally favourable to Labour.
Decisions reached in other areas of the country proved similarly controversial and the government was facing legal challenges from several councils when it paused the plans in September.
Announcing the pause, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner said: "In light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law."
The local government minister has now said all of the different proposals submitted by councils across Devon were back on the table and "as such it should not be assumed the same proposal will automatically be selected".
Devon County Council leader Julian Brazil said the announcement left a "Halloween horror show hanging over us" and warned it brought "more chaos, cost and confusion to local authorities which are already facing significant challenges".
"Instead of getting a firm decision from government, we have had more delay and indecision, and now a U-turn on how much it will contribute financially," he said.
"This makes it incredibly difficult for councils to plan their budgets, workforce and future."
He added the council would "continue to explore our legal options".
Tudor Evans, leader of Plymouth City Council, said: "Whilst we are disappointed that the government has decided to subject our local government reorganisation proposal to a further review process, this remains a once-in-a-generation opportunity to get local government reform right and that must remain the priority.
"We continue to believe our proposal offers the best future for Plymouth, Devon and Torbay and we will be ready to make that case when the review process begins."
David Thomas, leader of Torbay Council, said he was "deeply disappointed and frustrated" by the move.
He said: "Over the past year, we have invested significant time, effort and public money in developing proposals and preparing for implementation.
"At a time when local government finances are already under pressure, it is extremely frustrating that so much work has been undertaken only for the process to be delayed, creating further uncertainty for councils, residents and businesses."
While the minister has committed to all the new plans being published by the new year, he said some areas may hear sooner.

title: Spain Urda train crash: Shock of tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
text:
Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
The chaos and horror of Spain's second rail tragedy this year has been conveyed vividly by survivors of Wednesday's high-speed crash that has left at least 69 people dead.
But as Spain holds three days of mourning, revelations from leaked audio recordings of the apparent human error in a control room in the minutes before this disaster happened have given way to public disbelief and outrage, in a highly politicised climate, exactly a month before Spaniards go to the polls.
"You don't know what's happening, you don't know what has happened, you just know that you're being thrown around in a matter of seconds," said Iñaki García, 60.
He was on the stationary Iryo train that was rammed from behind by a Renfe train on the Madrid-Seville line near Urda, around 140km (87 miles) south of the capital.
"There were people injured, walking around, there were dead people," he said. "In the next carriage along there were a lot of dead people."
Recalling the horrific scenes around him, one young man told the BBC in a quivering voice: "I don't know if that's something I'll ever recover from."
Stories of tragedy have continued to emerge. A pharmacist from Urda was one of the first to reach the scene, bringing with him first aid supplies and medicine.
"One of [the passengers] was saying goodbye to his wife and children. His last words were 'God is good'," Antonio García told Spanish radio.
Similar scenes of grief played out only nine months ago in the southern village of Adamuz, when a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people.
Now, in the town of Urda, just like Adamuz, awful stories are combined with acts of kindness and solidarity.
Locals turned out to help the injured, bringing blankets, food and water to a nearby sports hall that was converted into a makeshift hospital for much of the day.
"We all started to turn out to help and we organised ourselves as best we could," said Rosa María Domínguez, a local woman, who described the scene as "a horror film".
However, the overriding sentiment that these two tragedies have generated is one of confusion and a failure to comprehend how this could have happened.
Not long ago, the speed, efficiency and safety of Spain's high-speed rail system, the largest in Europe, was the envy of its neighbours.
The Adamuz crash triggered a nationwide debate about whether the network was fit for purpose.
This latest incident intensifies pressure on the left-wing government of Pedro Sánchez, in the middle of an election campaign where his Socialist PSOE is behind the conservatives in most opinion polls.
On Wednesday night a demonstration protesting at the government's handling of the rail network saw far-right groups turn out and clash with police.
Although the main parties, other than the far-right Vox, have suspended campaigning, Sánchez has twice visited the scene of the crash and his People's Party rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo came to Urda on Thursday.
Sánchez's transport minister, Óscar Puente, made clear from the start that a computer failure followed by human error was the likely cause of the crash. By late evening, leaked audio recordings of a control-room operator talking to train drivers appeared to back that up.
Puente has long been a hate figure for the right, and with two of the worst rail tragedies in Spanish history taking place on his watch, the criticism is only going to increase.
Spain's biggest train drivers' union Semaf condemned the leak of audio recordings as irresponsible and slanted. The union had already called a strike for Thursday in a bid to ensure that "urgency to travel is never prioritised over safety".
One train driver, Vicente Almenar, told Spanish media: "They always look for the last link in the chain, where it's weakest, but here the entire procedure failed because we don't even know what our colleague was seeing on the screen," he told Spanish media.
Sánchez had not been expecting rail safety to dominate his campaign, but that now looks increasingly likely.
After two accidents and more than 100 deaths on the same high-speed line, Feijóo told reporters in Urda on Thursday: "The Spanish people need answers. They are wondering what is happening to high-speed rail in their country."
And he emphasised that politics was not about talking - it was about acting.
description: The latest train crash will pile pressure on the government of Pedro Sánchez, one month before the general election.

title: Jacksepticeye: YouTuber talks Hitman, Bloodborne and new projects
text:
'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out
The world's changed a lot since Seán McLoughlin, better known to 31 million subscribers as Jacksepticeye, began making YouTube videos.
He started uploading in 2012, in what many people consider to be the platform's "golden age" when vlogging, video game playthroughs and comedy escapism were all the rage.
Like many in the content creation space, he's been branching out in recent years, taking more acting jobs and getting involved in film production.
BBC Newsbeat caught up with McLoughlin to talk about his new role, his work on bringing one of his favourite video games to the big screen and why he misses the "whimsical" days of the internet.
McLoughlin got famous playing video games, and these days there's a good chance you'll see - or hear - him in one.
After a role in the 2025 superhero adventure Dispatch, McLoughlin's got a new role in Hitman, the successful "assassination simulator" from Danish studio IO Interactive.
He plays controversial content creator Finn Colton, known as Finnvictus.
Although the fictional character shares McLoughlin's likeness and voice, he says the "manosphere-adjacent influencer" is not based on him.
As the name of the game suggests, players aren't there to collab with him.
He's one of the celebrity "elusive targets" Hitman's developers occasionally place in the game to encourage returning fans.
"If you love me it'll be funny to play and you'll get to kill me in different ways," says McLoughlin.
"If you hate me maybe that's even more fun to play."
It's not the first time McLoughlin's worked with IO - he appeared, briefly, in their James Bond game 007: First Light earlier this year.
He'd hoped to watch other streamers react to the blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo, but says many of his friends missed it.
"This time you're forced to interact with me," he says, even if that does involve thinking of imaginative ways to kill him off.
Earlier this year, McLoughlin was also unveiled as a producer on an animated movie version of Bloodborne, one of the highest-rated video games of all time.
Some parts of its passionate fan base reacted negatively to the announcement, questioning the YouTuber's credentials.
McLoughlin reassured them he's a huge fan of the games and has a tattoo of a Hunter's Mark - one of the game's key items - to prove it.
He's described himself as a "vibe-checker" and sees it as his responsibility to make sure the adaptation is done properly.
"If it feels off, especially with something like Bloodborne, people can feel it immediately, even if they don't know what they're pointing towards," he says.
"They know the game so well that if the atmosphere, or the world, or the vibe feels off, they'll pick up on it pretty fast."
McLoughlin says he's been trying to pick people for the project who have ideally played Bloodborne and "have a feeling" for what it's all about.
"I feel like I have good instincts on what works and what doesn't and what I like and what I don't like," he says.
"So the producing side of it fits a lot more naturally for me right now."
'Rise of anti-communities'
Screen adaptations are a big trend in video games at the moment, but they're not the only thing seizing the industry.
Hitman's new mission lands just weeks before the launch of the hugely-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
It won't be released on disc at launch, a move that's arguably accelerated the game industry's move towards digital-only games.
McLoughlin, who fondly remembers PlayStation cases on a bedroom shelf and getting new games for Christmas, says "it would suck to see physical games disappear completely".
"Just in terms of the humanity behind it all, I think it would be a shame to see that stuff disappear because it's a magical experience," he says.
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in video game development is another hot topic at the moment.
Earlier this month, Epic Games, makers of Fortnite, announced a "pivot" towards using AI as a primary development tool.
Like many players, McLoughlin's opposed to its use.
So no chance of seeing a Jacksepticeye Fortnite skin any time soon?
"I think the chances of that happening were already zero before anything related to that even happened," he says.
"But now it's definitely, definitely unlikely."
Physical games, GenAI and content creators' career moves are sure to generate discourse, and conversations online are another thing McLoughlin thinks have changed since he started out.
He says there's been a "rise of anti-communities", where people will "rush to condemn a film or game before it's even been released".
"I'm just sad that the internet is such an angry place these days," he says.
"It's just zero to a thousand immediately. I think we're just not there in terms of having nuanced discussions about anything.
"But I think that's just endemic of the internet in general."
McLoughlin thinks that could be linked to people's real life worries.
"Right now, it's just people are angry in general, just at the world," he says.
"So it's harder to interact with stuff online these days.
"It's a less whimsical space. But hopefully that's something that can change."
McLoughlin's doing his bit to bring people together in December with his annual Thankmas event.
The fundraiser took a break last year but its returning to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation.
"I think it's a nice little pinprick of light in the middle of everything else going on," he says.
And while he's not afraid to speak his mind, he says he is mindful of letting others do the talking sometimes.
"I'm trying to get better about not giving an opinion about absolutely everything any more," he says.
"Because I think there's too much of that in the world."
description: He got famous playing video games but now you're more likely to see Seán McLoughlin in one.

title: Former Thames Valley University site to undergo £640m revamp
text:
Former uni site's £640m revamp plan gets go-ahead
A £640m regeneration scheme to "transform" a former university site and deliver more than 1,500 homes has been approved.
Homes England, the government's housing and regeneration agency, bought the former Thames Valley University site in Slough in 2023.
Its head of development, Ian Knight, told Slough councillors who approved the project on Wednesday that it is planning "transformational change" for the town centre.
The development, known as the North West Quadrant, is the latest major project for housing in Slough town centre, following plans to use the Queensmere Shopping Centre for 1,600 homes.
Homes England's project, which is a joint venture between developer Muse, also includes a multi-storey car park and an 86-pupil nursery.
The phased development will also bring forward restaurants, an office block, shops, cafes, gyms and other commercial spaces.
No affordable housing will be delivered at the site for now to keep the plan deliverable, councillors were told.
Daniel Ray, the council's director of planning, said a viability assessment was "rigorously interrogated" to ensure that was the case.
There are measures in place to review if affordable homes can be delivered later in the scheme, he added, but for the first phase, affordable housing is "absolutely" not viable.
Ray said: "We do know that [Homes England] will be committed, wherever possible, to deliver as many affordable homes as possible.
"That is within their mission statement. That's what they're doing on behalf of the government."
The redevelopment will be broken down into three main phases, with the first phase expected to start in 2027, which will deliver 501 flats and 325 co-living units.
Another 331 apartments will come forward in the second phase, as well as the children's nursery and a multi-storey car park.
The final phase, expected to start in 2034 and finish by 2037, will see a "substantial" office block and up to 382 apartments.
The former Thames Valley University, now known as the University of West London, closed its Slough site in 2010. It retains campuses in Reading, Ealing and Brentford.
description: Homes England and developer Muse plan to build 1,500 homes on the former university site.

title: Punch from Billy Allison which killed pub boss in Lichfield was 'loud and forceful'
text:
Punch that killed pub boss was 'loud and forceful'
The partner of a pub landlord who was killed by a single punch has told a jury the man accused of murdering him "appeared out of nowhere".
Rebecca Mullally told Stafford Crown Court she was with Matthew O'Gara and friends at the Ricco and Loren bar in Lichfield, Staffordshire, when Billy Allison punched O'Gara suddenly in the head.
She described the attack, which broke several bones in his neck and split an artery supplying blood to the brain, as quick, loud and forceful.
Allison denies murdering O'Gara but has admitted manslaughter. The 36-year-old also admitted inflicting grievous bodily harm against another man, Adam Cooper, during the same incident, but denied doing so intentionally.
Cooper, who was part of a group at the bar with O'Gara and others, suffered a fractured eye socket, a fractured nose and damage to a dental implant, the court was told.
Allison, of Cropthorne Road in Shirley, Solihull, was not someone O'Gara's partner had seen before and she had not seen any interaction between him and O'Gara or other members of their group, she told the court.
O'Gara had his back to Allison when the punch came, she said.
She was visibly upset at times while giving evidence in the witness stand.
"I'd never see a punch like that before," she told the court. "I did think 'has that killed him?' It was hard."
She said her partner had gone to get a drink from the bar and then went to the toilet. When he came back, a song he liked was playing and he was dancing to it.
"I was stood by him, dancing in the group, and then basically he just got punched in the left side of his head.
It was audible above the noise from the speakers in the bar, she said.
"It was really fast and really quick, really loud. I heard the punch because it was really forceful."
She described how her day had begun with looking after her horse and a dog walk, before heading to The Plough in Huddlesford, where O'Gara was landlord.
There, she chatted and drank with friends sat outside, adding that her partner was in a "happy" mood having just watched his team Tottenham Hotspur beat Everton on the television that afternoon.
They had decided to go out to Lichfield in the evening and the group hired two Ubers to get there.
They started off at the Duke of York before moving on to Ricco and Loren.
The jury was shown a map of the route and shown CCTV images of the moments leading up to the attack.
Mullally described Allison as being "really tall, really broad shoulders, he was very big."
He was much larger than her partner, who she said was 5ft 7 and "medium build".
She said that after the punch, she noticed O'Gara's face turning blue and called paramedics, urging them to hurry.
People from the bar assisted him, she said, before police and ambulance crews arrived.
She said she noticed Allison remained in the corner of the dance floor but then left through a back door, and had not seen him afterwards.
Later, she described seeing Cooper outside and noticing that he too had been hurt.
"He was crying and he looked like he'd got black eyes, blood on his face," she said.
Earlier, the jury had heard how Allison, had been visiting Lichfield with a group of friends including his girlfriend Charlotte Dean and friends Ryan Bridge and Ben Cullen, and had been drinking throughout the day before the attack on the two men, who he did not know.
Footage from a courtyard at the back of the bar taken after the attack showed Cooper receiving help in a wooden shelter and Allison leaving through a gate.
The jury was told how after he left the scene, Allison swapped t-shirts with Cullen, and had tried to pull the top over his head to conceal his face from a camera.
The trial at Stafford Crown Court continues.

title: Worcestershire north-south council split to go ahead in 2029
text:
Worcestershire north-south split to go ahead in 2029
A historic shake-up of councils across Worcestershire is set to go ahead despite a 12-month delay - with the county due to be carved in two.
Local government minister Jim McMahon has confirmed a prior decision to establish two new unitary councils for Worcestershire is now set to be implemented after a review - but only in 2029, a year later than planned.
The move will see all the county's current councils abolished - the biggest change since 1974.
Council leader Matthew Jenkins, said: "It's not ideal, but at least it gives us clarity of where we are going now." Adam Kent, his deputy, described the delay as "madness".
The new north Worcestershire council will provide services across the Wyre Forest, Bromsgrove and Redditch, while its southern counterpart will do the same in Worcester, Malvern and Wychavon.
The decision comes amid major financial problems at Worcestershire County Council, which will now have to plan to exist for 12 months longer than envisaged.
The authority, which is led by a Green-Lib Dem-independent coalition, is battling with an estimated budget shortfall of £98m next year and has already stated it will require more emergency government support.
Jenkins, Green councillor, added: "Particularly with our finances, we'd have preferred to have made these changes [in 2028], but the government will have its reasons for pushing it back.
"But at least the clarity is good - across local government many authorities are in the same position."
His deputy Adam Kent, who had been in favour of having just one unitary council for the county, described the 12-month delay as "madness"
"This means all the district council elections will have to go ahead next year, so we'll be asking people to vote for councils that will very soon be abolished," he said.
"It's absolutely barking - we'll have to prepare for another county council budget when we thought we'd be planning to wind the authority down."
Speaking in parliament, local government secretary Jim McMahon said the announcement was about "providing some clarity on what comes next".
"Yesterday's budget showed we're committed to giving local leaders, local councils and local communities the tools to shape their own future," he said.
"The decisions that we take now will be the building blocks for how this country is governed for generations to come."
He also said there would be a "short period of time" where people could make final representations to him, before the decision is fully signed off.
The leaders of all six district councils across Worcestershire have released a statement saying they are "in a strong position" to respond, due to all the "preparatory work" that has already been done.
It added: "We now look forward to moving forward and remain committed to continuing to provide services to our residents, while focussing on delivering the best possible outcomes for our communities across Worcestershire."

title: Motion laid to limit length of Budget debate speeches in Guernsey
text:
Motion to limit length of Budget debate speeches
Moves are being made to limit the length of speeches in the States' Budget debate.
There are 30 amendments lodged for the debate which is due to take place from 3 November, which include increasing social housing spending and free bus travel.
The Policy and Resources Committee has laid out a motion to limit speeches to either seven and a half minutes for opening speeches and five minutes for debates, or nine minutes for opening speeches and six minutes for debates.
Speeches were limited during the States' tax debate at the start of October, a change several politicians later credited with helping the assembly complete the debate within six days.
The Forward Guernsey Party pushed for limiting speeches during the tax debate.
Party member deputy Rhona Humphreys said she was "pleased" to see Policy and Resources' motion to limit them again.
"It worked very efficiently in the tax debate," she said.
"We got to an answer at the end of the tax debate, so I can understand why Policy and Resources have done the same thing again.
"I think we all know now we can prepare our speeches to the right length.
"So hopefully, 30 amendments, we've got four days, we should be able to get through it and have proper debate about the Budget, which, of course, comes after the debate on all the amendments."
Humphreys said she does not think limiting speeches will become the standard and she does not think they should.
"I think there is actually some really good value in having some time to rehearse arguments and understand things properly," she said.
"I do think it's beholden on us to make a decision about budget and it was beholden on us to make a decision about tax and these methods help."

title: Lanny actor, 9, shares joy at getting lead role in Bristol Old Vic play
text:
Boy's joy at getting lead role in play aged nine
A nine-year-old who landed a leading role in a play with no professional acting experience says he "screamed the house down" when he found out.
Atlas Johnson-Dutfield from Bristol is sharing the role of Lanny with fellow youngster Lucian Thomas, 10, in the stage adaptation of Max Porter's acclaimed novel Lanny.
Atlas' mum Jada Johnson-Dutfield said she initially "felt sick" with nerves when watching him perform - but this was then overtaken by pride.
The young actor got the part following an open audition by the Bristol Old Vic theatre.
Atlas said he felt "super-duper happy" when he found out he had got the role.
"I shouted yes and fist pumped... dad was so confused and wondering why we were screaming," he added.
Based on the bestselling novel by Max Porter, Lanny has been adapted for the stage by West Country playwright Bea Roberts.
The play tells the story of Lanny and his family moving to a village near Bristol and awakening Dead Papa Toothwort, a mythic figure listening from the woods.
"Lanny is different from all the other kids and is connected to nature in a different way that other people can't see. He's different in a good way," Atlas said.
He added that he and Lucian, who share the part of Lanny, are now "like stage brothers".
Atlas' mother said her son had gone to acting classes after watching children in the Lion King stage show at the age of seven, at which point he asked if he could be in a play one day.
Describing the moment she first watched her son on stage himself, Johnson-Dutfield said: "When I first saw him up there it was just odd. I'll be honest I felt quite sick.
"I couldn't focus on the play. I was thinking 'I don't want this to go wrong'."
"After that I got over it, there was pride. I was just watching him in the whole process and seeing him grow," she added.

title: CCTV shows frying pan used to stop Huntingdon train attacker
text:
CCTV shows frying pan used to stop train attacker
CCTV footage of a crew member using a frying pan to fend off a knifeman aboard a train has been shown in court.
Prosecutor Christopher Paxton KC said Samir Zitouni showed "sheer courage and bravery in seeking to save lives and defend others", during the mass stabbing on the Doncaster to London King's Cross train.
Jurors at Cambridge Crown Court saw footage of Zitouni using the pan against Anthony Williams, before the train made an unscheduled stop at Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025.
Williams, 33, of Langford Road, Peterborough, denies attempting to murder 10 people aboard the train, three people in Peterborough the day before and a boy at a London railway station.
The trial has been told that whether Williams carried out the attacks was not in question, but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill those individuals.
On the second day of the trial, Paxton told jurors the attack on Zitouni was "prolonged, persistent and brutal".
Zitouni was said to have told the defendant: "We love you, we can help you."
Other CCTV footage played in court showed people fleeing the train.
Zitouni, in what Paxton called a "blood-soaked shirt", appeared "to be one of the last off the train", and Paxton said he fell "between, essentially, the gap between the train and the platform".
The court heard both of Zitouni's lungs had been punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.
Paxton earlier said one of the passengers, Raza Aslam, had grabbed a frying pan, but was stabbed in the hand by Williams.
He said Zitouni started throwing things at the defendant and "saved" Aslam's life.
Jurors also heard that Aslam told police Williams "had the greatest delight on his face".
Aslam said: "I saw his eyes expand with pleasure. I saw the contempt on his face, like a person who's high.
"He was just loving every single moment. He loved seeing us in desperation."
Paxton also told the jury how there was hand-to-hand fighting on the train.
He said Sachin Balakrishnan was stabbed in the forearm and chest, which punctured a lung and was "just centimetres from his heart".
The jury heard a call Stephen Crean made to 999 from a locked toilet on the train, telling the operator he had been stabbed "all over" and left "covered in blood".
Commenting on CCTV footage, Paxton said: "You can see the panic, you can see the fear in the faces of those fleeing.
"In this storm of violence, and even when gripped by fear, many there on that train helped others and, as we will see, some stood tall, quite literally, against the defendant's violent onslaught."
Jurors also heard how Scott Green had been travelling on the train with his dog, Poppy.
Paxton said: "He thought he was going to lose his life on the train when the defendant tried to stab him for the third time.
"It seems, members of the jury, that Poppy the dog, for Mr Green at least, saved the day and sent the defendant running off.
"You will hear that in an unrelated incident the defendant had previously been bitten by a dog."
During Thursday's evidence, the court was also told of an attack on 73-year-old David Presland, who had been stabbed in the back while on his hands and knees.
Presland said he had been "helped by someone he knew as Kevin" - believed to be Kevin Deely, another of those Williams is accused of attempting to murder.
Paxton told the court the events were "all over in about five minutes", adding: "In that time, 10 men are stabbed by one man, this defendant, Mr Williams."
Williams is accused of attempting to murder Aslam, Balakrishnan, Crean, Deely, Green, Presland and Zitouni on the train between Peterborough and Huntingdon on the Saturday evening, along with Scott Bletcher, Jonathan Gjoshe and Michael Paffett.
He is also accused of attempting to murder a 14-year-old boy and Dawid Taborski on a footbridge near Henry Penn Walk in Peterborough on 31 October, and William Ogelby at Railworld car park in the city shortly afterwards.
The trial continues.

title: Rwandan genocide: Eric Nshimiye convicted in US for lying about role in the killings
text:
US convicts Rwandan man who hid genocide role for decades
A Rwandan man has been convicted in the US of lying under oath about his involvement in the 1994 genocide during the trial of a former university classmate.
A federal jury in Boston found Eric Nshimiye, 54, guilty of perjury and obstruction of justice charges stemming from his testimony in the 2019 immigration fraud trial of Jean Leonard Teganya, who was also accused of participating in the atrocities.
Nshimiye fled Rwanda for Kenya in 1994 and was admitted to the US as a refugee the following year.
About 800,000 people, mostly from Rwanda's minority Tutsi community, were killed by ethnic Hutu extremists during the 100-day genocide.
Prosecutors said Nshimiye concealed his involvement in the genocide to secure entry into the country.
Evidence presented at his trial showed that, while a student at the University of Rwanda in Butare, he took part in attacks of the Tutsi people, including by striking them on the head with a club.
He faces up to five years in prison for each of the four perjury counts and a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for obstruction of justice.
He is due to be sentenced on 26 January 2027.
"For nearly three decades, this defendant concealed his involvement in the 1994 Rwandan genocide and the heinous acts of violence he committed, including clubbing people to death," US justice department prosecutor Tysen Duva said.
"Then he lied to immigration officials in order to become a US citizen, and he lied to a federal jury to protect himself and a fellow perpetrator of the Rwandan genocide," Duva said.
Nshimiye's lawyer, Kurt Kerns, said in a statement that they were "obviously disappointed with the verdict" and would pursue "all avenues of relief".
During his opening statement at the trial in October, Kerns argued that the charges were based on "fabricated accusations", saying Nshimiye was not in Butare when the violence began.
He also said Nshimaye was charged only after testifying as a character witness for Teganya, his former university classmate.
Teganya was sentenced to eight years in jail in 2019 for what prosecutors described as "the most serious form of immigration fraud", after lying about his involvement in the genocide.
He was also accused of participating in at least seven murders and five rapes, but denied being involved in the genocide.

title: Surrey teacher banned over images with 'revenge porn' hallmarks
text:
Teacher ban over images with 'revenge porn' hallmarks
A teacher at a school for children with complex needs has been banned from the profession indefinitely for sending unsolicited images of female genitalia and a sex toy to a colleague.
Alastair Grandison, 51, sent the pornographic images to a colleague while employed at St Dominic's School, in Godalming, Surrey, in 2022.
The Teaching Regulation Agency (TRA) said his behaviour "had the hallmarks of revenge pornography".
A spokesperson for St Dominic's said the school did not wish to comment.
On the morning of 13 October 2022, Grandison messaged one colleague to say "thank you for being so tolerant of such an un-PC and quite probably offensive sense of humour".
He messaged the same colleague later that day: "Yikes! Actually, I like it when you get serious and tell me off. Not sure why exactly."
The colleague said Grandison's comments made her "skin crawl".
Grandison was given an informal warning for his behaviour, but the following month sent 13 explicit images, including of breasts and female genitalia, to another colleague.
Among those images were misogynistic comments.
This colleague told the TRA that prior to receiving the pornographic images he and Grandison had never exchanged messages.
The panel said Grandison's behaviour had the hallmarks of the offence of revenge pornography otherwise known as image-based sexual abuse - when an individual shares private, sexual material of another person without their consent.
In a disciplinary hearing in 2023, separate to the TRA hearing, Grandison blamed sending the messages on being drunk while taking anti-depressants.
The TRA looked at this as part of its investigation but said it found no substantiating medical evidence, nor any sign of alcohol misuse.
Grandison is now banned from teaching in England indefinitely. He may not apply for the ban to be overturned until 2031.
St Dominic's School told the BBC it did not wish to comment on the incident.

title: Cappadocia: Rock collapse kills two in Turkey's Cappadocia, local media reports
text:
Rock collapse kills two in Turkey's Cappadocia, local media reports
At least two people have been killed and five injured after a rock formation collapsed at a tourist site in Turkey's historical region of Cappadocia, local media is reporting.
One of the rock spires, which are known as fairy chimneys, reportedly disintegrated at the popular open-air museum in the central town of Göreme.
Nevşehir provincial Governor Hüseyin Kök said the victims' bodies had been recovered from under the rubble, but the justice minister warned there could be "other potential victims" still trapped.
The cause of Thursday's incident was not immediately known, however local media reported the collapse could have been triggered by heavy rain.
Turkish media reported that the collapse happened near the entrance to the museum - a Unesco World Heritage site - at about 15:15 local time (12:15 GMT).
In a later post on social media, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said that "according to initial assessments, two individuals have lost their lives in the incident, and five others have been injured".
He added that a search and rescue operation was continuing at the site.
The Cappadocia region attracts tourists from around the world, who want to see the ancient fairy chimneys - tall, cone-shaped rock formations that are created by volcanic activity.

title: Teen killed peacemaker with punch on Newcastle night out
text:
Teen killed peacemaker with punch on night out
A killer who fatally punched a peacemaker trying to break up a fight on a night out has been jailed for four years and 10 months.
Ethan Cockram was 19 when he struck Simon Beston to the side of the face, causing the 55-year-old grandfather to fall and hit his head on a kerb in Newcastle city centre, the city's crown court heard.
The victim's family said they could never forgive his killer and felt "anger and disgust" Cockram and his accomplices had been able to carry on enjoying their lives.
Now 21, Cockram, who at the time of the killing was on bail for punching two other men on a night out, admitted manslaughter. Lola Charlton and Shayne Cook, both 20, admitted affray.
The trio, who were all 19 at the time, had been drinking at Ladies Day at Newcastle Racecourse on 26 July 2025 before going to more bars in the city centre, prosecutor Emma Dowling said.
Simon Beston, from Sunderland, and his partner were out for a romantic meal when, at about 22:15 BST they stopped to give money and talk to a homeless couple on St Andrew's Street, the court heard.
As they were talking, a large group of young people "all dressed in racing finery" walked by, among whom were the three defendants, the court heard.
Cockram, of Durham Street in Wallsend, forcefully pushed an unknown man into a parked car, with Cook then punching the man, Dowling said.
Simon Beston intervened and tried to calm the youths down, the court heard, reminding them they were on a night out.
A verbal altercation then broke out between Simon Beston's partner and one of the young women in the group, which culminated with Charlton, of Fairhaven Avenue in Newcastle, grappling the victim's girlfriend to the ground, the court heard.
Simon Beston went to protect his partner and was kicked multiple times by Cook, of Winifred Gardens, Wallsend, and Charlton as he was on the floor, the court heard.
The 55-year-old got up and was "clearly" trying to pacify members of the group, the court heard, with his hands making a "placatory gesture", when Cockram punched him forcefully to the side of the face, the court heard.
The blow fractured the victim's cheekbone and knocked him unconscious, causing him to fall in an "uncontrolled" way and hit his head on the kerb, the court heard.
The attackers then left while Simon Beston's partner, nearby door staff and a nurse on a night out went to his aid, the court heard.
He was found to have suffered a fractured skull and severe brain swelling which led to him dying three weeks later on 16 August at Newcastle's Royal Victoria Infirmary, Dowling said.
The court heard Cockram was on police bail at the time having punched two strangers, one of whom was seriously injured, on a night out in Newcastle in April.
'Everything taken away'
Simon Beston's daughter told the court her father was "loving and caring" and "played a significant part" in her and her young daughter's life.
"He always made sure we were happy and had everything," she said. "I think of the future and everything he won't be there for."
His mother said she would "never forget or forgive the person who did this to my son".
She said she still waited to hear her son "opening the front door and shouting 'it's just me mam, do you fancy a cuppa?'".
In a statement read to the court, Simon Beston's partner said she felt "survivor's guilt" and the "horrific" attack had had "devastating consequences".
She said it was supposed to be just an "ordinary romantic evening" but "in one moment everything we had planned and everything I knew was taken away from me".
'Kind-hearted soul'
She said it took four weeks before she felt able to return to their home and found it "heartbreaking" to see her partner's jacket hanging by the front door and his pyjamas awaiting him in a neat pile on their bed.
Any reference to Ladies Day, such as seeing an advert or hearing people talk about it, was now "extremely triggering" for her trauma, she said.
She also said she felt "anger and disgust" at the three attackers continuing their "normal lives" while the consequences of their actions had been so devastating to others.
In mitigation for Cockram, Josh Normanton said the killer, who had moved to the North East to escape domestic violence, was "haunted" by Simon Beston's death.
Charlton had "expressed unrelenting remorse" while Cook believed he had been "protecting a friend" when he kicked the victim three times, the court also heard.
Judge Edward Bindloss said the three were all drunk and without the violent actions of Charlton and Cook, it was "unlikely" Cockram would have launched the fatal punch.
The victim was clearly a "kind-hearted soul" who was "loving and caring", the judge said, adding "many people had been robbed of a future" with "somebody they loved".
Cook was sentenced to 18 months of youth detention while Charlton got nine months, suspended for two years, with 120 hours unpaid work.

title: Fresh measures to secure Nottingham's derelict Debenhams building
text:
Fresh measures to secure derelict Debenhams building
Work is ongoing to stop youths accessing the roof of the former Debenhams building in Nottingham city centre, police have said.
Reports of young people accessing the building in Long Row, off Old Market Square, have led to a closure order, which has now been extended until 20 November.
Nottinghamshire Police said officers were working with the site owners and Nottingham City Council to "ensure the building is better secured".
Ch Insp Kylie Davies said buildings like Debenhams were "extremely dangerous".
On 22 October, police said a small group of young people were able to access the roof, putting themselves in danger.
Police said the individuals had now been identified, and their parents or guardians were being visited.
Earlier this year, two boys, 13 and 15, were arrested on suspicion of entering a closed premises in breach of a closure order.
It comes after a closure order was issued in May at the derelict store following concerns about anti-social behaviour.
The store closed in May 2021 as part of the wider closure of all Debenhams outlets, and the building has remained vacant since.
Davies said work was under way to make sure the building could not be accessed.
"Inside, they are structurally unsound and by scaling the roof you are quite literally putting your life on the line," she added.
"Should you lose your footing and fall, or part of the building breaks, the result will be catastrophic."
She said police were limited in what it could do to punish the people accessing the building.
"However, we are exploring youth injunctions, which are designed to ensure young people have stringent conditions set by the courts, which they cannot ignore," Davies added.
"These can include curfews and not being allowed to enter parts of the city whilst also offering diversionary support to try and change the cycle of behaviour.
"The closure order has certainly limited the activity at Debenhams and for some time we saw no children or young people attempting to enter the site.
"We have identified further issues and access points which are now being addressed.
"Officers have been in touch with the managing agents and they are looking to further target harden the site, particularly the roof area."
She said parents and guardians should speak to their children and explain the risks to them, and added: "We do not want to be reporting that someone has tragically lost their life due to behaviour which is completely avoidable."

title: Gloucestershire abuse victim speaks out about coercive control
text:
'I was not living a normal life, I was surviving'
A woman says she survived a nine-year relationship with her abusive ex-partner by shrinking herself "as small as I possibly could to fit in line with his rules".
Darren Kingscott, 54, of no fixed abode, was convicted of one count of engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour in an intimate relationship on 22 October.
Tashya told the BBC she had lost "every singe bit of confidence she had in herself", and even contemplated ending her own life to escape the daily torment.
At Gloucester Crown Court earlier, Judge Richard Mawhinney sentenced him to 20 months in prison, suspended for 18 months, along with a five-year restraining order.
Kingscott was also ordered to complete a 120-day alcohol abstinence and monitoring requirement, in addition to 100 hours of unpaid work.
In her victim impact statement to the court, Tashya said her "confidence, independence and sense of safety were taken" and the "psychological injuries" had "not healed".
The couple first got together in 2016 after meeting at a pub in Gloucestershire, during what Tashya described as a "vulnerable" time in her life as a single mother.
This meant initial "red flags" in his behaviour, namely aggression and verbal abuse while drinking, were overlooked at the time, she says.
But Tashya said his behaviour "changed significantly" when, within the first year of dating, he moved into the home she owned and began to exert more control.
"None of us could keep up with any of his demands," she said, adding her two children spent most of their time hidden away in their bedrooms out of fear.
"Everybody has arguments, but it's more that 'scared to go home, scared for him to walk through the door' feeling.
"I shrunk myself to be as small as I possibly could to fit in line with his rules, to try to keep myself and my children safe. I was not living a normal life, I was surviving."
The court heard Kingscott also convinced Tashya to sell her family home, which she had put all of her money into, so that he could be a homeowner.
Once he was in "his castle", Tashya said his threatening behaviour escalated further.
"Ultimately, I was going to take my own life, and I shared that with my children," she said.
She said "rightly or wrongly", telling them about how she was feeling "was probably the best thing I did, because my children helped me make the right choice in fleeing at that point".
The pair ended their relationship in 2024 after the family moved into a safe shelter for domestic abuse survivors. There has been no contact between the pair since.
Learned 'to anticipate danger'
"I still live with anxiety and nightmares," Tashya told the BBC. "I wake up in the middle of the night, vomiting. I still hear his voice every day."
She also had to leave her job, explaining it was another part of her life that she "was forced to give up because of the impact of what had happened".
"Coercive control changed the way I lived and the way I thought," she said.
"I learned to anticipate danger. I learned to be careful. I learned to live with fear. Even now, part of me remains on high alert.
"There is no way for me to get these years back for my [children] or undo the fear they experienced, but I am trying to rebuild."
In mitigation, the judge acknowledged "impressive" character references from Kingscott's new family and employer, "which either show a different side to your character or a changed man, I don't know which".
Tashya now hopes her story can raise awareness of coercive and controlling behaviour, and perhaps help other victims to recognise the warning signs.
"Out there, there is someone else living exactly how I was living, to the point they feel the only way out is to end their life," she added.
"It's not easy to go to court, but it is empowering. You are listened to, you are given care and respect and if you tell your story, the judges will see the truth."

title: Life in jail for Bradford pair who used iron to murder man
text:
Life in jail for pair who used iron to murder man
A man and a woman who beat another man to death using a domestic iron in what a judge described as a "brutal and merciless attack" have been jailed for life.
Jaroslav Daniszewski, 43, was found dead at the home of Zbigniew Chlebek, 67, in Stead Street, Shipley, on 22 April 2025.
Following a trial at Bradford Crown Court, Chlebek and Beata Walczak, 58, of Barkerend Road, Bradford, were both found guilty of his murder and were each sentenced on Thursday to nearly 15 years in prison.
Sentencing the pair, Judge Geoffrey Marson said Daniszewski had suffered a "brutal assault with multiple blows" and had "little or no chance of defending himself".
The trial heard Daniszewski was found dead on the living room floor at Chlebek's one-bedroom flat after having suffered significant injuries to his head and face when he was attacked during a night of heavy drinking.
"Precisely which of you delivered which blows we will never know, but it matters not because you are both equally responsible for this killing," the judge told Chlebek and Walczak while sentencing them.
'Intention to kill'
The court was told that Daniszewski suffered approximately 24 groups of injuries, mostly to his head and face, and two serious brain injuries - the second of which led to his death.
Marson said Chlebek, Walczak, Daniszewski and a man called Roj had met on 20 April for a day of heavy drinking and all had a "serious alcohol problem".
Both defendants maintained they had no memory of events.
"You spent the day drinking significant quantities of alcohol, but other than that we will not know what happened on that day," Marson said.
The court heard Daniszewski had been Walczak's boyfriend and they had had an argument, which was caught on CCTV, in the lead-up to the attack.
"We will never know what the motive or cause of this attack was," Marson told them.
"It is clear to me and I am sure that, from the ferocity of the attack and that final blow, each of you had the intention to kill.
"I am sure that from the totality of the evidence I have heard, including the scientific evidence relating to the distribution of blood, that you were both principals in this killing," Marson said.
The court heard that after Daniszewski's death, Chlebek and Walczak had remained in the flat.
"Your callous reaction after you must have known he was dead was to remain in the flat and you, Walczak, simply went to bed in the bedroom where he lay," said Marson.
The judge said neither had shown any remorse and chose to lie to the police during interrogation.
Following the pair's conviction, Senior Investigating Officer Matt Holdsworth said Daniszewski had been subjected to a "prolonged assault" and was left unconscious by those responsible.
"Rather than seeking help for a gravely injured man, the defendants left him to die," he said.
"The evidence gathered by the investigation team demonstrated not only the severity of the attack, but also the deliberate failure of the offenders to provide or summon assistance when it was clear the victim was in urgent need of medical attention."
Holdsworth said their conviction was a result of "meticulous investigative work" and added that he hoped the verdict would "provide some comfort" to Daniszewski's family.
Chlebek was sentenced to a minimum term of 14 years and 168 days and will remain on licence for the remainder of his life.
Walczak was sentenced to 14 years and 169 days and will remain on licence for the remainder of her life.

title: Island Energy: No plans to remove gas standing charge
text:
Island Energy: No plans to remove gas standing charge
The company which provides energy to households on the Isle of Man said it has no plans to change the charging structure, following announcements in the UK Autumn Budget regarding the removal of standing charges.
On Wednesday, Chancellor John Healy announced the removal of standing charges - fixed daily fees paid regardless of usage - from household gas bills in England, Scotland and Wales, with costs added to the unit rate instead.
Island Energy said any proposed changes would be subject to consultation with the Communications and and Utilities Regulatory Authority (CURA) on the island.
A spokesperson warned removing standing charges may benefit some customers but could see others pay more.
"The cost currently covered by the standing charge would instead be recovered through the unit price of energy," explained an Island Energy spokesperson.
"This means customers who use less energy could save money, while those who use more could see their bills increase."
Islands Energy Group supplies energy to homes and business in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man.
The gas utility and energy service provider, which serves about 40,000 domestic, commercial, and industrial customers across the three islands, said any change to the charging structure would need to have the clear support of the community, the regulator and government.
CURA have been contacted for a comment.
'Strike the right balance'
Treasury Minister Michael Crowe said his department was reviewing the various measures set out by the chancellor to understand what the implications might be for the island.
"As we look towards the Isle of Man Budget, in February 2027, our priority is to strike the right balance between supporting people and businesses today and maintaining strong, sustainable public finances for the years ahead," he said.
In accordance with the Autumn Statement, the island will extend the reduction in the VAT rate, from 5% to 0% on domestic electricity supplies, until 30 June 2027.
It will also honor the Customs and Excise Agreement with the UK and continue to apply the cut in fuel duty, by 5p per litre, until 30 June 2027.
A reduced duty rate for red diesel, introduced in June until the end of the year, will also be extended to 30 June 2027.
