title: Worcester farmer says Budget's minimum wage rise is 'massive blow'
text:
Minimum wage rise 'a massive blow' says farmer
A farmer has said the minimum wage increase announced in the Budget would be a "massive blow" for businesses like his.
The 3.9% rise was confirmed by Chancellor John Healey during his speech in the House of Commons on Wednesday.
It was among a raft of measures that he said were designed to help ease the pressures of the cost-of-living crisis by offering people "breathing space".
But Tristan Bennett, of Bennetts Farms in Worcester, said it seemed like "a lot of tinkering and gimmicks" and that he was "disappointed there was not anything substantial".
As well as a dairy farm, he also runs a glamping site and cafe, and said the minimum wage increase would hit them hard.
"That's going to have a massive blow, especially for the cafe side and hospitality, and a lot of the young people," he told BBC Hereford and Worcester.
"We are trying to take on apprentices on the farm but we're finding it so hard now to make it pay."
He said the increase in the small business rate relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 would help the glamping side of the business a "little bit".
But Bennett said the disappointment was the lack of relief or reduction in VAT for businesses like his.
"They did it for the pubs," he added. "We were hoping they would have been able to help the rest of the hospitality industry but sadly not."
He said he was "nonplussed" by the Budget and questioned why Labour "have not done anything with such a big majority".
"It just seems to be such a mess with things that need sorting out," Bennett said. "If you can't do it with that thumping majority, how else can you do it?
"I'm just completely despondent, really, about the political class and what they're failing to achieve."
'Massive difference'
Rachel Buchanan, co-owner of Elderwood Books in Brampton Bryan, Herefordshire, said she was currently challenging the business rate valuation of her premises.
She said her current rate was more than £18,000, but if her challenge was successful, her business would be below that figure, which would be a "relief".
"We're in an area subject to flooding. Tourists come or don't come, so if we have a quiet week in the winter, those business rates still have to be paid," she added.
"Having a much lower, or preferably zero, bill would make a massive difference."
She said a reduction in VAT was a "lovely dream" but she did not expect that to be included in the Budget, which she described as "tinkering around the edges".
"I didn't expect any big changes," she continued, "and here we are back to being reliant on ourselves and making sure we have customers coming through the door to pay those bills."

title: Jersey minimum wage increase accepted by minister
text:
Minimum wage increase accepted by minister
A recommendation to increase the minimum wage has been accepted by the social security minister.
The Jersey Employment Forum's latest report recommended hiking the minimum wage rate to £13.97 per hour from 1 April 2027 - an increase of 2.8% on the current £13.59 in line with the Jersey retail price index (RPI) in June 2026.
Senator Elaine Millar, Minister for Social Security, said she had "decided to accept the forum's recommendations in respect of the main minimum wage and trainee minimum wage rates".
Forum chairwoman Carla Benest said it had been "challenging times" for businesses and employees and "the forum has endeavoured to reflect that in our recommendations".
The report recommended minimum wage rates for year one and two trainees remained at £10.50 and £11.75 per hour respectively for one more year from 1 April.
It also recommended an equivalent increase in the allowances available to employers for accommodation and meals provided to employees earning the main minimum wage rate, which Millar said she accepted.
The minister said: "The forum's report also reflected on the debate about a youth rate and possible changes to the way in which the formal trainee minimum wage policy is currently set.
"I will consider carefully the arguments that have emerged from the forum's consultation exercise, and in particular whether a further consultation on these aspects should take place."

title: Milton Keynes expansion gets £50m for road links
text:
Milton Keynes expansion gets £50m for road links
Milton Keynes is to receive £50m to improve road links supporting the city's expansion.
The city council said the money would help unlock 5,500 homes and that new roads would also improve access to land earmarked for future growth.
The leader of the council said the money would help ensure infrastructure was "provided alongside new homes, not years afterwards".
The project has already received £94.6m from the government's Housing Infrastructure Fund, which has funded a primary school, road improvements and a community health hub.
The school and the hub are expected to open next year.
The Milton Keynes East expansion, approved in 2022, will include 40 hectares (99 acres) of employment land as well as 5,500 homes.
Jane Carr, the Liberal Democrat leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "People rightly expect roads, schools and healthcare facilities to be provided alongside new homes, not years afterwards.
"This additional £50 million investment will help ensure Milton Keynes continues to grow in the right way, with the infrastructure needed to support new communities from the outset."
She added that the "quality of life that makes Milton Keynes such a great place to live" would be maintained.
Stephen Kirwan, from the lead developers, Berkeley, said its partnership with the council "is on course to deliver 5,500 private and affordable homes, a 160-acre country park and a mix of community amenities.
"We are also delivering over 4,000 new jobs within the 4 million sq ft strategic industrial hub on the southern part of the site."
Analysis: Will infrastructure appear alongside homes?
The promise that infrastructure will be built alongside new homes is often one of the key issues for existing and future residents.
But many people will reserve judgement until construction is further advanced.
Developments elsewhere have become more expensive than expected and homes have sometimes sold more slowly than forecast, leading to changes in infrastructure plans.
There have also been cases where proposed schools were scrapped because fewer families moved into an area than anticipated.
In Milton Keynes East, however, both the school and health hub are already visible on the site, giving residents reason to be cautiously optimistic that those facilities will open as planned.

title: Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
text:
Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
Philippine police have obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from the former home of Thomas Markle, father of the Duchess of Sussex.
Earlier this month, it was reported that hundreds of images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle Sr, 82, had been found at the property in the Philippines.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.
Thomas Markle Sr, who is now in the US, has strongly denied the allegations made by his son, describing them as "sick lies".
Cebu Regional Prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that Thomas Markle Jr was "adamant" that the case should be investigated, and that he felt his father "has to answer for it".
Last week, the Sun on Sunday reported that Thomas Markle Sr's ex-wife, Roslyn Loveless, had sent a letter to the Metropolitan Police about the 2019 allegations, which was shared with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time.
Loveless, who has since died, is the mother of Meghan's two half-siblings. She divorced Thomas Markle Sr. in 1975, before he married the duchess's mother.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".
Speaking to the Sun, Thomas Markle Jr also apologised to Meghan for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement, and said he had "been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years".
Thomas Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May.
He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
The police say they must identify how the material was obtained before they can consider any criminal charges.
Campaigners describe Cebu as a known hotspot for the sexual exploitation of children, and authorities say they take any such allegations very seriously.

title: Emily Atack backs call for school uniform ban in porn
text:
Emily Atack backs call for school uniform ban in porn
Actress Emily Atack has supported calls for the government to ban the use of school uniforms in pornography.
The campaign was started by a group of teenage girls from The Cooper School in Bicester who say uniforms have been "tarnished… and warped by sexualisation".
Their petition has been signed more than 40,000 times and comes in response to new government legislation making it a criminal offence to possess or share pornographic content featuring adults pretending to be under 16.
But the students say the new law does not go far enough and a "loophole" means uniforms could be worn by those claiming to be playing someone over 16.
Taking to social media earlier this week, Atack shared a BBC News story about the campaign with her 1.8 million Instagram followers
Alongside, she wrote "with you all the way" - accompanied with a red love-heart emoji.
The actress has starred in TV shows such as the Jilly Cooper adaptation Rivals, but is best known to UK audiences for her role in the seminal noughties sitcom The Inbetweeners.
In it, she played Charlotte Hinchcliffe - a recurring, and highly-sexualized, schoolgirl who was an on-off love interest of Simon Bird's character Will Mackenzie.
"She was the popular girl at school," she previously told the BBC. "The issue is, that yes, it's a fictional character, but obviously people associate you with the characters that you play."
In 2024, Atack told The Guardian she "naively didn't think what narrative was being painted for me" by the character.
The Cooper School's Little Feminist Book Club, which started the campaign, previously said: "We're not 'sexy schoolgirls'. We're not objects. We're students, and more importantly, children."
They argued school uniforms were used in pornography to "evoke childhood and school-age identities".
Willow, 14, said she does not wear her uniform in public if she can avoid it: "I go home and change, because I feel vulnerable."
A 2018 survey of 1,004 girls in the UK found 35% of 14-21 year-olds said they had experienced unwanted sexual attention while wearing school uniform in public, according to children's charity Plan International UK.
Reacting to Atack's support for the campaign, 15-year-old Aylin said: "Seeing that so many other people can resonate and agree with our cause empowers us to keep going."
"It is still encouraging that despite calls for the ban being ignored people still want to combat this problem even after years," Mae, 15, added.
In April this year, the government agreed new legislation making it a criminal offence to possess or share pornographic content featuring adults pretending to be under 16, as part of the Crime and Policing Act 2026. It is set to come into force in November.
But Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and author of Exposed: The problem of Extreme Porn, said school uniform does not necessarily fall into this category.
"Where someone says they're pretending to be 17 and in school uniform, that's not covered by the law," she said.
"Let's face it, the reality is that school uniforms are trying to portray a young girl."
Minister for victims, tackling violence against women and girls and international justice, Alex Davies-Jones, said: "Young women and girls should not have to grow up seeing their school uniforms sexualised, and I commend these pupils for speaking out about something they feel so strongly about.
"Pornography must never normalise or glorify the sexual abuse of children. That's why we are changing the law so possessing or sharing pornography which depicts an adult pretending to be a child under 16 will be an imprisonable offence."

title: Cardiff Parkway £30m pledge is an insult, Welsh minister says
text:
Chancellor's £30m pledge for train station is insult to the people of Wales, minister says
A £30m rail funding pledge announced by Chancellor John Healey in the Budget is "an insult to the people of Wales", a Welsh government minister says.
Wales' Transport Minister Mark Hooper said the investment in the proposed Cardiff Parkway station was "a tiny fraction" of the cash needed to improve Welsh rail.
The Plaid Cymru-led Welsh government had called on Healey to bring forward £1bn of the £14bn the UK Labour government had promised for long-term rail funding in Wales.
UK government finance minister Emma Reynolds said the cash was part of a £445m package aimed at tackling years of "chronic under-investment" in rail.
Hooper made the comments after a meeting with the UK government in Whitehall on Thursday.
The proposed Cardiff Parkway in the city's eastern St Mellons area would link passengers on the South Wales Metro network to north Wales, Bristol, Manchester and London.
On Wednesday the chancellor's Budget announcement confirmed cash for three projects in Wales - £2.5m for a science park in Ynys Mon, £11m for a bridge in Port Talbot and £30m for Cardiff Parkway.
UK ministers said that rail funding was part of a £445m package that had been announced at the last Spending Review.
The UK government has already backed plans for five new stations in Cardiff, Newport and Monmouthshire, as well as upgrades in north Wales.
The UK government had previously claimed Cardiff Parkway - whose private developers had plans for the station approved in January 2025 after years of delays - could serve 800,000 passengers every year and support around 6,000 jobs.
Budget documents released on Wednesday said the £30m would "progress delivery" for the scheme.
UK government finance minister Reynolds told Radio Wales Breakfast on Thursday that the £445m to progress rail projects in Wales was because of "chronic underinvestment in Wales" during past Conservative and Tory-Liberal Democrat UK governments.
"We need to clear away the red tape and get the planning in place," she said.
"So the reason that we have given £30m to Cardiff Parkway Rail Station yesterday is because we've done the work together to get the planning in place, so we can get that money flowing."
She said she was "all ready to work" with the Welsh government and Transport for Wales to progress with the project.
Hooper met UK government ministers and officials in Whitehall later on Wednesday to discuss his plans for rail.
He told BBC Wales the £30m announced was a "tiny fraction" of what was needed, saying: "This figure is an insult to the people of Wales."
"The UK government's continued failure to invest in their network in Wales demonstrates, now, more than ever, the need for devolution of rail," he said.
"It's wrong to say these stations aren't shovel-ready. The UK government promised this money in February and since then we've agreed with Network Rail that Transport for Wales will deliver the stations.
"Transport for Wales are ready to start work we just need the UK government to keep their promise. I made this point to the rail minister when I met him today."
The Welsh government said that despite making up 10% of the rail network across Great Britain, just 1% of Network Rail's spending goes to Wales.
Developers had hoped Cardiff Parkway would be operational by 2024, but the planning process was dogged by delays.
Plans were approved by Cardiff council in April 2022, but the broader national interest in the project led the Welsh government under Labour to review the application, before former First Minister Eluned Morgan granted planning permission in January 2025.
Additional reporting by Reem Ahmed

title: 'Uneventful' Budget draws mixed reaction across Shropshire
text:
How people fighting rising costs reacted to Budget
The autumn Budget has sparked a mixed reaction as businesses and charities face "fighting" rising costs
A promise to shield households from some cost of living pressures was the focus of John Healey's first budget as chancellor - saying the plans would offer "breathing space".
But reaction across Shropshire was mixed, with businesses, charities and politicians divided over whether the measures will go far enough.
Harry Delves, who runs Tuffins Supermarket in Craven Arms, said there was little in the announcement that would significantly affect his business.
He said: "We all knew about the national living wage that was going to be increasing from April, so that's something that we just need to build into our forecast for the following year."
While he welcomed the extension of the 5p fuel duty cut, Delves said he did not see "any big announcements or major changes" that would "supercharge the UK economy.
"In all, it's quite uneventful. We shall see how everything starts to turn out."
Scott Adams, owner of Telford Exotic Zoo, described the Budget as "underwhelming" and said there was "really nothing in there" that would directly help visitor attractions.
Instead, he hoped any extra money in consumers' pockets could encourage more spending on leisure activities.
"If people feel maybe like they've got a little bit more money in their pocket, then maybe they'd be more willing to go out and spend money on luxuries, like going for days out," he said.
Adams said businesses continued to struggle with rising costs.
"Our electric costs have gone out of control. Animal feeds, anything that we're buying in since the pandemic, there's just been one excuse after another to double the price.
"Instead of enjoying running a business, it seems like you're always fighting. You're always fighting to make enough money to buy everything that you need."
He added: "There's not really any help or support out there at all at the moment."
Callum Jinks, financial controller at Joule's Brewery in Market Drayton, welcomed support on business rates but argued the measures did not go far enough for pubs and breweries.
He said: "The main things in there for us were the supports on the business rates, which does touch some of our sites and our tenants and will support them.
"But I don't think it goes anywhere near far enough to what the wider pub industry does need at the moment."
Jinks said there was a "big push" within hospitality for a review of VAT and further relief on alcohol duty.
He also criticised the current business rates system, arguing successful pubs could effectively be penalised.
"If you get a good operator and a pub that improves the business and makes that pub very successful in the local area, its business rates are then unfairly affected by increasing dramatically," he said.
He warned that despite some positives, more pub closures could lie ahead.
"I think in general we're going to see more pubs closing before anything does get better."
Mark Triggs, from debt charity Christians Against Poverty, said some of the headline announcements were welcome but questioned how much difference they would make as costs continue to rise.
He said: "The food tariffs, they reckon, will save an average household only £20 a year. So it's welcome, but it's a lot of little bits here and there with costs still running riot."
Triggs said energy costs remained one of the biggest concerns, particularly in Shropshire where many households are not connected to the gas grid.
"I think energy is the issue that most troubles in terms of what we'll see with people coming forward in the coming weeks."
He said more people were seeking help because they could not afford essentials.
"I see more and more people because they can't put food on the table and are looking for referrals to food banks."
Despite his concerns, Triggs said the chancellor had faced an "impossible sort of task".
"The proof will be in the pudding as time proceeds, but I think people won't feel that they're any better off than they were."
Responding to the criticism, Labour MP for Shrewsbury Julia Buckley described the Budget as "really positive".
She said: "You have to remember there's lots of uncertainty internationally. Our job really is to try and stabilise things and reduce some of our immediate costs to help people with this really difficult situation."
Buckley said changes to business rates would mean many smaller firms no longer paid the charge, and pointed to investment through the National Wealth Fund and Good Growth Fund.
She also highlighted measures aimed at reducing household costs, including support for households in council tax bands A to D.
"Our big project as a Labour government is to get people onto renewable energy because it's the cheapest form of energy," she said.
Liberal Democrat MP for North Shropshire Helen Morgan welcomed support on business rates and help for households, but argued the budget did not go far enough.
"Overall I think it was a timid budget," she said.
Morgan said rural communities needed greater support with heating oil and Liquefied Petroleum Gas costs.
"We need to help people to heat their homes over the winter because the prices are really astronomical at the moment."
She also backed calls for a temporary reduction in VAT for hospitality businesses and warned rural areas risked missing out on investment.
"At the moment, it looks like places that are rural are missing out in a significant way," she added.

title: President Tinubu to 'pray for Nigeria' during Saudi Arabia trip to Mecca
text:
President Tinubu to 'pray for Nigeria' during Saudi Arabia trip
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is travelling to the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia to perform the lesser Hajj pilgrimage, known as Umrah, where he will offer prayers for the West African nation, the presidency says.
The visit would provide the 74-year-old president with an opportunity for "spiritual reflection, devotion and prayers for Nigeria's peace, unity, stability and continued progress", his spokesman Bayo Onanuga said.
Tinubu, a Muslim from southern Nigeria, last travelled to Saudi Arabia for Umrah in 2022, while campaigning to become Nigeria's president.
The next election is in January and the country's widespread security challenges have become a major campaign issue.
Onanuga's statement said the president would "perform the religious rites associated with Umrah, seeking Allah's guidance and blessings for Nigeria and its people".
Unlike the Hajj, which has fixed dates once a year and is a pilgrimage that Muslims who are able to must perform at least once in their lifetime, Umrah can be performed at any time and involves a shorter set of religious rites.
Meanwhile, Tinubu's media aide Olusegun Dada has dismissed speculation that the real reason for the trip is that the president needs medical checks.
There was widespread discussion about the president's health last weekend after a video went viral on social media appearing to show First Lady Oluremi Tinubu popping something into Tinubu's mouth at the election campaign launch for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) party.
There has been no official comment regarding the incident.
In a post on X, Dada said the president's trip was intended to offer "supplications for the country" and to commit the president's re-election bid "into the hands of God" as he began "another major political journey".
According to a survey by US-based Pew Research Center, more than 90% of Nigerians say religion is "very important" in their lives - one of the highest proportions globally.
Nigeria - Africa's most populous nation - is roughly evenly divided between Christians and Muslims, with a small number of traditional believers.
"It is a regular practice among Muslims when they want to embark on any critical journey or attain a milestone," Dada said, reminding his followers that Tinubu had last done the lesser Hajj ahead of the APC's presidential primary in 2022.
The next elections are scheduled for 16 January when Tinubu's main challengers will again be former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.
As campaigning gets under way the economy and insecurity are major issues for voters.
The country faces an array of security challenges including an Islamist insurgency, attacks by criminal gangs - known locally as "bandits" who loot and kidnap for ransom - clashes over land and separatist unrest.

title: Royal British Legion fundraises on London Poppy Day
text:
Royal British Legion fundraises on Poppy Day
The Royal British Legion (RBL) has launched a city-wide fundraising effort for London Poppy Day 2026.
Thursday is the 20th anniversary of the charity's annual fundraising event in the capital for the armed forces community, and includes performances from military bands and choirs at more than 20 stations including Waterloo, Liverpool Street, Euston and London Bridge.
In 2025, the event raised almost £1.5m for the RBL.
Lucy Inskip, the director of the Poppy Appeal, said she hoped people would "get involved, and enjoythe various military bands and choirs performing across major stations across London - and give what they can".
EastEnders actor Ross Kemp joined the fundraising effort aboard a Thames Clippers service on the River Thames - a first for the event.
The 62-year-old, who appeared in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors, said: "I'll always be 100% faithful to the faithfuls and 100% faithful to the Royal British Legion.
"Twenty years of fundraising in the capital is a fantastic milestone, and it's always a pleasure to see so many people coming together to support the armed forces community."
Donations from London Poppy Day and the Poppy Appeal are used to support serving personnel, veterans and their families.
The campaign encourages the public to wear a poppy to recognise those who have served in the armed forces.
Mayor of London Sadiq Khan said he was "delighted" to support the event.
"This is the biggest one-day city collection of its kind in Europe, and I'd like to thank all the Armed Forces personnel and Poppy Appeal collectors who will be out fundraising across the city," he said.
Approximately 2,500 armed forces personnel and volunteers will collect donations at stations, transport hubs and other locations across the capital on Thursday.

title: Dispersal order issued for Beeston town centre on Halloween
text:
Dispersal order issued for town centre on Halloween
Police have issued a dispersal order in parts of Beeston for Halloween in a bid to prevent anti-social behaviour.
Nottinghamshire Police said a dispersal order was in place across the town centre, Broadgate Park and Dovecote Lane Recreation Ground from 15:00 on Saturday to 03:00 GMT on Sunday.
The order will give officers temporary powers to remove people without arresting them.
Police added additional officers would be on patrol "to remove any troublemakers from the town centre and recreation ground".
Insp Usha Madaraa, district commander for Broxtowe, said: "Halloween should be a time of fun and enjoyment for young children and their families, not an excuse for local youths to behave in ways that cause alarm and distress to others.
"So, for that small minority of young people looking to use this event as an excuse for poor behaviour, I want to be very clear that we will not tolerate it.
"In addition to this, anyone playing tricks we really don't like, can expect the treat of a ride home in a police car and an uncomfortable conversation between my officers and their parents."

title: Trainee guide dogs visit Warwick 'haunted' house ahead of Halloween
text:
Guide dogs visit haunted house event to prepare them for Halloween
A group of trainee guide dogs have been given a special tour of a haunted house to prepare them for their first Howl-oween.
The canines, from charity Guide Dogs for the Blind, visited the Grade-I listed St John's House in Warwick on Wednesday, to help them stay calm around spooky sights and sounds.
The mansion, which is open to the public until Saturday evening, has been dressed up with Halloween decorations as part of its Haunted House family trail event.
As the trainee guide dogs tackled a few frightening sights and sounds, Guide Dogs trainer Chris Roberts explained how the visit was designed to build their confidence.
"There's lots of things around the house that these dogs need to be confident and resilient enough to perform what they need to when they're guiding," he said.
"There's lot of kind of scary faces, make up, gear, flapping things, stuff like that can really upset a dog and make them quite anxious."
With Bonfire Night and Diwali also approaching, the festivities can sometimes be a little tail-raising for young dogs unaccustomed to the sights and loud sounds.
Roberts described how there was an incident where a skeleton fell over in one of the rooms and startled one dog, named Taylor.
"She was a little bit worried by that, so it's important for me to recognise that with her body posture," he said.
"[The dogs have] come in, they've had a bit of a sniff, they've had some play, they've had some food and we're really trying to create that positive environment, that [when] they see something that's a bit scary, bit worrying, actually good things happen."
Rebecca Coles, from St John's House, added the 17th Century mansion was open to visitors over the Halloween period.
"The event's for children, for younger children, so we're not too spooky, no jump scares and the dogs are welcome back, if they want to come when the public is here as well," she said.
When asked whether the house was haunted, Coles added: "If you believe in ghosts, then yes."
To help dogs feel relaxed and happy over Halloween, Guide Dogs' canine behaviour and welfare team shared the following tips:
- Slowly introduce costumes - Let your dog sniff and explore new items like wigs, hats or masks before you wear them and reward calm behaviour.
- Build up to new sounds - Play recordings of fireworks or doorbells quietly first, increasing volume only if your dog stays relaxed.
- Add decorations in stages - So your dog can gradually adjust to new sights and smells.
- Create a safe space with their bed and toys - Where your dog can retreat to if they feel unsettled.
- Avoid scary attractions - Pet dogs may find these overwhelming, skip noisy events or parties and skip the costumes.
- Keep treats out of reach - Chocolate, raisins and xylitol are toxic to dogs and sweet wrappers can cause choking or tummy upsets.

title: DNA testing in north Wales to identify dogs in livestock attacks
text:
Investigators to use DNA testing to identify dogs in livestock attacks
Warning: This article contains an image of an injured sheep
DNA testing will be used to track down dogs that have attacked livestock.
A change in the law in March has given police the power to take samples from dogs, and dog owners can receive an unlimited fine if their pets have been involved in any attacks.
Farmers are also being given testing kits as part of a project to make sure better DNA evidence is being gathered.
Insurance company NFU Mutual has estimated dogs attacking livestock in Wales cost insurers more than £300,000 last year.
Across Wales, police say there were about 300 dog attacks on farm animals last year.
Wales wildlife and rural crime coordinator Rob Taylor said 90% of attacks were resolved outside court.
"In most cases, owners are often very apologetic and are happy to pay compensation to the farmer and attend an approved online responsible dog ownership course," he said.
"The new power to take DNA is extremely useful in cases where an owner claims that it wasn't their dog involved, which assists evidentially with identification."
Dyfed-Powys Police has assigned two crime scene officers to support investigations into dog attacks.
PC Ian Nicholls, from North Wales Police Rural Crime Team, said reports of livestock attacks were "constantly coming in".
"The DNA test helps us to identify dogs, and also sends out a message that the police have got things that we can do to help investigate these crimes.
"These attacks cause farmers significant financial losses and are very distressing to farmers and to the wider public."
Researchers at Liverpool John Moores University will examine samples and draw up guidance on collecting DNA properly.
Dr Nick Dawnay said: "We're looking to improve the whole analytical pipeline from CSI - crime scene investigation - through to analysis.
"Looking longer term, we'd also like to see whether it would be possible for farmers or vets to collect DNA evidence themselves if a crime scene investigator can't get there in time."

title: Cambridgeshire Army Cadets leader guilty of sexual offences
text:
Ex-councillor guilty of sex crimes against cadets
A former city councillor has been convicted of sexual offences, many involving boys he had instructed as an Army cadet leader.
After 11 hours of deliberations, a jury at Ipswich Crown Court found Rylan Ray guilty of 23 crimes including the rape of a man he met on a night out.
The case involved 11 male complainants, many of them teenagers the former Conservative politician had met through his role with the Cambridgeshire Army Cadet Force.
Jurors heard how the 26-year-old, of Westgate, Peterborough, used social media apps such as Snapchat to groom the boys.
The jury, made up of four men and eight women, found Ray guilty of:
- Five counts of causing a child to watch a sexual act
- Five counts of sexual communication with a child
- Four counts of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity
- Three counts of sexual assault
- Three counts of making indecent photographs of children
- One count of rape
- One count of sexual activity with a child
- One count of possessing an extreme pornographic image
Ray looked straight ahead and displayed no emotion as the forewoman of the jury read the first 22 guilty verdicts, which were unanimous. His mum cried in the public gallery.
When the jury returned later to return a guilty verdict for the charge of rape, on a majority verdict of 11 to one, Ray refused to return to the dock.
He has been convicted of 28 offences in total, having already pleaded guilty to five offences against one teenage boy. They are two counts of causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, two of making indecent photographs of a child, and one of causing a child to watch a sexual activity.
Victims not identified
Det Con Gordon Logan, of Cambridgeshire Police, said the result "reflected the seriousness of his offending", which took place over a six-year period.
Ray will be sentenced at the same court on 8 January.
More than 700 indecent images of children were found on Ray's devices when they were seized by police, and not all of them have yet been identified.
"If you have any concerns that you may have been a victim of Rylan Ray then please come forward; please talk to our specially trained officers," said Logan, speaking to the BBC outside the court.
During the trial, Ray was cleared of one count of possession of prohibited images of children and another of causing a child to watch a sexual act, because of a lack of evidence.
Ray was elected to represent Eye, Thorney and Newborough on Peterborough City Council in May 2022.
He was removed from the Conservative group in February and continued to sit as an independent councillor until May's local election, when he did not contest his seat.
Ray also previously worked for HM Courts and Tribunals Service, the Ministry of Justice, and at two schools in the Peterborough area.

title: Scarborough Post Office closure plan 'disappointing', says MP
text:
Post Office closure plan 'disappointing', says MP
The planed closure of Scarborough's main post office in the coming months is "disappointing", the town's MP has said.
The Post Office confirmed its branch inside the TG Jones store on Westborough would close shortly before the store itself was shut as part of a wider restructuring programme.
The town's Labour MP Alison Hume has urged the Post Office to find an alternative location for this "vital lifeline" to be found.
The Post Office said a final closure date had not yet been confirmed and that it was reviewing applications from potential operators, meanwhile the Falsgrave Road and Newlands Park branches had been identified as alternative locations while a permanent replacement was found.
Hume said she had made it clear to the Post Office that any replacement for the Westborough branch must be "accessible and convenient".
"We need a town centre provision," she said.
"Post Offices are a vital role, particularly for older residents and vulnerable people, so this closure is not good news."
'Long way to go'
The planned closure of the Westborough branch has also prompted concern among local councillors, who said they feared it could leave many residents without easy access to key services.
Janet Jefferson, who represents Castle Ward, told the Local Democracy Reporting Service she was particularly worried about people who currently travelled into the town centre to use the branch.
"A lot of people use that branch. A lot of them get the bus, get off in the town centre and it's easy for them," she said.
Alternative branches at Falsgrave Road and Newlands Park would be less convenient for many users, Jefferson added.
"I know Falsgrave, if you have got a car, is fine - but if you have not, it's a long way to go."
The Post Office said in its letter announcing the closure plan that "the provision of a Post Office service to our customers in the area is important to us".
The letter added that the Post Office was "working hard to find a location nearby to continue offering services to the local community in Scarborough".
The closure follows similar changes elsewhere, including the recently announced closure of the main Post Office branch in York city centre following restructuring by Modella Capital, the owner of TG Jones.
TG Jones has been contacted for a comment.

title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
text:
'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.
Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.
Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.
The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.
In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.
But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.
"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.
"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.
However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.
In response to this "painful" situation the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.
Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains "already behind us".
Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.
The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.
Lost decade
Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.
The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.
The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.
Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.
However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.
While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.
The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.
Helen Miller, director of the influential think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the outlook was "depressing".
"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," she said.
"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."
'Fragile' finances
There would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament, Miller added.
"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.
"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.
Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.
Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.
He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.
Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.
But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" or the buffer that the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.
Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.
description: Budget forecasts show growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

title: Man who texted victim 'I feel bad' after violent rape jailed
text:
Man who texted victim 'I feel bad' after violent rape is jailed
A man who texted his victim "I feel bad" after a violent rape in Edinburgh has been jailed for seven years and three months.
Alquimedes Gabriel Duran Geraldino, a 35-year-old Venezuelan national, forced his way into a woman's home on 3 January 2024, before subjecting her to physical and emotional abuse.
During the trial at the High Court in Edinburgh, the jury heard that Geraldino had punched the 28-year-old woman in the face, leaving her with a broken nose, before kicking her body. He then raped her.
The woman, who cannot be named, told the court that during the attack he had described her as a "a street walker" and accused her of having "slept with half of Edinburgh".
He went on to leave his victim further traumatised by sending her a text message the next day saying he felt "bad" for what he had done.
In a recording played to the jury, the woman described how the attack left her feeling "humiliated", adding that Geraldino had been "very, very aggressive".
Geraldino was found guilty on rape and abuse charges at the end of his trial last month.
He had denied any wrongdoing throughout the proceedings.
Throughout the trial he had sat alongside a Spanish translator who explained the evidence presented against him in his native language.
At his sentencing on Thursday, Geraldino's defence advocate Victoria Dow told the court her client knew he would be going to prison but asked for leniency.
Judge Lord Cubie told Geraldino that his actions meant a custodial sentence was necessary.
He said: "The jury has found you to be controlling, violent and abusive.
"The victim impact statement is powerful. She has suffered physical injuries and she suffers from psychological injuries.
"There are mental scars.
"She suffers from panic attacks, flashbacks, sleep disturbance and shame.
"The consequences for her are long standing and far reaching."
Alongside the prison sentence, Geraldino will also be placed on the Sex Offenders Register for life.
Lord Cubie also handed him a lifelong non-harassment order prohibiting him from making contact with his victim.

title: Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
text:
Russian drone attack on Ukrainian train station kills at least 14, officials say
At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to the railway operator chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform" when the drone struck, he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit an electric civilian train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole in a platform that is strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal that was struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Moscow, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 25 others, including four children, were injured, he added.
A day of mourning has been declared for Chernihiv and Dnipro on Friday.
In the city of Kremenchuk, in the central Poltava region, three people were killed and 28 injured in a Russian drone attack that hit residential buildings and a school, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said.
The latest Russian strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricity for years.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The two-day event is attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real, and attacks on Ukraine's train infrastructure have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency.
Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in the capital Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.

title: Peterhead fish firm fined £245,000 after worker dragged into machine
text:
Fish firm fined £245,000 for safety breach after worker pulled into machine
A fish processing firm has been fined £245,000 after a worker was dragged into a machine in Aberdeenshire.
The 30-year-old man was trying to free a jammed box at Lunar Freezing and Cold Storage in Peterhead when his right arm was pulled into the mechanism.
He suffered a fractured jaw and injuries to his chest and arm, and needed surgery.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) into the incident in August last year found a safety guard had been removed during maintenance two weeks earlier and was not replaced.
The company, which pleaded guilty to health and safety offences at Peterhead Sheriff Court, has been contacted for comment.
The incident happened on 19 August 2025 after the worker entered the production line to clear a jammed box without first isolating the power.
He climbed onto the conveyor and pressed down the lid of the box to release the jam, but the machine then restarted and he was pulled by his arm into the mechanism until his head made contact with moving parts.
A colleague, hearing his shouts for help, shut down the machine but the worker was found to have suffered a fractured jaw as well as arm and chest injuries.
He needed surgery to insert metal plates into his jaw and spent three days in hospital but made a full recovery and returned to work about six weeks later.
Guard not put back
An investigation by the HSE found that a section of fixed guarding next to the production line had been removed during maintenance about two weeks before the incident and had not been put back.
Without the guard, workers were able to access the production line without the power being isolated.
Normally, they would have to pass through an interlocked gate which would have switched off the machinery as soon as the gate was opened.
Maintenance staff told HSE investigators they had noticed the guard was missing and had seen employees using the gap, but it was not reinstated.
The weekly inspection checklist used by the in-house maintenance team did not include checking the integrity of non-electrical fixed guarding.
'Wholly preventable'
HSE inspector Nicky Smith said: "This was a wholly preventable incident which left a worker seriously injured.
"A missing guard and an unchecked gap left the way open for a worker to be dragged into a machine.
"Guards must be kept in place, and checks must cover every guard, not just the electrical ones."
In a statement via law firm Digby Brown, the injured victim said: "I am relieved the Crown has held my employer accountable for the safety failures that led to my injuries.
"The substantial fine issued by the court reflects the seriousness of what happened. I hope this verdict serves as a clear reminder to all employers that worker safety must always come first.
"My focus remains on my ongoing recovery and finalising the remaining legal matters surrounding this incident."

title: Former police station in Paisley goes on sale for £75,000
text:
Former police station in Paisley goes on sale for £75,000
A former police station in Paisley that closed last year is to go on the market as a "potential development opportunity".
Offers in excess of £75,000 are being invited for Ferguslie Park police station, with surveyors saying the building has "scope for alternative use".
The station had not been open to the public for more than a decade when the force announced plans to dispose of it in May 2025, following a consultation.
Shepherd Chartered Surveyors said there had already been "keen interest" in the building.
The former police station occupies a prominent corner pitch on Ferguslie Park Avenue, near various schools, a community centre and a sports centre.
It includes a reception area with adjoining office, two larger rooms previously used as breakout spaces and multiple smaller storage and office spaces as well as W/C provisions.
A parking area to the rear of the building is secured behind a locked gate and houses a storage shed, as well as individual covered parking spaces for up to 10 vehicles.
Fraser McDonald, of Shepherd Chartered Surveyors, said: "This former police station with secure off-street covered parking offers a potential development opportunity with scope for alternative use, subject to planning.
"As such, we have already received keen interest in this opportunity."
Last year, Ch Supt Rhona Fraser said it was not necessary to have the police station there, given it was two miles from Paisley police station and three miles from Johnstone police station.
She said: "By merging resources, we can ensure our focus remains on delivering frontline policing and enhancing community safety, rather retaining underutilised buildings."

title: Northumberland Conservatives challenge Defra's Rothbury donation
text:
Conservatives challenge government estate donation
Local Conservatives have challenged the government's £1.9m donation to help conservation groups buy a vast upland estate.
The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust are raising £30m to acquire the 9,500-acre Rothbury Estate in its entirety as part of plans to boost wildlife, restore bogs and promote nature-friendly farming.
But as the groups close in on the target, chairman of Northumberland Conservatives, Guy Renner-Thompson, said the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) should instead focus its support on "our farmers and fishermen".
Nature minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter said purchase of the site would benefit local communities.
Earlier this year, tenant farmer Chris Armstrong, who oversees 1,000 acres (405 hectares) close to the Rothbury site, told the BBC local opinion was split with most of the farming community seeing it as a "folly".
Renner-Thompson said the government had "its priorities wrong", referencing difficulties farmers had faced accessing sustainable farming incentive (SFI) funding.
"Defra should be focusing on its support of our farmers and fishermen, the people producing our food and sustaining Northumberland's rural and coastal communities," he said.
The Rothbury Estate sale has attracted support from the likes of Sir David Attenborough and the window for public donations is open until the end of the week.
If successful, the organisations claimed there would be the potential to develop a "40 mile nature recovery corridor stretching from the North East coast to Kielder on the central Scottish border".
Renner-Thompson challenged ministers to stipulate if any conditions would accompany the grant and how farmers and food production would be protected.
"We support investment that benefits nature and our communities," he said.
"But that does not put this particular purchase beyond scrutiny."
Riddell-Carpenter said: "This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure one of England's biggest and most wildlife-rich landscapes for nature recovery and for the benefit of local communities.
"That's why the government is stepping in to help The Wildlife Trusts secure the future of the Rothbury Estate, after thousands of members of the public pledged their support."

title: No evidence of Corby cancer rise after waste scandal, says report
text:
No evidence of cancer rise in toxic town - report
An independent report has found "no clear evidence" of higher than expected cancer rates among children and young adults in a town at the centre of a toxic waste scandal.
Dust from work to dismantle the former steelworks in Corby, Northamptonshire, is believed to have caused birth defects and many families suspect pollution is also behind childhood cancers.
The National Disease Registration Service (NDRS) found cancer rates among adults and children living within 5km (3.1 miles) of Deene Quarry were not higher or lower than those seen in the rest of Corby, the East Midlands or England.
North Northamptonshire Council said the report was a "comprehensive analysis" of the data.
The Reform UK-led local authority commissioned the report after requests from local residents.
The report expanded on a previous analysis published in January - which also found cancer rates were not higher than average - and considered a wider age range and a longer time period.
The NDRS examined cancer registrations among children and young adults aged under one to 24 years that occurred between 2001 and 2023, while the previous report considered registrations among people aged under one to 19 years old that occurred between 2013 and 2022.
It comes after parents calling for "greater transparency" protested outside the council's Corby Cube headquarters in July.
The previous analysis found a slightly lower rate of cancer in children and young people in the area near Deene Quarry compared with other areas, while this expanded analysis found a slightly higher rate.
However, the council said none of these findings were statistically significant, meaning that the differences observed were likely to reflect natural variation rather than a genuine difference in cancer rates.
Des Collins, a solicitor who represents the campaigning families, pointed out the NDRS's findings did not "cover all cancers reported to date"
"Above all, it is wrong to put Deene Quarry as the centre of the investigation radius as it's the 'unknown dumping grounds' in and around Corby that are causing the most concern," said Collins.
"Only a fully independent public inquiry will get to the truth and allay local people's fears."
Dr Jane Bethea, the director of public health for North Northamptonshire Council, said: "We recognise that concerns about cancer rates in this area have been deeply felt by some residents, and it is important that those concerns are taken seriously and investigated thoroughly.
"This independent assessment provides the most comprehensive analysis available for this population and time period."
The council's leader, Martin Griffiths, added: "We recognise that a cancer diagnosis, particularly involving a child or young person, is deeply distressing for families, and that concerns about why it happened are entirely understandable.
"This expanded study has looked at a larger population, over a much longer time period.
It found no clear evidence that cancer rates among children and young adults living within the study area are different from those experienced elsewhere."

title: Call for removal of 'eyesore' boulders in Mow Cop laybys
text:
Call to remove 'eyesore' boulders in village laybys
A resident of a Staffordshire village is calling on a council to remove 'eyesore' large boulders and rubble blocking viewing laybys in the area.
Nicola Beckett said the boulders began appearing on Congleton Road in Mow Cop - on the Staffordshire and Cheshire border - in March, and residents believed they were in response to anti-social behaviour and "large gatherings" taking place there.
Beckett, from nearby Harriseahead, estimated that there was "in excess of about 40 tonnes of construction waste and excavated material".
Cheshire East Council said it was aware of concerns and was working with neighbouring local authorities to address the issues.
"Discussions are ongoing and we will continue to work collaboratively with our partners to consider appropriate next steps," it added.
Beckett said she believed that residents had "taken matters into their own hands".
"It started with a couple of the laybys being blocked off, and now it's totally inaccessible," she said.
"It's an area that's of huge local importance to people that live [here]."
"It provides panoramic views across the Cheshire Plains, it's the base of the Pennines, it's the start of the Gritstone Trail.
"There are areas of remembrance up there.
"Many people just use the areas in a very responsible manner to read a book or have their lunch, and we're no longer able to access these areas at all safely," she said.
Beckett told the BBC she wanted the authority to clear up the materials and speak to the local community.
"Come up with a solution that will reduce the likelihood of large gatherings, and maybe remodelling the lay-bys,... but still enabling those of us who would like to use the area responsibly... to have some access. And [to maintain] the local beauty of the area, which has been totally spoilt."

title: Pitlochry Town Hall to be sold to community for £1
text:
Pitlochry Town Hall to be sold to community for £1
Pitlochry Town Hall will be sold to the local community for £1 after councillors approved the move.
The sale follows a consultation that saw 96% of respondents back the Pitlochry Town Hall charity's community asset transfer request.
The charity's chairman Duncan Tannahill described the move as a "hugely significant milestone" in its journey towards securing the future of the 126-year-old building.
The charity has run the venue since July 2025 as part of an agreement with Perth and Kinross Council.
The aim of the takeover was to see the public building open more often for visitors and locals, following the loss of the Pitlochry Tourist Information Centre in 2024.
The two-storey town hall officially opened in April 1900 on a site gifted by Captain Archibald Edward Butter of Faskally.
The construction was funded by public subscription and gifts.
Independent councillor Xander McDade told the Pitlochry common good fund committee: "I live only a few streets away and can see the activity when I drive home and there are signs outside telling us what is going on inside the town hall today.
"That's a marked difference from when it was being run by Live Active Leisure when it was mostly closed up. I think that's a really positive thing for the community."
Tannahill said the level of public support had been "tremendous" and demonstrated "how important this building is to the people of Pitlochry".
He added: "Once ownership is transferred, we will be able to access funding to modernise and enhance the building, ensuring it meets the needs of current and future generations.
"Our plans include improving accessibility throughout the building, reducing its carbon footprint and creating a vibrant, sustainable community asset at the heart of Pitlochry."

title: Hospital payout after Covid-19 patient suffered stroke
text:
Hospital payout after Covid-19 patient suffered stroke
A hospital trust has agreed a six-figure settlement with a woman who suffered a stroke after a catheter was mistakenly inserted into an artery instead of a vein while she was being treated for Covid-19.
The woman, who was 32 at the time, had been admitted to Whiston Hospital on Merseyside suffering from breathing problems.
The woman said the incident had significantly affected her independence and quality of life and had left her with impaired vision and weakness.
A Mersey and West Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust representative said the trust was "sincerely sorry" over the mistake, which happened in February 2021.
An investigation by the trust found a central venous line had been incorrectly placed in an artery rather than the jugular vein.
This meant noradrenaline, an emergency medication used to treat dangerously low blood pressure, had been delivered directly to blood vessels supplying the brain instead of the major vessels leading to the heart.
The mistake went undetected for four days before scans revealed multiple areas of reduced blood supply in the left side of the woman's brain.
The mother-of-one spent more than two months on an acute stroke ward before being transferred to a specialist rehabilitation unit.
The woman, now 37, said she continued to suffer lasting effects, including impaired vision, weakness in her right leg, memory problems and difficulties with concentration and multitasking.
The case was resolved through an out-of-court settlement.
Mersey and West Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust said: "We are sincerely sorry for what this patient and her family have experienced and for the distress this has caused.
"The Trust fully investigated the incident at the time, and the learning identified has since been taken forward to further strengthen clinical practice."

title: County Durham miner welcomes pension release but urges speed
text:
Miner welcomes pension release but urges speed
A former miner has welcomed a move to end a decades-long battle over pension surplus.
They say they lost out when a deal was struck in 1994 when British Coal was privatised, meaning while the value of the fund would not decrease, the government was allowed to keep half of any investment surplus.
However, in his budget announcement Chancellor John Healey pledged that the 50-50 agreement would end and all surplus cash would be paid to pension holders.
Burt Moncur, who worked at Murton Colliery in County Durham, said it was "the best news" but urged pay-outs were made as quickly as possible as former miners were dying every day.
Former chancellor Rachel Reeves agreed in the last two budgets to release part of the fund and pay-outs from the two pension funds - the British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme (BCSSS) and the Mineworkers' Pension Scheme (MPS) -have since been made.
However, campaigners have been calling for the full transfer of the remaining funds.
In his budget speech on Wednesday, Healy said some work had been done but the job was not finished.
He stated: "For ex-mineworkers, I'm guaranteeing that every penny of the pension fund surplus now goes to miners."
Moncur said it was "the best news" for the 3,500 relying on miners' and miners' widow pensions across north-east England.
He said: "We never lost that hope, all the way along we've fought on, we've fought on, we've had setback after setback, the length of the campaign.
"It's just like one of the best things that's ever happened to us really."
The BCSSS has warned it could be several months before members could see any increase from any surplus.
And the MPS noted there had been "no specific timetable" for the distribution of the surplus currently locked up in the scheme.
Moncur said with miners dying every day it was important pay-outs happened as soon as possible.
"We really need the money back now, more so to the most vulnerable, when you can't heat and eat - and sometimes that's your choices - so any extra that goes back into their pocket, it's massive."
description: Bob Moncur worked at Murton Colliery and asks government to act fast as "miners are dying every day".

title: Scot arrested in Thailand over alleged phone theft faces six-week verdict wait
text:
Scot arrested in Thailand over 'phone theft mistake' loses flat and job in wait for verdict
A Scottish backpacker who was arrested in Thailand after he was accused of stealing a mobile phone, faces another six-week wait to find out if he will be allowed to return home.
Rory McColl, 37, claimed he mistakenly picked up a device belonging to a German tourist from a bar in Bangkok thinking it was his own after arriving in the city in March.
The father-of-one, from Edinburgh, spent two nights in a Thai jail, but seven separate court hearings have yet to produce an outcome.
Two police officers testified that the incident was a "misunderstanding" on Thursday, however the case has now been continued for a final verdict on 9 December.
McColl was released on bail following the incident, but had his passport seized meaning he is unable to leave.
His mother, Helen, 70, and dad John, 66, said he had lost his flat and his job as a result of being stranded in the country.
Helen told BBC Scotland News McColl was "frustrated" following the latest hearing.
"He just wants to see his son," she said.
"It has been so disappointing every time. It is out of our control."
McColl had been enjoying drinks in a bar on the world famous KahoSan Road after arriving in Bangkok following a 30-hour journey.
He claimed to have misplaced his phone before spotting one on the bar.
McColl put the phone in his pocket without realising it belonged to a fellow tourist.
It was returned to the woman a short time later and McColl explained what had happened to the bar's security and the police.
Helen said he had initially been taken to the police station to "sober up" but he was arrested and spent two nights "sleeping on a concrete floor".
After his release on bail, he briefly spent time living in in Pattaya, about 90 miles (150km) south east of Bangkok.
He is now living with a family in the north of country until the case is concluded.
December hearing
John said his son's mental health had suffered initially, but they were encouraging him to take each day as it comes.
He said: "Rory is very outgoing by nature, very personable. He never sleeps before the court hearings.
"With all the different cases and hearings, we just had to settle and encourage Rory to keep going."
Helen said she had come out of retirement and was looking after dogs to earn additional income for legal fees.
She said she was not completely hopeful the hearing in December will allow him to return home.
"We're trying not to get too excited," she said.
"There's been so many hearings, we don't give ourselves any great expectations that it will even be over on 9 December.
"But if it is, it will be euphoric, the whole family will be here. It will be like a homecoming."
description: Rory McColl was arrested in Bangkok in March over an accusation that he stole a woman's phone - but police say it was a "misunderstanding".

title: Victims appalled as deadly crush footage included in Call of Duty
text:
Bereaved families appalled by footage of Seoul crush in Call of Duty
Families who lost loved ones in a crush caused by overcrowding in Seoul's narrow streets four years ago say they're appalled to see footage of it on the latest Call of Duty game.
In an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4, video of rescue efforts from the 2022 disaster in Itaewon, South Korea, is used to show the aftermath of an imagined attack from North Korea.
Almost 160 people died and their families are calling on the game's makers Activision to delete the footage, saying including it was "senseless".
Activision confirmed it used recordings from that night but had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".
"In developing Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, we approached the subject matter with care and respect," a spokesperson said.
"The game's opening cinematic utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game's fictional narrative."
'Highly inappropriate'
Thursday marks the fourth anniversary of the crush, which happened when more than 100,000 people went out in Seoul's nightlife district to celebrate Halloween.
The narrow streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.
"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used as it was to create a scene in a game," the bereaved families said.
"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless," their statement continued.
"If the game developer has even a minimum of courtesy and empathy towards the victims, it should take corrective action without delay."
Activision did not comment on the request to edit the scene to remove the video from that night.
Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.
Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.
At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".
description: Modern Warfare 4 uses video from the Itaewon crush to show the aftermath of an imagined North Korean attack.

title: Mini-gardens for bees on Peterborough bus stop roofs approved
text:
Mini-gardens for bees on bus stop roofs approved
Plans to introduce "bee bus stops" aimed to boost biodiversity in urban areas have been approved for Peterborough.
Peterborough City Council said 34 bus stops could include Living Roofs, mini-gardens planted on top of bus shelters that are made up of wildflowers and other vegetation.
The initiative was included in its new plan for the city's bus stops, which will also see "comfortable seating" replace existing perch seats.
At a meeting of the cabinet on Tuesday, the plans were discussed and approved.
The council will award a new contract to Bauer Media Outdoor UK to manage the city's bus stops.
The agreement includes the company providing the council with an annual income of £140,000 from the sale of advertising space, plus 2.5% of its quarterly gross revenue.
The contract is expected to run for a minimum of 10 years, with options to extend it, and could provide the authority with £2.8m over 20 years.
There are more than 350 Living Roofs across the UK, including in Birmingham, Glasgow and Northampton.
Chris Wiggin, the council's Liberal Democrat cabinet member for environment, said: "We need to do everything we can to support biodiversity and support bees and other pollinators because without those there is no other life, so I'm very happy to see these [plans] come forward."
Other planned changes to the city's bus stops include providing up-to-date passenger information and installing digital advertising screens at most bus stops.
