title: South East Water worst for supply - how do the rest fare?
text:
South East Water worst for supply - how do the rest fare?
South East Water is the worst in the industry for supply issues, a new report says.
The company saw its average minutes of supply lost per property it serves increase sixfold compared to 2024, according to the first joint report by the regulators.
Southern Water and Thames Water also performed badly on their environmental performance.
Spokespeople for the water companies say they had made progress on performance.
SEW's poor rating on interruptions comes after customers across Kent and Sussex were hit by multiple water outages in 2025 and 2026 which left up to 70,000 people without water.
Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales (NRW), Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.
The report found Southern Water and Thames Water saw a combined 765 pollution incidents in 2025.
In the report, all of the area's water companies were found to have drinking water of an "exceptional standard".
Southern Water
For Southern Water, which provides water to parts of Sussex and Kent, and covers sewerage services for most of the South East, the company had its "strongest-ever performance for minimising water supply interruptions", according to the report.
But the water company also has a high number of pollution incidents and "has failed to complete all necessary environmental improvement actions on time", it added.
Southern Water customers also have the lowest satisfaction levels of the water industry, with the regulators saying it "must substantially improve customer interactions".
Customers have not been under hosepipe restrictions this summer, while South East Water customers have been.
Southern Water was, however, fined more than £7 million in July for dumping sewage off the Kent coast between 2019 and 2021.
Tim McMahon, the company's chief operating officer, said: "Ofwat's report says Southern Water's performance is 'improving', recognising the progress we're making in key areas, though we're not yet out of the lower category.
"Meaningful change won't happen overnight, but we've made significant progress since launching our turnaround plan, and we're determined to continue that improvement."
South East Water
In South East Water's area, covering parts of Sussex and Kent, the joint regulators report found that environmental performance was showing "areas of improvement", with the company recording 57 pollution incidents, none of which were classed as serious.
However, following several supply interruption incidents in 2025, the water company's performance was found to have "deteriorated significantly".
The company also ranked low for customer satisfaction, adding that it should improve customer interactions.
Regulator Ofwat placed South East Water under an independent monitor earlier this month, and the company was ordered to spend £30.5 million on improvements in July after several investigations into its performance.
South East Water customers have also been under hosepipe restrictions after the South East experienced its driest April to September period in over a century this summer.
John Halsall, the water company's new chief executive, said it "openly accepts that our past performance did not consistently meet the high standards our customers rightly expect".
He added: "Rebuilding trust requires decisive action, and we are already seeing clear, positive progress across our operations as a result of major strategic updates.
"We are doing all we can to prove that we mean what we say and that we are determined to rebuild trust in the communities we serve."
Thames Water
Thames Water, which covers parts of Surrey and London, had 464 pollution incidents, including 24 classed as serious, in 2025, according to the joint regulator report.
Ofwat has also placed the company under further oversight "following concerns with financial resilience, operational performance and ability to deliver for customers and the enviornment", the report added.
"The company must reduce leakage and household consumption to secure water supplies", it said.
Thames Water customers also remain under a hosepipe ban.
A spokesperson for the company said it has "made strides in our performance" and that it is "pleased Ofwat recognised our progress by designating Thames Water as improving".
It added: "This is a company improving its operational delivery, however, it will take time for the benefits of investment to be reflected in regulatory performance."
SES Water
SES Water, which serves parts of Surrey, recorded no serious pollution incidents in 2025, and only 10 pollution incidents across the year.
The company, which serves around 700,000 people, perfoms better than most of the industry in terms of water leakage per property, the report added.
The regulators also found it needs to "take action" to ensure there is enough water to meet future need.
"Customers report levels of satisfaction broadly in line with others in the industry, but it should do more to improve customer interactions and overall experience", the report added.
Affinity Water
Affinity Water, which covers a small section of the Kent coast, was found to have a "largely positive" environmental performance, and is taking actions to improve the environment both in the short and long term, the report found.
Reported leakages per property were also better than the industry average, but customers still reported relatively low levels of satisfaction compared with other companies in the industry, it added.
Affinity recorded 39 pollution incidents, but none of these were classed as serious, the report found.
Across the water industry, the environmental performance of companies fell last year despite investment in the industry, according to the joint report.
Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", while the chair of the environmental regulator said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".
Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.
Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.

title: Scottish ministers to work with councils on £100 energy payment rollout
text:
Scottish ministers to work with councils on £100 energy payment rollout
Scottish ministers will work with councils to ensure a £100 energy payment is passed on to households in Scotland following Chancellor John Healey's Autumn Budget announcement.
On Wednesday, Healey told a packed House of Commons that about 20 million households in England - in council tax bands A to D - would receive £100 this winter, paid directly into bank accounts.
The Labour minister said the payment would "help deal with rising energy bills and take the pressure off in the coldest months".
Scotland's deputy first minister and finance secretary, Jenny Gilruth, told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast the Scottish government would seek to replicate the scheme but it was "not a perfect solution".
"We will work with local government partners on how we roll out the funding," she said.
Healey said the Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish governments would receive funding proportionate to the £2.6bn scheme and urged them to replicate it.
"I call on them to do the same and give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter," he said.
There are about 1.9 million homes in Scotland in council tax bands A to D, according to government figures. To give each of those households £100 would cost at least £190m.
Existing council tax bands are based on 1991 valuation of homes.
There is cross-party agreement at Holyrood that the outdated system should be reformed but no consensus as to how that should be done.
Gilruth said the Scottish government would not be able to re-band the council tax valuations between now and winter.
"The important thing is that people get this money in to their accounts and they benefit financially from this because bills are so high at the current time," the deputy first minister said.
"There are always challenges around the ways in which the UK government administers funding to those most in need.
"But we need to ensure the people get the money that is needed."
Gilruth added that she did not know about the scheme prior to the Budget announcement and would have liked to have seen the UK government "go further".
"This is not a scheme of our making and we are now having to play catch-up with the UK government on this," she said.
"I do think it is regrettable they were not able to share details of the scheme in advance of the Budget but that is a decision they have taken."
Also speaking on BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast, Chief Secretary of the Treasury Emma Reynolds said she had spoken to Gilruth on Wednesday morning before the announcements.
"I'm sorry she feels like that," Reynolds told the programme.
"I shared with her information that we had not shared publicly on the trust she would keep it private, which she did.
"She had some heads up to the Barnett consequentials of the Budget that were going to be announced later that day."
She added that she welcomed the Scottish government's decision to give people in the bottom four council tax bands the £100 payment.
"The prime minister has said he wants to work closely with the Scottish government and it is my impression that I am working closely with Jenny on some of the big issues around the Budget," she said.
How can I find my council tax band?
Scotland currently has eight council tax bands, from A to H, based on estimated property values as of 1 April 1991 - the same valuation date as England.
However, Scotland uses different band thresholds assigned by the local Scottish Assessor.
Band A in Scotland covers properties valued at up to £27,000, compared with £40,000 in England, while band H is for properties worth more than £212,000.
Earlier this year, the Scottish government announced two new council tax bands, which are set to be added from April 2028 - band I for homes valued between £1m and £2m, and band J for properties above £2m.
You can find your council tax band in Scotland by searching your address or postcode on the Scottish Assessors Association website or on your council tax bill.

title: Rare beetle find in Gloucestershire shows species is 'on the move'
text:
Rare beetle find shows species is 'on the move'
New sightings of one of the UK's rarest beetles shows the species is on the move, scientists say.
The great silver water beetle - which is usually found on the Somerset Levels and in the east of England - was spotted in two places in Gloucestershire - far further to the west of the country than usual.
Citizen scientists Gordon Kirk and Bill Watkins made the discoveries during routine moth monitoring in the Severn Vale and Beachley respectively.
Tina Bouttle, from Gloucestershire Centre for Environmental Records, said: "The great silver water beetle's conservation status is listed as near threatened. These are both significant records as it shows this species is on the move."
Despite looking black on land, when the beetle is in water where it predominantly lives, it holds a film of air against its belly which gives it the silvery sheen it is named after.
Bouttle said it was not yet known why the beetles were moving - although the team did have theories.
"We think that it's moving around the country looking for new wetlands as wetlands currently are suffering from pollution and habitat destruction.
"Or they just might be doing really well where they are and needing to find new places to move into," she explained.
Citizen scientists are members of the public who aid with scientific discoveries by - for example - monitoring wildlife around them and sending photos to scientific organisations to help identify them.
The People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES) promotes the importance of such volunteers.
"Citizen science drives so much of conservation and by reporting sightings to your local wildlife trust, environmental record centres or organisations like PTES, people across the country are helping to protect and better understand our wildlife," its conservation research and strategy officer David Wembridge said.
Members of the public are being encouraged by the Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust to become citizen scientists and submit beetle sightings to help track the biodiversity of the county.
"The majority of this year's records would have come from citizen scientists, so this shows you do not need to a professional ecologist to help towards the understanding of this species.
"Each record is a piece in the puzzle to understanding the movement of this species into Gloucestershire and beyond," Bouttle added.

title: Harrogate town centre transformation to start in new year
text:
Town centre transformation to start in new year
Work on a multimillion-pound redevelopment of Harrogate town centre is due to begin in the new year after contractors were appointed by North Yorkshire Council.
The Harrogate Station Gateway scheme, aimed at improving access to the town's railway station for pedestrians, cyclists and bus passengers, was first announced in 2022, but has since faced opposition.
Some residents and businesses claimed the end result would not justify the disruption and expense, but the latest legal challenge to the plans was rejected by the Court of Appeal in March.
Malcolm Taylor, the council's executive member for highways and transport, said the scheme represented a "significant" investment in the town centre.
The £13.4m Transforming Cities Fund project would be carried out by NY Highways, a commercial company set up by the authority in 2021, the council said.
'Listen to businesses'
The scheme includes the redevelopment of One Arch and Station Square, improved traffic signals, a bus lane, a southbound cycle lane on Station Parade, new paving for pedestrians and cycle parking at Harrogate Station.
There would also be improvements to traffic signals on the A61, North Yorkshire Council said.
Construction work had previously been given the go-ahead by the authority last November, with work due to start this year and be completed by autumn 2027.
After the Court of Appeal ruled earlier this year in favour of North Yorkshire Council when the Get Away campaign group had appealed against parts of the project, the authority said it was working with partners to secure the necessary funding and agreements.
Taylor said the work would not now begin before 2027, to "avoid impacting businesses over the busy trading period" and to reduce disruption.
"Before and throughout the programme, we will be talking with local businesses to explain what is happening and listen to them," he said.
"We understand that any scheme of this scale can raise questions, particularly around how it will affect trade, so those ongoing discussions are important."
Discussions would include drop-in sessions and visiting businesses directly, the council added.
It was hoped the work would be completed by autumn 2028, a North Yorkshire Council spokesperson said.

title: Man who broke ribs of 25-day-old baby in Reading attack jailed
text:
Man who broke ribs of 25-day-old baby jailed
A man who broke a 25-day-old baby's ribs has been jailed for five-and-a-half years.
Joshua Grant, 32, from Reading, admitted breaking two of the baby's ribs and causing them brain, spinal and retinal haemorrhaging in March 2023.
He also punched a security guard in the face at the Tesco Express in Bath Road, Reading, in January this year. Grant left the man with lasting injuries to his teeth, before he fled with stolen goods.
He was found guilty in his absence of robbery and theft relating to those offences and was sentenced at Reading Crown Court on Monday.
Det Con Sam Haselgrove, from Thames Valley Police's Major Crime Unit, said: "Joshua Grant caused extremely serious injuries to a defenceless baby who was just 25 days old.
"The harm he inflicted could have had devastating consequences, and I am pleased he has now been held accountable for his actions."
Haselgrove added: "Grant's offending was not limited to this incident. He also used violence against a shop worker who was simply carrying out his duties.
"I welcome the sentence imposed by the court and hope it provides reassurance that offenders who commit such serious crimes will be brought to justice."

title: Ormeau Road: Restrictions imposed on parade
text:
Apprentice Boys banned from parade along lower Ormeau Road
The Parades Commission has imposed restrictions on the Apprentice Boys, banning them from walking along the mainly nationalist lower Ormeau Road.
The Belfast Walker Club had submitted an application for 7 November to parade from Ballynafeigh Orange Hall along the Ormeau Road, across Ormeau Bridge and onwards to Donegall Pass.
The parade has not been permitted to proceed down this part of the road since 1999.
The commission received submissions from a number of groups and individuals, including the organisers, residents of the lower Ormeau Road and the wider area as well as the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) and political parties.
It said allowing the parade to proceed along the proposed route would cause significant disruption to the local community, with the potential for disorder and harm to community relations.
A protest involving 1,500 participants had also been notified to take place at Ormeau Bridge at the same time.
In its determination made on Thursday, the commission said the loyalist parade "is prohibited from crossing Ormeau Bridge at its junction with Annadale Embankment, or from entering that section of Ormeau Road between the junction of Ormeau Bridge and Annadale Embankment and the junction of Ormeau Road and Havelock Bridge."
It also said police had highlighted increased tensions over parading following recent events at Garvaghy Road in Portadown, as well as sectarian attacks on memorials in the lower Ormeau Road area.
The organisers of the parade told the Parades Commission that "they would like to have an agreement with residents of the Lower Ormeau Road, whereby all cultures are respected".
Lower Ormeau Concerned Community (LOCC) spokesperson Gerard Rice said many people had been in touch to express their relief at the decision.
"Following the recent events at Drumcree there was a natural concern that the Parades Commission might get it wrong," he said.
"We hope that today's decision will be maintained through the year ahead."
The local residents' group, previously joined others in expressing support for those living on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
In a joint statement, the groups, which also included representatives from the Bogside in Londonderry and Crumlin Road and Ardoyne Residents Association in Belfast, said they had developed "accommodations" around Orange Order parades in their respective areas.
"Our concern is that such accommodations could unravel if the Orange Order continue to insist on parading down Garvaghy Road, or indeed pursue the same demands in other nationalist/Catholic areas," they said at the time.
Sinn Féin assembly member Deirdre Hargey said that Thursday's "decision is the correct one".
"There was never any basis or justification for taking the community of the lower Ormeau Road back 27 years."
description: The parade is prohibited from crossing Ormeau Bridge at its junction with the Annadale Embankment.

title: Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
text:
Record number of purges as Xi emphasises 'party discipline' at China political gathering
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Since then, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", Zhang Fuhai, from the party's disciplinary commission, told a press briefing on Friday.
He also said the party would enhance its efforts to ensure officials "dare not, cannot, and do not want to be corrupt".
Anti-corruption purges continue
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
Who are the key figures purged?
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violated [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Xi's plans for the future
Analysts believe one reason for the increased emphasis on discipline – which many interpret as loyalty – is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder of Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."
description: Xi's anti-corruption campaign has become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", observers say.

title: South West Water given lowest environmental rating
text:
South West Water given lowest environmental rating
South West Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency over high levels of pollution.
The regulator downgraded the firm from two stars out of a possible four to one, meaning it is now considered a "poor performing company" for its environmental impact.
It said it had performed "significantly below target" for sewage pollution incidents for the 15th year in a row.
South West Water, which has 1.8 million customers across Devon, Cornwall, the Isles of Scilly and parts of Dorset and Somerset, said it knew there was "much more to do" and was taking action to improve areas that "matter most" to customers and the environment.
The annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.
For 2025, South West Water was among four companies rated as poor performing, or one star, while four others were rated as requiring improvement, two stars.
Severn Trent Water was the only company to achieve the highest rating of four stars.
The Environment Agency's report card comes a month after South West Water was fined almost £8m for a series of pollution-related offences over six years.
In the last year it also recorded the sharpest rise in customer complaints of any water company.
Serious incidents in the past year include pollution in St Austell River, killing thousands of fish, while pollution at Exmouth meant beachgoers had to leave the water.
Industry regulator Ofwat said the company met seven of its 23 targets in 2025-26, with below target performance for "most areas".
It noted its performance in relation to water supply interruptions "deteriorated substantially" and, despite improving annual performance by 38%, said the company's total pollution incidents performance remained more than double its target.
Customer satisfaction also remained challenging, ranking 15 out of 17 in the sector.
While storm overflows performance improved by 19%, it still fell short of its target, the Environment Agency said.
'Under new management'
It was, however, the only company to have met its target for internal sewer flooding, or how often wastewater enters a property, every year since 2020-21.
A spokesperson for South West Water said: "We are under new management with a renewed focus on improving our performance.
"We know there's much more to do and although it will take time, we are taking action and making progress in the areas that matter most to our customers and the environment."
They said the firm had "reduced spills from storm overflows by 17% last year alone, with spill duration down by 25%, and we have insourced over 40 new leakage specialists".
"We are working hard to build on the progress we're making, backed by record levels of investment across the region," the spokesperson said.
"We are transforming our network to improve long-term resilience of our water supply; protecting the environment and tackling leaks as part of our multibillion-pound plan to deliver the long-term improvements our customers and communities expect."
A separate report from the Drinking Water Inspectorate, the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales and Ofwat said South West Water's drinking water quality "remains exceptional, and consumers can be confident that their water is safe to drink".
It noted although its internal sewer flooding performance had deteriorated, "it is still performing better than the industry average".
However, it said overall environmental performance "is poor".
In a summary, the report said overall water supply interruptions "remain a significant concern, and it is one of the worst performers in the industry".
To improve the company needed to reduce interruptions and complete a transformation programme to address the root causes of its failures and "substantially improve customer interactions and overall experience", it said.
Surfers Against Sewage described the latest performance ratings as "another league of shame for water companies" but she added they were "a mere slap on the wrist that means absolutely nothing".
Head of campaigns Jo Morley said: "What is the point in these environmental performance ratings when year after year water company behaviour gets worse?"
description: The water firm is performing "significantly below target" for pollution, the Environment Agency says.

title: Two veterans can make further MoD compensation claim over LGBT ban
text:
Two veterans can make further MoD claim over LGBT ban
Veterans who say they lost out on tens of thousands of pounds under an "unfair" compensation scheme for those affected by the military's LGBT ban have won the first stage of a legal battle.
The ban between 1967 and 2000 meant those who were, or thought to be, gay or transgender were subjected to interrogation and dismissal.
Steven Stewart and Mark Shephard were "forced to resign" and so were eligible for the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme. They received £7,000 and £5,000 respectively but claims for larger sums were refused as they were not formally dismissed or discharged.
On Wednesday, Mrs Justice Eady ruled at the High Court they could take their claim against the MoD to a full hearing.
Amanda Jones, representing the MoD, said the claim was "not arguable", adding the scheme had a "limited total budget" and was set up to "mark and alleviate harm", but did not concede any legal liability.
The compensation scheme, set up by the MoD in 2024, offers two payments: a flat-rate payment of £50,000 for those who were dismissed or administratively discharged under the ban, and "impact payments" of up to £20,000 for those affected by it.
Isabelle Agerbak, representing Stewart and Shephard, said this meant those who were dismissed were eligible for a total of £70,000, whereas those who resigned after an ultimatum are only eligible for a maximum of £20,000.
Departure was 'devastating'
The court was told Stewart, from the south west, had served as a corporal in the Royal Military Police from 1988 until 1995, when he was "stripped of his duty pistol and escorted into the office of his commander" and told "incriminating letters" had been found.
Stewart was interviewed under caution and resigned after being told he would face a court martial and potential prison sentence.
"Leaving under those circumstances was devastating," Stewart said.
"My military career ended overnight. The impact of that decision has stayed with me ever since.
"I rebuilt my life, but what happened has stayed with me for nearly three decades.
"It affected my confidence, my relationships and how I saw myself."
Shephard, from Taunton in Somerset, served in the Royal Air Force (RAF) from 1995 as a senior aircraftman technician.
In 1999 he broke down in front of his commanding officer after persistent bullying and told her he was gay, as he was unaware of the ban at the time.
He later applied to leave the RAF after being told he would otherwise be summarily dismissed.
Shephard said he was "driven out of the career I trained hard to achieve and excelled at" and had only recently told his friends and family the real reason he left the RAF.
He received an official apology in 2024 as part of a programme of restorative measures for those affected by the ban, which was presented by Taunton MP Gideon Amos.
In written submissions, Agerbak said the scheme was "irrational and unfair".
She said: "It is entirely unclear how and why the defendant arrived at an outcome whereby those who were compelled to resign would be eligible for tens of thousands of pounds less than those with similar experiences, but who were dismissed or discharged."
Jones, for the MoD, said £75m had been spent on the scheme and that making it available to those who were forced to resign would result in "a very significant additional sum".
She said there had been benefits for the claimants of resigning rather than being dismissed, including being given a positive employment reference and not having to repay a £4,000 bonus.

Woman, 92, dies after being struck by lorry in Inverness city centre
A 92-year-old woman has died after she was struck by a lorry in Inverness.
Emergency services including fire engines and a critical care paramedic were sent to Academy Street in the city centre at about 09:50. The woman was pronounced dead at the scene.
The street was closed for about seven hours while police investigations took place, and reopened at about 17:00.
Police Scotland said extensive inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances and has urged anyone with information to get in touch.

title: Thousands of fake clothes and perfume seized in Accrington
text:
Thousands of fake clothes and perfume seized
More than 3,000 items of counterfeit clothes and perfumes worth £60,000 have been seized following tip-offs from members of the public in the Lancashire area.
Three van loads of items with brand names including Nike, North Face, Dior, Berghaus and Hugo Boss were confiscated after they were found for sale at two premises in Accrington, Lancashire County Council said.
A trading standards officer posing as a customer was able to buy branded perfume for £10, which was later confirmed to be fake.
On 27 October, officers returned with police and seized the counterfeit goods.
Joshua Roberts, cabinet member for rural affairs, environment and communities, said: "Seizing three van loads of counterfeit clothing, trainers, perfumes and other goods shows just how valuable information from the public can be.
"Our trading standards officers work hard to stop illegal goods reaching Lancashire's communities and to protect legitimate businesses, which play by the rules.
"I'd encourage anyone who suspects counterfeit goods are being sold to report it. Information from residents really can help us to take action."

title: Call for better internet in Charlwood after Openreach issue
text:
Calls for better network after village goes offline
Internet outages in a Surrey village left people "unable to carry out daily tasks" for two days, prompting calls for better connectivity in rural parts of the county.
Parts of Charlwood lost access to broadband services on Monday and Tuesday, with the impact amplified by poor 4G and 5G reception in the area.
The problems have led to the Dorking and Horley MP pushing for the government and companies to improve mobile signal in more rural areas of the constituency.
Openreach, which operates the broadband network in the area, apologised for the disruption and confirmed services were now working again.
Feargal Hogan works from home but had to travel to neighbouring towns to get signal during the outage.
He told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "It's been pretty poor.
"It was very difficult to get information about what was going on and when it would resolve itself."
Hogan said he used to run both fibre and copper to ensure there was a back up if one went down, but the older service has since been shut off, leaving the town to rely on its fibre connection.
He added: "When we were trying to call to report a fault we couldn't get a signal, we were having to drive to Redhill, or Horley."
MP Chris Coghlan said: "Several people in Charlwood came to me after being left without internet all day on Monday and parts of Sunday.
"People were unable to work or carry out everyday tasks, with some complaining that communication about the issue was non-existent from providers.
"The 4G and 5G coverage in this area is also very poor, leaving many stranded with no connection all day."

title: Backpacks contain basics for East Yorkshire youngsters in care
text:
Backpacks have essentials for young people in care
Hundreds of backpacks containing essential items are being made available to children and young people who enter care unexpectedly.
East Riding of Yorkshire Council has received 400 backpacks provided by the HEY Smile Foundation and Nurture a Child charities.
They contain things including shampoo, a toothbrush and toothpaste, deodorant and sanitary products.
"These backpacks are a simple idea, but they can make a real difference. They mean that when a child or young person arrives into care unexpectedly, there is something ready for them – something practical that is theirs to keep and use," said Jamie Lewis, of HEY Smile Foundation.
"We can't change the circumstances that have brought a child into care, but together with Nurture a Child and East Riding of Yorkshire Council, we can help make that moment a little easier, and give a child some dignity, comfort and reassurance when they need it most."
The backpacks are being held by the council so they can be got hold of quickly when needed.
"Having experienced the care system myself as a child, I know that arriving into care can be an incredibly uncertain and unsettling time," said Lewis.
"You may not know what is going to happen next or even have the basic things that you need with you."

title: Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
text:
Russell Brand's wife tells his rape trial he is 'kind and a wonderful father'
- Warning: This story contains graphic content.
Russell Brand's wife Laura has told a court her husband is "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".
The 39-year-old told the jury at his rape and sexual assault trial that "the way he treats me is to know me", adding: "I feel very seen by him... I love him very much."
The media personality faces seven charges - three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.
Giving evidence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday, Laura Brand was asked by the defence barrister if her husband respected her when she didn't want to be sexual with him, and she replied: "Yes absolutely."
Laura Brand is the daughter of former golfer Bernard Gallacher and sister of TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher. She married Brand in 2017 and they have three children.
She told the court she first met him at the Edinburgh festival in 2006, explaining that he took her number and they started a relationship soon afterwards.
She said that after his performance: "I went over and said, 'I'm Laura, Kirsty's sister. That was a great show'."
He contacted her the next day, she said. When they met, she said they had oral sex, adding: "He might have wanted to have sex but I didn't want to."
Laura Brand said she knew before they met that "he liked women", and found out that while they were dating that he had been having sex with others.
"I wasn't interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people", she said.
"I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous."
She said she remained friends with Brand while he was married to singer Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012, and got back together with him in 2015.
Asked if she was "aware of his promiscuity" during their time apart, she said: "I was very aware of it. I could read about it regularly in the papers, so I was aware of it and he also told me."
Turning to their relationship now, she said: "We have a very honest, frank, and clear relationship and marriage.
"It is one of the most important parts of our marriage, and our relationship has always been honest."
The charges against Brand relate to allegations made by six female complainants spanning a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.
The entertainer has displayed little emotion during the course of his trial, but was seen smiling broadly during parts of his wife's evidence.
He let out a laugh when she told the court: "We do have many friends and there are colleagues, and we are grateful for those people."
Her evidence came a day after the star appeared in the witness box himself.
He told the jury the allegations had a "devastating" impact on his relationships with friends and colleagues, meaning they would not touch him "with a bargepole".
He also said on Wednesday he had been promiscuous but believes sexual consent is "fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself".
On Thursday, the court also heard statements from two of Russell Brand's ex-girlfriends
Elia Alvarez Diaz said they were in a relationship and lived together for about a year from 1998 to 1999, and described the defendant as "gentle" and "loving".
She described him as being "highly persuasive... a complex character" and "exciting to be with".
"When I said no, however, he accepted it," she said in a statement.
Their relationship ended because he cheated on her repeatedly, she said.
Amanda Alguero Alejos told the court in a statement that Brand had also repeatedly cheated on her.
"He was undoubtedly promiscuous, never in front of me and never when I was around. That was not what mattered to me at the time," she said.
She recalled women "circling" around Brand "like birds", even when they were out as a couple.
The trial continues, with the jury likely to retire to consider the verdicts on Tuesday.

title: Ivan Toney: England striker nightclub assault trial set for 2028
text:
Ivan Toney nightclub assault trial set for 2028
England striker Ivan Toney will face trial in 2028 over the alleged assault of a man at a central London nightclub.
The 30-year-old footballer, from Northampton, previously pleaded not guilty to attacking Saber Da Silva at a nightclub in Wardour Street, Soho, on 6 December 2025.
He formally entered this plea at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday, where a provisional trial date was set for the same court of 12 June 2028.
Judge Christopher Hehir told the defendant he was "sorry" about the delay, adding: "As you may know, the crown courts are operating under a great deal of pressure. We have got a massive backlog of work for various reasons."
Toney is accused of headbutting and punching Da Silva during a confrontation at the 100 Wardour Street club.
The criminal case came after a Metropolitan Police investigation and the charge was announced in July.
Toney, who represented England at this summer's World Cup, was released on unconditional bail after the hearing on Thursday.
His provisional trial date of 12 June 2028 falls during the group stages of the men's European Championship, which is being jointly hosted by England, Republic of Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

title: Swansea: Trafle Mill bridge in Wales is struck again
text:
Watch the moment bridge hit at least 45 times is driven into again
A railway bridge considered the "most bashed" in Wales, having been struck almost 50 times, has been hit again.
In 2020 Network Rail said Trafle Mill bridge in Gowerton, Swansea, had been hit 33 times in the preceding decade, the most of any bridge in Wales and the border areas. There have been 12 reported strikes since 2023.
Despite sensors being installed to alert drivers of the height restrictions, CCTV footage shows a utilities lorry with wooden poles and a crane arm colliding with the bridge on 25 October.
Swansea council said it was disappointing and the warning system was functioning normally. It urged delivery companies to remind drivers of the restrictions.
In the footage, the lorry appears to slow just as it approaches but the crane arm smacks into the underside of the 11ft (3.3m) bridge, causing a loud bang.
According to residents the driver reversed onto nearby Fairwood Terrace and then headed back on Victoria Road in the opposite direction.
Video footage from Victoria Road resident Mark Needs shows a number of lorries and other vehicles getting into difficulty over the years, despite warning signs alerting drivers to its presence.
"The worst one was when a van with a cherry picker got stuck under it, it took four to five hours to get it out," he said.
"Another time a lorry coming down the hill hit the bridge, then a car and a telegraph pole."
Needs said there were sensors on poles set some way back on either side of the bridge. He said they activated flashing signs close by the bridge when vehicles of a certain height drove past.
The flashing sign on the Fairwood Terrace side of the bridge did not appear to flash when the lorry approached on 25 October, but Swansea council said the sensor system was functioning correctly.
Needs said there had been some interesting collisions, including a lorry transporting potatoes that got stuck.
"Everybody had free potatoes that day," he said.
Network Rail said staff carried out precautionary safety inspections following the latest incident but identified no damage.
Network Rail said: "Alongside collision protection beams, which have been in place since 2014 to protect the main railway structure from vehicle impacts and reduce the risk of damage, the bridge is also clearly marked with low-headroom warning signs, with additional advance and illuminated LED signage on the approaches to alert drivers before they reach the structure.
"We continue to work closely with Swansea Council to improve highway signage, and make sure these warning systems remain operational and effective."
Gowerton councillor Susan Jones said: "Obviously that bridge is a problem. When they extended the railway station it was strengthened - if they hadn't, I dread to think."
description: Despite sensors and warnings, Trafle Mill bridge in Gowerton is often crashed into.

title: Man admits throwing petrol bomb at Islington asylum seeker hotel
text:
Man admits asylum seeker hotel petrol bomb attack
A man has admitted throwing a petrol bomb at a hotel used to house asylum seekers in Islington, north London.
Mark Neville, 65, who pleaded guilty to attempted arson when he appeared at Snaresbrook Crown Court on Wednesday, was captured on CCTV carrying out the attack at Thistle City Barbican in Dingley Road on 24 September 2025.
The fire was discovered shortly before 23:00 BST and was put out by security guards. It did not cause any injuries.
Det Ch Insp Paul Ridley said the attack was "designed to terrify residents and the local community", and that Neville had been "motivated by hate."
Neville was identified on CCTV throwing the petrol bomb at the hotel before returning to the door of his flat on Pear Tree Street.
A London Fire Brigade forensic dog also discovered a glove with Neville's DNA in a bin close to the hotel.
Police said analysis of his computers showed internet searches on far right activism and asylum seekers.
In a police interview, Neville stated that his friends had often sent him articles about immigration and that he had attended anti-immigration marches, including one outside the hotel he had targeted.
Neville initially denied petrol bombing the hotel, claiming he was visiting a friend who had been diagnosed with dementia, but after being confronted with the evidence, he admitted he was the person in the footage.
Ridley said his actions could "easily have caused horrific injuries".
"Police will relentlessly pursue those who seek to cause fear and harm, bringing serious offenders to justice," he said.
The hotel no longer houses asylum seekers.
Neville pleaded guilty to attempted arson being reckless as to endanger life, possession of a bladed article and possession of a prohibited weapon (a stun gun) in a private place.
He will be sentenced on 8 December.

title: Concern over cut to young people's mental health crisis scheme
text:
Concern over cut to young people's mental health crisis scheme
Concerns have been raised over the reduction of a specialist mental health support service for children and young people in the north west.
The Card Before You Leave scheme ensures young people experiencing a mental health crisis who present at a hospital's emergency department are given a written appointment with specialists before leaving.
The Western Health and Social Care Trust (WHSCT) said due to financial pressures the scheme is now only operating on a Monday to Friday basis and not at all on weekends and bank holidays.
Londonderry GP Dr Joe McEvoy said the reduction was a further "chipping away at an already threadbare service".
"It's already difficult for families when they're dealing with a young person who is distressed to know how they should manage it," McEvoy told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.
In a statement, WHSCT said the reduction was introduced in August as "part of wider savings measures" and would remain under review.
It said the reduction in the scheme's operating hours applied only to young people "who present out of hours and are assessed as low risk".
"These patients are now assessed by Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) on the next working day rather than the next calendar day," the trust said.
It added: "There has been no change to arrangements for young people assessed as high risk, who continue to receive the appropriate assessment and support based on their clinical needs."
The trust said it remains "committed to providing safe and effective mental health services for children and young people".
In August, Northern Ireland's health trusts announced proposals on how they intend to make savings of up to 12% over three years.
At that time the Permanent Health Secretary, Mike Farrar, said health and social care in Northern Ireland is facing enormous challenges, with a current funding gap of £800m.
There have been no changes to the Card Before You Leave scheme in the Belfast Health Trust, Northern Trust, Southern Trust and South Eastern Trust areas.
McEvoy said weekends and bank holidays are "the times when we actually see peaks in mental health distress in young people".
The reduction, he added, means "a young person in distress on a Friday evening will now have to wait until Monday morning on a normal weekend, Tuesday morning on a bank holiday weekend and maybe a Wednesday morning on a weekend which as two-bank holidays, such as Christmas or Easter.
"It's a small change but it is a significant one," he said.
Foyle DUP MLA Julie Middleton said the decision to reduce the scheme's operating hours should be reversed.
"We should be united on calling for the service to be reinstated and we have to acknowledge that while someone could be deemed to be low risk that could move quite rapidly," she told BBC Radio Foyle.
"We need to provide a pathway where they know it's okay to ask for help, that they've asked for help and the help is coming."
'Going to impact people'
SDLP MLA Mark H Durkan said the Trust's need to save money was directly "impacting on the services, not the services that people want, but the services that the population need."
He said parents should not be deterred from seeking help for their child.
"Any reduction in that service you know is going to impact people. We have to be sure the message goes out there that those deemed more at risk, even medium or high risk, that they won't be just sent home," Durkan said.

title: Guernsey housebuilding at 10-year high, report says
text:
Housebuilding at 10-year high, report says
The number of homes being built in Guernsey has reached its highest level in a decade, according to the latest figures.
The Island Development Plan report showed 408 homes were under construction at the end of June, the highest figure recorded since 2016 and well above the 10-year average of 325.
Officials said there were 1,264 homes in the island's development pipeline, equivalent to between nine and 11 years' worth of housing supply based on current demand forecasts.
The largest residential schemes include Leale's Yard in St Sampson, which has outline permission for 314 homes, along with the Mallard Complex, the Tyre Yard and Pointues Rocques developments.
Despite the increase in construction activity, housing approvals slowed during the second quarter of 2026.
Planning permissions granted between April and June resulted in a net increase of 44 dwellings, down from 74 in the first quarter and below the three-year quarterly average of 69, according to the figures.
The report showed, from the adoption of the development plan in November 2016 to the end of the quarter, the cumulative number of units under construction was 942 in the private market and 184 classed as affordable housing.
The report highlighted a continuing trend of commercial buildings being converted into housing.
A total of 2,691 sq miles (28,966 sq ft) of office space was lost during the quarter, with four planning permissions involving the conversion of office accommodation to residential use.
Planning officials said the cumulative loss of office space since 2023 reflected the conversion of older secondary and tertiary office accommodation that no longer met modern requirements.
The number of affordable homes in the development pipeline remained unchanged at 154.
A focused review of the Island Development Plan is continuing, with the current plan having been extended until 2030.

title: Lego shop builds on Norwich's shopping success story
text:
Lego store builds on city's shopping success story
The number of empty shops in a city centre has fallen to its lowest number in 18 years as crowds gathered for the opening of a new Lego store.
A report by Norwich City Council said the decision by companies such as Lego to open new outlets was proof the city was "a good place to invest".
Hundreds of people queued outside the Chantry Place shopping centre on Thursday ahead of the Danish toy giant opening its latest branch.
Figures from surveys the council conducted showed that 9.8% of retail units were empty last month, down from 15.2% in September last year.
However, the report conceded that the demolition of Anglia Square shopping centre – where 40 units were knocked down – had impacted the numbers.
Ian Stutely, the cabinet member for planning at the Green-run authority, said the figures were "a real vote of confidence in Norwich as a shopping destination".
The council's report covers some of the highs and lows for retail in the city over the past 12 months.
While some notable names have closed – including River Island, Select and Claire's – others such as Swarovski and Menkind have opened branches.
It also highlighted the decision by Lego to open its 24th store in the UK, which is the first in East Anglia.
In her report, the council's head of planning, Sarah Ashurst, said this was "the first time that vacancy rates for units [have] dropped below 10% since July 2008".
"This is a really positive sign and demonstrates that Norwich has a robust and thriving city centre," she said.
Another contributing factor to the fall in empty stores has been the demolition of Anglia Square, on the edge of the city centre, which began last year.
The removal of 40 units in the precinct and surrounding area, many of which were empty, helped bring down the percentage of vacancies.
One of the main retailers based at the site was the discount chain QD, which opened its first store in Anglia Square in 1985.
When speaking to BBC Radio Norfolk about the opening of a new branch in Harleston, QD's head of operations Andy Jermy said the firm hoped to return to the the city one day.
"We would love to be back in Norwich, but it is finding the right opportunity to do so," he said.
Norwich City councillors are due to discuss the report on Monday.

title: Storm-stricken swan released after rescue from beach rocks
text:
Storm-stricken swan released after rock rescue
A swan rescued after becoming trapped in rocks on a beach during Storm Austen has been released back into the wild.
The bird was spotted on Barton on Sea beach on Friday afternoon trapped in a small gap in a cluster of large rocks close to the sea's edge by passers-by who alerted the RSPCA.
RSPCA inspector Jo Story climbed among the rocks to reach the male swan where she said after "carefully folding his wing in to his chest" she was able to pull him free.
He was taken to Bournemouth-based charity Wildlife in Need where he stayed to be checked over. After being found to be healthy and cleared to return to the wild he was released at Christchurch Town Quay on Wednesday morning.
Story said: "The poor swan had been blown into the rocks by the high winds that battered the south coast during Storm Austen.
"He'd somehow got trapped in a small gap in a cluster of large rocks and couldn't get himself out.
She said that after wrapping the swan in a towel, a kind passer-by stopped to help her get out from the large rocks.
After releasing the swan, she said: "It's wonderful to see them healthy and back in the wild where they belong."
Storm Austen caused disruption as it swept across Dorset, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight on Friday.
Provisional Met Office data showed it brought a maximum gust of 69 knots (about 79mph) to the Isle of Wight.

title: Plymouth Parkway sell out FA Cup first round tie against Berkhamsted
text:
Plymouth Parkway sell out FA Cup first round tie
Plymouth Parkway have sold out the ticket allocation for their first-ever appearance in the FA Cup first round.
The seventh-tier side will host Southern League Premier Division South rivals Berkhamsted on 9 November at Bolitho Park, with the match due to be televised.
Parkway reached the first round proper after a 2-0 win over another seventh-tier side, Chertsey Town, at Bolitho Park on 19 October.
Parkway would not confirm the exact number of tickets sold, but said it well exceeded 2,000.
Plymouth Parkway are based less than two and a half miles from League One side Plymouth Argyle and their maiden appearance in the FA Cup first round is the latest positive for a club formed as a park football team less than 40 years ago.
They currently occupy one of their highest-ever league positions and are in talks about overseas investment with the aim of one day reaching the English Football League.
Speaking after the win over Chertsey, Plymouth Parkway boss Karl Curtis said FA Cup progression was a boost for the club's finances but added it was also about continuing their upward trajectory.
"The obvious thing is the finances, but from a footballing perspective for me it's belief and it's continuing the momentum," he said.
"We've done absolutely nothing yet, but we've had a really positive start and it just continues that momentum.
"The boys in that changing room are starting to really believe in themselves as a group and what we could do."
If Curtis' side can get past Berkhamsted they will pick up £47,750 in prize money and will have their eyes set on drawing a team from the EFL in the second round.

title: Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate
text:
Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate
The Republican governor of Alaska has ordered an investigation into an alleged "scheme" which led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the state's US Senate race.
Governor Mike Dunleavy said he was responding to a New York Times (NYT) story which said the team of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
The governor's post on X said he would investigate "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws". He did not say which laws he had in mind.
Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. Peltola's team deny any wrongdoing.
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," the Peltola campaign said in a statement.
They say they did not encourage the second man, Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand. He has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress. Americans head to the polls across the country on Tuesday.
Dunleavy's statement, which did not name the Peltola campaign, said the NYT reporting had supported findings by the state Division of Elections earlier this year.
"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," he wrote. "The evidence will determine what happens next."
The NYT report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Sullivan the schoolteacher to stand in the Senate race.
This was part of a broader effort to encourage other would-be "spoiler" candidates to enter the race and dilute the support of the sitting Republican senator, the newspaper reported.
The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the NYT's reporting.
"The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan," the non-incumbent candidate, said Monica Robinson, a committee spokesperson, in a statement.
The ballot paper is set to list the two men as Dan S Sullivan, who will be described as the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Senator Dan Sullivan told Fox News on Wednesday night that Peltola should "come clean" and described it as a scandal of the highest order.
His fellow Republican senator in Alaska, Lisa Murkowksi, accused the Democratic campaign of engaging in a "pattern of lies". President Donald Trump has called for Peltola to be barred.
Previous efforts by the Republicans to remove the non-incumbent Sullivan from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court which found no state laws had been broken by him running in the race.
Though officials at the state and federal level have called for investigations in the wake of the New York Times reporting, election law experts said it was unlikely to dislodge the second Dan Sullivan from the ballot and it was unclear at this point if any state laws had been violated.
"It turns out that convincing somebody to run for office is not a crime, even if their name happens to be the same as an incumbent," said Justin Levitt, an election law expert at Loyola Law School and a former justice department official.
The non-incumbent Sullivan had a constitutional right to run and have his name on the ballot, added Ruth Greenwood, an election expert at Harvard Law School.
The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.
On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the Times reporting, citing significant sections of the story as well as Dunleavy's announcement.
Some legal experts expressed scepticism of the merits of the lawsuit, and their chances of success given Alaska's courts had already allowed the second Sullivan to remain on the ballot.
The actual legal arguments the justice department made were a "frivolous theory," Rick Pildes, an election law expert at New York University, told the BBC.
He noted the lawsuit did not cite a specific provision that the government wanted to enforce, merely a general preamble taken from a sweeping US voting law.
Alaska election officials asked a federal court to dismiss the lawsuit "because the complaint has no legal basis".
The justice department has pledged continued action in the wake of the New York Times' reporting.
"They are cheating, let's call it what it is," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Fox News on Wednesday.
In a series of Truth Social posts, Trump too pointed to the report and made a variety of allegations against Peltola, who he argued should be removed from the ballot. He repeated his endorsement for Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator, writing: "Dan is a GREAT man, has ALWAYS delivered for Alaska."
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
The battle threatens to delay the full picture of nationwide results following the midterm elections. The ultimate question of which party controls Congress will have a significant bearing on the remaining two years of Trump's presidency.
A statement from an Alaskans for Mary spokesperson, written prior to Dunleavy's call for an investigation, said: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight.
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."
In a statement given to US media, the DSCC likewise denied that it had been involved in any such scheme.
Peltola earlier this week paused campaigning activities in order to recover after she and her family sustained "minor injuries" in a car crash.

title: Under-used Lancaster and Preston park and rides could be scrapped
text:
Under-used park and rides could be scrapped
Two under-used park and ride services which cost £1,800 a day to run could be scrapped in Preston and Lancaster.
The Walton-le-Dale Park and Ride near Preston and the Caton Road Park and Ride in Lancaster are both at risk of closure, as the number of people using them was below the level needed to cover their costs, Lancashire County Council has said.
The sites currently cost the council about £550,000 a year to operate combined, but regularly see fewer than half of the spaces filled.
The sites were established to encourage more sustainable travel into Preston and Lancaster city centres in a bid to reduce congestion and improve air quality.
'Significant public subsidy'
Parking at both sites is currently free, with income generated through the £2.50 return bus fare.
However, Walton-le-Dale costs about £1,020 a day to operate but is only used by 200 of the needed 550 return customers to cover its costs.
Meanwhile Caton Road costs about £780 a day to operate and is used by 150 return customers, with 400 needed to cover its costs.
The council said that as both sites had about 600 parking spaces each, it meant current park and ride use was "well below capacity, with income from fares falling well short of covering the costs for these services".
Proposals to consult on the potential closure of both sites as well as possible alternatives are set to be considered by the council's cabinet next week.
Any future decision about the Caton Road site would also take account of the county council's wider work to support the Eden Project in developing its transport offer, the council said.
County Councillor Warren Goldsworthy, cabinet member for Highways and Transport, said: "I want to be clear that no decision has been made to close either park and ride.
"Both sites require significant ongoing public subsidy, so we need to consider whether this represents the best use of public money, while also looking carefully at what any changes could mean for people who rely on the services."

title: 'Unforeseen staffing issues' close Kirkwall's air traffic control
text:
'Unforeseen staffing issues' close Kirkwall's air traffic control
Flights to and from Kirkwall in Orkney were cancelled after "unforeseen staffing issues" closed the airport's air traffic control.
Loganair's Edinburgh - Kirkwall return service and the Aberdeen - Kirkwall flight on Wednesday - as well as Thursday morning's Kirkwall - Aberdeen service - were affected.
Highlands and Islands Airports Ltd (Hial) said that "regrettably" it had not been possible to plan the closures around the flight schedule.

A Hial spokesperson said: "Wherever possible, we try to plan such closures around our flight schedule but regrettably this has not been possible on this occasion, and a limited number of flights are affected.
"Passengers should contact their airline directly for the latest information on their flight. We apologise for the inconvenience this will cause."
Loganair said its services were affected by the closure of air traffic control.
The airline said it arranged welfare support and overnight accommodation for passengers affected on Wednesday.
A spokesperson said an additional Edinburgh - Kirkwall return service would depart Edinburgh at 15:30.
They added: "We apologise for the inconvenience caused, which is outwith Loganair's control, and thank our customers for their patience and understanding while we work to get them to their destinations."

title: Developer loses appeal for Oxenhope green belt site
text:
Developer loses appeal for Bronte Country site
Housing plans for a green belt site in Bronte Country have been refused for a second time after the developer appealed against the planning inspector's original ruling.
Earlier this year, Bradford Council refused an application for nine homes on land off Moorhouse Lane in Oxenhope, submitted by the trustees of the Holmes Family Trust of 2017.
Council planning officers said the development could cause harm to the land, which is close to the South Pennine Moors Special Protection Area, a protected natural habitat.
The applicants challenged the decision, saying the council's reasons for refusal were "unsubstantiated" and applied for the costs of the appeal to be paid for by Bradford council.
The application said there were "significant benefits in bringing the site forward" and that it would "contribute to the vitality of the village", according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
However, government inspector Chris Mayes dismissed the appeal, as well as the appeal for costs, arguing more evidence would be needed to show there would be no impact on wildlife.
"Residential development of the type proposed could result in the loss or deterioration of land that supports qualifying Special Protection Area bird species outside the designated site boundary," he said.
"A net increase in dwellings is also likely to increase recreational use of the sites, with potential effects including disturbance to breeding birds, trampling and erosion of sensitive habitats, increased fire risk and dog fouling."
The plans had been seen as an early test of the recently introduced "grey belt" planning policy, which applies to green belt land that is previously developed or makes a limited contribution to the core purposes of the green belt, allowing for sustainable development under strict conditions.

title: Colchester charity goes into administration after 60 years
text:
Charity placed in administration after 60 years
A charity that has served its local community for almost 60 years has gone into administration.
Community360 provided transport, mobility vehicles, advice and networking opportunities for people and organisations in Essex.
While costs scarcely changed, the Colchester-based charity saw its income drop from £5.39m in 2023-24 to £2.76m in 2024-25.
In a public statement, the trustees said it was "with enormous sadness" that the decision had been made "following a prolonged period of financial challenges".
It said services delivered through Community Roots would continue independently.
The charity has 82 employees and 46 volunteers.
The statement read: "Despite the considerable efforts of our trustees, staff and supporters, it has not been possible to secure a sustainable financial future for the organisation.
"Our immediate thoughts are with the people who rely on our services, as well as our dedicated employees, volunteers and partners.
"We recognise the uncertainty and concern this news will cause."
It expressed its "sincere gratitude" to supporters over the years and said the formal appointment of administrators was expected to take place in the coming days.
Colchester City Council said it recognised the "positive contribution" the charity had made to Colchester and beyond for many years.
A spokesperson said: "Our focus now is on understanding the impact this will have on residents, volunteers, community groups and service users, and we will continue to work with partners to help minimise disruption and support those affected wherever possible."
Simon Collyer, founder of the Association of Pension and Benefits Claimants CIC in Colchester, said: "Community 360, in its day, helped steer and train many small charitable organisations in North Essex, and their contribution will be sadly missed."

title: Three jailed as part of East London people smuggling gang bust
text:
Gang who smuggled people from UK into France jailed
A gang who smuggled people into France from the UK by hiding them in lorries passing through Dover have been jailed.
The gang of 21 people were sentenced to a combined total of 84 years, said the National Crime Agency (NCA), which investigated 10 different smuggling runs between July 2025 and January 2026.
The migrants paid around £1,400 to enter France and most were in the UK legally at the time but were trying to avoid restrictions on entering the EU, an NCA spokesperson said.
Shuhal Ahmed, Robiul Islam and Qasim Jan were the latest members to be sentenced on Wednesday at Canterbury Crown Court.
In January, the NCA found an operation where 23 people were taken from London to a location near Whitstable, where they loaded onto a lorry bound for Dover.
The court heard how Ahmed, 44, was one of the heads of the East London-based gang and would charge people in return for helping them to avoid border and immigration checks to enter France illegally.
Taxi driver Islam, 50, would then drive mostly Pakistani and Bangladeshi migrants from London to Kent, where they would plan the channel crossings.
'Entire network dismantled'
Ahmed was given eight and a half years in prison, while Islam was given a five year sentence and Jan, 55, another taxi driver, was sentenced to four years in prison.
Senior investigating officer John Turner said: "Our investigation has seen the entire criminal network dismantled, from the organisers right down to the drivers employed to transport migrants illegally.
"I hope it sends out a warning to those who would consider getting involved and think there is money to be made from smuggling people in either direction across the Channel.
"The chances of getting caught have never been higher, it simply isn't worth it."
