title: Von der Leyen lays out vision for new Canada-EU partnership at Montreal summit
text:
EU chief lays out vision for new Canada partnership at Montreal summit
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her vision for what an "associate membership" status for Canada to the EU would look like as officials gather in Montreal to discuss closer ties.
It is "a partnership that comes close to membership than anything we have done before," she said on Thursday's remarks at the two-day Canada-EU summit.
She added it is a type of relationship that would be open "only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together."
It includes close alignment on governance and policies, and partnering in research and innovation.
For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this year's meeting in the Canadian city.
Thursday and Friday's summit is being closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Von der Leyen first proposed "opening the door" to Canada last month for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.
The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.
According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month.
While there is broad support for closer ties, the concept of "associate membership" is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada, he said.
"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Despite some opposition, von der Leyen has continued to use the term has not addressed the disagreement over the term.
Later on Thursday, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.
But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.
Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.
Polls show the majority of Canadians support forging closer ties to Europe, though the Conservative opposition in Canada has criticised the effort as a distraction from other issues, like the high cost of living.
"No one's mortgage or grocery bill will come down," said Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre in a statement, adding that Canada already has a free trade pact with the EU.
Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
On Thursday, Canada released its new National Security Strategy, the first in two decades, which underlines supporting security and stability in Europe as a priority.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, Carney has said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.
description: Ursula von der Leyen continued to use the term "associate member" for Canada despite some opposition of the bloc's members, including Germany.

title: Wang Fuk Court: Hong Kong leader John Lee apologises for deadly high-rise fire at Tai Po
text:
Hong Kong's leader apologises for deadly high-rise fire
The chief executive of Hong Kong, John Lee, has apologised for a massive fire that ripped through an apartment complex last year and killed 168 people.
Speaking at a press conference, Lee promised major reforms to government departments to ensure such an incident would not happen again.
A report by an independent committee, released by the government at the press conference, found that the fire was caused by "misconduct" by the private sector as well as "decades of failure" by government bodies.
The massive blaze at Wang Fuk Court in November 2025 was the deadliest the city had seen in decades. Dozens of people have been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, fraud or corruption.
At the start of the press conference on Thursday, John Lee said he was "deeply sorrowful" about the fire and that on behalf of his government, "I apologise to the victims as well as the city's residents".
He then stood up and bowed, along with several top officials.
Later he announced that the city's housing secretary Winnie Ho had resigned to take accountability for the fire.
The independent committee's report found that the fire was most likely caused by a "glowing source, likely a cigarette" which ignited "paper materials" at the apartment complex, which was undergoing extensive renovation at the time.
Officials have said the government may start using AI and drones with infra-red cameras to detect and identify smokers on construction sites.
The report also found that the construction companies in charge of the renovation used sub-standard building materials and had unsafe procedures.
This included using scaffolding nets that were not fire retardant and covering up windows with inflammable foam boards for a prolonged period of time.
The companies had also used fake information in paperwork to "feign compliance" with regulators' rules, according to the report.
The committee said the main contractor and consultant for the renovation, as well as several individuals associated with the project, deserved "the most severe criticisms" for the fire.
But had the various government departments involved in the project possessed a "sense of crisis" and "paid sufficient heed" to the possibility of misconduct, it added, such behaviour as well as the fire hazards at Wang Fuk Court could have been rectified.
The report also said there were "widespread, systematic and long-standing" practices in the construction sector that were "unlawful and dubious". There was also bid-rigging and other misconduct by various parties, including some who had connections with local mafias, it said.
Lee said that the various government bodies involved in the case would be investigated, and that a unit in the housing bureau which conducts independent checks would be replaced.
Lee also promised to crack down on bid-rigging, including criminalising the practice, and introduce long jail terms and heavy fines.
Built in the 1980s, Wang Fuk Court in Hong Kong's north-eastern Tai Po district housed about 4,600 people.
Nearly 40% of the residents were 65 or older, and many of the fire's victims were elderly people.
Thousands of firefighters were deployed to bring the fire under control. One of them, 37-year-old Ho Wai-ho, died during the firefighting operation.
The fire deeply shocked and worried Hong Kong, a densely populated city where many residents live in similar ageing high-rises, and sparked calls for accountability.

title: Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
text:
Burnham 'ready to support' Poundland staff as retailer faces collapse
Andy Burnham has said the government was "ready to support" Poundland staff as the retailer teeters on the brink of collapse.
The prime minister called for answers over why an offer to buy the business from its current owners, which would have protected jobs, had been rejected.
"This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families," Burnham told the BBC.
The discount chain is teetering on the edge after its US-based owners Gordon Brothers cut off a vital funding supply and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).
The uncertainty surrounding Poundland's future has left some of its 12,000 members of staff fearful about the future of their jobs.
Burnham said: "We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn't been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.
"We stand ready to support the workforce however we can."
The retailer's bosses have filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, giving the business 10 days to find a rescue deal.
The move comes after managing director Barry Williams told staff that the chain's US owner had cut off a vital supply of funding despite Poundland's strong sales.
It is understood Gordon Brothers wants to break it up, with rivals Poundstretcher, B&M and Lidl interested in potentially buying up its stores.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds earlier said he was "very much concerned" by the uncertainty clouding Poundland's future.
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland, which had been struggling, from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1. A little over a year later, it put the business up for sale.
Despite an offer on the table for the business, Poundland's managers and owners have not been able to agree on a buyer.
It could still be purchased out of administration in a so-called pre-pack deal, but the most likely option is for it to be broken up and for Poundland's stores to be sold off.
Poundland was founded in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent and has around 20 million customers per year.
It has across its 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades as Dealz.
It sells low-cost everyday products, general merchandise and fashion on local high streets.
A Gordon Brothers insider said breaking the firm up would allow creditors to recover more money and that this process would ultimately offer the best outcome for staff. The US investment firm's position is that current employees may be able to get employment with new store owners.
If this type of insolvency happens, it would let interested parties firm up offers.
These include Poundstretcher owner, Fortress, which according to one insider is interested in taking on between 200 and 250 stores.
Another large retailer is understood to be interested in buying up more than 100 other sites.
More than half a dozen retailers, include Iceland, Lidl, and B&M, have expressed interest in Poundland's store estate.
Bally Auluk, a national officer at the shopworkers' union Usdaw, said this week had been "incredibly distressing" for Poundland staff.
He claimed staff were having to "watch from the sidelines as a multi-billion pound company jeopardises their livelihoods as it tries to extract £30m from a business it bought for £1".
He said Williams had "reluctantly" kicked off the administration process to give the business time to find a rescue deal, adding that Usdaw was urging Gordon Brothers to reconsider.
Staff at Poundland's customer support centre in Walsall held a protest on Thursday, with some dressing as the Poundland "Pound Hound" mascot.
One employee said they were trying to "save our jobs".
Situation 'wholly avoidable'
There is also a split between the owners and the management running Poundland, who described the situation as "unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable".
"As you all know, our sales are strong and our recovery is taking root. This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration," the chain's managing director Williams said in a message to staff this week.
He revealed that Gordon Brothers had limited Poundland's access to funds that help it run its day-to-day business.
"I'm disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have given instructions that restricts our access to funds that we would, in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement," he added.
Williams said in the memo, seen by the BBC, that the offer from Martin Property Group was a "fully funded, ready to go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we've made".
Three independent directors who were appointed earlier this month to help oversee a sale resigned with immediate effect after disagreeing with Gordon Brothers' decision not to accept MPG's solvent offer.

title: Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment, say regulators
text:
Serious pollution by water industry remains high despite £5bn investment
The environmental performance of water companies worsened again last year despite industry investment, according to the first joint report by the regulators.
Eight of the nine companies in England were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement", with only Severn Trent receiving the highest rating.
Companies were praised for reducing service disruptions but serious pollution into the environment remained a "major concern".
The chair of the environmental regulator, Alan Lovell, said the results showed the industry continued to "fall well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public".
"I'm very angry," he told BBC News. "I think it's extremely disappointing to see the level of pollution incidents... and I completely sympathise with the public."
Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said she was "demanding answers from the companies that are failing" and would be "shining a spotlight on the worst offences around the country".
Four different regulators currently oversee water companies in England and Wales - the Environment Agency (EA), Natural Resources Wales (NRW), Ofwat and the Drinking Water Inspectorate - and this marks the first time they have come together to assess the industry.
It is a nod to the commitment made by Sir Keir Starmer's government to merge the organisations covering England into a single body as part of efforts to streamline regulation.
But it is on environmental performance that the report is most critical.
Serious pollution incidents in 2025 were a "major concern", the Environment Agency said, and remained at similarly high levels to those seen in previous years.
Overall, England's water companies were awarded 16 out of a possible 36 stars for environmental performance - the worst total on record.
The EA said this was due to "declining performance in some areas but also due to our tighter performance standards".
And in Wales, Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water was given a two-star rating, out of four, by NRW.
Industry body Water UK acknowledged that "the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough".
But it also pointed out that more than half of all pollution incidents were as a result of "blockages or vandalism, which are not in the direct control of the water companies".
"It will take time, but record investment will help secure water supplies, support growth, and end sewage entering rivers and seas," a spokesperson said.
Today's report did highlight some "strengths to build on", with UK drinking water quality remaining "among the best in the world".
And the regulators also noted that "leakage has reduced over the long term" but said improvement was still needed.
Will record investment deliver improvement?
Water companies have committed record levels of investment up to 2030 to upgrade their networks and sewage treatment works. But customer bills are expected to rise 36% on average between 2025 and 2030 as a result.
There has already been £5bn invested over the last five years to try and tackle environmental pollution.
But Alan Lovell from the EA said: "Not all companies have delivered the environmental improvement schemes they have been funded for."
In September, it was reported that the number of complaints made by households about water companies to the Consumer Council for Water (CCW) rose by 84% in a year - the highest in 20 years.
Mike Keil, chief executive of the CCW, said that "many customers have not noticed any improvement in customer service or performance" despite recent bill rises.
"People support investment and understand it takes time to bear fruit," he said, but added that "bill payers are already questioning whether their money is being well spent".
The government is planning to introduce new legislation next year to overhaul the structure and regulation of the industry - including combining the regulators in England.
The Welsh government plans to set up a new regulator alongside Natural Resources Wales.
In his Labour conference speech last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that a strengthened Water Bill would also remove limits on government ownership of shares in England's major water companies.
He also promised new powers for local leaders. The BBC understands further details on the idea of "regional bodies" to oversee water companies are likely to follow in the coming weeks.
Water consumption fails to fall, risking supplies
The joint report, published on Thursday, also found that household consumption in England and Wales in 2025 remained similar to the previous year, at 137 litres per person per day.
Government advisers have said that demand for water will likely have to fall to safeguard future supplies, which are facing pressures from climate change, a growing population and historic underinvestment.
Hosepipe bans remain in place across large parts of England and Wales as companies have sought to shore up supplies following drought this summer.
Mark Owen, head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said the industry also needed to take more responsibility and cut leakage rates further.
"Every litre lost has already been taken from the environment while our rivers, fish and wildlife are under immense pressure," he said.
description: All but one of England's water companies were rated as "poor" or "requiring improvement" for environmental targets.

title: Yeadon recycling centre closed due to nearby fire
text:
Recycling centre closed due to nearby fire
A fire on an industrial estate has led to the closure of a waste recycling site in north Leeds.
West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service attended SBT Skip Hire on Milners Road in Yeadon at about 08:30 GMT on Thursday after the blaze broke out.
Yeadon's household waste recycling centre, which is further along the road, has closed as a result of the fire, according to a Facebook post by Guiseley and Rawdon's three Labour councillors.
A spokesperson for the fire service said nearby residents should keep windows and doors closed and warned drivers to avoid the area due to possible traffic disruption.
It is not yet clear how the fire started.

title: Michelle O'Neill blocked from PM meeting in Glasgow
text:
DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has been blocked by the DUP from attending an economic summit involving Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The Sinn Féin vice-president and Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly were both invited to attend the National Economic Council in Glasgow on Friday with other devolved leaders.
The DUP leader Gavin Robinson confirmed that his party colleague Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill and permission will not be granted for the first minister to operate on a solo basis.
The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order march in Portadown from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
A meeting of the party's ruling officer committee was held earlier on Thursday.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the first minister's "arrogance will have consequences", but O'Neill accused the party of being "reckless and irresponsible".
"Her complaints today that she's frustrated from engaging with the British Prime Minister within the sovereign United Kingdom will so be it because her law breaking must have consequences," Robinson said.
O'Neill said the DUP leader's comments were "arrogant and supremacist" adding that the DUP "is consumed with their own internal leadership troubles and divisions".
She said she would be at the Assembly on Monday with her party colleagues to "keep showing up every day for people".
Earlier she described the move to block the meeting with the prime minister as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented".
"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems," she said in a statement posted online.
The prime minister revived the National Economic Council over the summer to encourage greater collaboration between the nations and regions.
Earlier Little-Pengelly said the concerns arising from O'Neill's conduct and the "anger and hurt felt by many people across Northern Ireland, cannot simply be ignored or minimised".
She said the decision comes after stopping a separate planned engagement with the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly.
"I have requested a separate meeting with the Prime Minister to ensure Northern Ireland's interests, including the urgent budgetary and funding challenges facing the Executive, continue to be represented directly," she added.
The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it was "deeply frustrating" that the Northern Ireland executive would not be represented at the National Economic Council.
"I understand feelings are running high but it must be in the interests of the people of Northern Ireland that everyone gets round the table."
O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating last month's unnotified demonstrations in Portadown, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.
The Sinn Féin deputy leader has defended her involvement, saying it was the "right thing to do".
The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said "the DUP's sham response today was beyond pathetic" adding "the DUP is interested only in clinging to office, not principle".
Alliance leader Naomi Long said refusing to attend or preventing others from attending the meeting with the prime minister was reckless and put party interests ahead of Northern Ireland's economic future and the needs of the public.
The Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows told BBC's Evening Extra programme the situation was a "political fudge" that was "all choreography and no consequences," adding that the move would "probably galvanise Sinn Féin further at the ballot box."
The Social Democratic and Labour Party's (SDLP) Matthew O'Toole said "plunging this place into more political chaos is not a sensible strategic move for unionism".
"Ultimately it's only going to make reasonable people here conclude that the largest unionist party simply doesn't want to make the status quo work," he added.
The DUP has been under pressure from unionist rivals and some within its own ranks over how to respond to the row over Drumcree.
Last week, DUP MP Carla Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer board over their leader Gavin Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.
On Thursday Lockhart said she will follow her "own course" if the party does not seek to remove Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill as Stormont's first minister.
Robinson said that while O'Neill and her party colleagues "should be punished, that does not include punishing the rest of Northern Ireland".
The Upper Bann MP, who last week quit the DUP's ruling officer board in opposition to party leader Gavin Robinson's approach, outlined her position in a letter to colleagues which she later posted on Facebook.
Other DUP representatives including assembly member Diane Forsythe have since backed Lockhart's calls for O'Neill to be "removed from office".
On Tuesday, Forsythe said that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".
On Wednesday, a second DUP assembly member called for O'Neill to go.
Maurice Bradley said removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the Assembly to collapse".
Bradley added that the party "must stand together" and "support Carla Lockhart".
Other party members including former MP Lord McCrea and Mid Ulster councillor Clement Cuthbertson have also backed Lockhart.
Party leader Robinson said last week that he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".
Speaking on the BBC's The View programme, Robinson said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.
He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".
"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.
Last week, a court heard Police Service of Northern Ireland intelligence information that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on police had officers cleared a path for the parade.

title: Theni jailbreak puts spotlight on overcrowded Tamil Nadu prisons
text:
Audacious Indian jailbreak saga ends with 17 prisoners recaptured
A fake medical emergency, an audacious jailbreak and a 36-hour search operation that ended with 17 prisoners being recaptured.
Those are the highlights of a story from India's Tamil Nadu state that has captured headlines across the country.
It began on Monday night after 17 men escaped from a prison in Theni district in the southern state after overpowering guards, and ended almost two days later with police catching them in batches.
The incident has drawn attention to overcrowding in Indian prisons. Police say the Theni prison was housing 334 inmates against a capacity of 200, leaving authorities unable to maintain control once chaos broke out.
The state police said it has suspended nine staff at the prison for alleged negligence in connection with the incident.
All the men who escaped were undertrials - inmates on trial or awaiting one - and 18 of them were in one cell at the prison in Thekkampatti in Theni.
On Monday night at 2230 local time (17:00 GMT), one of the prisoners acted like he was going through a seizure. The other cellmates shouted for help and a jail official responded. He was soon overpowered by the prisoners, police said.
The prisoners then got out of the cell, reportedly attacked two other jail guards and took away keys which they used to open the main gate and flee. While 17 escaped, one returned to the prison immediately.
Several prison personnel were injured in the attack.
Police sources told BBC Tamil that they were examining the possibility of collusion between some prison officials and the escaped men.
Sandeep Rathore, Director General of Police for Prisons in Tamil Nadu, said in a press briefing that the jailbreak was caused by "human error".
"There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel," he said.
On Thursday, he was replaced as the head of state prisons and transferred to a different department.
At the time of the incident, only four guards were on duty, far below the staffing required to maintain the prescribed 1:6 guard-to-inmate ratio recommended by the state - which should have worked out to 34 guards against the approved strength of 200 prisoners.
The police then launched a manhunt, calling forces from across the state.
"Advanced technology, drone surveillance, CCTV footage analysis, and the tireless efforts of police personnel played a crucial role," the department said in a statement on X.
Four men were arrested at a bus station in a nearby village, and the fifth was caught while he was travelling in a tuk-tuk.
A drone search of a forest near the prison led to eight more escaped prisoners being caught. Videos of the arrests showed the men obeying police instructions even as they did not answer questions from reporters who were also seen at the scene.
Two more were captured with the help of drone surveillance, police said, while the last two men surrendered on Wednesday.
News agency PTI reported that all 17 recaptured prisoners have been moved to high-security correctional prisons.
Rathore told media that all prisons across the state would be audited to check if rules were being followed.
The incident evoked memories of one of the biggest jailbreaks in Tamil Nadu in 1995 when 43 suspected militants escaped from a special camp after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel beneath a historic fort. Some of them were never recaptured.
While the investigation is going on, the incident has sparked a conversation on overcrowding in Indian prisons. The National Crime Records Bureau's last Prison Statistics India report from 2023 showed a national occupancy rate of 120.1%.
Data shows that undertrial prisoners - individuals who are detained while they await police investigation or court trials - make up more than 73% of India's total prison population. Human rights groups and legal experts have also raised concerns about delays in investigations and trials that lead to people languishing for years behind bars.
Additional reporting by Siraj and Prabhurao Anandhan
description: The jailbreak began with a fake seizure and ended 36 hours later with all the inmates back behind bars.

title: John McGuirk: Family tribute after Liverpool One bus fall
text:
Tribute to 'familiar face' who died after bus fall
A "familiar face" of Liverpool has been remembered by his family after he fell and died while travelling on a bus.
John McGuirk, from Croxteth, spent many years working in pubs across Liverpool before running a kiosk at the city's Lime Street railway station, his family said.
The 83-year-old was the only passenger on board a bus when he fell at Liverpool One bus station at about 12:55 BST on 3 October, said Merseyside Police.
He died a week later, said a force spokesperson, who added both that the Serious Collision Investigation Unit was continuing to investigate what had happened and that a 65-year-old man was assisting officers.
In their tribute, John McGuirk's family described him as a "true character, full of life, who could talk to absolutely anyone".
"You could never keep John quiet for long, and wherever he went, he was sure to know someone," they said.
His family said he was a much-loved brother, uncle and great-uncle who had dedicated much of his life to caring for his late brother Tommy.
"We have lost John far too soon, in the most heartbreaking of circumstances," they said.
"Liverpool has lost a familiar face, and we have lost someone irreplaceable.
"John will be remembered for his warmth, his stories, his unmistakable character and the countless memories he leaves behind."

title: Derry: Council withdraws support for future jobs fairs with British Army
text:
Council pulls support for future jobs fairs with Army
Derry City and Strabane District Council has voted to withdraw any involvement in the organisation or marketing of any future jobs fair that includes the UK's armed forces.
Proposed by Sinn Féin councillor Christopher Jackson, the motion stated that their presence at a recent jobs fair organised by the Department for Communities (DfC) had acted as a "barrier" for some people seeking employment opportunities.
Jackson said the legacy of the armed forces in Londonderry had been one of "trauma, hurt and destruction".
However DUP councillor Niree McMorris said the motion would limit employment opportunities and accused the council of politicising employment opportunities.
A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said it was disappointed by the council's decision and said it would "continue to work openly and cooperatively with councils across Northern Ireland".
The MoD welcomed opportunities to attend jobs fairs across Northern Ireland and "share the wide range of careers available to potential recruits".
Previously, the Army pulled out of a jobs fair at the council-owned Foyle Arena last year following opposition from nationalist councillors after the MoD, which had initially registered as an employer for the event, decided not to go ahead with a stall.
Speaking in support of his motion, Jackson said: "The legacy of the British armed forces in this city has been one of trauma, hurt and destruction of many people."
He added: "To have the British armed forces present at a jobs fair has become a barrier for many people who are seeking employment or looking to advance their careers."
"It has caused hurt to families and victims," he said.
Jackson told the full council meeting on Wednesday that preparations were already underway for a council-run jobs fair without the presence of the military.
"We as a council have an opportunity to hold our own jobs fair and preparation to host a jobs fair is already underway," he said.
"We can't have people who are resident in this council area who want to seek and further their careers be intimidated out of it."
SDLP councillor Rory Farrell said his party fully supported the motion.
"We do not support any organ of the British military being invited to a jobs fair anywhere across this city and district," he said.
"In the event that they are present, there should be no council role whatsoever in facilitating that jobs fair."
'Jobs fair should be inclusive not selective'
DUP councillor Niree McMorris opposed the motion, arguing that jobs fairs should provide equal access to a range of employment opportunities.
"A jobs fair should be inclusive not selective," McMorris said.
"Whatever our individual political perspectives may be, employment fairs should be about opportunity, choice and equal access to careers.
"Excluding the British armed forces from participating sends entirely the wrong message and denies local people the chance to hear about a legitimate and respected career path."
McMorris said many former members of the armed forces lived in the city and district and "deserve neither discrimination or exclusion".
"This council should not be in the business of deciding which lawful employers are politically acceptable and which or not," she said.
"If we start excluding organisations because some disagree with their role, where does that end?"
She added that residents deserved access to a range of employment opportunities and said "they can make informed decisions for themselves".
UUP councillor Darren Guy also raised concerns about the motion, while acknowledging the reasons some councillors opposed the armed forces' presence at jobs fairs.
He said he could understand opposition given "what happened on the streets in our city and in their homes", but stressed that "a jobs fair is all about choice".
"The armed forces is a legitimate employer," he said.
'High levels of poverty in our city'
Guy questioned whether the motion could go "against the equality and good relations policy of this council".
He also criticised what he described as the removal of an employment option for people who might lack the qualifications or skills needed for other jobs advertised at the fair.
"The constant shouts of oppression of the Irish people and the high levels of poverty in our city and district yet all we hear now is elected representatives looking to remove an avenue of employment that may be the best option for someone who doesn't have the skills or qualifications for other jobs on offer at the fair," he said.
"If this council excludes the armed forces from a jobs event for political reasons there is a credible argument that the decision is inconsistent with section three, four and five of our equal opportunities policy because it limits opportunities available to those seeking potential employment."
A senior solicitor at council told members at the meeting that, as with any motion passed, it would result in a paper being brought before all elected members, "where relevant matters would be addressed and considered".
Communities Minister Gordon Lyons said it was a "deeply disappointing" decision by the council adding "it is not fair, it's exclusionary and shows a complete disregard for inclusivity".
"Due to the intolerance of some councillors, people interested in a career in the Royal Air Force, Royal Navy or Army will be denied the opportunity to learn more about those professions," he said.
He said no one should have "the right to dictate which lawful career opportunities are showcased".
"But that is exactly what has happened," he continued.
"Shame on them. Yet again those who claim to champion equality have demonstrated that this is only extended when it is on their terms. That hypocrisy will not be lost on the public."
description: Councillors were divided on whether the armed forces should be welcome at any future council job events.

title: Man who died in double fatal crash during Storm Boelo was a loving grandfather
text:
Man who died in double fatal crash during Storm Boelo was a loving grandfather
An 84-year-old man who died in a crash that also killed a 20-year-old man has been described as a "gentle and loving" grandfather.
Jim McCollum was pronounced dead at the scene of the crash which happened on the B708 Lower Bathville road in Bathgate at about 12:15 on Sunday, during Storm Boelo.
It involved McCollum's blue Peugeot 208, a white BMW 116D and a blue Citroen Saxo.
The BMW driver was also pronounced dead at the scene - but has not yet been named by police - while his 19-year-old passenger was taken to hospital for treatment.
A 20-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman in the Citroen were assessed by paramedics at the scene.
In a statement, McCollum's family said: "Jim was a gentle and loving husband, father and grandfather and will be deeply missed by his heartbroken family.
"The family wishes to thank the emergency services who attended the scene of the crash."
Sgt Dave Waddell, of the road policing unit, said: "We are continuing to appeal for information and would ask anyone who witnessed the crash or may have dashcam footage which could assist, to contact us as soon as possible."

title: Jersey gas leak causes series of road closures
text:
Gas leak causes series of road closures
A gas leak has caused a series of road closures in Jersey as repair work takes place.
St Saviour's Hill has been shut at the junction of Deloraine Road and St Saviour's Hill, and firefighters were at the scene, police said. People were advised to avoid the area.
Island Energy said it was alerted to the leak by a member of the public who smelt gas on St Saviour's Hill on Wednesday evening.
Engineers found the leak in the mains network near the junction of Deloraine Road and Chasse Brunet, with work carried out overnight and continuing until it is fixed, the firm said.
The gas company said work to repair the leak was expected to be completed later with testing and tarmacking to then take place.
"We expect St Saviour's Hill will open fully tomorrow evening," it advised.
States of Jersey Police said the following closures were in place:
- St Saviour's Hill (from the junction with St Saviour's Road when travelling uphill)
- St Saviour's Hill from Five Oaks roundabout
- Langley Avenue/St Saviour's Hill junction
- Chasse Brunet
- Sunshine Avenue
- Deloraine Close
Jersey Fire and Rescue Service watch commander David Fish said crews were standing by in case the gas company needed help.
Kevin Hart from LibertyBus said the 3, 13, and 23 buses were being diverted via Wellington Road in both directions.
He said there was less traffic about because of the half-term break and hoped conditions would be back to normal when schools return.

title: Ethiopia receives 12 Russian fighter jets and air defence systems as Tigray war escalates
text:
Ethiopia acquires Russian fighter jets and air defence systems amid war in Tigray
Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity.
He said Ethiopia and Russia had agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow.
The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.
Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in sub‑Saharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology".
"If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said.
Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military.
Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Su‑35 jets and S‑400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country.
The Su‑35, he noted, was equipped for both air‑to‑air and air‑to‑ground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200km (124 miles).
Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts".
According to him, the jets are highly manoeuvrable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning.
When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority", Qalaab said.
Abiy said in addition to the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence.
Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts.
"We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said.
The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies.
Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty.
Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea.

title: Section of M2 in Kent to close for resurfacing after fatal crash
text:
Section of M2 to close for works after fatal crash
Part of the M2 will close overnight for emergency resurfacing after days of disruption following the death of a pedestrian in a crash.
Motorists faced disruption on Thursday as one eastbound lane between Chatham and Sittingbourne remained closed following the crash at about 21:00 GMT on Tuesday.
The whole eastbound carriageway between junctions three and five had closed for clear-up but one lane later reopened.
Kent Police said a man in his 50s had died after he was struck by several vehicles near Medway Services.
The London-bound carriageway of the motorway, which was previously closed between junctions five and four, reopened on Wednesday afternoon.
National Highways said the still-closed eastbound lane would remain closed for all of Thursday.
The whole carriageway would then be closed from 20:00 on Thursday until 05:00 on Friday.
It is understood that police investigation work at the site has concluded, but detectives said they wanted witnesses to the crash, including anyone with dashcam footage, to get in contact.
The man's next of kin has been informed, Kent Police added.

title: 'Big brother' and AI fears over Lincoln University filming
text:
'Big Brother' and AI fears over lecture filming
A university policy making it compulsory to film lectures has raised concerns about the footage being misused or used to train artificial intelligence (AI), unions said.
The University of Lincoln said it was "standard practice" for lectures to be filmed, and confirmed that was a change from it being "best practice" in the previous academic year.
The university said the policy would ensure "all students have access to the teaching materials and support they need to succeed".
However, Lincoln and Districts Trades Council said the policy was like a "big brother state", while the University and College Union said its members were concerned the content could be repurposed by AI without consent.
Branch chair Dr Katie Hunt said the union was concerned about lecturers being "filmed against their will".
"The university policy does allow for lecture recordings to be used as part of investigations into complaints about staff misconduct.
"So they become, instead of teaching tools, tools for surveillance of us as workers," she said.
Bradley Wall, the chair of Lincoln and District Trades Council, echoed the concerns, and said the policy was akin to a "big brother state constantly following you around, recording you so they can point out when you've done something bad".
"I don't think there's a single person out there that would be arguing this is a policy they would be happy with," he said.
Hunt said the previous policy, where staff could opt out of recording lectures, had "worked well" and said it should remain "voluntary".
"Colleagues are worried about AI, about our voice, our comments, our images being repurposed without our consent, perhaps used to train AI or being distorted," she said.
"Some of us are concerned about safety. Some of our migrant colleagues who come from more authoritarian regimes are concerned about comments that they make in an unguarded, spontaneous way, getting out and attracting negative consequences."
A University of Lincoln spokesperson said it was commited to an "inclusive and high quality learning experience" for students.
They said "choosing not to record teaching sessions risks creating inequalities" in students' access to learning resources and the policy allows "for exceptions and reasonable adjustments" where recording is not appropriate.
"We remain committed to constructive engagement with our recognised trade unions as we implement the policy," the spokesperson added.
"Our priority remains ensuring that all students have access to the teaching materials and support they need to succeed."

title: Sixty police officers recruited for new Bee Network unit
text:
Sixty police officers recruited for new Bee Network unit
Sixty police officer have been recruited to patrol Greater Manchester's trams and buses.
The new Transport Policing and Crime Command has been created to tackle crime and antisocial behaviour on the Bee Network.
The new squad will deliver a "significant increase" in visible policing and enforcement across the transport network, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said.
The dedicated unit, which will also cover the city's active travel routes and roads, has been formed with funding from the Mayor of Greater Manchester's budget.
It will be supported by control centre staff at GMP and Transport for Greater Manchester, which has access to CCTV cameras across bus stations, interchanges, tram stops and train stations.
Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson said the aim was to "make the roads and public transport among the safest in the UK".
Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester said the move would "bring together up to 300 police and safety officers, with high-profile patrols across our roads and the Bee Network".
She added: "It means a stronger presence in our communities and faster action when people need help."
The unit would also "crack down on dangerous driving to reduce the number of deaths and serious injuries on our roads", she said.

title: ITV seeks to continue lucrative Emmerdale set tours
text:
ITV seeks to continue Emmerdale set tours
The producers of Emmerdale are hoping to continue its popular visitor tours which generate millions of pounds a year.
The set of the Yorkshire-based soap in Harewood, Leeds, attracts more than 40,000 visitors a year and fans can see behind the scenes of the fictional Emmerdale village, home to the famous Dingle family.
ITV Studios has applied to Leeds City Council to continue the two-hour experience after the current planning permission expires and requested that visitors can also arrive by bike or on foot.
Emmerdale has been running since October 1972 and is watched by millions of people in 120 countries.
According to the planning report, the tours contribute £7.7m a year to the local tourist economy and have been running for more than 10 years.
The report said: "The Emmerdale Village Tour is a popular tourist attraction.
"It provides fans of the popular television continuing drama the opportunity to visit the exterior, particularly the core set at Emmerdale Village."
The report also said visitors could access the tour via car, bicycle, a public walking route or collection from a nearby bus stop, removing the need for coach travel.
"Two coaches operate in rotation to facilitate the maximum of two tours per hour whilst allowing for reasonable boarding, alighting and travel between locations, in line with the planning conditions.
"This application seeks to remove the requirement for coach travel as visitors will travel direct to site."
Separately, ITV has already lodged a separate application to permanently film the show at Stub House and Burdon Head Farm, on Harrogate Road, after consent runs out next June, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
A full change of use planning application is out for consultation until 13 November.

title: Plaid child poverty payment talks positive, says Welsh Secretary
text:
Talks over Plaid £10 child poverty payment positive, says Welsh secretary
Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock says "positive" talks are taking place over Plaid Cymru's flagship plans for a payment for Wales' poorest parents.
Plaid ministers in Cardiff want to trial offering £10 a week for 15,000 children aged under six, in households already receiving universal credit (UC).
Finance Minister Elin Jones has asked for the payment - known as Cynnal - to be exempt from taxation and disregarded from benefits.
Jones said she could not see a reason why the UK government could not move quickly.
Kinnock told BBC Wales that officials in the Welsh government and the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) were "working together" on the issue.
Cynnal was a key pledge of Plaid's election campaign in May.
There have been concerns the payment could be treated as regular income, unless the UK government made an exemption for it.
Kinnock said: "We are clear that officials in the Department for Work and Pensions and Welsh government officials are working together on Cynnal.
"We are absolutely positive about that.
"We need to make sure that the numbers work and there are no unintended consequences."
Cynnal was one of the items put in a list of requests to the UK government by Jones, ahead of Wednesday's budget.
Jones said: "It was in the UK government's gift to confirm a decision on that in the Budget. They've not done so, which means that we're still uncertain as to whether this exemption will be given to the Cynnal child payment.
"I don't see any reason why the UK government can't move reasonably quickly now on this decision, because it is something, hopefully, that is in their interests as well, to see Welsh government look to tackle child poverty in Wales.
"We can't start this payment before we've had the clarity from the UK government that the payment will be exempt from taxation and benefits."
Jones wrote for the Chancellor John Healey's support in September to ensure payments made through the Cynnal programme remained "exempt from taxation and disregarded for benefit calculations".
The Budget on Wednesday saw an extra £450m for the Welsh government over three years.
Much of it is triggered by two schemes in England - cuts to business rates and a £100 payment scheme to help people with their energy bills.
The Welsh government announced that it would implement a similar assistance programme for households in council tax bands A-D.
Ministers said the extra money amounted to a "real-terms cut" below the rate of inflation, but that was denied by the UK government.

title: M23 Rebels: US sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over Congo war
text:
US sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over DR Congo conflict
The United States has imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its alleged support for the M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, increasing pressure on Kigali to withdraw its troops and halt support for the rebels.
"Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops from eastern DRC," US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The sanctions come months after Rwanda and DR Congo signed a US-brokered peace agreement aimed at ending the conflict.
Fighting has continued in eastern DR Congo since early 2025, when M23 seized the cities of Goma and Bukavu. Rwanda denies backing M23.
The US Treasury says Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
The M23 has seized mineral-rich areas, including gold-mining sites in South Kivu and Rubaya, a major coltan-producing area in North Kivu. Washington says minerals from rebel-held territory enter Rwanda's supply chains, alleging that Rwanda exports more minerals than it produces.
The sanctions are intended to reinforce the Washington Accords, signed by the Congolese and Rwandan presidents in December 2025 under US mediation. The deal aimed to end the conflict and expand regional trade and investment, but fighting has continued.
On 24 October, ahead of the sanctions announcement, DR Congo President Félix Tshisekedi urged the international community to increase pressure on Rwanda.
"We must firmly demand that the international community impose concrete sanctions against Rwanda and exert increased pressure, so that we may finally secure a lasting peace in our country," he said.
In a statement to Reuters, DR Congo foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and urged Rwanda to honour its commitments under the Washington Accords, respect the UN Charter and withdraw its troops from Congolese territory.
"The Washington Accords contain clear commitments regarding Rwanda's security, specifically the neutralization of the DR Congo-sponsored FDLR genocidal militia, which are wholly unmet, and with no accountability," Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo told the BBC.
The FDLR is a militia linked to perpetrators of Rwanda's 1994 genocide. Kigali considers it a security threat and cites its presence in eastern DR Congo to justify its military posture.
"Rwanda remains ready to fully implement the Washington Accords, concurrently with the willingness of the DRC to fulfill those commitments, and with the mediator holding all parties accountable," she said.
The US also sanctioned Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a popular bank and financial institution serving Rwanda's security services.
Washington alleges it facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions for M23 and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance, helped pay for military equipment for Rwandan forces from China and enabled gold to be transported from rebel-controlled areas to Kigali.
The sanctions freeze the designated entities' assets under US jurisdiction and generally prohibit US individuals and businesses from conducting transactions with them, unless authorised or exempt. Violations can result in penalties for US and foreign parties.
The measures follow earlier US sanctions against Rwanda's army and four senior military commanders in March 2026. The US imposed further sanctions on Gasabo gold refinery and three mining companies accused of smuggling conflict minerals in June 2026.
Pressure is also mounting over Rwanda's international sports partnerships. Two US senators have urged the National Basketball Association (NBA) to reconsider its commercial relations with Kigali, questioning whether it aligns with the league's stated commitment to human rights.
In a letter sent to NBA commissioner Adam Silver on 23 October, senators Jeff Merkley and Marsha Blackburn questioned the league's continued partnership with Rwanda amid allegations of human rights abuses.
The NBA has yet to issue a substantive response to the letter.
Rwanda has used sports high-profile sports sponsorship to raise its international profile. Early this month, it secured a 10-year deal to host Formula 1's African Grand Prix in the early 2030s.
The country's sponsorship of Arsenal ended in 2026, while Bayern Munich has also ended its commercial partnership with Visit Rwanda.
The M23 has recently joined a new rebel coalition, known as the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) and led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, which wants to oust Tshisekedi's government.

title: Gurkha band plays to veterans in new Colchester home
text:
Gurkha band plays to veterans in new Colchester home
A Gurkha military band has performed for the first time since relocating from Kent to Essex.
The Band of the Brigade of Gurkhas played traditional folk music of Nepal to Gurkha veterans in Colchester on Wednesday, ahead of its first public appearance at the city's Remembrance Sunday parade.
Tuba player Ankit Rai said taking part in the performance felt "like a home away from home" and that it reminded him of his grandfather, "who was in the British Army and I followed his legacy".
"Our Gurkha veterans are a foundation for us," he added. "They have built up the legacy that we are following today and seeing them dancing was quite overwhelming for us."
Following the partition of India in 1947, an agreement between Nepal, India and Britain meant four Gurkha regiments from the Indian Army were transferred to the British Army, eventually becoming the Gurkha Brigade.
Gurkhas have been part of the British Army for almost 200 years and more than 200,000 fought in the two world wars.
Gurkhas have also served in Hong Kong, Malaysia, Borneo, Cyprus, the Falklands, Kosovo and now in Iraq and Afghanistan.
The band relocated to the city from St John Moore Barracks in Folkestone in the summer.
Rai said performing traditional and popular folk songs, like Resham Firiri, at the event was "a very privileged and honourable thing to do" and encouraged a sense of pride towards his heritage.
Retired Maj Udai Bahadur Gurung MBE watched the performance and said: "They were excellent, I've seen them playing in the late 1990s and it's now 2026 - a lot of time has gone past.
"This is my first time seeing them on parade playing their music."
He said there were more than 3,000 members of the Gurkha community in Colchester.
Cpt David James Hatton, director of music for the Band of the Brigade of Gurkhas, said the performance was "fantastic and lovely to see the Nepalese community really engaged with us".
Hatton said it is an honour for people to be in the Gurkhas.
He added that the day consisted of "a few traditional Nepalese tunes, some really modern and some very very old and really famous and that obviously strikes at the heart - remembering home".
"This is something we do annually, we play to the veterans in Nepal, but it is really lovely to connect to the local community here."

title: Mum pilots daughter and Framlingham classmates on Iceland flight
text:
Mum pilots daughter and classmates on Iceland flight
An airline pilot had a flight to remember when she flew her daughter, classmates and teachers to Iceland for a school trip.
Marnie Munns captained a flight from Stansted Airport to Reykjavik with her 17-year-old daughter Lillian and about 30 others from Framlingham College, Suffolk, on board.
She managed to swap a shift to make sure she could be in the cockpit for the flight on Monday.
"It isn't every day you get to go to Iceland, and it certainly isn't every day your mum flies you there," said Lillian.
Munns, of Cambridge, said it was a "huge privilege" to be at the controls of the Jet2 Airbus A321neo with her daughter and her fellow pupils on board.
She had initially planned on surprising geography student Lillian on the morning of the flight but had to come clean during a parents' evening.
"When I first told her I was doing it, she couldn't believe that I was actually going to do it and had followed through on it," said Munns.
"Pilots will try to fly their family because it is such a unique experience and it is just a real pleasure, so it was nice to have a really lovely, personal day out."
Lillian's party were joined on the 232-seater's full flight by pupils and staff from other schools embarking on a similar trip.
Her teachers were not the only people excited to learn who the pilot would be.
"What surprised me was the excitement of my fellow crew members when I told them I had the pleasure of flying my daughter and had the whole school trip on board," said Munns.
"The first officer was so excited about it and the crew were fantastic and they found out where she was sitting and it was really nice and quite funny."
Women make up about 6% of commercial airline pilots worldwide, according to the Civil Aviation Authority.
Munns has been a pilot for 25 years and a captain for 19 years but had never flown her daughter on a commercial flight before.
She said while she tried to do her best on every flight, she did feel added pressure when flying her daughter – especially in making the flight announcements, as Lillian was keen for a "shout-out".
"I was mindful we had many other schools on board, and so I wanted to make sure everyone felt they were special to be on the flight, but of course, my daughter," she said."

title: A143 near Stanton full of potholes again despite repair
text:
Road that melted in summer full of potholes again
A busy commuter road that saw its surface reportedly melt during the summer heatwaves is again facing issues with potholes.
The A143 between the villages of Ixworth and Stanton, north-east of Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, was closed in July for urgent repair work.
Conservative county councillor for Blackbourn, Harry Richardson, is calling for a public meeting "where Suffolk's political leaders can explain to residents how they will fix this ongoing saga".
A spokesperson for the county council's Suffolk Highways team apologised for the "ongoing road surface issues" and said it "recognised the frustrations of motorists, residents and businesses".
Commuters use the road heavily, which runs between Gorleston-on-Sea in Norfolk and Haverhill.
Permanent repair work was scheduled for early August but defects have appeared again.
The spokesperson said: "Following the original surface dressing works, defects emerged which have been the subject of inspections and remedial works over the past year, but further deterioration of the road surface has occurred and we do appreciate the concern this is generating locally.
"Suffolk Highways is developing a plan for further works, which we expect to be finalised shortly and implemented as soon as possible.
"In the meantime, the site will continue to be monitored and warning signs remain in place. We would ask motorists to take care and drive according to the prevailing road conditions."
Richardson said: "I am deeply concerned about reports of a further deterioration in the road surface.
"This follows months of chaos and I have asked Suffolk Highways to investigate urgently."
Previously, West Suffolk district councillor Jim Thorndyke, who lives in Stanton, told the BBC that problems started when the road was resurfaced in September 2025.

title: Bury St Edmunds pitstop for the busker cycling with a piano
text:
Quick pitstop for the busker cycling with a piano
A busker who is cycling across the country with an upright piano in tow has taken his foot off the pedals in Suffolk.
James Tofalli, known as the Piano Man, tickled the ivories during a brief stop off in Bury St Edmunds.
The pianist set off from Land's End in Cornwall on 11 July and has been joined on the 874-mile (1,407 km) cycle to John O'Groats by his faithful cocker spaniel, Jeff.
Tofalli told BBC Radio Suffolk his aim was to bring smiles to people's faces, raise awareness of mental health and autism, and eradicate barriers to music by campaigning for more pianos to be installed in public spaces.
"People are surprised, shocked and confused at the route I'm taking, but the majority of responses are positive, and that's the joy of what street music is," he said.
"I've busked in Bury St Edmunds a lot in the past and it is a great place to play - I've had a lot of positive experiences, but for me Bury is a big part of this journey."
Tofalli, who has battled homelessness and mental health issues, first started taking his music seriously after plucking up the courage to have a go on a public piano at London's St Pancras station 10 years ago.
At the time he said he was battling an addiction, but having a musical outlet gave him an "opportunity to phase that addiction out and bring the piano in".
He credits public pianos with helping him to "overcome addiction and find his footing with ADHD".
"I still get nervous playing, but it is a happy excitement and I've done what I've set out to do and that's bring music to people," he added.
"I can't even put it into words [how the piano changed my life] - I genuinely wouldn't be here today without playing the piano."
Tofalli first set himself the challenge of travelling the country on his purpose-built cargo bike in 2021, but his trip was curtailed when he was stopped by police.
He said he was subsequently charged with illegally "driving a piano" on the A92 in Arbroath, Scotland.
This time, therefore, he is even more determined to cross the finish line – although when that will be remains a "work in progress".
"Loads of people have done Land's End to John O'Groats, cycling or walking in many different ways," he said.
"And I believe it had been done with a keyboard, but nobody's ever done it with a full upright piano with an iron frame."
Tofalli said his mission was to raise money to "acquire, refurbish, place and maintain pianos in public spaces, town squares, stations, parks, community hubs and family homes".
He is funding the journey himself by busking in towns and cities along the way.
"The idea is to give people the opportunity I had when I was struggling with addiction," he added.
"There's no-one to say, 'You can't try it, you can't have a go', even if you go up and just press a few notes – there's no barriers, there's no boundaries."
The Piano Man's efforts went down well with people in Bury St Edmunds - not least Steven Hooper, who has seen him busk before and always gives him £20.
"He has come a long way with his mental health and everything else and he is just spectacular, to just sit here and play music to everyone is unbelievable," he said.
"I had not seen him for a while, but then I saw his face and I came over - it's lovely and just brilliant."

title: 'Our son was ill and we felt dismissed as worrying new parents'
text:
'Our son was ill and we felt dismissed as worrying new parents'
When Becca and Harvey first raised concerns over their newborn son's rash, they said they felt dismissed by healthcare workers as "worrying new parents".
Their son Roman, who was born in July, had become increasingly unwell during his first few weeks of life, with the couple describing him as swelling, "screaming for hours" and "clawing at his own face".
Becca and Harvey, from Ipswich, said they repeatedly sought medical advice and were reassured by medics that his symptoms were normal or attributed to conditions such as baby acne.
In September, two months after his symptoms first appeared, Roman was diagnosed with a cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA).
"We felt brushed off, but he'd been to hospital more times in two months than I have in my entire life. If we hadn't been so persistent, he'd still be ill now," Becca said.
Harvey, 27, said: "After two weeks [from his birth], we noticed he was getting rashes and hives after his bottle.
"He'd become irritated, clawing at his face, leaving scratches even with mittens on.
"We initially thought it was just all part of having a newborn, their skin becoming used to their surroundings. We quickly realised it wasn't that."
CMPA can be life-threatening and Allergy UK said 2% to 3% of children have the condition, making it the most common food allergy in childhood.
The charity said cow's milk was responsible for more than a quarter of fatal food-anaphylaxis cases in children.
Dr John Chapman, a consultant paediatrician at the James Paget Hospital in Great Yarmouth, Norfolk, said the allergy can be difficult to diagnose and doctors often rely on symptoms and parents' accounts.
"Only about one in 10 babies with a milk allergy will have a positive allergy test. That means nine out of 10 are diagnosed from their history and the story parents give you, which makes it difficult," he added.
The couple said Roman became increasingly distressed after feeds, and they began questioning whether they were overreacting, despite feeling sure something was wrong.
"Whoever you go and see, they will ask if you are a first-time parent," said Harvey.
Becca, 29, added: "A lot of the time it's followed with, 'it's normal' or 'first-time parents are overprotective', and you're told you're worrying too much.
"Even on our third GP visit, we listed all his symptoms. The scratching, blood in his poo and continuous crying.
"A CMPA symptom is losing weight, but Roman was gaining weight, so we were told he was OK when we knew he wasn't."
'We felt brushed off'
After noticing periods where Roman appeared to stop breathing, Becca called NHS 111.
After paramedics found his oxygen levels dropped when he lay flat. He was initially diagnosed with silent reflux and prescribed medication, but his symptoms continued to worsen and he began to develop hives and have diarrhoea and feeding difficulties.
Becca said seeing her newborn in an ambulance was the "hardest time of our lives".
"He was so swollen and there was nothing that we could do to fix it. It was really hard. In fact, it was hell," she said.
The couple began to research Roman's symptoms and found them to match those for CMPA.
In September Roman reacted badly to a hypoallergenic formula and was taken to the children's assessment unit at Ipswich Hospital, where doctors diagnosed him with CMPA.
Becca said receiving the diagnosis felt like a "weight had been lifted" off her, with Harvey adding: "To have that CMPA diagnosis, and know we weren't overreacting, was a huge relief."
Diagnosis difficult
After Becca shared Roman's story on TikTok, hundreds of other parents responded with similar experiences of living with CMPA.
The couple have since launched a petition calling for mandatory CMPA training and specialist referral pathways in primary care, which Harvey said would help similar families.
"It seems there's a gap in knowledge. We believe there could be more specialised training in primary care to build awareness and understanding of the allergy.
"That would go a long way towards helping families in the future and empowering them to advocate for their children.
"Roman can't talk. We need to be his voice."
Chapman, a consultant paediatrician, said: "I think GPs have got a lot better at diagnosing milk allergy.
"I would always support increased education for general practitioners, who have very difficult jobs. I don't think there is one thing you could do to help them recognise it.
"GPs need to spot unusual or unexplained symptoms and not brush them off. They must think: 'Could this be a milk allergy?'"
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said: "We know living with an allergy can be frightening for children and their families.
"We are committed to improving care and support for people with allergies and are working closely with NHS England, clinicians and experts, including the National Allergy Strategy Group, to consider how services can be strengthened and patient outcomes improved."

title: Nurseries face 'difficult balance', minister says
text:
Nurseries face 'difficult balance', minister says
The politician with responsibility for nursery provision in Jersey has said she wants to "open lines of communication" with the sector to address challenges including staffing levels.
The Assistant Minister for Education, deputy Lucy Stephenson said she was due to meet those who had expressed concerns.
It comes ahead of the permanent closure of the Busy Bees Leeward Nursery in St Helier at the end of this week.
The Jersey Early Years Association (JEYA) has previously warned that the island does not have enough "appropriately qualified staff" to meet increasing demand.
In a statement, Busy Bees Leeward Nursery said it had "worked hard to find a way to keep the nursery open" but due to "ongoing challenges in recruiting the qualified early years staff needed to operate the nursery sustainably" it would have to close.
It said affected families had been offered places at other sites owned by Busy Bees.
In the States Assembly, Deputy Louise Doublet asked the assistant minister what could be done to ensure nursery workers receive a fair wage and conditions.
'High-pressure job'
Stephenson said the annual Childcare Providers Survey consistently highlighted "recruitment and retention is a challenge".
However, she also said that "many providers were paying the living wage and offering other benefits to staff".
She said one of the key areas for government was "how it can help to upskill and the courses that are offered", and she was keen to "check in" with providers about what more could be done.
She told the BBC: "We can't expect government to have all the answers.
"I also would acknowledge it's quite a high-pressure job.
"I've got young children and I can only imagine how difficult it must be in a very, very busy early years setting."
Stephenson said there was a "difficult balance" to be struck "to have the incentive for people to enter the industry... but you need to keep the cost of childcare down".
'Workforce challenges'
One childcare provider who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC the closure of Busy Bees Leeward Nursery "illustrates the seriousness of the situation".
They said "recruiting from outside Jersey is increasingly difficult because of the island's high cost of living".
They added childcare workers were "skilled professionals" and "financial constraints make it extremely difficult to reward these professionals appropriately".
The result was the industry was "losing experienced practitioners to better-paid and less stressful employment elsewhere", they said.
While the provider said they support financial assistance for parents, they cautioned that there has been "no corresponding investment in the sector to address the underlying capacity and workforce challenges".
"There is a very real concern that the places simply will not be available, including for parents wishing to use the additional funding to increase the number of hours their children attend," they said.
Meanwhile, a nursery in Trinity said it had no problems with staffing and there were even people wanting to work there should a post become available.
The owner who runs Acorn Nursery School, Vicky Scarborough, said all the hours for their children who are aged between two and four were met by the government so childcare costs were also not an issue.
But she said the difference in how funded hours are administered for each age group remained an issue.
The government pays nurseries directly for funded hours for 3-4 year olds, reducing bills for families at the outset.
For 2-3 year olds, parents must pay the full cost of fees before claiming back funded hours.
Scarborough said: "It would be more practical and less stressful for the parents, and indeed easier for the government, if there was one form of administration to cover both areas of funding."
Previously JEYA warned "a number of providers... do not currently have additional capacity either to take more children or to offer additional hours to children already attending their settings".
JEYA Chair, Belinda Lewis said "increased financial support for parents will therefore not, by itself, necessarily translate into increased access to childcare".
