title: Concerns raised in Jersey as reserves used to fund pension pot
text:
Concerns as reserves used to fund pension pot
A former civil servant has told the BBC islanders are unaware of the "scale of cuts" to the Social Security Fund and Social Security Reserve Fund which pay towards pensions and benefits.
Accountant Alisdair Macleod said the States' use of reserve funds to offset cuts "doesn't feel healthy".
The Social Security Fund receives contributions from islanders; their employers and the government pay a contribution through the States Grant, though this was paused from 2020-2023 due to finance pressures connected with the Covid pandemic.
While a reduced grant into the Social Security Fund has since been reinstated, the government strongly rejects the claim the funds are being cut.
Social Security Minister, senator Elaine Millar told the BBC the government has continued to reduce the states grant to the Social Security Fund so that money can be freed up for "essential public services" like health.
In the 2026-2029 budget the government made the decision to temporarily reduce the value of the grant to £50 million a year into the Social Security Fund. Had the government paid the full value in it would be between £92-95 million a year.
Money from the Social Security Reserve Fund has been used to make up the deficit.
Millar said: "The Social Security Fund is actually very healthy, so we're not taking money out of the fund.
"I'm always at pains to point out - there is not money coming out of the fund as a result of the grant being reduced - it's a bit less going in."
The Social Security Fund functions as a current account for pensions and benefits, while Jersey has a separate Social Security Reserve Fund, which functions as a savings account to top up funding pensions in the long-term.
As the government is reducing the states grant into the Social Security Fund, it is drawing on money from the reserve fund to supply the shortfall.
Millar explained this was always the plan when the Social Security Reserve Fund was set up as it was meant to be a buffer for the Social Security Fund.
"The reserve fund was established to recognise that there might be a turning point where we could have more pensioners than we have working people.
"So, it's just to create that safety net that we don't need to increase contributions because have got that reserve."
'Big sum of money'
Between 2020 and 2026, £396 million has been taken out of the Social Security Reserve Fund into the Social Security Fund.
The government is now proposing further transfers of £133 million over three years to cover the reduction in the states grant.
Millar said this was not a cause for concern as the Social Security Reserve Fund is "approaching 3 billion".
"That is a big sum of money and that is what it is there for, to help pay for pensions in cases of need."
"If we kept the States Grant at the full amount it would be like putting money in your savings account when you cant afford your electricity bill."
'Significant amount'
Alisdair Macleod, an accountant and former civil servant, said this policy "concerns him a lot" as the Social Security Reserve Fund has been built up over many decades and is "designed to cushion the impact of an ageing population".
"Since 2020, a significant amount of money has been taken out of that pensions pot [Social Security Reserve Fund] as a result of the government cutting the amount it's paying into the Social Security Fund and it's continuing to do that in this budget."
Macleod disputed Deputy Millar's view that the social security fund was "healthy".
"I've heard this fund described as 'healthy', yet the last full actuarial assessment of the fund in 2021 projected that on current levels of migration, the fund would run out entirely by 2082, and to me that doesn't feel healthy."
"Furthermore, when they last updated their projections to include the impact of a cut in the money being put in by the government last year, they projected that that would reduce the life of the fund by a further 10 years."
Jersey's Fiscal Policy panel warned that drawdowns and contribution cuts to the Jersey Social Security Fund should only occur after a comprehensive actuarial review of future pension liabilities.
However, States Members are being asked to vote on reducing the states grant to the fund for the 2027 budget before the review has been done.
When asked if that was problematic, Senator Millar said: "I think its fair because of of the size of the social security funds as a whole.
"There is plenty of money - nobody needs to be worried about the pensions. We can pay pensions for a very long time with the money we've got.
"Even if no contribution went in at all, we could still pay pensions for seven years.
"There not many countries with that level of funding for their pension schemes."

title: Isolation of stroke tackled in Guernsey charity support group
text:
Isolation of stroke tackled in charity support group
The husband of a stroke survivor has told how a communications support group has provided a "lifeline" for his wife.
Andrew Ingrouille's wife Bridget had a stroke three years ago and now has aphasia, meaning she can no longer read or write and her speech is limited.
Andrew said "it was devastating," adding "one day you're going through life normally... and suddenly your whole world collapses".
He and Bridget now both attend Stroke Association Guernsey's communications club, a group which helps rebuild key communication skills and enable people affected to connect with others, something which Andrew said had given him and his wife a "stepping stone back into the future".
Andrew said: "We didn't have this when my wife was discharged, but to have it now is a lifeline...
"You realise that everybody has a different journey, but we are all in it together."
Stroke Association Guernsey helps those who have either suffered a stroke or know someone who has through its communication club and support groups.
A new topic is introduced through the club each week, with support for transport, holidays, technology and a monthly singing session.
Andrew said: "It's not what we lost, it's what we still have and what we can do together going forward, which is what this group reinforces."
As well as the weekly club, a free event is held at Le Marchant Ward dining room of the Princess Elizabeth Hospital every third Wednesday.
The sessions, designed for those who have been affected by a stroke or know someone who has, offer support within a community that breaks the barriers of isolation.
Beth Brown, engagement officer at Stroke Association Guernsey, said the charity does not want people to feel alone when they are discharged.
"We want them to know that there is this support on island and there is a community of stroke survivors and their loved ones where information, advice can be shared to make them more aware and what there is to help recovery," she said.
"Being able to see other people who are further on in their stroke journey when you may have just recently had your stroke yourself, is so inspiring."
World Stroke Day takes place on 29 October 2026 to raise awareness and bring people together improving understanding of stroke.

title: Northamptonshire Police steps up Halloween and Bonfire patrols
text:
Police step up Halloween and Bonfire Night patrols
Police will be stepping up patrols of town centres and events during Halloween and Bonfire Night to tackle robbery, burglary, theft and shoplifting.
Northamptonshire Police says the operation comes as "evenings become darker and towns and neighbourhoods become busier with seasonal events".
Det Insp Hayley Thurston hoped everyone would enjoy the season, but urged people to remain "alert" and take "simple precautions to protect themselves and their property".
She said the force aimed to make the county "a hostile environment for offenders".
The force has advised people to be aware of their surroundings, particularly when walking alone after dark, and to keep mobile phones, jewellery and other valuable items out of sight.
Also, it asked people to stick to well-lit routes and, where possible, travel with friends or family.
Thurston said: "Robbery can have a devastating impact on victims, and we will be increasing our visibility in hotspot locations.
"We would also encourage residents to report suspicious behaviour to us," she added.

title: Guernsey social tenants frustrated by delays for repairs
text:
Social tenants frustrated by delays for repairs
A social housing tenant whose home has damp and cracks in the wall has said she has "given up" asking for help after waiting months for issues to be fixed.
Mother-of-one Shannon Shell and her partner Declan Askew said they had experienced a series of problems at their property in the estate in St Peter Port, Guernsey.
"You give up about it because you know it's going to take forever," said Shell, adding: "They don't help."
The housing committee's president, Steve Williams, admitted the committee needed to provide a better service for tenants but he said additional funding for maintenance was needed.
An attempt to increase the amount of money spent maintaining States houses in the last political term was put forward by former deputy Peter Roffey but the proposal failed.
Williams has now requested an extra £795,00 for the maintenance of social housing as he said the budget had dropped in the last decade from £10.9m to £9.9m last year.
Askew said his parent's property on the same estate had similar issues with damp.
"We were just told to open windows," he said.
"Then we found out it was a leak in the roof. It actually made my brother and me move out there for a little while."
Another social housing tenant the BBC spoke to who did not want to be named said she had to wait 18 months for someone to fix a leak in her roof which was causing water to enter her bedroom.
She said she was still waiting for someone to fix her fence as it was dangerous for children to play near. Another resident on the same road raised a similar issue.
Kylie Roussel, who lives on Skins Lane, said she had had very few problems with her property except for an issue with her outside toilet.
"My husband did phone up a while ago and asked for a replacement, but nothing ever happened," she said.
"The only thing they did was replace the window in the shed and that's full of condensation because it wasn't done properly."
Amy, another resident in the St Peter Port estate, said her property was generally good but there were issues with the windows.
"It's freezing in this house in the winter, they do try and maintain it, but things like the child locks on the windows don't work," she said.
She said her downstairs windows were "about to fall out" but crews "came around and just put some sealant on".
Williams said the lack of investment meant his committee had been forced to use contractors who had longer waiting times in exchange for lower prices.
"We're not doing certain jobs, we're putting stuff off," he said.
"You've got to look after your home, your property, otherwise in the long run it will be worse and we'll end up spending more money."
He said the committee "want to do a heck of a lot more" but "there's obviously a limit and everyone's asking for money".
"It's difficult times and we're trying to make the best use of that money," he said.
"The staff work really, really hard to obviously make every pound count but we do need to look after the properties and we do need to provide a better service for the tenants."
Debate on the 2027 budget starts on Tuesday next week and there are 30 proposals to change it including attempts to introduce a free bus service and create new benefits.

title: Hot water for Guernsey pier's showers fuelled by cooking oil
text:
Hot water for pier showers fuelled by cooking oil
Treated vegetable oil is being used to heat marina facilities used by visiting boat crews, Guernsey Ports has said.
It said the fuel was being used as an alternative to kerosene to heat the building and hot water for showers at the facilities on Crown Pier.
The renewable biofuel comes mostly from used cooking oils in the food industry and could lower carbon emissions by about 90% compared with fossil fuels, Guernsey Ports said.
Head of port operations Kieran Higgs said the switch was a "clear step towards lowering emissions" across the marina's operations.
Head of sustainability Lisa Duggan said about half of Guernsey Ports' direct carbon emissions across the harbour and airport were from fossil fuels for heating, back-up generation and fleet vehicles.
She said the conversion was therefore an "important step in our journey to becoming a greener organisation".
Boiler installers Rubis helped convert the three boilers which service the visitor facilities.
The company's Nick Crolla said renewable fuels provide an "immediate and practical route to reduce emissions, using the systems and vehicles already in place".

title: Rare Narnia book sold in Cornwall charity shop sells for £1k
text:
Narnia book found in charity shop sells for £1k
A rare first edition of The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe has sold for £1,000 after it was spotted at a charity shop.
The 1950 copy of the first of the Chronicles of Narnia by CS Lewis was identified by a sharp-eyed volunteer at the Oxfam bookshop in Truro, Cornwall.
The children's fantasy novel was put up for sale on the charity's online selling portal and was quickly snapped up.
Store manager Barnaby Attwell said: "It's great to know that money will be going to help people in need."
The Chronicles of Narnia is a series of seven novels - the most famous being The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe - published between 1950 and 1956.
They have been the subject of multiple screen and stage adaptations, most recently a Netflix production of The Chronicles of Narnia.
Jane Rickard said she had been sorting through some newly donated books when she came across the rare volume "completely by chance".
"It looked like an old copy of it, I looked inside to see if it was a reprint, and it wasn't, and I got quite excited," she recalled.
"So I checked online for what a first edition would look like and that's when I thought, 'It's a first edition!'"
The volunteer worker said "my jaw dropped" when she realised what the book might be worth, adding: "For us, it's very unusual.
"We do get some excellent donations, and it's not that rare to have a £30 book, a £50 book, but £1,000 has never happened.
"I can only think it was the magic of Narnia because there was no reason for me to even be looking at that section - I'm normally behind the counter or in the shop. It just looked like a small hardback book."
Barnaby Attwell, manager of Oxfam Books Truro, said he was amazed "when Jane plucked the book out amongst many other similar-looking books".
"Another volunteer looked it up and saw that, even without a dust jacket, a first edition is worth over a thousand pounds.
"A couple of other volunteers checked it too and we all agreed.
"Another volunteer wrote a description of it, and I photographed it and put it online for £1,000. So it was a real collaborative effort."
Attwell said "we were all over the moon" when the book sold.
"I haven't stopped thanking Jane, and gave her a bunch of flowers at our shop general meeting recently," he said.
"It's great to know that money will be going to help people in need."

title: Northants actor Robert Rhodes targets 'scarred villain'stereotype
text:
Actor targets 'scarred villain' screen stereotype
An actor is backing a charity's call for more positive roles for performers with scars and visible differences.
Northamptonshire-based Robert Rhodes, who has appeared in Silent Witness and House of the Dragon, said: "The media industry needs to start reflecting the true experience of people with visible difference."
The charity Changing Faces wants the film and TV industry to stop using scars, burns and other visible differences as marks of villainy and has started a petition calling for more positive representation.
One casting agency said visible differences were often used as a shorthand for villainy, but that these casting briefs could be successfully challenged.
New research by the Centre for Appearance Research (CAR) at the University of the West of England showed that people who are exposed to visible difference via villainous characters go on to have a more negative perception of people with visible difference in the real world, the charity said.
Rhodes, who was recently in the BBC One show, The Rapture, was born with a large facial birthmark as a result of congenital melanocytic nevus and was left with scarring following multiple surgeries to remove it as a child.
He said: "We can't wait for action any longer.
"Yes, there is often trauma associated with a scar, but we experience joy, love and success just like everyone else.
"More neutral and aspirational characters on screen will improve real perceptions of the whole visible difference community."
Fellow actor Beau Bradfield said: "As an actor with facial scarring, I know how important it is to see people with visible differences represented on screen as real, complex people.
"I want children growing up with visible differences to see characters who look like them being heroes, friends, parents and love interests – not just villains."
About 4.9 million people in the UK have a visible difference, the charity said.
As part of its work to monitor visible difference representation, it has worked with the Creative Diversity Network to include visible difference as a category in its diversity data monitoring and reporting.
Louise Wright, chief executive of Changing Faces, said: "For years we've asked the industry to think about the stories it tells about visible difference.
"Now, for the first time, we have proof that those stories don't stay on screen – they shape how people with visible difference are treated in real life.
"Halloween is the moment this is impossible to ignore, which is why we're asking industry, and the public, to help us change it."
Bailey Frances, from Cambridge-based Shakyra Dowling Casting, a member of the Casting Directors' Association, said: "Getting it right matters.
"Villains are often written with visible differences (eg facial scars) as shorthand, but asking whether a character could be interpreted differently, or whether that difference is essential to the story, leads to better, more truthful storytelling," she said.
"We regularly present actors who don't match the description on the page but fit the character perfectly, and they're often the ones who get the job.
"Casting directors are in a unique position to widen the search and open up the conversation with writers and directors, challenging the initial casting briefs where needed."

title: Two swans killed in suspected King's Lynn catapult attacks
text:
Two swans killed in acts of 'deliberate cruelty'
An RSPCA inspector described suspected catapult attacks that killed two swans as "one of the worst types of deliberate cruelty" he had seen in recent times.
On 8 October, an injured swan was rescued from a drainage ditch in the King's Avenue area of King's Lynn, Norfolk, after concerns were raised by the public.
A ball bearing had fractured its skull, and it was put to sleep at East Winch Wildlife Centre to prevent further suffering.
At the same location, another swan was found dead with a ball bearing inside it. The RSPCA has appealed for information to track those responsible.
Dean Astillberry, the attending inspector, said: "This is just shocking that two beautiful birds have been targeted in this way.
"This is one of the worst types of deliberate cruelty I have dealt with this year.
"These birds would have suffered horribly as a result of this attack and it is a shocking crime.
"Wild birds feel pain, fear and distress, and deserve our care and respect.
"Deliberately harming them causes immense suffering and can have devastating consequences for both individual animals and local wildlife populations."

title: Cornwall woman saved by quick CPR encourages others to learn
text:
Woman saved by CPR has 'another chance at life'
A woman at a concert who survived a cardiac arrest thanks to the fast actions of event staff has encouraged more people to learn CPR.
It comes as South Western Ambulance Service is holding a series of tuition events across the region, teaching basic resuscitation techniques.
A trainer said there were around 14,000 defibrillators in the region and the service wanted more people to have confidence using them.
Esther Baker, who survived her cardiac arrest, said "the reality is if you do nothing they will die" and the quick intervention of others had given her "another chance at life".
Baker was attending a concert at Plymouth Pavilions in 2020 when she began to feel unwell and suffered a cardiac arrest at the age of 51.
She said she "went to the toilets because I felt sick" and she "collapsed into the arms of one of the events team called Peter Bickley" and he and his team "worked on me and saved my life".
"When you survive something like that and you know it was the actions of somebody else - I needed to meet them and thank them."
She said: "When we all met up it was very emotional.
"Getting people to be confident with CPR can save more lives like it did mine.
"Some people are really nervous about intervening but the reality is if you do nothing they will die.
"I've had another chance at life thanks to early intervention."
Andy Collins is a community engagement and training officer with South Western Ambulance Service NHS Foundation Trust (SWASFT).
He said: "There are nearly 14,000 defibrillators publicly accessible across the South West and it's vital that people have the confidence to use them.
"It's the worst day of someone's life to suffer a cardiac arrest and for bystanders it's really difficult as well.
"We need to give them the confidence to know that their early intervention can make such a great difference in that patient's outcome."
'Low survival rate'
One of the trainers, Adam Wildes, is retired doctor and volunteer community responder.
He said: "We know in this country there's a low survival rate for cardiac arrests outside of the hospital - around 8%.
"But simple training can really improve things. Some countries have 25% survival rates, partly because of better CPR training for the public.
"We've normally got about three to five minutes to intervene in order to give people a much higher chance of surviving.
"Doing this can be really scary so we want to give people the tools to do this almost like they're on autopilot, which can be quite hard with other people getting upset."

title: Norfolk fire service praised for explosion-risk ship response
text:
Fire crews praised for explosion-risk ship response
A fire service chief said preparing for major incidents would remain a "focus", after a review praised its response to a ship carrying a potentially explosive cargo docking in the county.
His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) found Norfolk Fire and Rescue Service had improved in 16 problem areas since its last inspection in 2023.
The watchdog rated it "good" overall and investigators said it "responded well" to the damaged MV Ruby docking at Great Yarmouth port in 2024, amid fears its cargo of fertiliser could explode.
However, it did find the service's preparedness for major incidents required improvement.
The ship ended up in Great Yarmouth after several other countries had turned it away.
It was carrying 20,000 tonnes of ammonium nitrate fertiliser destined for Africa.
MV Ruby damaged its hull and propellor after running aground in July.
It led to concerns it could explode, following the 2013 incident in Beirut, Lebanon, when 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate detonated while being stored in the city's port.
Its arrival in Yarmouth led to a major incident being declared. Fire crews played a key role by investigating the vessel, using body-worn video cameras to identify any risks.
Scott Norman, deputy chief officer, said the use of this "innovative" technology meant crews could immediately feed back information from the scene to all agencies involved.
The HMICFRS said the incident showed the service had "effective plans to respond to a major incident and work with other emergency responders".
But it also found staff needed more training for major incident responses, such as marauding terror attacks.
Ceri Sumner, chief fire officer, said it would continue to improve responses to major incidents, acknowledging "anything can happen" in a county with a "range of risks".
Overall, the fire service has improved significantly since 2023, when just three areas were rated "good". This year, there were eight.
Sumner said the service was particularly proud of its prevention work, which had "required improvement" following the last assessment.
Crews carried out 8,294 home fire safety visits in 2024-25 - almost four times the 2,233 managed in 2022-23. They targeted vulnerable residents and people living in deprived areas.
Sumner said the service was "really delighted" at the positive report and that it followed "hard work being put in by all of our teams".
She added: "We've been really focused on assessing the risks in Norfolk, being clear on what they are and then building strategies around that, and then working collaboratively as a team to make sure we really focus our resource where it can have the most impact."
Looking ahead, the fire chief said funding pressures could become an increasing challenge.
This year, the service is expected to go £1m over its initial budget, with costs exacerbated by wildfires over the summer months.
August was its busiest month on record.
Sumner said budget pressures would need to be addressed, as demand for services was expected to continue to increase.
But currently, the service is delivering on cost-effectiveness, with its £41.58 spend per resident being below the national average of £51.72.

title: Stormont budget: NI Executive 'losing £117m' to defence spending
text:
Stormont to lose £117m due to defence spending - O'Dowd
Stormont is to receive less infrastructure funding than expected from the UK government as a result of money being reallocated into defence spending, the finance minister has said.
John O'Dowd said that over the next four years the Northern Ireland Executive would get £117m less than previously planned.
"The reason we lost that money is because it is going to military spend," he said.
The Treasury has been asked for comment.
It is understood the change relates to a budget "reprofiling" which was first announced by Sir Kier Starmer's government.
That involved shifting some infrastructure, or capital, spending into defence from other departments.
That was confirmed by the Chancellor John Healey in Wednesday's Budget.
"I am fully funding the Defence Investment Plan, including through capital reprioritisation across Whitehall," Healey said.
'A major blow'
That has a negative impact on Northern Ireland's budget because of the way the devolution funding formula works.
Northern Ireland gets a population-based share of additional spending allocated to public services in England, so long as those services are devolved.
Defence is not devolved so moving money into it from other areas means the devolved administrations lose out.
O'Dowd said the move was "a major blow at a time when additional investment in areas such as critical infrastructure and social housing is urgently needed".
The government makes the case that additional defence spending benefits all areas of the UK through contracts for arms manufacturers and other businesses.
For example Thales, the French arms company, is expanding its Northern Ireland operations after winning a large contract to supply missiles to Ukraine.

title: Devon and Cornwall Police adopt protocol to find missing veterans
text:
Police adopting protocol to find missing veterans
An initiative designed to help police respond more effectively when a serving member of the armed forces, military veteran or reservist is reported missing has been rolled out in Devon and Cornwall.
Devon and Cornwall Police have adopted the Forcer Protocol, which allows family and friends to pre-submit information before someone reaches a crisis point and goes missing.
The protocol is named in honour of solider Alan Forcer, who took his own life after going missing in 2020.
The force said information submitted was completely confidential and officers could only access it when someone was reported missing, adding: "Once located, they can be signposted to the appropriate support services."
Claire Lilly, former wife of the Army lance corporal, acknowledged the South West had a "strong connection with the armed forces".
She said: "Alan served in Kosovo and Northern Ireland, but, like many other service personnel, he struggled with mental health issues.
"The aim behind the Forcer Protocol is to help other personnel and their families, by identifying if a person being reported missing has an armed forces history and providing information which can help the police to find them."
Veterans and service personnel can self-refer to the protocol, or friends and family members can register them.
Det Supt James Dowler, missing persons lead for Devon and Cornwall Police, said: "The more information we have about the person we're looking for, the easier it is for us to assess the risk and locate them safely.
"By registering that information in advance through the Forcer Protocol, vulnerable people and their loved ones are providing us with an invaluable head start when someone with a service background is reported missing."

title: Small businesses in Bilston say Budget failed to deliver the help they need
text:
'We need help for small businesses, not punishment'
"We need more help for small businesses instead of punishing them," said butcher Kevin Evans, in response to the government's new tax and spending plans.
In the Budget, set out by Chancellor John Healey on Wednesday, a number of measures were announced, including a one-off £100 payment for up to 20 million households in council tax bands A-D in England.
However, for those living and working in Bilston, Wolverhampton, not enough is being done to tackle the rising cost of living.
"The electricity is a killer, it's a big one, it's mega money. It's just out of control now," added Kevin Evans, a butcher and business owner.
"Six sausages would have cost you £1.50 last year, but it's around £2.50 now."
The Budget also included a 3.9% rise in the legal minimum wage from April, as well as a new flat-rate state pension increase of £488 a year, equivalent to 3.9%, under the triple lock policy. The old basic state pension will rise by £374.40.
Evans told BBC Radio WM the measures would make things harder for his business, not easier.
He added: "I would love to take another person on but I can't afford to because National Insurance and the minimum wage keep going up. I might as well just do the hours myself.
"You have less time at home. I don't get a day off now. It's not feasible, it comes out of my pocket which is already being emptied.
"It doesn't benefit you to be a businessman in this country anymore."
The sentiment was echoed by plasterer Glen Gandy, who said he also could not afford to expand his workforce or absorb the rising cost of materials.
The father-of-two said: "There is nothing in the new Budget that will help my business.
"Minimum wage up by 3.9% is good for kids, but you're going to employ someone with more experience if you have to pay them extra anyway, so it will push people out of work.
"We haven't put our wages up for two and a half years to absorb the costs, but there is nothing you can do about the materials.
"I pay around £350 a week on fuel just going around Wolverhampton. It costs us a fortune."
Lutfu Efe, who owns a chip shop, said he now pays nearly £800 a month for electricity and £600 a month for gas.
"This is why we are struggling. Many years ago it was around £300, but it has sky-rocketed," he said.
"It's not just me, everyone is in the same boat. Everything has gone up. We have two options: the government helps us or we have to close down.
"There is nothing in this Budget to help me."
For households across England, Scotland and Wales, standing charges, fixed daily fees customers pay regardless of usage, will be removed from gas bills, while the VAT cut on electricity bills has been extended until July.
Import taxes are to be removed on more than 100 food products, including gherkins and marmalade, as well as kerosene and fertilisers.
For mum-of-six Gwyneth Totney, the one-off £100 payment will "help but not much, it will cover about two weeks of gas and electric".
She added: "My weekly shop has gone from about £100 to about £130 a week.
"I've started going to the butcher's for my meat now as it's cheaper than the supermarket.
"We're working more to get more money but we have less time. We still have our pizza night and cinema night at home, but it's way too expensive to take all the kids to the cinema."
Reacting to the Budget, she said: "It feels like they are trying to bring the cost of living down, but they are not actually doing it."

title: Swindon's Wyvern Theatre 'will need to be replaced'
text:
Theatre faces being replaced but show must go on
Repairs and improvements are continuing to be carried out on a town theatre even though the director admits the ageing venue "needs to be replaced".
Laura James, director of the Wyvern Theatre in Swindon, has been overseeing a series of small improvements, such as re-upholstering seating, but she says the town "needs and deserves a bigger and brand new venue".
Swindon Borough Council recently said it would not be good value to spend millions on the building but it does want to keep the theatre open until a new venue is finished.
The council wants to have a business case ready to put in front of councillors in February.
The Wyvern currently has a rolling programme to re-upholster the auditorium seating.
Last year, there was a project to refresh backstage areas, there are new automatic doors in the foyer replacing ones from the 1970s when it opened, and there have been improvements to the boiler system.
James explained there is always a lot going on in terms of maintenance, but much of it is not "always visible to the public".
"It'll be a be an incredibly sad day when the Wyvern does close but no building can last forever and we know the time is approaching when we need to find a new space," she said.
James would like to see a venue with larger capacity because there is "appetite" for larger shows that currently can not be accommodated at the Wyvern.
Councillor Matthew Vallender, the cabinet member for culture, said it is a "lovely space" that accommodates community groups as well as the usual big shows.
But he said: "We're past our economic lifespan. Trying to do wholesale refurbishment is not going to be cost effective.
"It's how we can find a way to continue to deliver a new theatre in Swindon without risking a closure here at all."
He said the council does not intend to close the Wyvern until a new venue is ready and finished to move into.
A new venue is expected to cost about £45m, with £20m already secured from the government and the council hopes that the rest can be found from private investment.
Vallender said they are getting the numbers together for the business case in February.

title: Best of north Devon showcased by young filmmakers in competition
text:
Best of north Devon showcased by young filmmakers
What people love about the area they come from has been showcased in a set of short films made by young people.
Thirty of these films have been entered in a filmmaking competition named "Place", organised by North Devon District Council.
The aim of the competition for under 25s, is to explore what makes north Devon special through themes including the coast, the countryside, communities, culture and wildlife.
Clare China, project officer for the council, said: "It's their home. It's where they live. It's where they work and study. We wanted to see that through their eyes, and for them to tell us what they think is important about North Devon.
Harry Deakin, whose film is among the 30 submissions, recently returned to Barnstaple after studying film at university in Birmingham.
He said his film would show "there is life here, as most people often think of Devon as a place to retire or to raise children".
Deakin insisted young people can still "have a fruitful life" in the area.
Submissions from students from the media studies department at North Devon College are also among the entries with many of their films choosing to focus on the natural landscape and beautiful beaches.
Fifteen shortlisted entries will be screened publicly at a red carpet event to be held at Ilfracombe's Landmark Theatre,.
Six finalists will receive a behind-the-scenes tour of a professional editing studio in London and support to help develop their creative careers, while two runners up will be given mentoring.
The winner's material and ideas will inspire an official video celebrating the area from a young person's perspective, to feature on the council's website, social media and elsewhere.
A winner will be announced on Monday 2 November.

title: Yorkshire Water given lowest environmental rating by regulator
text:
Yorkshire Water given lowest environmental rating
Yorkshire Water has been given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency (EA) after a sharp rise in pollution incidents.
The regulator formally downgraded the company from two stars out of four to one, meaning it is now classed as a "poor performing company" for its impact on the environment.
The firm, which serves 2.4 million homes in the region, said its environmental performance was "not where it needs to be".
The company has pledged to spend £8.3bn over five years on improvements, but said customers' bills would provide most of the money to achieve that figure.
The EA's annual Environmental Performance Assessment grades England's nine water and sewerage companies, largely on how often they pollute rivers, streams and the sea.
The new figures published by the regulator showed Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, up from 151 the year before - a rise of more than 70% and the highest total since 2011.
It also failed to complete six legally required environmental schemes in west Leeds on time.
Stephanie Pullan, Yorkshire Water Director of Asset Management, said: "Our pollution performance isn't where it needs to be, and we haven't delivered on time six of our Water Industry National Environment Programme schemes."
She said the company was "looking at our operational performance, making sure that we're being as predictive as we can be", as well as "investing in the long-term and our assets".
The business said it was investing £8.3bn between 2025 and 2030, including £1.5bn to cut discharges from storm overflows, which release diluted sewage into rivers during heavy rain.
It said 300 schemes had been delivered across the region since April 2025.
Average bills for customers in the region rose by about 30% in April 2025 and by a further 5.6% in April of this year.
Asked whether customers or shareholders were paying the bigger share of the improvements, Pullan said: "That would be our customers."
Prof Becky Malby of the Ilkley Clean River Group, which campaigns to improve water quality in the River Wharfe, said: "They have trailed this for some time.
"Of course, this performance is shocking.
"It's amazing how Yorkshire Water continues to reduce its ability to treat and manage our sewage and increase its ability to pollute our environment at the same time as it increases our bills."
Questioned on whether she could understand customers' anger, Pullan said: "I can absolutely understand that, and our bill profile is set in line with Ofwat [the Water Services Regulation Authority], and it's making sure that we're delivering the £8.3bn investment."
In its latest annual report, Yorkshire Water said shareholders had put £500m into the company over the past five years to aid its improvement programme, and had committed a further £600m by March 2027.
In 2020, Yorkshire Water was given the top rating of four stars by the EA, described at the time as "industry leading".
This year's one-star rating is the first time the company has received the lowest grade since the ratings began in 2011.
The company was rated three stars in 2022, the first year in charge for its current chief executive, Nicola Shaw.
Over the past year, Shaw has faced continued scrutiny over her pay.
She received £732,000 from Yorkshire Water in the year to March 2026.
Over the past three years she has also received three further payments totalling £1.98m from Kelda Holdings, the Jersey-registered parent firm of the water company.
Yorkshire Water has said the Kelda payments were for separate work for the group and were funded by shareholders rather than customers.
The industry regulator Ofwat ruled the payments were not performance-related pay.
Shaw has also waived some bonuses.
In 2025 a group of local Labour MPs wrote to the company branding the additional payments "disgraceful".
Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions before Wednesday's Budget, York Outer Labour MP Luke Charters explained that he had seen "sewage pouring into the River Ouse whilst doing a BBC interview on pollution".
He went on to urge "stronger public control" of the region's water.
In his response, Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the water industry as "a symbol of what has gone wrong".
Yorkshire Water told BBC News that Shaw was not available to be interviewed about the EA's decision. Pullan said the chief executive was meeting Ofwat.

title: Owner 'overwhelmed' after dog lost in Storm Boelo is found
text:
Owner 'overwhelmed' after dog lost in storm found
A dog which escaped from the garden of her new home during Storm Boelo has been found after four days on the run.
Natasha Lapsley said she had only owned Suzie the cocker spaniel for about 90 minutes when strong winds blew open her garden gate.
After tracking her new pet around housing estates in Ramsey for more than an hour, Natasha said she lost sight of Suzie and contacted Noodle's Canine Rescue (NCR).
"I just felt sick with anxiety worrying about her," she explained. "The weather was so bad and she was out in a place she didn't even know."
The Isle of Man was hit by 70mph (113km/h) winds during the storm that peaked on Saturday night and Sunday morning.
"I'd only just brought her home and all sorts went through my head," said Natasha. "I don't know how I'd have got through it without Noodle's. They were amazing."
Volunteers from NCR printed and distributed flyers across the area while thermal binoculars and 4G wildlife cameras were used to try to track Suzie's movements.
The charity said that because of the severe weather, its drone could not be flown above the area where the cocker spaniel had gone missing.
NCR said: "Given Suzie's temperament and the awful weather, we suspected she would hunker down somewhere safe.
"With no sightings for two days, searches continued morning, day and night."
Suzie was eventually spotted on Tuesday in a garden two estates away from Natasha's home.
'Huge relief'
A resident contacted Natasha after recognising the dog from social media appeals and flyers distributed by volunteers.
Natasha said receiving the call had come as "a huge relief".
"She said 'I think your dog's in my garden', and I was just hoping it was definitely her," said Natasha, who added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the community's support.
"People I didn't even know were messaging me to say they were taking their dogs for walks in the area to look out for her.
"It was lovely knowing there were so many people looking out for her."
NCR said the operation highlighted the limitations of its current drone in severe weather.
The charity said it was fundraising for a more advanced model that can be deployed in stronger winds.
description: Suzie the cocker spaniel was found four days after going missing during Storm Boelo on the Isle of Man.

title: Wiltshire owner charged £700 over lost dog's missing records
text:
Owner charged £700 over lost dog's missing records
A dog owner has been ordered to pay nearly £700 for failing to ensure her lost dog could be traced back to her.
Allison Prudence Collin, 61, of Short Street, Ludgershall, was found guilty of failing to ensure a dog wore a collar displaying the owner's name and address and failing to comply with a formal notice requiring the dog's microchip details to be updated.
It follows an incident in April 2026, when a terrier-type dog named Cookie was found wandering through the Short Street area without an owner present.
At Salisbury Magistrates' Court on Tuesday, Collin, who did not attend the hearing, was fined £220 and ordered to pay £389.21 in costs and a £88 victim surcharge.
It marks the seventh successful prosecution brought by Wiltshire Council for failure to comply with legislation relating to dog microchip records.
Councillor Paul Sample, cabinet member for public protection, said: "We hope it serves as a reminder that keeping a dog's identification details up to date is both a legal responsibility and an important way of helping lost pets return home safely."
It is a legal requirement for dogs over eight weeks old to be microchipped, and for the owner's details to be kept up to date.
Although Cookie was wearing a collar, it did not display the owner's name and address as required by law.
The dog was taken to a local veterinary practice where it was scanned and found to be microchipped, but the information recorded on the database was incorrect and the registered owner could not be contacted.
The council's dog wardens collected Cookie and arranged temporary kennelling until ownership could be established.
The following day, Collin collected Cookie from the council's holding kennels, provided proof of ownership and paid the required fees.
She was also served with a formal notice requiring the microchip details to be updated within 21 days.
Despite further attempts to contact Collin by letter, phone and email, the microchip details remained incorrect and prosecution proceedings were initiated.
Sample said: "Our officers provided multiple opportunities for the issue to be resolved, but the necessary action was not taken.
"When dogs aren't microchipped, our officers have to spend valuable time and resources resolving the issue.
"Microchipping is one of the quickest and most effective ways of reuniting lost dogs with their owners, but it only works when the information recorded on the database is accurate and up to date."
Owners can check or update their dog's details by contacting the database where the microchip is registered.

title: Isle of Man heritage railways mark end of 2026 season
text:
Heritage Manx transport set for season finale
The Isle of Man's heritage railways will close for the season this weekend, with special services and events planned to mark the occasion.
Two of the Manx Electric Railway's oldest trams, dating from 1893 and 1894, will be in service, while a historic steam locomotive will mark 140 years of the Foxdale branch line.
Smaller railways and heritage groups across the island will also put on Hop-tu-Naa ghost trains, open days and vintage bus trips.
Isle of Man Railways said it "looked forward to welcoming people to close the season".
Some of the line's original 1890s tramcars will be brought out on Saturday, with Car 2 making one last round trip before closing for the winter.
Car 2 and its sister Car 1 hold the Guinness World Record for the oldest trams still carrying paying passengers.
Steam finale
The Steam Railway has carried passengers between Douglas and Port Erin since 1874, and is the last surviving line of a network that once reached Peel, Ramsey and Foxdale.
On Sunday, Caledonia, a locomotive built in 1885 to climb the steep route out of Foxdale, will haul four trains with a newly restored coach to mark 140 years since that line opened.
'Two-horse tram'
On Douglas promenade, the horse tramway's 150th anniversary season will come to an end with Saturday's tram decorated for Hop-tu-Naa.
Double-decker tram 18 will then be pulled by two horses for special journeys along Douglas Promenade.
Some of the Snaefell Mountain Railway's collection of wagons will also be on display at Laxey station.
Groudle Glen Railway and the Great Laxey Mine Railway will both run Hop-tu-Naa ghost trains on Saturday and Sunday.
In Ramsey on Sunday, the Jurby Transport Museum will run heritage bus trips from the Manx Electric Railway station, and the Queen's Pier will hold an open day to show its restoration work.
Meanwhile, an exhibition at the House of Manannan in Peel marks 50 years of public ownership of Bus Vannin.

title: Wooden Burnham-on-Sea low lighthouse needs repairs
text:
Wooden 194-year-old lighthouse in need of repairs
Repairs to a nearly two-centuries-old wooden lighthouse on the Somerset coastline will take place in the next few months to help "future proof" it.
The Burnham-on-Sea Low Lighthouse has helped guide ships and vessels since it was originally built in 1832 and remains a fully operational navigational aid.
Repairs needed include rusting metalwork, damage to one of the legs and paint peeling away from the Grade II-listed structure, as first reported by Burnham-on-Sea.com.
Somerset Council said: "We're developing plans and seeking funding to repair and repaint it. The work will be carried out when weather and operating conditions are suitable, helping to protect the lighthouse."
Captain Jessica Tyson MNM is the Harbour Master and Marine Pilot for Somerset Council. She previously told BBC Radio Somerset's Secret Somerset series that it is a "very well known landmark" in the South West.
"The marine environment is never a kind one and things to start rusting quite quickly. We do try and use the right things to keep it maintained.
"People sometimes don't realise, the lighthouse is still very much in use.
"Coming into Burnham or the port of Bridgwater, we have a lot of sandbanks, a lot of tide and there's quite flat countryside. This was built to provide a landmark for the seafarers to see the coastline so they didn't run aground.
"At one point, the port of Bridgwater actually rivalled Bristol - this was and still is a busy area."
Three beams of lights come out of this building to help "guide" sea traffic along the Somerset coastline, according to Tyson.
She continued: "We have a red light for port, a green light for Starboard and a white light for what we would call down the middle.
"The sectored light is just a very visual guide really for ships coming in or out to see their situation. It's very windy and can get very shallow towards the Steart flats.
"We've had big steel structures heading towards Hinkley Point construction site and that's why we’re here - to help ships navigate.
"The light above is a steady white light, that's for shipping across Bridgwater bay - we're providing a navigational aid for transiting traffic down the Bristol Channel.
"The Red stripe - we have a similar one on the Esplanade - they are lined up and that's where I believe it has come from to help the vessels guide to the port of Bridgwater."

title: El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers
text:
El Salvador sends 2,000 troops to Haiti to rescue four missing soldiers
El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti as part of a mission to retrieve four nationals who went missing in the Caribbean country almost two weeks ago.
The "robust deployment" was communicated by El Salvador President Nayib Bukele to the Prime Minister of Haiti Alix Didier Fils-Aime earlier this week, the foreign ministry of El Salvador said in a statement on Wednesday.
Bukele said the soldiers would also assist ongoing "security efforts against gangs in Haiti", the statement continued.
Tensions between the two central American countries have escalated over the disappearance of the four air force technicians working as part of a UN-backed anti-gang organisation in Haiti.
The four soldiers with the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) were travelling back to their base in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets.
No gang has so far claimed responsibility.
The Salvadoran foreign ministry said the "large-scale operation" was "supported by various countries and international organisations".
Earlier this week, Haiti handed four bodies over to special forces claiming they belonged to those of the missing servicemen, but Bukele said they did not match.
He said one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's military uniform.
Bukele threatened last week in an X post to wipe out Haiti's gangs, saying he will replicate action he has taken in El Salvador, if they did not release the Salvadorans.
In October last year, the UN Security Council approved expanded powers for the GSF to tackle worsening gang violence in Haiti.
The multinational force has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway. More than 5,700 people were killed in gang-related violence in Haiti this year, the UN says, and armed gangs control much of the capital.
Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in 2021.

title: Cars falling off damaged Saltburn road, resident warns
text:
Cars falling off 'accident waiting to happen' road
It is "only a matter of time" before someone is seriously injured on a dangerous bend, a resident has warned.
Allan Pennock said the verge on a stretch of Grinkle Lane, in Saltburn-by-the-Sea, dropped away years ago and six cars had gone over the edge of it since 2023.
The 76-year-old said he contacted the council after the first car went over, but little had been done to fix it.
A spokesperson from Redcar and Cleveland Council said daily inspections were carried out at the site and it was the process of appointing a contractor for a "bank stabilisation scheme".
Pennock said there was a field on the side of the road which slopes down to a river and there was "nothing to stop" someone going over the edge.
"Fortunately there have been no fatalities, but it's only a matter of time before some poor devil goes over the top and finishes up rolling to the bottom and not coming back out again," he said.
Pennock said the traffic was "virtually constant" on the road, with buses and farm traffic which often meant people had to reverse back up the blind bend, or reverse down into the dip itself.
"It's just an accident waiting to happen," he said
"Somebody's going to get seriously injured."
The spokesperson for the council said it aimed to start work on the road in the new year.
"The council is aware of the issue and is currently in the process of appointing one of the Framework Contractors to deliver a bank stabilisation scheme at this location," they said.
"A consultant was previously appointed to undertake an independent assessment and the corresponding recommendations following this assessment were implemented."

title: Bid to turn meadow in Welwyn into village green refused
text:
Bid to turn meadow into village green refused
A bid to turn a meadow into a village green has been refused by a county council because it has already been designated as a Local Nature Reserve (LNR).
Singlers Marsh in Welwyn, Hertfordshire, is a 15-acre meadow by the River Mimram which is regularly used by dog walkers and families.
Applications to have the site registered as a village green were lodged in 2020 and in 2022, with more than 1,000 local people backing the application.
At a meeting of the Hertfordshire County Council's Development Control Committee on 21 October, councillors refused to grant the application.
At the meeting, councillors heard the site – which is, in parts, owned or leased by Welwyn Hatfield Borough Council – had been declared as LNR in 2009.
County council officers, in line with an inspector's report, recommended that the application be refused.
Russell Haggar, from the Welwyn Planning and Amenity Group (WPAG), said the village green proposal was "supported widely" in Welwyn village.
He told the meeting there was no piece of legal documentation that said a LNR could not also be a village green.
He cited examples of sites elsewhere in the country where LNRs and village greens co-existed.
He said the site had been used as open land since the 1700s, with people describing having unfettered use and access since the 1950s.
He told the committee he thought WPAG deserved "a fair hearing" and felt it had not had that to date.
Richard Cuthbert, the team leader for the county council's countryside and rights of way service, told the committee the conservation purpose of a LNR took precedence over the recreation purpose of a village green.
However, it was also recognised that Welwyn Hatfield Borough Council, as the landowner, could opt to deselect the site as a LNR.
Nigel Taylor, the chair of Development Control Committee, suggested that it be recorded in the minutes that the committee urged Welwyn Hatfield Borough Council to reconsider the designation, but it was a matter for it to decide the area's future.

title: Home Guard training World War Two documents discovered in attic
text:
Home Guard training documents discovered in attic
A set of documents showing how local Home Guard volunteers were trained during World War Two have been discovered in an attic.
The typewritten pages show scenarios to test how officers from E Company of the 4th (Forest of Dean) Battalion Home Guard, based in Mitcheldean, would respond to different situations, including finding four dead Germans lying near motor cycles at Westbury on Severn.
Found in his attic in Ruspidge, Bill Acland said he does not know who the "fascinating" papers, dating back to 1943, belonged to.
The documents have now been added to a collection of Home Guard artefacts at the Dean Heritage Centre, which will go on display over remembrance.
Full of local references, the documents include scenarios such as "Tayton (sic) Church Bells were ringing after a few enemy aircraft had passed from Tewkesbury way. About an hour or so later we saw some men in basin-shaped helmets go into the woods by Byfords".
Another scenario in the papers talks of Home Guard volunteers engaging German paratroops near the railway line in Longhope and that a "Section commander cannot afford a runner to go to Platoon HQ as he has had three men killed and a runner from Platoon HQ was seriously wounded on route".
It asks what message the section leader would send to the commanding officer.
Forest of Dean historian, Roger Deeks, said the 4th Battalion was divided into companies that covered various areas of the Forest of Dean and "they became more and more sophisticated".
He said the documents were "real evidence of how they were training people and making sure they understood how to respond to situations", including what messages would they send and would they send reinforcements.
"It's really putting what is potentially an NCO [non-commissioned officer] or an officer through their paces," he added.
What was the Home Guard?
Originally called the Local Defence Volunteers, the Home Guard was formed in May 1940 as the Government realised the threat of invasion was becoming more severe.
Bands of armed men were reportedly already patrolling the countryside at the time, so the then prime minster Winston Churchill and his staff decided the best outcome was to legitimise such operations.
Announcing the creation of the Local Defence Volunteers on the BBC Home Service, Sir Anthony Eden said: "Men of all ages who wish to do something for the defence of their country... Here, then, is the opportunity for which so many of you have been waiting."
Serving as a secondary home-defence militia, the force was made up of unpaid soldiers who were ineligible for regular military service.
The force later became known as the Home Guard on 23 July 1940 after Churchill coined the phrase during a BBC broadcast.
While the Home Guard at first was mostly made up of make-do uniforms and weaponry, the soldiers soon received military training and performed roles such as bomb disposal.
According to the Imperial War Museum, over the course of the war 1,206 men of the Home Guard were killed on duty or died from their injuries.
Bill said he decided to give the documents to the Dean Heritage Centre as he felt they "belonged in a museum somewhere".
"Its part of local history and there must be people out there with Grandparents or Great-Grandparents that actually served in these platoons," he said.
"It would be nice to 'bring it home' [the papers] to them, [the families]" he added.
Nicola Wynn, collections officer at the Dean Heritage Centre, said Bill's papers are a welcome addition to the collection as it "really helps understand what the men were doing during the war".
"It shows how serious they took the training and all the different scenarios they had to face".

title: New Stafford market hall welcomed despite parking fears
text:
New market hall welcomed despite parking fears
Businesses and shoppers in Stafford have welcomed plans to transform the former Guildhall Shopping Centre into a new market hall, although some have raised concerns about a lack of town centre parking.
The redevelopment will see the site converted into a venue housing 28 independent businesses, including shops, food stalls, cafes and bars, alongside space for events and live performances.
The project has been backed by £10m of government funding secured following a campaign by Stafford MP Leigh Ingham.
"People want to see Stafford town centre doing well again. So do I. And this is a big step towards making that happen," she said.
However, while traders said investment in the town centre was needed, some questioned whether enough had been done to make it easy for customers to visit.
Tim Sandy, owner of French & Byrne cafe bar, said he was excited by the plans but worried about the loss of parking spaces.
"We're very close to where the new market will be and it's really exciting. Anything that happens for town centres now is really, really important," he said.
"My only concern is I've seen the plans and there's no parking being allocated at all, no town centre car park."
He said the town had already lost parking at the former Guildhall Centre and would also lose the car park on the former Wilko site as part of plans for a new college development.
"I do wonder where all this trade and all these customers are going to come from," he said.
"You can see the success of retail parks around Stafford and places like McArthurGlen at Cannock, but all of them have convenient and easy access for vehicles."
Despite those concerns, he said Stafford had the potential to thrive.
"Stafford is a terrific town and lots of us independents are ready to look after you," he added.
Gary Brightwell, co-owner of Hadleigh Jewellers on Gaolgate Street, also questioned whether sufficient parking would be available.
"We're knocking down buildings and we're redeveloping, but we aren't bringing new car parking areas," he said.
"What we need to get into town is proper car parking spaces first and foremost to get people wanting to come into the town."
Brightwell said his business had traded in Stafford for 36 years but had noticed a decline in footfall.
"Without those repeat customers coming back, then sadly we could possibly be a victim of the high street," he said.
"What all shops here are sadly missing is just general footfall."
However, he agreed the funding was positive news for the county town.
"We are the county town and over the last five or six years I think it would be fair to say we've suffered a lot of losses of businesses and big retailers pulling out of the town.
"It is looking a little bit tired, so any investment has got to be positive news."
Residents also broadly welcomed the proposals.
Trish Hill said the redevelopment was preferable to leaving the site vacant.
"It's got to be better than nothing, hasn't it?" she said.
"When you look at Stafford now, they've got to do something with it."
She said bringing a market back to the town would appeal to many residents.
"A lot of older people do like markets and things like that, so anything like that would be good."
She added Stafford's retail offer had changed significantly over the years because of online shopping and out-of-town retail developments.
"They need to rejuvenate in a different way, I suppose," she said.
Dennis Dunn also supported the plans, although he said success would depend on the mix of businesses attracted to the development.
"The town's dead, but the top end, it's all right," he said.
"I think if you've got plenty of variety for eating and things like that, then yeah, maybe."
"It'd be nice if there were some smaller traders as well."
John and Gloria Wilson said they were pleased to see progress being made on the site.
"We could do with the market, couldn't we?" Gloria said.
"It just looks as though they've knocked it down and forgot about it."
John Wilson added: "Honestly, for a county town, it's disgusting.
"Why don't they get on it and start using it? [the £10 million] At least it shows some sign of improvement."
Under the plans, the new market hall will provide space for 28 independent businesses and a business hub aimed at helping local firms start up and grow.
Ingham said Stafford had lost an important part of its identity when the market closed.
"We lost more than somewhere to shop, somewhere to go and something to do," she said.
"We lost a place where people met and where people had another reason to come into our town centre."
She said securing the funding would help Stafford become "a proud market town again", while bringing more visitors and businesses into the town centre.
Wider investment plans
The market hall funding was announced alongside plans for a new Mayoral Strategic Authority for Stoke-on-Trent and Staffordshire.
Labour MPs from across the area welcomed the proposal, saying it would give local leaders more control over investment, transport, skills and economic growth.
In a joint statement, they said: "This is an important step towards making sure our area has a stronger voice and can shape its own future."

title: Residents report concerns over ongoing postal delays
text:
Residents report ongoing postal delays
Some people in parts of the South West say they are currently getting Royal Mail post delivered about once a fortnight.
The BBC has been contacted by people in the region, frustrated they are missing hospital appointments, bank cards are being cancelled and debt collection threats are being issued because of late parking fines.
Torbay MP Steve Darling told Parliament the problems were affecting people's health, citing missed medical appointments caused by delayed mail.
Royal Mail said it had experienced "short-term local challenges" in the area but had "taken steps to improve performance".
Jean Tomkow from Torbay in Devon said she had been receiving post about once every two weeks and was "constantly worried" about missing important correspondence.
On one occasion, among nine items of mail delivered together were two letters from a life insurance company which had been sent more than six weeks earlier.
One required a response by a specified date, while the second informed her the company had proceeded because no reply had been received.
"This could have been disastrous for us," she said.
"We're constantly worried we are going to miss something else important."
Tomkow also said her husband previously missed a hospital appointment after a letter notifying him of the time and date never arrived.
"I have let the MP know that we are experiencing problems as I don't know where we can go, on our own," she said.
Nikki Prentice said postal delays had worsened problems for her, when she started receiving parking fines in error and the notices arrived almost three weeks after they were issued.
She said she later received debt collection letters that were also significantly delayed.
"If I had needed to pay the fine, I would have missed the opportunity to pay the lower cost," she said.
"I've got no idea if this parking situation is resolved, whether I'm missing other things, have I received other fines?
"It's left me feeling frustrated, irritated and certainly absolutely no faith in the Royal Mail system as it stands at the moment.
"They need to review what they are able to do and deliver on those promises."
In Plymouth, John Allan said his gliding licence arrived on the 19 of October but was postmarked 14 days earlier.
"I was waiting for my gliding licence for at least two weeks," he said.
"I asked a neighbour if they'd had any post and they said not for three weeks.
"There has been no mail since."
Alison Hassall from Torpoint in Cornwall said since April she has been getting important mail "way too late".
"We go days and days with no post but you do see plenty of post people delivering mail so what really is the issue here?
"You're paying for, but not necessarily getting, the service promised. Stop prioritising parcels."
Darling recently raised the issue in Parliament, saying missed appointments were having an impact on people's health.
He said: "We need to make sure that we are maximising the powers of Ofcom, giving them teeth and encouraging them to use those teeth."
A Royal Mail spokesperson said 87.4% of first-class letters in the TQ postcode area, which includes Torquay, Paignton, and much of south Devon were delivered the next working day.
For the PL postcode area, which includes Plymouth, west Devon and east Cornwall, it said 83% of first-class letters were delivered the next working day, up from 79.1% the previous quarter.
In the TR postcode area which covers mid and west Cornwall, 84.1% of first class letters were delivered on time, compared to 74.6% the previous quarter.
"We know there is more to do and remain focused on improving the reliability of our service," they said.
"We have experienced some short-term local challenges across the Torbay area, but have taken steps to improve performance, with services becoming more consistent and additional recruitment underway.
"Where deliveries are missed, our teams work to deliver any outstanding mail as quickly as possible."
description: People in Devon and Cornwall say they are not receiving important letters on time.

title: Springwell villagers fighting back over repeated developments
text:
Villagers 'hacked off' over repeated developments
A group of residents say they are repeatedly having to fight plans for large-scale projects in what they call the most overdeveloped village in their area, with a concrete processing plant at one end and a large underground covered reservoir at the other.
People in Springwell Village near Sunderland said they had to deal with excessive dust and noise from approved developments.
Those living opposite Springwell Quarry said they also feared pollutants in the dust after the demolished Gateshead flyover was processed there.
The Ashcourt Group, which runs the quarry, said it "monitors dust levels in accordance with the planning conditions" and results show it was compliant.
Sunderland City Council said it was working with residents regarding concerns raised.
Since 2020, plans for several significant projects have been approved, including the creation of 75 homes, a 43,000,000 litre (9,000,000 gallon) reservoir and the continuation of operations at the quarry, which had been due to close in 2022.
The Springwell Village Residents Association (SVRA) said the village had become a target for cheap development at the expense of village life.
David Bain, who lives opposite the quarry on Railway Close, discovered through media reports that remnants of the 1960s-built Gateshead flyover would be processed there.
Residents in the area had believed the quarry would cease operations when its 20-year licence expired.
Bain said had he known work would continue he would not have purchased his home.
The Environment Agency (EA) recently found the quarry failed to stick to dust-control measures and said it had taken action against the operator.
"My biggest fear is that there is things like silicates, because concrete has silicates in which is harmful to your lungs and, a few doors up, virtually everybody has small children," Bain said.
Although plans were approved for the continued waste recycling and concrete production at the quarry, three tall blue silos which are part of a further industrial facility were installed without planning permission.
An application for retrospective permission has been made.
Washington West Labour councillor Brandon Feeley said the silos "shouldn't have been allowed" to remain, and criticised quarry operators for applying to run the site from 0700 which he said disturbed neighbours.
Other approved projects include the reservoir on land off Mount Lane which was completed in May for Northumbrian Water (NWL).
Graeme Moffitt, who has lived in his home opposite the site for the last 32 years, said he had considered "walking away" if further applications are approved.
"It's a strong community but people are fed up with it," he said.
"It's just non-stop, on and on.
"The village, it's been attacked... I'm hacked off."
Campaigners previously told the BBC the reservoir was bigger than expected and have criticised NWL for changing plans for the surface to be covered in gravel, instead of grass, claiming it now resembles a car park.
Moffitt said: "We had grazing horses and really fantastic views and we've had, for the last four years, nothing but interruptions [from works].
NWL said it had "worked closely" with the community "keeping residents informed" and said the updated reservoir roof was "in line with industry guidance to protect water quality".
Parts of the village remain surrounded by greenbelt land but campaigners said it was a constant fight to protect that from development.
Springwell Village Residents Association (SVRA) vice chair Liz Reid said campaigners had successfully fought plans for 60,000 solar panels to be installed on greenbelt land off Fairhaven in 2025.
Days later, however, plans were submitted for land in front of the proposed solar farm to build up to 17 bungalows for those aged over 55.
New plans leave them thinking "oh not again", she said.
"Something happens almost every day that seems to attack the greenbelt here."
She said it was "pretty obvious the village is a target" because of the proximity to Sunderland and Newcastle and its cheaper land.
Reid accepted the accusation of being NIMBYs - coined for those opposed to developments from the phrase "not in my back yard" - was something "often levelled at us".
But she said the village had already seen "every bit of brownfield land" developed, which the SVRA was not against, and their current fight was about "getting the rules stuck to" regarding greenbelt land.
Sunderland City Council said: "All planning applications are consulted on and determined in line with local and national policies."
It had refused the solar panel farm in 2024, and the decision was upheld by the planning inspector, it said.
Gateshead Council, which commissioned the flyover demolition, said all materials containing asbestos had since been taken to separate facilities, and disposed "correctly".
The EA said remnants of the flyover were no longer being processed at the quarry but it understood the concerns of people living nearby and said they "should not have to put up with unacceptable impacts".
It had taken action against the operator, which included issuing an enforcement notice to "fix breaches of its permit", and was reviewing data after it "closely monitored dust levels".
The Ashcourt Group said environment consultants were monitoring to ensure no dust was escaping from the site and it had challenged the EA on its "regulatory notices".
The firm said it went "further than the planning permission conditions and environmental permit requirements" with live dust monitoring and its results showed levels for particulate matter and dust were within guidelines set by the Institute of Air Quality Management.

title: Bingley teenage violinist wins top spot in national orchestra
text:
Teen violinist wins top spot in national orchestra
A teenage violinist from West Yorkshire has been chosen to lead a prestigious youth orchestra.
James Jet Uttley, 17, from Bingley near Bradford, has played violin in the National Youth Orchestra (NYO) for four years and has been selected to be first violinist and lead the 160-strong ensemble in 2027.
James undertook two rounds of auditions to secure the opportunity, which he said was something he had always "dreamed" of doing.
"It's something I've worked quite hard for and I couldn't really imagine from when I first started that I would be leader," he said.
"My dad was also a member of NYO, so he inspired me to get into NYO," he explained.
"He had an amazing time and he said my life would change completely through music if I joined - and he was right."
The NYO consists of teenage musicians from across the UK and was founded in 1948.
James said the orchestra gave young players the chance to perform on some of the biggest stages in the country - including the Bridgewater Hall in Manchester and the Barbican in London.
"This is my fourth year as part of the orchestra, and in my first year I started out on the very back 'desk' of the violins," he said.
"It's been a journey working my way up and having more opportunities."
James explained that in his role as first violin, he would have "a few more responsibilities than the average musician in the orchestra".
"I will be in touch and communicating and forming a relationship with our conductor," he said.
"Then, I'm also in charge of relaying information to the rest of my section and communicating with the other sections of the orchestra."
He said he had first picked up the violin aged six, inspired by his dad.
Now he is preparing for auditions for music conservatoires and making applications for the Royal Academy of Music and Royal College of Music in London and the Royal Northern College of Music in Manchester.
"I do hope to go into the profession," he said.
"I think anyone can survive the music industry if they're innovative and they're thinking about transforming the music industry."
