title: Needle exchange: Vulnerable at risk as 'life-saving' drug needle site closes
text:
Vulnerable at risk as 'life-saving' drug needle site closes
A drug needle exchange in Belfast is set to close within days because the charity which runs the service is losing its city centre premises.
The exchange, run by Extern, allowed people who inject heroin or cocaine to safely dispose used needles, receive clean needles and access health services.
The service will shut on 2 November and move to a "significantly reduced street-based service" following the loss of Extern's Royal Avenue premises.
The charity described the needle exchange as a "life-saving service" and warned that its closure meant vulnerable people would have "nowhere to go" to access support.
"The people who use this service are someone's son, daughter, brother, sister, parent or friend," said Mal Byrne, Extern's director of harm reduction and mental health services.
"They are members of our community, and, for many, this service is one of the few places where the door is open for them and where they can ask for help without judgement.
"That door is now closed until a space is secured to operate from."
Extern has also warned that the closure may mean substance use becomes more visible to the public in the city centre, along with an increase in drug-related litter.
The charity's premises is to be redeveloped as part of the Belfast Stories project and Extern has tried for more than a year to find an alternative site in the city centre.
The search was assisted by Belfast City Council, the Public Health Agency (PHA), the Department of Health and landlords but a new location is yet to be found.
'13,000 discarded needles removed'
In addition to clean needles, the exchange provided a wound-dressing service and advised the vulnerable about accessing temporary accommodation and healthcare.
"Loss of a premises means people who need support to reduce harms from substance use have nowhere to go to access life-saving harm reduction advice and interventions, healthcare support and wider practical assistance," Byrne said.
"This is a life-saving service. This work will be suspended."
The forthcoming closure is happening at a time when cocaine use is believed to be on the rise in Belfast city centre, according to Extern.
"We suspect that there are between 1,000 and 1,500 people at any one-time experiencing difficulties with their drug use," the charity said.
"Last year alone, almost 20,000 used needles were safely returned by individuals who came to the premises on Royal Avenue," it added.
"Extern's city centre outreach team removed more than 13,000 discarded needles from Belfast's streets.
"This is an increase of roughly 20% from previous years."
A service user said going to the exchange was not just about exchanging needles but also the people who work there.
"Over the last number of years, I've built up a bond with a couple of the workers," they said.
Adding that there are days when they go in "feeling very low, not going in to use equipment, but just to go in to get a chat".
Speaking about the impact the closure will have on their mental health they described their lifestyle as lonely and isolating and said the people at Extern "become like family".
"You kind of hold them close, it will have a big impact with our mental health with this going."
Independent councillor Paul McCusker warned the closure puts vulnerable people "at even greater risk" and he has lobbied the council to explore alternative locations.
"I am deeply concerned that any reduction in this service will have a devastating impact on the people who rely upon it," he said.
"I have known individuals who have suffered life-changing consequences as a result of addiction, including the loss of limbs, and sadly, the loss of life itself.
"Belfast is currently in the midst of a drug epidemic, yet the political response has not reflected the scale of the crisis."
McCusker founded a soup kitchen in north Belfast in 2017 and regularly campaigns on issues regarding homelessness, poverty and addiction.
"Over recent years, we have witnessed a substantial increase in the number of people injecting drugs, which has led to an increased risk of blood-borne viruses, serious infections, abscesses, and addiction-related health complications," he said.
McCusker added needle exchange services "play a vital role in reducing harm" and insisted the "fears and misconceptions" surrounding them must be challenged.
"They provide an opportunity for drug support workers to engage with individuals, build trust, minimise health risks, and ensure that those who need help can be referred to appropriate treatment and support services."
How often are needle exchanges used?
The PHA commissions charities and participating pharmacies to deliver the Enhanced Needle and Syringe Exchange Service (NSES) across Northern Ireland.
In 2024-2025, a total of 32,667 transactions were recorded by the NSES in Northern Ireland, an increase of 7.4% on the year before.
About 721,000 needles and syringes were given out, which is a 7.5% increase compared with the previous year.
The PHA said needle exchange sites "are located in areas where there is an existing pattern of injecting behaviour"
"Providing services locally is vital, as people who inject substances are often vulnerable, may be in poor health, can be dealing with complex social issues, and may be without local access to sterile equipment and advice.
"So support needs to be targeted in a way which maximises access.
"Needle exchanges are particularly valuable for engaging these people, because it may be the only service they are willing to use and provides opportunities to direct them to additional support and information," the PHA added.
description: Belfast charity workers warn people who use the "life-saving" service will be left without support.

title: A fresh roll of the dice for Shrewsbury board game cafe N3rdy's
text:
A fresh roll of the dice for board game cafe
A board game cafe which kept its community going for more than a year after being forced to close, finally has a physical home again.
Nerdy's in Shrewsbury shut in May 2025 because of rising costs and the owner, Katie Petrovic, said "walking away would probably have been the easier option".
But she believed the cafe had become a "home from home" for many people and she kept it alive by running pop-up events for its supporters around Shropshire.
After a fundraising campaign raised more than £8,000 to support the reopening, the cafe is back in new premises on Mardol Gardens, close to its old home.
Now known as N3rdy's, the cafe continues to offer customers the chance to play with its stock of board games while having a drink.
It has become a not-for-profit Community Interest Company - a type of limited company run with a social purpose.
Petrovic said this made the cafe more accountable and money would go back into events and support for the local games community.
It also helps the business secure funding and she said it would give it a more stable future.
Petrovic said she had discovered the original Nerdy's after the coronavirus pandemic, when it was a place to "hang out, play and feel welcome".
"We were part of the family there," she said.
Later she joined the staff and eventually became owner of the business
She said it was especially important to "those who have real difficulty finding anywhere they feel they can be themselves".
Petrovic said that was especially true for people who are "neurodivergent, LGBT+, socially anxious, isolated, or just plain different".
"Now more than ever, we need spaces like that," she said.
During the 18 months the cafe was closed, the Nerdy's team attempted to keep their community together with events at venues including Shrewsbury Unitarian Church, Hickory's Smokehouse and The Bell Inn at Tong.
During that time, she also raised funds to pay for their new home and said the £8,000 raised was "absolutely humbling".
As well as being a substantial sum, she said it was also important to her, because she believed it showed people were saying "we want it back, it's important to us".
But while one board game cafe in Shropshire is back with a new home, another which won a BBC Make a Difference award for its community work is facing a less certain future.
The Boardroom Cafe in Wellington is also a Community Interest Company and it said it had been told its landlord was looking to sell the building, so it was exploring its options.
Co-owner Jenni Drew said included "the possibility of purchasing the building or finding a way to do that as well as looking at alternative locations".
She said and her team were "not panicking", however, and nothing would change immediately.
To help attract grant funding for their next move and to help them plan, she has asked people to fill in a survey, to say what the cafe means to them.
Drew said: "I'm proud of what we've built together and we'd want to do everything we can to secure the future of Boardroom."

title: Cathedrals finding creative ways to stay financally afloat
text:
Cathedrals finding creative ways to stay afloat
Cathedral bosses say they have been forced to find creative ways to raise money as financial pressures mount.
Ben Silvey, chief operating officer at Bristol Cathedral said they had began holding events including silent discos and street food markets to generate extra funds, as it posted a budget deficit for the last two years.
Meanwhile, Nerys Watts, chief operating officer at Wells Cathedral, which costs £9,000 a day to stay open, said they introduced charges for visitors outside of timetabled worship two years ago in a bid to preserve its income streams.
Describing it as "incredibly challenging", Watts said: "It's hard when you're caring for what are the nation's most important treasures."
Watts said while visitor numbers to the cathedral, which was recently named by writers of the magazine Time Out as the nation's most beautiful building, had held since charges were introduced, it had not stopped costs overtaking income this year.
"We're running a deficit budget this year for our core costs," said Watts.
She said the cathedral, which was built in the 1300s, was also in the process of restoring its organ and was looking at having to potentially replace its roof, which could cost close to £30m.
The cathedral is also redeveloping Vicars' Close, a medieval street that dates back to 1348.
The plan is to fund the projects through grants such as the National Lottery Heritage and fundraising.
"Every single penny we raise is about looking after this building, keeping it open as a church, and a place of worship, and caring for the fabric of the building."
Watts said staff salaries are their largest outgoing and the target for 2027 was to break even.
Elsewhere, Gloucester Cathedral is currently re-structuring with some staff possibly facing redundancy as they say operational costs add pressure.
In a letter to supporters The Revd Canon Andrew Zihni, Dean of Gloucester Cathedral, said: "Despite considerable efforts to increase that income and to manage our costs, we continue to face substantial financial pressures."
The Revd Canon Zihni added that the wish is to create a "resilient organisation" saying "no final decisions" have been made concerning staff.
For Bristol Cathedral, Silvey said while the budget deficit had fallen from £300,000 in 2024 to £120,000 in 2025, it was still projected to have a shortfall of £55,000 next year.
"We're moving in the right direction but we can only run a deficit for as long as we've got cash to cover it," he said.
"Our cash reserves will run out at some point if we carry on like this," he added.
Silvey said the cathedral had taken measures to try and recoup some of the money, including reducing staff.
"We've lost good people in that process," he said.
He said the cathedral had also shifted emphasis towards finding new income streams, hiring specialist events and venue hire manager Nat Gearing and putting on "a huge array of events".
Gearing said balancing the opportunity of using the cathedral as a commercial venue with its primary role as place of worship and celebration had meant they "often have to push boundaries a little bit and challenge perceptions".
"Cathedrals have for hundreds of years have been places not just for worship but for celebration. These are just updated ways of celebrating," she said.
Gearing said the events had helped to bring in a whole new group of people who have possibly never visited Bristol Cathedral before.
Silvey said the cathedral was following a progression that goes back since it was built.
"This cathedral has been here for 900 years and it's been all sorts of things to all sorts of people.
He said while the cathedral was very much still for worship, the shift in focus to commercial events was all about making the "building viable and sustainable" as well as "accessible to as many people as possible".
Watts said a similar approach was also taking shape at Wells Cathedral.
"We have to be very entrepreneurial and creative about how we bring in a wider range of people. To welcome them to the cathedral, to come and see all of the fantastic things that we have here."

title: Northumberland's new data centres must bring 'local benefits'
text:
New data centres must bring 'local benefits'
Government plans to impose "strict tests" on data centres before they can be built have received a cautious welcome in an area which could soon be home to three such facilities.
During Wednesday's Budget speech, Chancellor John Healey said new centres would face requirements to "invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies".
The Conservative leader of Northumberland County Council, which gave US firm QTS the go-ahead for a £10bn facility at Cambois and is considering two more applications, said the sector was "absolutely critical" for the economy.
Meanwhile, the local Labour MP welcomed Healey's pledge but warned the "devil is in the detail".
Last month, Blyth and Ashington MP Ian Lavery called on the prime minister to regulate data centre developments like those in his constituency, fearing they would take up "scarce industrial land that could be used for other industries that create far more local jobs".
On Wednesday, the chancellor told the House of Commons: "When the NHS uses AI to treat patients, we want that data here, when our armed forces use AI to keep us safe, we want that data here."
He said if companies invested locally, created jobs and protected resources, they "will get the grid connections they need and, where necessary, be allowed to build onsite generation while they wait".
Speaking to the Local Democracy Reporting Service afterwards, Lavery said: "We have to listen to the residents much more than we have been."
He said the chancellor's pledge "broadly speaking does address the issues" being raised, but he was "not sure it could cover the impact of having three or four data centres within two square miles".
Northumberland County Council leader Glen Sanderson said of the QTS plans: "If it is done right and carefully then data centre development is absolutely crucial for a new economy and a new generation of people."

title: Girl, 11, praised for calm response after teacher's school seizure
text:
Girl's 'calm' actions during teacher's seizure praised
An 11-year-old girl has been praised for her quick thinking and composure after helping her teacher who was having a seizure in the classroom.
Tom Ray began to feel unwell during a maths lesson before suffering an epileptic seizure and losing consciousness.
While some pupils thought he was joking, Lily-Mae - who has been a Sea Cadet for three years and has had some first aid training - immediately realised something was seriously wrong.
"At first we all thought it was a joke but then Mr Ray started losing focus and he hit his head on the whiteboard, and I knew he doesn't really joke like that," she said.
'Incredibly proud'
Lily-Mae said she "literally jumped over a table" to help him before getting her classmates out of the room and alerting school staff who called for medical help.
She said she had drawn on her cadet training during the incident.
"We have been learning how to be calm in difficult situations," she said.
"Before you act, always take a breath and assess the situation because it is also about are you OK doing this, rather than calling someone who has better skills than you?"
Reflecting on her response, she said: "I thought I was only going to have to do bandages, like, say someone gets hurt on the playground.
"I feel very proud of myself for acting. I feel like I've accomplished something very big for my age."
Ray, whose epilepsy is managed with medication, said he had never experienced a seizure like that in the classroom and praised Lily-Mae's actions.
He said her calm and measured response during a stressful situation was something many adults would have struggled to maintain.
"It's very scary for other people to see," he explained.
"It was amazing Lily-Mae was so calm in that situation."
Lily-Mae's mum Jennifer said she was "incredibly proud" of her daughter.
Lily-Mae said she hoped to join the Royal Navy when she is older and also has an ambition to be an astronaut for Nasa.
description: An 11-year-old girl is praised for her quick thinking when her teacher suffered a classroom seizure.

title: Inside the control room dealing with fires and floods
text:
Inside the control room dealing with fires and floods
"In your most terrifying moments, the voice of calm is the control room staff."
Those are the words of Theresa Hurford, who has been working in a fire service control room in Shropshire for nearly 19 years - taking countless calls from the public and deploying firefighters across the county.
"It's worth remembering when the blue lights turn up - before that, there [was] a voice at the end of the line," she said.
Her colleagues around the globe are being celebrated by International Control Room Week, acknowledging the hard work of people who deal with crises day in, day out.
It has been a busy year for Shropshire Fire and Rescue Service, with fires over the summer putting crews under "immense pressure".
Hurford described "very chaotic" scenes "with lines ringing non-stop".
The major challenge facing control centre staff was working out how to cover the blazes when there were "more incidents than fire engines", Hurford said.
As well as incidents in their own area, Shropshire crews were deployed to help colleagues in the West Midlands and south Wales in August with larger fires.
It was reassuring to know "we can call upon our neighbours and they'll support us", Hurford added.
But in the midst of autumn, with temperatures and rain falling, the control room is now preparing to deal with a very different concern - flooding.
This time of year sees a "constant" high volume of calls, "similar to wildfires," Hurford said.
"The rain keeps coming, the calls keep coming, and we keep mobilising," she added.
"But for us, it's the expected and it's what we train for and what we plan for."
There are "definitely" more weather-related incidents in recent years, Hurford said.
"When I started, we would probably have one flooding season, which lasted maybe a month at the beginning of the year," she explained.
But now, these seasons have steadily increased in length - an issue the fire service is hoping to tackle with specialised training.
"Some of the calls we take can be very stressful, very hard to handle, and those certainly take their toll," Hurford said, though the team had worked to build a sense of "family" to help improve mental health.
Ruth Walkerdine is a watch manager at fire control - who came to the role after serving as an on-call firefighter in Hodnet, Shropshire.
"I think my favourite part is coming into work every day, and you don't know what you're going to be faced with," she said.
Walkerdine explained how her first-hand experience helps her "visualise what incidents look like and what resources they're going to need".
Distressing calls and major incidents are part of the job, but Walkerdine said the team "talks about it together to make sure we are okay."
Facing down high-pressure scenarios is something the team "thrives on", she added.
"I think the pressure is part of what attracts us to the job."
Hurford routinely answers the phone to people experiencing the worst days of their lives - be it a traffic accident or a burning home.
"It gives me a real sense of pride, knowing that I'm going to be able to help somebody," she said.
Dealing with hoax calls, however, is "frustrating" and a "massive waste of resources".
"If we've got a fire engine committed to a hoax call, then there's obviously a risk if a genuine emergency call comes in, it will delay the response," she explained.
To have a week dedicated to celebrating people like Hurford and her team makes her "really proud."
"All calls start with control [rooms] right across the globe," she said.

title: Council leader aims to 'keep historic' Prescot Cables in town
text:
Council leader aims to keep football club in Prescot
Knowsley Council wants to ensure Prescot Cables' future but does not have the money to pay for a new stand at the ground the local authority has owned since 2018, its leader has told the BBC.
While the historic non-league side may not be the most famous football club on Merseyside, Cables can claim to be older than neighbouring Liverpool FC.
However, its fans are worried the club may have to relocate from its Valerie Park home because the main stand is "nearing the end of its life".
Council leader Graham Morgan said the estimated cost for a new stand would be about £2m, money which he said the local authority did not have.
Knowsley Council stepped in to secure Cables' future in 2018 when it bought Valerie Park for £300,000 from private owners and granted the club a 99-year lease.
Cables fan Mike Kostrzewski called BBC Radio Merseyside's Hot Seat phone-in to raise his concerns directly with Morgan.
He said supporters were finding the uncertainty around the club's future "unsettling" and added: "I know it's not Everton or Liverpool, but it's important to the local community."
'Lifeblood of town centre'
Morgan said the council would work "closely" with the club's board.
He said the local authority had previously provided a £63,000 loan which had enabled the club to secure funding for £200,000 in ground improvements.
Morgan said a recent assessment had concluded that it could cost about £2m to replace the main stand and that "unfortunately at the moment the council hasn't got that kind of money".
Kostrzewski said it would be great if other facilities could be built around the stadium to help keep the club there.
He said: "I think we'd lose a little bit of the soul of the club if we moved."
Morgan said "Prescot Cables fans are the lifeblood of the Prescot town centre regeneration, and I want to see Cables stay at Valerie Park, not just for the short term but for generations to come."
The club's name comes from the largest local employer in Prescot, British Insulated Cables, which was founded in 1890 as the British Insulated Wire Company.
The football club, which has also been called Prescot Town, was formed six years earlier.
The fan-owned club's board previously said it was "exploring all options" and was in discussions with the council and its landlord about moving to a new home.

title: Jury says care failings contributed to ex-Southend player's death
text:
Missed opportunities before ex-footballer's death
An inquest jury has found missed opportunities contributed to the death of a former footballer who had Alzheimer's disease.
Ex-Southend and Cambridge United player Colin Flatt seriously injured himself and fell from height at Basildon Hospital in July 2021. He later developed an infection and died that September.
His former partner, Melanie Leahy, who campaigned for the Lampard Inquiry into mental health deaths in Essex, said she did not want to hear that "lessons had been learnt" but wanted to know "who would take responsibility".
Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust (MSEFT) said it had already changed how patients at risk of delirium or confusion are monitored.
During the two-week inquest, the 81-year-old, who also played for Leyton Orient, Wisbech and St Albans, had been described as a fit and active man who enjoyed golf, walking his dog and sailing before his dementia worsened.
The 10-member jury at the hearing in Chelmsford concluded there had been several missed opportunities to assess Flatt's mental capacity and the risk of him leaving care settings unsupervised and coming to harm.
Jurors found one missed opportunity occurred when a mental health tribunal approved his discharge from Goodmayes Hospital in Ilford in June 2021, after he had been detained under the Mental Health Act.
They said his release led to an "unsettled period", during which he moved between care settings and his own home while becoming increasingly confused and aggressive.
The jury also identified failures including the lack of a referral to a specialist mental health team and a failure to complete a handover when he was admitted to Basildon Hospital from a care home.
They said there was an absence of risk assessments for him leaving care, and shortcomings in handovers when he was transferred between wards.
The inquest heard Flatt was admitted to Basildon Hospital with heart issues.
Once medically fit for discharge, staff struggled to complete a full assessment because of his agitated behaviour. The inquest heard there were a limited number of security guards at the hospital who were not trained in restraining patients.
On 27 July 2021, Flatt took a pair of scissors being used to cut another patient's hair, and stabbed himself in the abdomen. He then left the ward area and climbed over a landing before falling about five metres.
The jury concluded the probable cause of death was the self-inflicted injury, the fall and a subsequent infection.
Dr Fitzpatrick, a cardiac pathologist described his medical cause of death as an acute infection of the lungs, damage to the lungs and an enlarged heart.
Leahy said: "To see him deteriorate so rapidly under supposed professional care is something I will never recover from."
Christine Blanshard, chief medical officer at MSEFT, said: "We offer our sincerest condolences to Colin's family and loved ones.
"We have worked to address the recommendations made following an independent investigation last year. All the actions have been completed, and learning has been shared across the trust."
Blanshard said changes had included tighter medicines management, improved observation of patients at risk of delirium or acute mental health crises, better record keeping and information sharing, and reducing unnecessary ward moves.
A spokesperson for Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust said: "All of us across healthcare have a responsibility to work together to improve care and treatment for all, and to take careful note of the coroner's conclusions."

title: Troubles legacy plans a 'backwards step', says former DPP Barra McGrory
text:
Troubles legacy plan a backwards step, says former senior prosecutor
A former director of public prosecutions (DPP) in Northern Ireland has accused the government of running "coach and horses" through the independence of the office.
Barra McGrory KC SC said a plan by the government to give the attorney general for England and Wales the final say in Troubles-related prosecutions in Northern Ireland was a "significant backward step".
He said had the proposed arrangement been in place when he was first appointed, he would not have applied for the job.
The Northern Ireland Office said the attorney general was also the advocate general for Northern Ireland, and the plan was a recommendation from Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights.
The plan is one of a number of changes proposed by the government to the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, which is currently passing through Westminster.
Speaking to BBC News NI, McGrory warned the plan will be damaging for public confidence in the office he once held.
"If the director of public prosecutions can't be trusted to independently take decisions on troubles-related cases. Well, then, people are going to start questioning whether or not the DPP can be trusted to take decisions locally, and that is not healthy," McCrory said
McGrory was appointed DPP in 2011 and held the office for six years.
He took up the role after the criminal justice reforms in 2010 which ensured the office for the first time was completely independent. The reforms were a key part of the Good Friday Agreement.
But McGrory warned the government proposal would now "wipe away that independence in relation to Troubles-related cases".
"It has significantly undermined that very carefully crafted suite of reforms that were introduced back in the early 2000s. So it's a backward step," he added.
He also warned against a "two-tier" justice system with Troubles-related prosecutions being decided by the Attorney General of England and Wales with all other cases being considered by the local DPP.
"The public will say we are expected to have belief and trust in our DPP as someone who can take his decisions independently and impartially and on the evidence.
"But when it comes to this class of suspect, we're told that our DPP isn't good enough. So what does that say?"
He added: "We will have a hierarchy of victim, and that is not healthy."
McGrory also revealed that he would not have taken the job as DPP had the proposed new arrangement been in place when he was appointed.
"I was the first DPP to be appointed who was wholly independent and that was the reason why I applied for the job," said McGrory.
Asked how his former colleagues in the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) might react to this proposed new arrangement, he said he didn't want to speak for the people he used to lead but he "can't imagine they are entirely happy about it".
He commended the staff of the PPS, which he described as "highly-skilled... independent people", and said they will address any Troubles-related cases that come to them from this legacy unit in that way.
"But the decision will no longer be made by their director; it will be made by an English attorney general, and I think that's not healthy for internal confidence."
McGrory also questioned the lack of response from the Irish government as a co-guarantor of the Good Friday Agreement, who supported the criminal justice reforms.
"I would have thought the Irish government would be deeply concerned about this reform. It is a reform that the Irish government would not tolerate in its own jurisdiction," he said.
He also questioned if the current Labour leadership appreciate the significant of this proposed change.
"I would have been shocked had Keir Starmer allowed this to happen as I know how much he valued the independence of prosecutorial decision making and he had a deep understanding of this jurisdiction," he said.
"I worry that the current occupant of Downing Street and the current secretary of state may not appreciate just how significant and potentially damaging this change is."
A Northern Ireland Office spokesperson said: "The Troubles Bill will repeal the Legacy Act's immunity scheme and enable families to seek answers and accountability about the deaths of their loved ones.
"To ensure confidence and consistency in any decisions to prosecute, the bill will introduce a requirement for the attorney general, who is also the Advocate General for Northern Ireland, to provide consent. This was a recommendation of parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights.
"In making such decisions, the attorney general must act quasi-judicially and independently of the government, applying well-established prosecution principles of evidential sufficiency and the public interest.
description: Former DPP Barra McGrory says Troubles legacy plans will be damaging for public confidence in the office he once held

title: Community helps shape art tribute to Uriah Rennie
text:
Community helps shape art tribute to Uriah Rennie
A public artwork in tribute to history-making referee Uriah Rennie is being developed with the help of the community.
Rennie, who was the Premier League's first black referee, died in June 2025 after being diagnosed with cancer.
In honour of the trailblazing official, members of the public were invited to collaborate with artist Nicole White to help shape the bespoke artwork.
The finished piece will go on display at the Uriah Rennie Leisure Centre in Arbourthone, which is due to be completed by Autumn 2028.
The event, organised by Sheffield City Council, took place at Springs Leisure Centre.
People were encouraged people to share their ideas, memories or reflections to explore Rennie's legacy in the city.
White said she hoped the consultation would bring together "different perspectives and different ways that he's impacted lives".
"We're going to try to make something that the community can be proud of," she added.
Both those who knew Rennie personally and others whose lives had been touched by his work came the event to share their connection to the man.
Colin Swaby, 60, described him as a "trailblazer".
"He's done a lot for the community, but in particular people who are minorities and misrepresented," he said.
Levi Ashton, 34, Project Officer for the Sport Leisure and Major Events team at Sheffield City Council, engaged with schemes championed by Rennie as a child growing up in Arbourthorne.
"Uriah Rennie was an incredible character for the city and an absolute juggernaut of a man," he said.
"I'm really hoping that this leisure centre and public art piece in his name will allow young people from surrounding areas to come and say, 'wow, this person was from here, they've achieved all this and I can do that too'."
Rennie made history as the Premier League's first black referee in 1997 when he officiated a match between Derby County and Wimbledon.
During his 20-year career in football, he took charge of more than 300 top-flight matches.
His impact extended beyond football through his efforts to tackle deprivation, improve equality and inclusion in sport, and support mental health initiatives.
In 2023, he received an honorary doctorate from Sheffield Hallam University for his work with local communities, before being appointed Chancellor in 2025.
Before he could fully begin his role as Chancellor, he died aged 65.

title: Maryport businesses shocked and saddened by bus cuts
text:
Shop owners shocked and saddened by bus cuts
Shopkeepers say they are shocked and saddened by a council's decision to cut a bus service only a year after it was launched.
Cumberland Council will stop subsidising the MD1 service from Maryport to Dearham, which runs through the centre of Maryport, due to poor usage.
The service was introduced in 2025 using part of a £3.5m government pot and was supported with a golden ticket scheme by local businesses, giving passengers perks such as discounts for using the service.
The owner at The Three Frogs clothing shop Michelle Mayman said the news was a "big disappointment" for the town. The council said the decision had been made with a "heavy heart".
Mayman said it was "such a shame" for non-motorists, adding: "To be able to get from town to town is really important for local businesses and the people themselves."
She said the loss was "a bit of a shock" but she did not believe the service had been well advertised.
"If more people knew about it hopefully more people would have used it," Mayman said.
Marie Buckley, owner of The Curiosity Shop on Senhouse Street, also felt more could have been done to promote the service.
"I never got one person coming in with a golden ticket, maybe it was used more with the cafes, but not directly to me," she said.
Katy Walton from nearby Essence Wellness said many people travelled to Maryport from nearby towns and the bus would be a loss.
"Public transport around Cumbria is shocking," she said, adding: "To lose another form of transport for people that live here or people just travelling around is just a shame."
The assistant director of highways and transport at the Labour-led council, Karl Melville, said the contract to run the MD1 would end on Thursday, but the authority was hopeful the service would briefly resume from early November before being scrapped at the end of the year.
Though they do not travel through the main shopping area of Maryport, two other buses serving the town - the 60 from Silloth and the 68 from Cockermouth - would continue to be subsidised for another 12 months, together with other buses introduced around the same time as the axed Maryport to Dearham route.
Melville said: "[Councillors] make these decisions with a very heavy heart. We don't want to put subsidised bus services in place only to remove them a year later."
He said the council made it clear when it launched 18 new services they would have to be supported by passengers.
The authority had also held meetings with MPs about the struggling routes, he said.
"We've done a lot of campaigning on our socials as a council, basically along the lines of use it or lose it," he said.
"We have to balance the books at the end of the day."
The MD1 will be one of six services to have their funding cut from the new year.
The DR1 from Carlisle city centre to South Carlisle Health Centre, which was designed to help patients get to appointments, will also be scrapped.
Melville said the council did consider the importance of the route, but considered there were two other services running close to the surgery.
"It leaves a very, very short walk to the surgery, but we looked at the numbers and on average that bus was taking [fewer] than 12 people a day."
The 93S Sunday service between Carlisle, Kirkbride and Anthorn, is also among the axed routes, together with the the extra 93AM morning peak journeys on the same route and extra services added to timetables on the 64 serving Cargo, Rockcliffe and Durdar.
A council report said due to low use, the cost per passenger to deliver the routes was at least £20 per person.
Daily passenger numbers recorded ranged between three on the 93S and 25 on the MD1.

title: Fuel prices blamed for diesel theft from Worcester haulier
text:
Fuel is now liquid gold, haulier says after theft
A West Midlands haulage company has said thieves are motivated by rising fuel prices after they stole 400 litres of diesel.
Martin Pinches, director of M Pinches & Sons Ltd in Worcester, said the fuel was stolen from two vehicles at the weekend.
"[It happened] because of the price of fuel," he claimed, adding that it was "an added cost that everyone has been burdened with."
Pinches said fuel had become "liquid gold" and estimated the missing diesel was worth about £800.
Because we're a business, and we use more fuel, it's a bigger burden on us really," he added.
"It's always a bit disappointing, isn't it?"
Pinches said the thieves also broke numerous fuel sending units and fuel caps on the vehicles, resulting in lost revenue as they were out of action for a day being repaired.
"It does mount up."
West Mercia Police told the BBC it had "received a report of a burglary after a business was broken into sometime between 24 and 25 October.
A force spokesperson said: "It was reported that a large quantity of fuel was stolen from two lorries on the site. Inquiries are ongoing."
During Wednesday's budget, Chancellor John Healey said the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, would be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.
It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52p per litre.
Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.
The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.
Pinches said something like this happening again is "always in the back of your mind".
"[To prevent it] we will maybe tell the drivers not to fill the lorries up until the morning they're going out".

title: Katherine Kelly lends voice to Barnsley Remembrance installation
text:
Actress lends voice to Remembrance installation
Actress Katherine Kelly has lent her voice to an art installation dedicated to the memory of the men and women of who have served in the Armed Forces.
The former Coronation Street star has helped record the names of more than 2,000 people commemorated on war memorials and in honour rolls across Barnsley, which will be "whispered" from the town's three Yorkshire Rose sculptures.
The Roses Remember installation, which runs from 7 to 14 November, will also see the sculptures lit up in red to represent poppies.
Sam Burdett, Barnsley Council's cabinet spokesperson for communities, said the "unique and powerful" tribute would ensure that "those who made the ultimate sacrifice are never forgotten."
Barnsley-born Kelly helped record the names at the Lamproom Theatre, alongside local veterans, including several councillors.
Councillor Stan Bryan, who was one of the veterans who took part in the recordings, said: "I found it moving and humbling to be able to play my own small part in this act of gratitude and remembrance.
"The Roses Remember is a poignant project to honour those from Barnsley who have made the ultimate sacrifice."
Burdett added: "Through every name whispered from the Yorkshire Roses, we honour not only those who served and died for our country, but also the enduring impact their sacrifice had on the people and place they called home."
The first showing of The Roses Remember will take place on 7 November at 18:30.
Between 8 and 14 November the installation can be seen and heard at 08.30 (audio only), 16.30 and 18.30.

title: Pier mistress' memoir tells of boy bands, bombs and Emma Thompson
text:
Pier mistress' memoir tells of boy bands, bombs and Emma Thompson
Stories about a One Direction music video, actor Emma Thompson and a bomb disposal team all feature in a woman's memoir about her time running England's only Grade I-listed pier.
Linda Strong was pier mistress, or manager, at Clevedon Pier, North Somerset, from 2005 to 2015, and her new book Tales of a Pier Mistress - Bombs, Bands and Bumps in the Night tells some of the zanier incidents during her time in charge.
Strong was the only staff member who knew One Direction were coming to film the video for You & I in 2014 and was sworn to secrecy because there were concerns fans would turn up in large numbers from across the country and beyond.
"They asked me if there was anywhere you could land a helicopter," she said.
People in Clevedon knew something was happening, however. There were broadcast vehicles parked outside the pier and posters were put up around town saying an episode of Countryfile was to be filmed there.
But as the big day approached, people started getting wind that One Direction - one of the UK's biggest bands at the time - were going to be there.
Strong told BBC Radio Bristol presenter John Darvall she was initially told "a band" was coming to film.
"I remember saying that whoever this band was, they must be big - someone like One Direction," she said she had joked to the visiting location manager.
"His reply was: 'You're heading in the right direction'."
"I was the only one allowed to be at the pier - because they needed someone to let them on."
When the band came, they took over the site and Liam Payne, who died in 2024, endeared himself to Strong.
"My office was turned into a dressing room," she said.
"Liam [Payne] had his hair cut, food was in abundance. The irony was, come lunch time, they wanted fish and chips.
"I remember Liam being the gentleman - quiet but caring. He was the only one who offered to do a photo."
She added: "So sad to have lost such a young man."
The book also tells the story of when actor Emma Thompson went there on holiday in 2005.
"I just happened to come down the stairs and I looked at this lady and I thought 'I know that face'," Strong recalled.
"The guy with her was really handsome and I know at the time she was married to Greg Wise.
"I looked at her and I said, 'I know your face', and she laughed and said 'yes you do'.
"And I thought 'let the floor open up and swallow me'.
"But she was so gracious and I told her that even though she'd been in loads of films, my favourite was Nanny McPhee.
"She just said, 'I'll let you into a secret - we're about to start another one'. And that was Nanny McPhee and the Big Bang. So I knew what was going to happen before that film ever came into being."
Strong also recalled the concern she felt one day when the pier had to close when an object that "looked suspiciously like the nose cone of a bomb" was spotted lodged in sand nearby.
She sent the image to the coastguard, but heard nothing back. She called again.
"Within half an hour, several coastguards turned up with blue lights flashing," she said.
The team agreed it looked suspicious and sent it to another group in Plymouth.
"All went quiet," Strong added.
"Four weeks later, the police arrived in the morning and told me that the pier would close at 12 noon as the bomb squad were on their way from Plymouth.
"At low tide they went out in a small rib [rigid inflatable boat] to inspect the item.
"It was decided the object was hollow and had a tiny hole in the tip. It was not a bomb and possibly an old piece of metal leftover from parts of the old pier head."

title: A127 pigs saved from being shot after Essex community rallies
text:
Escaped pigs saved from being shot thanks to locals
Pigs who escaped onto a busy dual carriageway have been saved from slaughter after the community rallied together.
The animals caused mayhem on the A127 at Dunton, near Basildon, when they darted between cars last week, leading to the road's closure.
Essex Police said five pigs had to be shot at the scene for safety reasons, but one ended up at Tower Hill Stables, in Asheldham, after seeking refuge in a resident's garden.
Eight of the pigs were due to be slaughtered on Tuesday, but an online fundraiser has saved their bacon after almost £6,000 was raised towards their upkeep.
Martin Morgan from Tower Hill Stables said: "We are hopefully taking eight; we've already got one that managed to get into somebody's garden... and it was also due to be shot, but the people whose garden it got into weren't too keen on that."
It is still unclear where the pigs originally came from. Police previously said 20 had escaped on the A127. The BBC does not know the whereabouts of seven.
Morgan initially thought he would only be welcoming one pig to the sanctuary after receiving a phone call from a resident about the animal in her garden.
"We managed to get the little pig into the van and thought that was the end of it," he said.
But he soon found out there were lots more also looking for a home.
"I didn't sleep the night we were told about it because I did not think we could fit them in - like most sanctuaries, we are struggling," he said.
He felt the weight of the situation, knowing his decision could mean the difference between whether the "pigs live or die".
He was thankful when a fundraiser was set up and praised people for coming together to help the pigs.
"I'm very grateful to everyone who has donated and continues to donate for the feed bills because looking after 400 animals is a tall order," he added.
Morgan said males and females will be kept separately and three pigs have already been reunited with what appears to be their mum.
Speaking about the other swine, he hoped they remembered each other, as "introducing the pigs to other adult pigs is a nightmare".

title: Lambeth council estates saved from demolition
text:
Council estates saved from demolition, 12 years on
A south London council has pledged to repair two housing estates rather than demolish them, ending 12 years of uncertainty for residents.
Green Party-led Lambeth Council voted to remove Central Hill in Norwood and Cressingham Gardens in Tulse Hill from its redevelopment programme, at a cabinet meeting last Wednesday.
Councillor Scott Ainslie said residents had "lived under the threat of demolition", adding: "That ends now. These homes will be kept, maintained properly, and repaired."
Residents have welcomed the move, but said they were still living with the "legacy of that disastrous decision back in 2014".
'Misery'
Anne Cooper, a Cressingham Gardens resident, told the meeting: "I really welcome this decision.
"I do think, however, we are living with the legacy of that disastrous decision back in 2014, and we've heard from both Cabinet members and residents about the misery that has caused."
Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens are two post-war developments that were designed by a team of Lambeth architects led by Ted Hollamby, who was renowned for creating modernist housing that aimed to improve everyday life for social housing residents.
But for more than 12 years, residents have been in limbo and have campaigned to stop the council from knocking down their estates and replacing their homes.
According to a cabinet report, council officers found comprehensive redevelopment of both Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens, which would involve demolition and rebuilding, to be financially unviable.
The council said it would focus on delivering "genuinely affordable homes" while respecting the borough's architectural heritage by avoiding demolition of the sites.
Former Central Hill resident and councillor Pete Elliot, cabinet member for housing, said: "Far too long, previous Labour administrations pursued demolition as the default answer to complex housing challenges.
"Millions of pounds were spent developing schemes that never materialised or were substandard. Residents were left living with uncertainty, anxiety and disruption and depression."

title: The hospital accordion player who has been busking for 35 years
text:
The accordion player who has been busking in hospital for 35 years
For 35 years, volunteer John Jones has been entertaining patients and visitors at Macclesfield District General Hospital by playing the accordion.
The 84-year-old retired engineer discovered his love of the accordion as a child, watching his father play the instrument.
"My dad played the accordion all the time and I could play the piano a little bit," he said.
"When he died, I started messing around with his accordion.
"One half is like a piano, but the other half is completely different with buttons.
"I had to teach myself, but I really enjoyed it."
He has since been using his musical talents to raise money for East Cheshire NHS Charity.
John's volunteering began after visiting the hospital with his mother-in-law in 1991 where he saw an appeal for a CT scanner.
He has since raised hundreds of thousands of pounds for the charity.
"One of the nicest moments was about five years after helping to raise the money for the scanner, I had to have a CT scan myself," said John who has an MBE for services to charity.
"The nurse said, 'That's ironic, you're using the scanner you helped pay for.' That really stayed with me."
The money has been used to fund a family room at the hospital intensive care unit, where his wife June died from sepsis in 2020.
"She'd been in intensive care five years earlier with sepsis as well, but she managed to survive that one," said John, who also performs in care homes.
"I asked if I could specifically collect for intensive care unit which is very close to my heart really because my youngest daughter is matron in intensive care in Australia.
"Obviously I know all the staff personally because they've been here all that time."
Zara Jones, chief executive at East Cheshire NHS Trust, said: "It's a privilege having so many people who are willing to give up their time to work here.
"A number of the volunteers I've met also have their own stories about care they've received here or their family or friends have had care here as well so it means a lot to them personally and we're really keen to support them."
description: Volunteer John Jones, 84, has been entertaining patients and visitors with his musical talents.

title: Roof repairs approved to tackle leaks at Yorkshire Museum
text:
Roof repairs approved to tackle museum leaks
Roof repairs at a Grade I listed museum have been approved in a bid to tackle significant and regular leaks which it is feared could eventually lead to historic items being damaged.
The Yorkshire Museum in York's Museum Gardens has seen several near misses, with leaks threatening to affect artefacts and fossils.
Senior curator Dr Andrew Woods said the museum was closing its galleries five times a year on average due to major leaks, which were preventing investment.
The repairs are set to take place over the next two years, following a £2m funding grant from Arts Council England.
The museum, which was completed in 1830, houses a number of Iron Age, Roman, Viking and Medieval artefacts and prehistoric remains, including dinosaur bones.
In the last three years, one leak had led to a pool of water forming on top of a cabinet housing Iron Age artefacts, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
Meanwhile, water had also been found running down the back of a case containing a Jurassic Ichthyosaur specimen and dripping into a cabinet full of Roman burial finds.
Woods said it was mainly down to luck that there had not been more damage to the museum's collections.
"There are galleries and spaces within the museum where we cannot put our most important or sensitive collections," he said.
"While we have a strong connection, it can be enhanced by loaning objects from other institutions.
"But there are galleries within the museum where this is not possible because the water risk is too high.
"Without confidence to invest in our permanent galleries, we are missing out on up to 75,000 visitors per annum - this would equate to the loss of potential annual revenue in excess of £500,000."
Woods said this would threaten the financial viability of the museum over the long term.
The first phase of repairs funded by the Arts Council grant is set to focus on the roof above the museum's Tempest Anderson hall and its main entrances.
Kathryn Blacker, York Museums Trust's chief executive, said the funding would help address some essential building works, improve the experience for visitors and ensure the museum remained sustainable.

title: Hillingdon Council to scrap all 700 dog waste bins to save money
text:
Dog waste bins in Hillingdon scrapped to save cash
All 700 dog waste bins in a west London borough are to be removed to save money, the local authority has said.
Hillingdon Council said dog owners should use litter bins or their own bins at home and a separate dog service was no longer necessary.
The change will save £160,000 a year, with £60,000 of that to be spent on extra street cleaning.
On its website, the Ruislip Residents' Association said some of Hillingdon's dog bins already overflowed under the current collection service, and that the council had not published a list or map to show any alternative bins.
The council's report acknowledged the risk of an increase in dog fouling, but said it could be managed with signs, communications and enforcement, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service.
The 14.5 tonnes of dog waste collected each month will now go into general waste, which the council said its existing bins could handle.
The plan was signed off without a formal public consultation, which the residents' association criticised.
Officers considered keeping the bins or removing only those already near litter bins, but rejected that because a separate collection service would still be needed.
Stickers reading "I can take dog waste too" will go on litter bins in parks and dog walking spots before the bins are removed in phases.
The report described removal as "the most effective and efficient option available to the council".

title: 'Albinism means you are never invisible', say Coventry siblings
text:
'Albinism means you are never invisible'
Growing up in Coventry, Naseem Akhtar and her family faced judgement because of the way they looked.
Although they come from Pakistani heritage, albinism runs in the family - both of her parents, all six of their children, herself, and various other relatives have the genetic condition.
Albinism affects the production of melanin, which can affect eyesight as well as they way people with the condition look. This means the family have very pale skin and white hair - something which Akhtar said they faced mistreatment for.
"I used to hate bonfire night because you knew that the fireworks were going to come through the letterbox," she told the BBC.
Growing up in the city in the 80s, Akhtar found it difficult.
"When I came along, the stigma was a lot more prominent... it would have been more prominent for my father and my mother and my uncle and aunt who had the condition, because they were born in Pakistan... they came to Coventry at about 11 and 12.
"You're never invisible... you will stand out in any community and that takes a lot of strength and courage to fit in to that and to grow into yourself."
"I think that the traumas that we suffer as a child not fitting into your skin, into your identity, I think that then can play out later in life," she said.
"You have to kind of deal with those feelings... your nervous system got programmed by feeling that feeling of threat because when you were walking around as a child and you were experiencing bullying because you look different."
Despite this, Akhtar wanted to raise awareness of the condition from a young age.
"I was about 11 years old, I went onto the local radio to talk about albinism... I did that because I wanted to change that perception that people had - that we weren't the family that could just be dumped on or to be bullied."
Akhtar is 14 years older than one of her siblings, Mohammed Rafi, now 32, and said the treatment he received growing up was a lot more accepting.
"We stayed in the same same area in Coventry, so our neighbours, community... they know us that way and there was more awareness over the years," said Rafi.
Akhtar added: "And that shows progression, that Rafi's experience is completely different to mine, which I think can only mean that we as a society are more accepting of difference, and we are more integrated a little bit."
"The main thing that we struggle with is the vision," added Rafi, who has poor eyesight.
The reduced amount of melanin in albinism can cause eye problems, including poor eyesight, astigmatism, or photophobia, according to the NHS.
In 2022, they received a Guinness World Record for the most siblings with albinism.
Akhtar described this as a "mark that that it's OK to be different and and it's all right".
None of their children have albinism, but do carry the gene.
The siblings said they were not sad that the condition could end in the family in their children's generation.
"Although we carry this uniqueness, we also know the struggle of how it has been to find our way in life and to live life in this unique way," said Akhtar.
"Our children will not struggle with the difficulties of having a disability and a long-term condition, I think that's the blessing.
"Although we have learned to grow into ourselves... it's hard work trying to grow into your skin."
'If I inspire others, I've done my bit'
Akhtar added that in talking about the condition, she hoped she could help the next generations of those with albinism.
"We're able to advocate for that, we're able to like have a voice for that and to change that because a lot of it is your perception, the more you change your perception about how you feel about yourself you will have a better life.
"I was inspired as a child, my specialist teacher that came to support me when I was younger, he had albinism.
"He inspired me, so if I as a person can give something back to this world - to inspire others - then I feel like I've done my bit on this earth."

title: Dorset man stockpiles 600 cans of food in case of an emergency
text:
'I stockpiled 600 cans of food for an emergency'
A man who purchased 600 cans of food in case of an emergency has said that it is something he began to do following the start of the war in Ukraine and Covid-19 pandemic.
The government has told us to have three days' worth of food and water on hand to get through a national emergency in its 'Be Ready' campaign.
Ian Ferguson from Weymouth, Dorset has been collecting tins for the last two years.
"Six cans would last me a day and then I have enough to hand out to other people if they need it."
The Governments "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need to get through a rocky few days.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said unexpected events "seem to becoming more common" and everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
Recommendations include having enough supplies in the kitchen to last three days, including bottled water and non-perishable foods.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash are also recommended – some of which Ferguson has stored in a shed.
"I do have lots of bedding and stuff like that indoors, so if I couldn't put my heating on, I've got a couple of sleeping bags." he said.
The 71-year-old explained why he started. "It was about two years ago I started and there'd been some various things and obviously Covid was a huge lesson, people panic buying, taking stuff.
Ferguson continued; "Ever since the Ukraine conflict I'm thinking if if that could happen there then we are really susceptible to some sort of attack you know and even if it's not an actual physical attack of soldiers on the floor and cyber attacks.
"Everything's controlled by computers now, so we are really susceptible to living in a digital world and somebody turning the switch off."
Every time Ferguson visited a supermarket to do his food shop he has purchased six extra cans just in case.
The 71-year-old has also bought a gas stove with canisters and water filters for his water butt in his back garden.
"I've got my filtration sticks that I can use so I can drink that water.
"You know a lot of people talk about you know what about having a bath or a shower well I think when push comes to itself staying alive is probably a bit more important than minor points of personal hygiene."
The business owner believes having 600 cans is necessary "If I was going to eat six tins a day, which would be more than ample, I've got 100 days' supplies.
"but I've got family, I've got friends, I've got neighbours, I would be looking to share, I wouldn't be looking to keep it to myself."
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said the advice - which is similar to guidance issued by the previous government - was not triggered by any "particular piece of intelligence", but rather about improving "national resilience" more generally.
The government's announcement focused on extreme weather events, which are becoming more frequent because of man-made climate change - but Streeting also referred to the threat of "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, and supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".
description: Ian Ferguson from Weymouth wanted to be prepared and thinks other people should be too.

title: Archway tower block residents face 'nightmare' over scaffolding
text:
Tower block residents plagued by intruders in scaffolding 'nightmare'
Residents of a north London tower block said they are living a "nightmare", with intruders accessing the scaffolding that has surrounded their homes for the past six years.
The scaffolding was erected at Archway Heights in 2020 as a precautionary measure after a piece of external cladding fell off, according to the housing association, Places for People.
It said it was waiting for approval from the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) to begin repairs.
The regulator said an application submitted in 2024 had been invalidated, with further information required to demonstrate compliance with building regulations.
'Saw something outside'
Natasha Dyett moved into the nine-storey block two years ago, with the scaffolding already in place.
"We've had the heatwave this summer; I've spent most of it with everything shut because we've had people breach the scaffolding all summer long," Dyett said.
She said that in July she was terrified to see someone outside her window.
"I climbed into bed, I turned over and I saw something outside. I rubbed my eyes because my vision is failing and I could still see it and it moved," she said. "I realised it was a person standing there."
She shouted at the person to go away and contacted her landlord, who advised her to call the police. However, she said the CCTV footage was wiped before it could be examined.
"It seems that every week someone is reporting people on the scaffolding," Dyett said. "They just walk around. I think they can get all the way up to the roof."
She added that the scaffolding meant she sometimes had to keep the lights on during the day, particularly in her son's bedroom which is obscured by a metal guard.
"I try not to because it's becoming quite expensive using the light in the daytime, and then we go out into the actual daylight and squinting our eyes because we've been in darkness for so long."
Ciara Squires, a 34-year-old nurse, said she had also seen at least two people outside her window and found it frightening to return home because people were often loitering outside.
She said CCTV had captured one incident involving five men.
"It was five youngish men. It was just terrifying. Luckily, I wasn't on my own. I was looking after my mum who is recovering from cancer," she told BBC London.
Jameel Choudhury, who lives at Archway Heights with his wife and three children, said the scaffolding had attracted rough sleepers who moved into the building's cycle and storage room.
"We are regularly seeing people going up into the scaffolding, going where they shouldn't be, breaking into the cycle store, dealing drugs: the type of antisocial behaviour you really don't want to see," he said.
Pointing to an area where his bike had been stolen, Choudhury said people had brought duvets, chairs and a microwave into the storage area, where they cooked food and charged devices.
"Just behind these walls there is a child's bedroom and [the child] used to be able to hear all the stuff they got up to," he said.
Residents have also raised concerns about the lack of information about the cladding and whether it is safe.
Choudhury said he feared it could be flammable or come loose, as had happened previously.
"We just want a clear answer from them. What's going on? Is it safe?" he said.
A Places for People spokesperson said extra security had been brought in at the block.
They said planning approval was secured in 2023 and a contractor appointed, but changes introduced by the Building Safety Act concerning higher-risk buildings meant further approvals were required.
Origin Housing, which merged with Places for People in April 2024, submitted an application in 2024 that had to be resubmitted in January 2025. The full integration of the organisations, bringing around 9,000 homes under the Places for People umbrella, was completed in April 2026.
'As quickly as possible'
Places for People said it was awaiting a decision from the BSR before work could begin.
"The challenges at Archway Heights are complex, multi-faceted and will take some time to resolve. We know it has been in place for far longer than anyone would have wanted and we want to progress these works as quickly as possible," the spokesperson said.
The BSR was established to reform building safety laws following the Grenfell Tower fire.
A spokesperson said the regulator was "working closely with the applicant to secure approval for proposed remediation works to a non-compliant wall façade originally identified in 2020 prior to BSR being formed".
They added: "This complex case was originally submitted to BSR in April 2024 and was invalidated. A subsequent application was made in January 2025 and has required several requests for further information and ongoing engagement with the applicant for them to be able to demonstrate compliance with building regulations."
Acorn Community Union has been helping residents raise their concerns. Its media spokesperson, Dan Newcombe, said they had been left in limbo.
"Our members have been told for the last six years there will be a decision this month or that month, and that date keeps changing. The housing association is saying one thing, the Building Safety Regulator says another, and our members are left in the dark with no end in sight," he said.
Places for People said residents would receive a detailed programme of work once approval was granted. The repairs are expected to take 12 months to complete.

title: RAF base chemical contamination worst in UK, report finds
text:
RAF base chemical contamination worst in UK, report says
Chemical contamination at a former RAF base earmarked for 9,000 homes is the worst found in the UK, a report has said.
Testing at RAF Upper Heyford carried out on behalf of a developer found "unacceptable" levels of polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), referred to as forever chemicals.
Fears have been raised previously that the site could be the source of pollution in nearby waterways, after earlier testing by campaigners and the Environment Agency.
Roughly 1,300 homes have already been built on the site. Paul Silver, chief executive of developer Dorchester Living, said separate soil samples taken from residential areas showed the area was "safe for use".
PFAS are a group of thousands of man-made chemicals, some of which can cause cancer, which are often referred to as forever chemicals because they do not break down easily.
The results of the site investigations were uploaded to Cherwell District Council's website as part of a planning application.
The author of the report said they were higher than the village of Bentham, Yorkshire, "determined as having the highest level of PFAS in the UK".
The Environment Agency (EA) said military sites and airports were hotspots for PFAS, which were used extensively in firefighting foams for decades.
At RAF Upper Heyford, firefighters would practice putting out an aeroplane set on fire above a "pond" of fuel.
This training area was found to be "the most significant ongoing source of PFAS contamination identified" - a few hundred metres north of existing developments.
Another report into ground and surface water found contamination was "widespread" at the site, with all samples exceeding environmental standards.
Subsequent independent testing by Gallos Brook Environmental Group found elevated levels of the chemicals in more than a dozen streams that flow from beneath the base.
The results have prompted concerns from residents about existing and approved developments near the site, including a planned primary school.
Groundwater and surface water results from the school site in another report showed PFAS exceeded safe levels by environmental quality standards.
Calum Miller, MP for Bicester and Woodstock, said: "The most important thing is to understand fully what level of contamination, if any, there is in that area.
"And in the case of a primary school that people have real confidence that it's a safe environment for children."
The BBC has spoken to residents living on and near the site who would like their blood tested to determine if they have been disproportionately exposed.
One of them, Leigh Radwell, said she was concerned for her health after eating vegetables from her garden, which borders a stream suspected to be polluted with the chemicals.
She said: "My little countryside haven and my dream of growing my own veg and having chickens and supporting wildlife is ruined.
"I hate living here now."
Helen Christie, from Gallos Brook Environmental Group, said the results confirmed what campaigners had been saying: "That the site is contaminated."
But she said the testing done so far had been "inadequate".
"The duty of care now must be towards the 1,300 houses already built and those living in the surrounding areas," she added.
'Further investigation'
The report carried out for Dorchester Living said the PFAS contamination could be managed through a phased remediation approach.
CEO Paul Silver said: "This testing was the first step and an outline strategy for further investigation has been submitted as part of the planning application.
"We anticipate that this will include further investigation work on a phased basis with any necessary remediation to be secured through the planning process."
He continued: "The levels of contamination found on site are significantly lower than we had expected given its historic use.
"Soil samples taken from residential areas show that homes are safe for use."
The results of these further tests have not been made public.
Silver added: "We continue to recognise our responsibilities as a landowner and developer and are continuing to work with the Cherwell District Council, Environment Agency and other relevant government bodies."
The local authority previously called on the government to support it on the issue and a working group has been set up alongside the developer and the Environment Agency.
Cherwell District Council has been approached for comment.
description: Testing at RAF Upper Heyford finds "unacceptable" levels of polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

title: Hunt for Tameside millionaire as £1m lottery jackpot unclaimed
text:
Hunt to find owner of £1m winning lottery ticket
The hunt is on to find Tameside's next millionaire.
The owner of a lottery ticket bought in the Greater Manchester borough this summer now only has two months left to claim their £1m prize.
Under National Lottery rules, winners must submit their claim within six months. In this case they must do so before 00:00 GMT on 28 December.
"The winning ticket could be tucked away somewhere completely ordinary while its owner has absolutely no idea they are a millionaire," said Andy Carter from National Lottery operator Allwyn.
"We'd love to find the person we've been looking for and turn this search into a celebration," Carter added.
"So, if you bought a ticket in the area, dig it out, check those numbers and help us find Tameside's missing millionaire.
"It could be you."
The winning numbers were 5, 8, 26, 33, 39, 42 and the Bonus Ball was 54.

title: The motor racing couple speed dating with no brakes
text:
The motor racing couple speed dating with no brakes
A young couple who are both speedway riders have spoken about going head-to-head on the track.
Jody Scott, 19, from King's Lynn in Norfolk, who this year claimed the British under-19 championship, shone riding for the Oxford Chargers.
Towards the end of this season he lined up for the Chargers against Edinburgh Monarchs Academy, which included his 19-year-old Australian girlfriend Anika Loftus.
Scott said racing your girlfriend "is something that's never happened before" as they both talked about their adrenaline-fuelled romance.
Speaking to BBC Radio Oxford's Gemma Hill, Scott said he did not know anything about Loftus before they met in May.
On 4 September they rode against each other in the WSRA National Development League fixture at Armadale Stadium in Scotland which ended with a 51–39 victory for Edinburgh.
Loftus was the only female rider in the league and it was the first time she and her boyfriend faced each other on opposite sides.
"Edinburgh's got the big screen there and I had a cheeky look at it and I see Anika was putting her helmet on and getting ready to go out," Scott said.
He explained that they left from different gates and he "made sure I went the other way".
"I expected I was going to be racing her at some point and then when we got together - it's kind of a mind-blowing thing to think."
Loftus said "it's not like you get the opportunity every day".
"We've been pretty, pretty excited actually and maybe down the track I think it'll be cool to look back on."
Scott also raced against Anika's brother, 17-year-old Jordy Loftus.
Loftus said of her and her brother's achievements: "Ever since we were little we'd always dreamt of riding together on a professional level and then to actually have it come true, it's just been such an amazing experience
"It's not every day you race your brother and your boyfriend on the track at the same time."
She said Scott and Loftus have been racing each other for a while, "so they're quite comfortable with each other on the track".
"Throwing me into the mix I was like 'Hopefully, I can just stay out of it and ride my own race'."
Loftus says she "never expected to be given the opportunity" to race in the UK but was "excited" when Edinburgh's manager Scott Wilson called her.
"Every meeting I've improved and I've scored more points and contributed to the team," she says, reflecting that not many women are riding in the UK leagues.
"To be one of the first it's really honourable and hopefully in the near future a few more girls can be on the track."
The couple are now preparing for a long-haul trip for the speedway season in Australia.
Despite racing in places such as Poland and all over UK, Scott has always previously taken his bike in a van and this will be his first flight.
"It's is going to be the furthest distance possible for me but I'm looking forward to it."
description: Oxford speedway rider Jody Scott said racing against his girlfriend Anika Loftus was "mind-blowing".

title: Plan approved to turn Old Day School in Bluntisham into a house
text:
Plan to turn school into three-bed house approved
A Grade II listed school is set to get a new lease of life after fears it would be lost forever.
Councillors have approved a plan to turn The Old Day School in Bluntisham, Cambridgeshire, which has been empty for about five years, into a three-bedroom house.
Huntingdonshire District Council's planning officers had recommended refusing the planning application, saying it would cause "substantial" harm to the building because the school hall would need to be divided to create the third bedroom.
Seventeen letters supporting the proposal had been submitted by residents. The authority's development management committee voted 10 to one in favour of the scheme.
According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service, Philippa Hope, of Bluntisham Parish Council, told committee members the building needed "to be preserved".
Hope added: "To convert any building into a home internal changes are inevitable – the school building is the same and any changes are justifiable in securing the long-term future of this vacant listed building."
A previous proposal had been refused in 2025, despite concerns the building had not been maintained since the school closed in 1968.
Councillors had been worried about a proposed rear extension, but that had been reduced in size in the resubmitted plans.
Simon Claridge, the applicant, told the committee he cared "deeply about the building" which had continued to "deteriorate through vandalism, broken windows, water ingress, roof damage and even attempted arson".
He added: "We've listened, compromised and repeatedly amended our proposals. Given the resources already invested though, this really is our last attempt to save this building."
