title: Artists angry as The Point Theatre in Eastleigh cuts staff and plays
text:
Artists angry as theatre cuts staff and shows
A community theatre is cutting down on original productions, including its Christmas show, and has let go of key staff members.
Local freelance artists and creatives expressed anger at not being consulted about the changes at The Point Theatre in Eastleigh, which one composer called a "mind-bogglingly bad decision".
The venue's artistic director and theatre programmer were both made redundant following an internal staff consultation, which ran from July to August.
Eastleigh Borough Council (EBC), which owns the venue, said the changes reflected a move to prioritise commercial activity and funded community-based events.
They said the changes would ensure future financial resilience and "support a cultural offer that is affordable and sustainable in the long term".
A group of 27 artists and creatives wrote to the council in July to express their concerns about the then-ongoing internal consultation.
The BBC understands that several upcoming original productions have been pulled - including this year's Christmas show, The Frog Princess.
David Lewington is a freelance sound producer and composer who has worked with the theatre for 15 years. He was contracted to work on three upcoming productions, including the Christmas show.
He said the changes effectively meant the theatre would now become a venue for touring acts and tribute bands.
"Nobody outside of the venue was asked about this process," he said.
"For a venue like The Point, which is a community asset, it beggars belief that the consultation didn't go any further than internal within the council."
He said the timing of the decision to axe shows had also left him and other freelance artists in a precarious position.
"We've essentially been dumped mid-way through a contract, so I've lost all of that work at Christmas… it's too late to find alternative work," he said.
"We're just left with nothing."
Several other artists told the BBC they were disappointed that the council did not engage with them further or seek out their views.
Lucy Rachel, a singer-songwriter from Southampton, has close links to some of the creatives affected.
"There was a chance to work together, and they didn't," she said. "They bulldozed through this culturally vibrant thing."
"The Point has been a really vital, creative starting point for me as an artist...for that to not continue in the same way for other young people, that's where it hurts my heart."
The council said it had provided a net subsidy of £712,020 to support its Arts and Culture service, including The Point and its sister theatre, The Berry, in 2025/2026.
In a statement it said: "We appreciate that some artists and creatives are disappointed that particular productions and projects will no longer go ahead.
"We must ensure that substantial public investment delivers good value for council taxpayers."
It continued: "We fully recognise that arts venues deliver social, cultural and educational benefits beyond their financial return.
"But that does not mean their operating models, staffing arrangements or levels of public subsidy should be beyond review."
description: Changes at The Point Theatre in Eastleigh are being implemented following an internal consultation.

title: Blackpool Multiversity: Views sought on £65m campus plans
text:
Views sought on town's £65m multiversity plans
People in Blackpool are being asked what they think about a £65m college campus being built in the town centre.
The multiversity, near Blackpool North railway station, will be expected to bring about 3,000 students, apprentices and staff into the town centre when it opens in September 2028.
Blackpool and The Fylde College said the development would aim to make higher education more accessible and help people gain skills and qualifications.
The survey, designed to find out what residents and businesses make of the project, takes about 10 to 15 minutes to complete.
Meanwhile, construction firm Morgan Sindall has opened a training facility called the Knowledge Quad at the building site, giving people opportunities to learn about construction skills and careers.
Blackpool councillor Mark Smith said the facility would allow young people to "learn construction skills and gain qualifications on a live site" and help them to start careers in construction.

title: Parking reduced for development plans near Hampton Court Palace
text:
Housing plan near palace sees parking scaled back
Plans to scale back the parking spaces of a housing scheme opposite Hampton Court Palace have been submitted to the council.
The new proposal for the former Jolly Boatman pub site in East Molesey, sent to Elmbridge Borough Council, would cut the originally agreed 207 parking spaces down to 93.
The planning application cited increased costs and slow sales for the decision, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).
A South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex spokesperson said it was working with authorities involved to consider the plans and "ensure the needs of customers, local residents and the wider community are properly taken into account".
The original planning application from Alexpo and Network Rail included 97 flats, an 84-bed hotel, retail units and a car park. It received more than 1,800 objections and 131 letters of support at the time.
This was approved by a government inspector on appeal in 2022 after being refused by the council a year earlier for being "excessive".
Permission was then sought and granted in 2024 from Lisa Nandy, the Secretary of State for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, due to the development's planned height and proximity to the palace.
Local concerns raised
The latest application has so far received 157 objections and two letters in support, according to the LDRS.
Steve Bax, who represents the Molesey East ward on the council, shared concern that the proposal could impact parking for the surrounding area.
He said on Facebook: "Anyone who has tried parking in Palace Road, Wolsey Road, or nearby streets knows how difficult it already is."
The joint spokesperson for South Western Railway and Network Rail Wessex added: "We recognise the importance of parking provision at Hampton Court and understand the concerns that have been raised locally."
They said an updated seven-day parking survey was undertaken in October 2025 to inform the proposals.
"Our focus remains on achieving a deliverable development that balances regeneration of the site with the needs of our customers and the local community at the heart of this."

title: I couldn't move, walk or talk after stroke, says Wisbech survivor
text:
'I couldn't move, walk or talk after my stroke'
A former primary school teacher said her "life has changed beyond belief" after having a stroke in 2019.
Priscilla Zuta, from Wisbech, Cambridgeshire, was 42 when she had a stroke in 2019, which left her with right-sided weakness and aphasia, a condition that affects communication.
Zuta, now 48, has shared her experience on World Stroke Day as part of a campaign by the Stroke Association, which aims to raise awareness of the condition's prevention, symptoms, treatment and survivor support.
"I was so frightened and had no idea what my life would be like. I couldn't move, walk or even talk – I felt so alone," she said.
Zuta added: "Over the years it took everything out of me – but now I'm slowly feeling like I can be myself."
In April 2019, when she was attending an interview for an assistant head teacher position, Zuta lost consciousness and was taken to Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge where she was placed into a coma.
She woke up several days later unable to speak or move her body.
"I never expected I would have a stroke. I was healthy, happy, and at my prime - I was going about life as normal."
'I am a miracle'
In the UK, someone has a stroke every five minutes and 1.4 million people currently living with a brain injury caused by stroke, according to the charity Stroke Association.
Research conducted by the charity found that out of 2,000 adults surveyed, a third aged 18-34 (34%) and almost a quarter of 35 to 44-year-olds (24%) believed they were too young to have a stroke.
Juliet Bouverie, the chief executive of the charity, said: "This new research shows that people still don't understand a stroke happens in the brain and wrongly believe a stroke only affects older people."
Zuta is sharing her story as part of the charity's Survival Is Not Enough campaign, which aims to raise awareness of the impact of a stroke.
The 48-year-old said: "My life has changed beyond belief. I am still the same woman, but very different.
"I have a physical disability – the weakness down one side of my body makes every task difficult, my speech condition makes speaking, thinking, reading and writing really complex – but I'm stronger and feeling like I'm becoming a better person."
Zuta's husband, Emmanuel, is now her full-time carer.
"My children and husband are my world, they've stuck by me and although it's been a long six years, I'm ready to raise awareness of this cruel condition.
"I want more people to understand what stroke is, and how a stroke can make someone feel. I am a miracle."

title: Isle of Wight neighbours win Postcode Lottery
text:
'Lottery win means I can pursue my dream'
Abbie West-Long was preparing to change her dream to move to Canada with her partner, when she had a knock at the door.
After learning she'd won £333,332 in the Postcode Lottery, the charity volunteer said she "just started crying".
Now, the 34-year-old from Cowes on the Isle of Wight says she can chase her dream and build a new life with partner Daryl Marlow in the Canadian Rockies.
Ms West-Long is one of five neighbours in her street to share £1m worth of winnings.
The Postcode Lottery team arrived on Tuesday to deliver individual tickets worth £166,666.
But as Ms West-Long has been playing with two tickets for the last three years, her prize was double.
"They phoned me and all they told me was I'd won 'a prize'. Then there was a week of sitting in lots of anxiety and waiting for that knock on the door," the childcare practitioner explained.
"For around five years we've wanted to move to Canada. We've put random timers on it to save between the jobs we've had and life happens and obviously things get in the way.
Ms West-Long continued: "But we had started a new timer a couple of months ago and said 'if we can't get it done it will be this, or we'll change our plans'.
"Then literally a month later got that knock on my door and it changed everything."
Ms West-Long and Mr Marlow, 39, had been aiming to save a minumum of £10,000 for a new life in Canada, which they'd pencilled in for 2028.
Now, their timeline has sped up and they're hoping to move in six months' time.
She added: "Our dream move and plan has accelerated massively.
"I do feel like I'm dreaming because this isn't something that happens to me. I usually expect bad news.
"We've been sat going through every dream possible and then thinking, 'oh my God, I don't deserve this, why would I get this?'"
"We've been out to Canada a couple of times and it just felt right. [The money] has ticked all the boxes, it's more than enough."
The couple, who have been together for 13 years, are hoping to start a family there.
Mr Marlow added: "We have literally not been able to provide the level of stability that we've wanted to start a family, until now."
With the prize worth more than $620,000 in Canadian dollars, the pair are hoping to buy a home in British Columbia, where they envisage living for the rest of their lives.
"A house, land, a dog, a snow shovel, a car," Ms West-Long said.
Her partner adding: "Everything we could want."
description: Abbie West-Long plans to use her winnings to pursue a dream of moving to Canada with her partner.

title: Painted Gruffalo stones spark passion to reclaim Sutton Park
text:
Hidden Gruffalo stones spark passion to reclaim park
When artist Lizzi Chambers from Sutton Coldfield decorated her son's nursery, she came up with the idea of painting Gruffalo themed stones.
Once the room was finished, she had a few left over, and knew they couldn't go to waste.
After seeing local residents post on social media that they were avoiding Sutton Park because of antisocial behaviour concerns, she came up with an idea: to hide her decorated stones for children to find.
"I thought I might do something nice and then, you know, maybe that'll have the same effect in a different way - just to get people into the park because there's something nice happening there as well, amplifying the good stuff," Chambers said.
After an overwhelmingly positive reaction from the local community, she continued to decorate stones for the park.
Over the past few months she has hidden dozens of them, featuring characters from Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, The Lion King, and even Celebrity Traitors.
"I sort of made it a bit of a project and I thought... a nice thing would be to do children's book and classic children's characters to really make it a thing for children to go and do," she said.
"I'm really enjoying it and it's been lovely to see how many people have really bought into it and you know, it's just over the way from the children's play area.
"So I've even been putting them out myself or taking my own children to the park and I've even seen people looking and that's lovely."
Reaction from local residents has been positive, with Chambers even making Traitors and Halloween themed stones, to keep up with the demand.
The mum plans to continue hiding them until Christmas, while people are still interested in looking for them.
"It's getting harder because obviously I've got my own children and it's half term and we all, we've all been ill so just sort of squeezing it in," she added.
"I thought, you know, I'll definitely do it until Christmas."

title: Basingstoke Canal users warned after poisonous plant seen in Ash
text:
Canal users warned after poisonous plant spotted
Visitors to a canal towpath have been warned to avoid a poisonous plant after it was spotted along the route.
Parish councillor Richard Lucas said hemlock water dropwort had been seen along the Basingstoke Canal in Ash Vale, Surrey.
The native plant is "extremely poisonous" and should only be touched wearing gloves, according to the Royal Horticultural Society.
Lucas said the plant was "quite widespread" in the area and "extremely dangerous".
He told BBC Radio Surrey the species "grows naturally in ditches and on the edge of stagnant waterways" so was present along the canal, in ditches and along the edge of the Blackwater River.
Ash Parish Council said hemlock water dropwort appears similar to harmless members of the carrot and parsley family and has white flower heads, which disappear by the end of summer.
"Residents are advised not to touch or pick any plant they suspect may be hemlock water-dropwort, and to keep children and pets away," the council said.

title: Wessex and Thames Valley mayors: What would they mean for you?
text:
What would new regional mayors mean for the South?
Plans for two new regional mayors have moved a step closer after they were named in the Budget.
The government said it was in the "final stages" of agreeing mayoral authorities for Wessex and the Thames Valley, as part of 10 new devolution deals across England.
Supporters say a mayor would bring more money and control over transport, housing and skills, with decisions made locally rather than in Westminster.
But some council leaders and MPs have questioned the areas being covered and whether the benefits will outweigh the costs.
Is this the same as my local mayor?
Unlike civic and ceremonial mayors, regional mayors are directly elected by the public.
They preside over mayoral strategic authorities, also known as combined authorities, which comprise a group of local councils.
Regional mayors, like those in Greater Manchester and London, are intended to provide strong local leadership, giving people a single prominent individual they can hold to account.
They also give central government a single point of contact when delivering work in a particular area.
Local councils would continue to run day-to-day services such as bin collections, social care, schools and local planning.
What could a mayor actually do?
The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act, passed in April, set out a standard set of powers for strategic authorities.
They typically include control over aspects of transport, skills, housing and local infrastructure investment.
In some cases they also hold power over planning, policing, health and employment support.
Police and crime commissioners are due to be abolished in 2028, with their powers passing to mayors where possible.
The Budget also said mayors would receive a share of business rates from next year and a share of income tax from 2028.
The government also plans to give all strategic authorities the power to introduce an overnight visitor levy.
Regional mayors can also exercise soft power as champions of the areas they represent.
Why does the government want more mayors?
The government says people who know their places best should have more power to shape their future.
Ahead of the Budget, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, himself the former mayor of Greater Manchester, said he was "calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster".
The Budget included £120m for areas moving towards a devolution deal, ahead of a £1.5bn borrowing facility for mayoral authorities being introduced from 2028.
Is a Wessex mayor finally happening?
The combined bid for a Heart of Wessex authority and mayor, comprising Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole (BCP), Dorset, Somerset and Wiltshire councils, was rejected by the government in January 2025 for not being advanced or developed enough.
Speaking during Prime Minister's Questions on 21 October, West Dorset MP Edward Morello urged the prime minister to "commit to a mayor of Wessex by 2028".
Andy Burnham said: "Yes, I'm always happy to create more mayors. Let's move quickly to get a fully devolved Wessex and south west of England."
Speaking to BBC Radio Solent on Wednesday, Morello said the decision meant "more buses" and "more investment" for residents.
"This means we can steam ahead with those plans," he said.
In a joint statement, the four council leaders added: "Wessex is ready. We have done the groundwork."
Why has the Thames Valley plan been so rocky?
Oxfordshire County Council and the Royal Borough of Windsor and Maidenhead had vetoed earlier proposals, with concerns over Swindon's inclusion and calls for a mayor from the start.
Oxfordshire council leader Tim Bearder said what he had vetoed was a non-mayoral authority, and it had been "quite wise to make sure that we held out for something that's far, far better".
Authorities in Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Swindon have spent the last two years drawing up plans for devolution.
The 13 councils involved say the government has proposed £9.1m of funding as the plans are developed.
They say a consultation is planned for the new year, with a formal proposal going to government in spring and mayoral elections expected in 2028.
Oxford City Council leader Susan Brown described it as "a once-in-a-generation opportunity".
Reading Borough Council leader Liz Terry said the authority would "unlock enormous benefits for residents in Reading".
Neighbouring Hampshire and the Isle of Wight are further down the same path, with their strategic authority launched in July and a first mayoral election due in May 2028.
What do the critics say?
Despite backing the next stage, Bearder said he had "serious, unanswered questions" about whether the benefits would justify "the costs and disruption involved".
He said leaving out Buckinghamshire, which shares some services with the rest of the Thames Valley, could have "significant" implications for policing, the NHS and fire services.
South Oxfordshire District Council leader Maggie Filipova-Rivers said councils had been given "just two working days" to consider proposals that "could reshape public service boundaries across the Thames Valley for years to come".
In Dorset, Poole's Labour MP Neil Duncan-Jordan has said there was "no real public support for creating an artificial entity called Wessex".
Conservative North Dorset MP Simon Hoare warned the BCP conurbation had "an entirely different economy" to the rest of the area.
The Local Government Association said "genuine devolution must go beyond mayors and strategic authorities to empower councils themselves".
description: Dorset, Berkshire and Oxfordshire are among 10 areas named in the Budget for new devolution deals.
